translations.an10.13:1: "Mendicants, there are these ten fetters. What ten? Five lower fetters and five higher fetters. What are the five lower fetters? Identity view, doubt, misapprehension of precepts and observances, sensual desire, and ill will—these are the five lower fetters.
translations.an10.15:1: "Mendicants, among all sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; with form or formless; percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, is declared to be the foremost. In the same way, all skillful qualities are rooted in diligence and converge upon diligence. Diligence is declared to be the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:2: Just as the footprints of all creatures that walk can fit inside an elephant's footprint, so the elephant's footprint is declared to be the foremost of them in terms of size; in the same way, all skillful qualities are rooted in diligence and converge upon diligence. Diligence is declared to be the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:3: Just as all the rafters of a peaked house lean toward the peak, slope toward the peak, and converge upon the peak, and the peak is declared to be the foremost of them; in the same way, all skillful qualities are rooted in diligence and converge upon diligence. Diligence is declared to be the foremost among them.
translations.an10.15:7: Just as all lesser kings become vassals of a wheel-turning monarch, and the wheel-turning monarch is declared to be the foremost among them; in the same way …
translations.an10.15:8: Just as the radiance of all the stars is not worth a sixteenth part of the moon's radiance, and the moon's radiance is declared to be the foremost among them; in the same way …
translations.an10.15:9: Just as in autumn, when the sky is clear and cloudless, the sun, rising into the sky, dispels all darkness from space as it shines and blazes and radiates; in the same way …
translations.an10.17:1: "Mendicants, live with a protector, not without a protector. One who lives without a protector suffers. There are these ten qualities that serve as protector. What ten? Firstly, a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and seeking alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they've undertaken. The fact that a mendicant is ethical … this is a quality that serves as protector.
translations.an10.17:2: Furthermore, a mendicant is very learned, remembering and keeping what they've learned. These teachings are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that's entirely full and pure. They are very learned in such teachings, remembering them, reciting them, mentally examining them, and comprehending them theoretically. The fact that a mendicant is very learned … this is a quality that serves as protector.
translations.an10.17:3: Furthermore, a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates. The fact that a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates, this is a quality that serves as protector.
translations.an10.18:10: Furthermore, a mendicant is mindful, with utmost mindfulness and alertness, able to remember and recall what was said and done long ago. 'This mendicant is mindful, with utmost mindfulness and alertness, able to remember and recall what was said and done long ago.' Senior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them, middle mendicants … junior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them. When they are cared for by senior, middle, and junior mendicants, only growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This is a quality that serves as protector.
translations.an10.18:11: Furthermore, a mendicant is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering. 'This mendicant is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering.' Senior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them, middle mendicants … junior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them. When they are cared for by senior … not decline. This is a quality that serves as protector.
translations.an10.18:2: "Mendicants, live with a protector, not without a protector. One who lives without a protector suffers. There are these ten qualities that serve as protector. What ten? Firstly, a mendicant is ethical … they keep the rules they've undertaken. 'This mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and seeking alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they've undertaken.' Senior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them, middle mendicants … junior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them. When they are cared for by senior, middle, and junior mendicants, only growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This is a quality that serves as protector.
translations.an10.18:4: Furthermore, a mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates. 'This mendicant has good friends, companions, and associates.' Senior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them, middle mendicants … junior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them. When they are cared for by senior, middle, and junior mendicants, only growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This is a quality that serves as protector.
translations.an10.18:5: Furthermore, a mendicant is easy to admonish, having qualities that make them easy to admonish. They're patient, and take instruction respectfully. 'This mendicant is easy to admonish, having qualities that make them easy to admonish. They're patient, and take instruction respectfully.' Senior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them, middle mendicants … junior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them. When they are cared for by senior, middle, and junior mendicants, only growth is to be expected in skillful qualities, not decline. This is a quality that serves as protector.
translations.an10.18:6: Furthermore, a mendicant is deft and tireless in the diverse chores for their spiritual companions, understanding how to go about them and how to get things done. Thinking: 'This mendicant is deft and tireless in the diverse chores for their spiritual companions, understanding how to go about them and how to get things done,' the senior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them, as do the middle and junior mendicants. When they're treated with such kindness by the senior, middle, and junior mendicants, they can expect only growth in skillful qualities, not decline. This too is a quality that serves as a protector.
translations.an10.18:7: Furthermore, a mendicant loves the teaching and is a delight to converse with, being full of joy in the higher teaching and training. Thinking: 'This mendicant loves the teaching and is a delight to converse with, being full of joy in the higher teaching and training,' the senior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them, as do the middle and junior mendicants. When they're treated with such kindness by the senior, middle, and junior mendicants, they can expect only growth in skillful qualities, not decline. This too is a quality that serves as a protector.
translations.an10.18:8: Furthermore, a mendicant lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They're strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to skillful qualities. Thinking: 'This mendicant lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They're strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to skillful qualities,' the senior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them, as do the middle and junior mendicants. When they're treated with such kindness by the senior, middle, and junior mendicants, they can expect only growth in skillful qualities, not decline. This too is a quality that serves as a protector.
translations.an10.18:9: Furthermore, a mendicant is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. Thinking: 'This mendicant is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick,' the senior mendicants think they should advise and instruct them, as do the middle and junior mendicants. When they're treated with such kindness by the senior, middle, and junior mendicants, they can expect only growth in skillful qualities, not decline. This too is a quality that serves as a protector.
translations.an10.20:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadamma. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants …
translations.an10.20:10: And how does a mendicant have tranquil physical processes? It's when a mendicant, giving up pleasure and pain, and ending former happiness and sadness, enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness. That's how a mendicant has tranquil physical processes.
translations.an10.20:11: And how does a mendicant have a well-freed mind? It's when a mendicant's mind is freed from greed, hate, and delusion. That's how a mendicant has a well-freed mind.
translations.an10.20:2: "Mendicants, there are these ten noble abodes in which the noble ones of the past, present, and future abide. What ten? A mendicant has given up five factors, possesses six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has eliminated idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth, has totally given up seeking, has unsullied intentions, has tranquil physical processes, and has a well-freed mind and well-freed wisdom.
translations.an10.20:3: And how has a mendicant given up five factors? It's when a mendicant has given up sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. That's how a mendicant has given up five factors.
translations.an10.20:4: And how does a mendicant possess six factors? It's when a mendicant, seeing a sight with their eyes, is neither happy nor sad, but remains equanimous, mindful and aware. Hearing a sound with their ears … Smelling an odor with their nose … Tasting a flavor with their tongue … Feeling a touch with their body … Knowing a thought with their mind, they're neither happy nor sad, but remain equanimous, mindful and aware. That's how a mendicant possesses six factors.
translations.an10.20:5: And how does a mendicant have a single guard? It's when a mendicant's heart is guarded by mindfulness. That's how a mendicant has a single guard.
translations.an10.20:6: And how does a mendicant have four supports? After appraisal, a mendicant uses some things, endures some things, avoids some things, and dispels some things. That's how a mendicant has four supports.
translations.an10.20:7: And how has a mendicant eliminated idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth? It's when a mendicant has dispelled, eliminated, thrown out, rejected, let go of, given up, and relinquished the various idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth espoused by the many different ascetics and brahmins, such as: 'The world is eternal,' or 'The world is not eternal,' or 'The world is finite,' or 'The world is infinite,' or 'The soul and the body are the same thing,' or 'The soul and the body are different things,' or 'A Realized One exists after death,' or 'A Realized One doesn't exist after death,' or 'A Realized One both exists and doesn't exist after death,' or 'A Realized One neither exists nor doesn't exist after death.' That's how a mendicant has eliminated idiosyncratic interpretations of the truth.
translations.an10.20:8: And how has a mendicant totally given up seeking? It's when they've given up seeking for sensual pleasures, seeking for continued existence, and seeking for a spiritual life has been stilled. That's how a mendicant has totally given up seeking.
translations.an10.20:9: And how does a mendicant have unsullied intentions? It's when they've given up intentions of sensuality, ill will, and cruelty. That's how a mendicant has unsullied intentions.
translations.an10.24:10: Suppose a person who was rich claimed to be rich, who was wealthy claimed to be wealthy, who was affluent claimed to be affluent. When some need for wealth arose, they would be able to produce wealth, grain, silver, or gold. People would know this about them: 'This venerable is rich and claims to be rich, is wealthy and claims to be wealthy, is affluent and claims to be affluent. Why is that? Because when some need for wealth arises, this venerable is able to produce wealth, grain, silver, or gold.'
translations.an10.24:2: A mendicant who claims to have knowledge, saying: 'I know this teaching, I see this teaching.' If, friends, that mendicant is overcome by greed, overcome by hate … delusion … anger … hostility … denigration … contempt … stinginess … bad envy … bad desire, they should be understood thus: 'This venerable does not understand in such a way that one who understands has no greed, for this venerable is overcome by greed. This venerable does not understand in such a way that one who understands has no hate … delusion … anger … hostility … denigration … contempt … stinginess … bad envy … bad desire, for this venerable is overcome by bad desire.'
translations.an10.24:3: A mendicant who claims to have developed, saying: 'I have developed body, ethics, mind, and wisdom.' If, friends, that mendicant is overcome by greed, overcome by hate … delusion … anger … hostility … denigration … contempt … stinginess … bad envy … bad desire, they should be understood thus: 'This venerable does not understand in such a way that one who understands has no greed, for this venerable is overcome by greed. This venerable does not understand in such a way that one who understands has no hate … delusion … anger … hostility … denigration … contempt … stinginess … bad envy … bad desire, for this venerable is overcome by bad desire.'
translations.an10.24:5: Suppose a person who was poor claimed to be rich, who was without wealth claimed to be wealthy, who was without affluence claimed to be affluent. When some need for wealth arose, they would not be able to produce wealth, grain, silver, or gold. People would know this about them: 'This venerable is poor and claims to be rich, is without wealth and claims to be wealthy, is without affluence and claims to be affluent. Why is that? Because when some need for wealth arises, this venerable is not able to produce wealth, grain, silver, or gold.'
translations.an10.24:9: A mendicant who claims to have knowledge and to have developed, saying: 'I know this teaching, I see this teaching, I have developed body, ethics, mind, and wisdom.' If, friends, that mendicant is not overcome by greed, not overcome by hate … delusion … anger … hostility … denigration … contempt … stinginess … bad envy … bad desire, they should be understood thus: 'This venerable understands in such a way that one who understands has no greed, for this venerable is not overcome by greed. This venerable understands in such a way that one who understands has no hate … delusion … anger … hostility … denigration … contempt … stinginess … bad envy … bad desire, for this venerable is not overcome by bad desire.'
translations.an10.29:1: As far as Kāsi and Kosala extend, as far as King Pasenadi of Kosala's realm extends, King Pasenadi of Kosala is declared to be the foremost there. But even King Pasenadi of Kosala is subject to change and alteration. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it. Being disillusioned with the foremost, they become dispassionate toward it, let alone toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:10: One who perceives the formless internally sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance. Just as a flax flower is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance, or just as Benares cloth smoothed on both sides is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance; so too one who perceives the formless internally sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance. They perceive thus: 'Having mastered them, I know and see.' This is the fifth dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:11: One who perceives the formless internally sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance. Just as a kaṇikāra flower is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance, or just as Benares cloth smoothed on both sides is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance; so too one who perceives the formless internally sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance. They perceive thus: 'Having mastered them, I know and see.' This is the sixth dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:12: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees visions externally that are red, with red color, red appearance, and red glow. Just as a bandhujīvaka flower is red, with red color, red appearance, and red glow; or a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is red, with red color, red appearance, and red glow; in the same way, not perceiving form internally, someone sees visions externally that are red, with red color, red appearance, and red glow. They perceive: 'Having mastered them, I know and see.' This is the seventh dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:13: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees visions externally that are white, with white color, white appearance, and white glow. Just as the morning star is white, with white color, white appearance, and white glow; or a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is white, with white color, white appearance, and white glow; in the same way, not perceiving form internally, someone sees visions externally that are white, with white color, white appearance, and white glow. They perceive: 'Having mastered them, I know and see.' This is the eighth dimension of mastery. These, mendicants, are the eight dimensions of mastery.
translations.an10.29:14: This is the best of these eight dimensions of mastery, that is: not perceiving form internally, someone sees visions externally that are white, with white color, white appearance, and white glow. They perceive: 'Having mastered them, I know and see.' There are beings who perceive in this way. But even for beings who perceive in this way, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with even that. Being disillusioned with the best, they become dispassionate toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:15: There are these four ways of practice, mendicants. What four? Painful practice with slow insight, painful practice with swift insight, pleasant practice with slow insight, pleasant practice with swift insight—these are the four ways of practice, mendicants.
translations.an10.29:16: This is the best of these four ways of practice, that is: pleasant practice with swift insight. There are beings who practice in this way. But even for beings who practice in this way, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with even that. Being disillusioned with the best, they become dispassionate toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:17: There are these four perceptions, mendicants. What four? One perceives the limited, one perceives the expansive, one perceives the boundless, one perceives the dimension of nothingness: 'There is nothing.' These are the four perceptions, mendicants.
translations.an10.29:18: This is the best of these four perceptions, that is: one perceives the dimension of nothingness: 'There is nothing.' There are beings who perceive in this way. But even for beings who perceive in this way, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with even that. Being disillusioned with the best, they become dispassionate toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:2: As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and illuminating the directions, so far extends the thousandfold world system. In that thousandfold world system there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sineru kings of mountains, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Western Continents, a thousand Northern Continents, a thousand Eastern Continents, four thousand great oceans, four thousand Great Kings, a thousand realms of the Four Great Kings, a thousand realms of the Thirty-Three, a thousand realms of Yāma, a thousand realms of Tusita, a thousand realms of gods who delight in creation, a thousand realms of gods who control what others create, a thousand Brahmā realms. As far as the thousandfold world system extends, the Great Brahmā is declared to be supreme there. But even for the Great Brahmā, mendicants, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with even that. Being disillusioned with the best, they become dispassionate toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:20: There are, mendicants, some ascetics and brahmins who describe the ultimate purity. This is the best of those who describe the ultimate purity, that is: having completely transcended the dimension of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. They teach the Dhamma for direct knowledge of that and for its realization. There are beings who hold such views. But even for beings who hold such views, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with even that. Being disillusioned with the best, they become dispassionate toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:3: There comes a time, mendicants, when this world contracts. When the world is contracting, most beings are reborn in the realm of streaming radiance. There they are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the sky, steadfast in beauty, and they remain for a long, long time. When the world is contracting, the gods of streaming radiance are declared to be supreme. But even for the gods of streaming radiance, mendicants, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with even that. Being disillusioned with the best, they become dispassionate toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:4: There are these ten dimensions of the totality, mendicants. What ten? One perceives the earth totality above, below, across, non-dual, and boundless. One perceives the water totality … One perceives the fire totality … One perceives the air totality … One perceives the blue totality … One perceives the yellow totality … One perceives the red totality … One perceives the white totality … One perceives the space totality … One perceives the consciousness totality above, below, across, non-dual, and boundless. These are the ten dimensions of the totality, mendicants.
translations.an10.29:5: This is the best of these ten universal dimensions, that is, when someone perceives the universal dimension of consciousness above, below, across, non-dual, and limitless. There are beings who perceive in this way. But even for beings who perceive in this way, there is change and transformation. Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with it. Being disillusioned with the best, they become dispassionate, let alone with what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:6: There are these eight dimensions of mastery. What eight? Perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally that are limited, beautiful or ugly. Mastering them, they perceive: 'I know and see.' This is the first dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:7: Perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally that are limitless, beautiful or ugly. Mastering them, they perceive: 'I know and see.' This is the second dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:8: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally that are limited, beautiful or ugly. Mastering them, they perceive: 'I know and see.' This is the third dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.29:9: Not perceiving form internally, someone sees forms externally that are limitless, beautiful or ugly. Mastering them, they perceive: 'I know and see.' This is the fourth dimension of mastery.
translations.an10.51:3: And how is a mendicant skilled in the ways of their own mind? Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornment. They'd examine the reflection of their own face in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. If they saw any dirt or blemish there, they'd try to remove it. But if they saw no dirt or blemish there, they'd be pleased with that, thinking: 'How fortunate that I'm clean!' In the same way, reflection is very helpful for a mendicant in skillful qualities: 'Do I usually live with covetousness or without covetousness? Do I usually live with ill will or without ill will? Do I usually live overcome by dullness and drowsiness or free of dullness and drowsiness? Do I usually live restless or calm? Do I usually live with doubt or have I gone beyond doubt? Do I usually live angry or without anger? Do I usually live with a defiled mind or an undefiled mind? Do I usually live with an agitated body or an unagitated body? Do I usually live lazy or with energy aroused? Do I usually live without immersion or with immersion?'
translations.an10.51:4: If, upon reflection, a mendicant knows: 'I usually live with covetousness, ill will, overcome by dullness and drowsiness, restless, with doubt, angry, with a defiled mind, with an agitated body, lazy, and without immersion,' then that mendicant should apply intense enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to give up those bad, unskillful qualities. Suppose your clothes or head were on fire. You'd apply intense enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to extinguish the fire on your clothes or head. In the same way, that mendicant should apply intense enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to give up those bad, unskillful qualities.
translations.an10.54:2: And how is a mendicant skilled in the ways of their own mind? Suppose there was a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornment. They'd examine the reflection of their own face in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. If they saw any dirt or blemish there, they'd try to remove it. But if they saw no dirt or blemish there, they'd be pleased with that, thinking: 'How fortunate that I'm clean!' In the same way, reflection is very helpful for a mendicant in skillful qualities: 'Do I gain internal serenity of mind or not? Do I gain the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena or not?'
translations.an10.54:5: But if, upon reflection, a mendicant knows: 'I don't gain internal serenity of mind, and I don't gain the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena,' then that mendicant should apply intense enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to obtain those skillful qualities. Suppose your clothes or head were on fire. You'd apply intense enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to extinguish the fire on your clothes or head. In the same way, that mendicant should apply intense enthusiasm, effort, zeal, vigor, perseverance, mindfulness, and situational awareness to obtain those skillful qualities. After some time they gain both internal serenity of mind and the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena.
translations.an10.54:6: But if, upon reflection, a mendicant knows: 'I gain internal serenity of mind, and I gain the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena,' then that mendicant, established in those skillful qualities, should practice further for the ending of the defilements.
translations.an10.60:10: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of cessation? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all attachments, the destruction of craving, cessation, extinguishment.' This, Ānanda, is called the perception of cessation.
translations.an10.60:11: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the whole world? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant dwells abandoning and not clinging to whatever attachments, mental standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies there are in the world. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of non-delight in the whole world.
translations.an10.60:12: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-desire for all formations? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant is troubled by, ashamed of, and disgusted with all formations. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of non-desire for all formations.
translations.an10.60:13: And what, Ānanda, is mindfulness of breathing? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, having folded their legs crosswise, set their body straight, and established mindfulness in front. Just mindful, they breathe in; mindful, they breathe out. Breathing in long, they know 'I breathe in long.' Breathing out long, they know 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, they know 'I breathe in short.' Breathing out short, they know 'I breathe out short.' They train: 'I will breathe in experiencing the whole body.' They train: 'I will breathe out experiencing the whole body.' They train: 'I will breathe in calming the bodily formation.' They train: 'I will breathe out calming the bodily formation.' They train: 'I will breathe in experiencing rapture.' They train: 'I will breathe out experiencing rapture.' They train: 'I will breathe in experiencing pleasure.' They train: 'I will breathe out experiencing pleasure.' They train: 'I will breathe in experiencing the mental formation.' They train: 'I will breathe out experiencing the mental formation.' They train: 'I will breathe in calming the mental formation.' They train: 'I will breathe out calming the mental formation.' They train: 'I will breathe in experiencing the mind.' They train: 'I will breathe out experiencing the mind.' Gladdening the mind … concentrating the mind … liberating the mind … contemplating impermanence … contemplating dispassion … contemplating cessation … They train: 'I will breathe in contemplating relinquishment.' They train: 'I will breathe out contemplating relinquishment.' This, Ānanda, is called mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:14: If, Ānanda, you were to recite these ten perceptions to the mendicant Girimānanda, it is possible that having heard these ten perceptions, the mendicant Girimānanda's illness would immediately subside.
translations.an10.60:3: What ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of unattractiveness, the perception of danger, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the whole world, the perception of non-desire for all formations, and mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:4: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.' Thus they dwell contemplating impermanence in these five aggregates of clinging. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of impermanence.
translations.an10.60:5: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of not-self? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant—gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—reflects thus: 'The eye is not-self, forms are not-self, the ear is not-self, sounds are not-self, the nose is not-self, odors are not-self, the tongue is not-self, tastes are not-self, the body is not-self, tactile objects are not-self, the mind is not-self, mental phenomena are not-self.' Thus they dwell contemplating not-self in these six internal and external sense bases. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of not-self.
translations.an10.60:6: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of unattractiveness? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant reviews this very body, up from the soles of the feet, down from the top of the hair, enclosed by skin, as full of many kinds of impurities: 'In this body there are head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach contents, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, and urine.' Thus they dwell contemplating unattractiveness in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of unattractiveness.
translations.an10.60:7: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of danger? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant—gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—reflects thus: 'This body has much suffering, much danger. Thus various afflictions arise in this body, such as: eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, outer ear disease, mouth disease, tooth disease, lip disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, fever, aging, stomach disease, fainting, dysentery, griping, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, tuberculosis, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, skin eruptions, scurvy, hemorrhage, jaundice, diabetes, hemorrhoids, fistulas, diseases originating from bile, diseases originating from phlegm, diseases originating from wind, diseases originating from their combination, diseases produced by change of season, diseases produced by improper care, diseases produced by assault, diseases produced by the result of kamma, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, and urination.' Thus they dwell contemplating danger in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of danger.
translations.an10.60:8: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of abandoning? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensuality, but abandons it, dispels it, eliminates it, and obliterates it. They do not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will, but abandon it, dispel it, eliminate it, and obliterate it. They do not tolerate an arisen thought of harming, but abandon it, dispel it, eliminate it, and obliterate it. They do not tolerate arisen bad, unwholesome states, but abandon them, dispel them, eliminate them, and obliterate them. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of abandoning.
translations.an10.61:1: Mendicants, a first point of ignorance is not evident, such that before this there was no ignorance and afterwards it came into being. Nevertheless, it is evident that ignorance has a specific condition.
translations.an10.61:2: I say that ignorance has fuel, not that it is without fuel. And what is the fuel for ignorance? It should be said: 'The five hindrances.' I say that the five hindrances have fuel, not that they are without fuel. And what is the fuel for the five hindrances? It should be said: 'The three kinds of misconduct.' I say that the three kinds of misconduct have fuel, not that they are without fuel. And what is the fuel for the three kinds of misconduct? It should be said: 'Non-restraint of the sense faculties.' I say that non-restraint of the sense faculties has fuel, not that it is without fuel. And what is the fuel for non-restraint of the sense faculties? It should be said: 'Lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension.' I say that lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension has fuel, not that it is without fuel. And what is the fuel for lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension? It should be said: 'Careless attention.' I say that careless attention has fuel, not that it is without fuel. And what is the fuel for careless attention? It should be said: 'Lack of faith.' I say that lack of faith has fuel, not that it is without fuel. And what is the fuel for lack of faith? It should be said: 'Not hearing the true teaching.' I say that not hearing the true teaching has fuel, not that it is without fuel. And what is the fuel for not hearing the true teaching? It should be said: 'Associating with bad people.'
translations.an10.61:3: Thus, mendicants, when associating with bad people is fulfilled, it fulfills not hearing the true teaching; when not hearing the true teaching is fulfilled, it fulfills lack of faith; when lack of faith is fulfilled, it fulfills careless attention; when careless attention is fulfilled, it fulfills lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension; when lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension is fulfilled, it fulfills non-restraint of the sense faculties; when non-restraint of the sense faculties is fulfilled, it fulfills the three kinds of misconduct; when the three kinds of misconduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the five hindrances; when the five hindrances are fulfilled, they fulfill ignorance. This is the fuel for ignorance, and this is how it is fulfilled.
translations.an10.61:4: Suppose, mendicants, when it is raining heavily on the upper mountain with big drops (…) that water, flowing according to the slope, fills the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies. When the mountain clefts, crevices, and gullies are full, they fill the small pools. When the small pools are full, they fill the large pools. When the large pools are full, they fill the small rivers. When the small rivers are full, they fill the large rivers. When the large rivers are full, they fill the great ocean. This is the fuel for the great ocean, and this is how it is fulfilled.
translations.an10.61:7: Thus, mendicants, when associating with good people is fulfilled, it fulfills hearing the true teaching; when hearing the true teaching is fulfilled, it fulfills faith; when faith is fulfilled, it fulfills careful attention; when careful attention is fulfilled, it fulfills mindfulness and clear comprehension; when mindfulness and clear comprehension is fulfilled, it fulfills restraint of the sense faculties; when restraint of the sense faculties is fulfilled, it fulfills the three kinds of good conduct; when the three kinds of good conduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the four establishments of mindfulness; when the four establishments of mindfulness are fulfilled, they fulfill the seven factors of awakening; when the seven factors of awakening are fulfilled, they fulfill true knowledge and liberation. This is the fuel for true knowledge and liberation, and this is how it is fulfilled.
translations.an3.15:3: Then the wheelwright rolled the wheel that was finished in six days. When rolled, it went as far as the force of the effort carried it, then wobbled and fell to the ground. But the wheel that was finished in six months less six days, he rolled that. When rolled, it went as far as the force of the effort carried it, then stood as if fixed on an axle.
translations.an3.15:5: Now, mendicants, you might think: 'Surely the wheelwright at that time must have been someone else.' But you should not see it like that. I was the wheelwright at that time. Back then, mendicants, I was skilled in the crookedness, faults, and defects of wood. But now, mendicants, I am the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One, skilled in the crookedness, faults, and defects of body; skilled in the crookedness, faults, and defects of speech; skilled in the crookedness, faults, and defects of mind. For any monk or nun who has not abandoned crookedness, faults, and defects of body; who has not abandoned crookedness, faults, and defects of speech; who has not abandoned crookedness, faults, and defects of mind—they have fallen away from this Dhamma and Vinaya, just like that wheel finished in six days.
translations.an3.12:5: Furthermore, mendicants, the place where a mendicant truly understands: 'This is suffering,' truly understands: 'This is the origin of suffering,' truly understands: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' truly understands: 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' This is the second thing a mendicant should remember for life.
translations.an3.15:2: Once upon a time, mendicants, there was a king named Sacetana. Then King Sacetana addressed a wheelwright: 'My dear wheelwright, in six months I will have a battle. Can you make me a new pair of wheels?' 'I can, Your Majesty,' the wheelwright replied to King Sacetana. Then the wheelwright finished one wheel in six months less six days. Then King Sacetana addressed the wheelwright: 'My dear wheelwright, in six days I will have a battle. Is the new pair of wheels finished?' 'Your Majesty, in these six months less six days, one wheel has been finished.' 'But can you, my dear wheelwright, finish the second wheel in these six days?' 'I can, Your Majesty.' Then the wheelwright finished the second wheel in six days, took the new pair of wheels, and approached King Sacetana. Having approached, he said to King Sacetana: 'Your Majesty, your new pair of wheels is finished.' 'My dear wheelwright, what is the difference between this wheel finished in six months less six days and this wheel finished in six days? I don't see any difference between them.' 'There is a difference, Your Majesty. Let Your Majesty see the difference.'
translations.an3.15:6: For any monk or nun who has abandoned crookedness, faults, and defects of body; who has abandoned crookedness, faults, and defects of speech; who has abandoned crookedness, faults, and defects of mind—they are established in this Dhamma and Vinaya, just like that wheel finished in six months less six days.
translations.an3.1:3: Thus, mendicants, the fool is beset with danger, the wise one is free from danger. The fool is beset with disaster, the wise one is free from disaster. The fool is beset with calamity, the wise one is free from calamity. There is no danger from the wise one, no disaster from the wise one, no calamity from the wise one.
translations.an3.20:1: "Mendicants, a shopkeeper who has three factors soon acquires great and abundant wealth. What three? It's when a shopkeeper has an eye for business, is responsible, and has supporters. And how does a shopkeeper have an eye for business? It's when a shopkeeper knows the goods: 'When this item is bought and sold in this way, it will bring this much capital and this much profit.' That's how a shopkeeper has an eye for business.
translations.an3.20:2: And how is a shopkeeper responsible? It's when a shopkeeper is skilled at buying and selling goods. That's how a shopkeeper is responsible.
translations.an3.20:3: And how does a shopkeeper have supporters? It's when householders or their children who are rich, wealthy, and affluent know of that shopkeeper: 'This good shopkeeper has an eye for business and is responsible. He is able to support his wife and children, and pay us back from time to time.' They provide him with money: 'With this money, good shopkeeper, do business and support your wife and children, and pay us back from time to time.' That's how a shopkeeper has supporters. A shopkeeper who has these three factors soon acquires great and abundant wealth.
translations.an3.20:4: In the same way, a mendicant who has three qualities soon acquires great and abundant skillful qualities. What three? It's when a mendicant has an eye for the teaching, is responsible, and has supporters. And how does a mendicant have an eye for the teaching? It's when a mendicant truly understands: 'This is suffering.' They truly understand: 'This is the origin of suffering.' They truly understand: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' They truly understand: 'This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.' That's how a mendicant has an eye for the teaching.
translations.an3.20:5: And how is a mendicant responsible? It's when a mendicant lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and embracing skillful qualities. They are strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to developing skillful qualities. That's how a mendicant is responsible.
translations.an3.22:1: "Mendicants, these three kinds of sick people are found in the world. What three? One kind of sick person, whether or not they get suitable food, suitable medicine, and a suitable carer, will not recover from that illness.
translations.an3.22:3: One kind of sick person will recover from that illness only if they get suitable food, suitable medicine, and a suitable carer, not if they don't.
translations.an3.22:4: Now, it is because of the sick person who will recover from that illness only if they get suitable food, suitable medicine, and a suitable carer, not if they don't, that food for the sick, medicine for the sick, and a carer for the sick are allowed. And it is because of this sick person that other sick people should also be cared for. These are the three kinds of sick people found in the world.
translations.an3.22:5: In the same way, these three people similar to the sick are found in the world. What three? One kind of person, whether or not they get to see the Realized One, whether or not they get to hear the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One, will not enter the sure path with regards to skillful qualities.
translations.an3.22:6: One kind of person, whether or not they get to see the Realized One, whether or not they get to hear the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One, will enter the sure path with regards to skillful qualities.
translations.an3.24:1: "Mendicants, these three people are very helpful to another person. What three? The person depending on whom another person has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. That person is very helpful to this person.
translations.an3.24:2: Furthermore, the person depending on whom another person truly understands: 'This is suffering' … 'This is the origin of suffering' … 'This is the cessation of suffering' … 'This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.' That person is very helpful to this person.
translations.an3.24:3: Furthermore, the person depending on whom another person realizes the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom in this very life, and lives having realized it with their own insight due to the ending of defilements. That person is very helpful to this person. These are the three people who are very helpful to another person.
translations.an3.2:1: "Mendicants, a fool is known by their deeds, an astute person is known by their deeds, and wisdom shines in action. A fool should be known by three things. What three? Bad conduct by way of body, speech, and mind. A fool should be known by these three things.
translations.an3.2:2: An astute person should be known by three things. What three? Good conduct by way of body, speech, and mind. An astute person should be known by these three things.
translations.an3.30:4: A person of upturned wisdom, stupid and undiscerning, even if they often go into the presence of the mendicants,
translations.an3.30:5: such a person cannot learn the beginning, middle, and end of a talk, for they have no wisdom.
translations.an3.30:6: A person of lap-wisdom is said to be better than that. Even if they often go into the presence of the mendicants,
translations.an3.30:8: A person of widespread wisdom is said to be better than these. Even if they often go into the presence of the mendicants,
translations.an3.33:1: Then Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to Venerable Sāriputta as he sat to one side: 'Sāriputta, I could teach the Dhamma in brief; I could teach the Dhamma in detail; I could teach the Dhamma both in brief and in detail; but those who understand are rare.' 'This is the time, Blessed One, this is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma in brief, to teach the Dhamma in detail, to teach the Dhamma both in brief and in detail. There will be those who understand the Dhamma.'
translations.an3.33:4: 'The abandoning of perceptions of sensuality, and of dejection too; the dispelling of dullness, and the warding off of remorse.
translations.an3.34:1: 'Mendicants, there are these three sources for the arising of actions. What three? Greed is a source for the arising of actions, hatred is a source for the arising of actions, delusion is a source for the arising of actions.
translations.an3.34:10: When, mendicants, an action done without delusion, born of non-delusion, sourced in non-delusion, originated from non-delusion—when delusion has faded away, that action is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.
translations.an3.34:11: Suppose, mendicants, there were seeds that are unbroken, unspoiled, undamaged by wind and sun, fertile, and well preserved. A person would burn them with fire. Having burned them with fire, they would reduce them to ashes. Having reduced them to ashes, they would scatter them in a strong wind or let them be carried away by a swift river current. Thus, mendicants, those seeds would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future. In the same way, mendicants, when an action done without greed, born of non-greed, sourced in non-greed, originated from non-greed—when greed has faded away, that action is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.
translations.an3.34:13: Born of greed, born of hatred, and born of delusion—for one who has discarded these, whatever action they have done, whether little or much, is to be experienced right here; no other basis is found.
translations.an3.34:2: When, mendicants, an action done through greed, born of greed, sourced in greed, originated from greed—wherever their personal existence arises, there that action ripens. Where that action ripens, there they experience the result of that action, either in this very life, or in the next rebirth, or on some subsequent occasion.
translations.an3.34:5: Suppose, mendicants, there were seeds that are unbroken, unspoiled, undamaged by wind and sun, fertile, and well preserved, planted in good soil that is well prepared. And the sky would provide timely rain. Thus, mendicants, those seeds would come to growth, increase, and maturity. In the same way, mendicants, when an action done through greed, born of greed, sourced in greed, originated from greed—wherever their personal existence arises, there that action ripens. Where that action ripens, there they experience the result of that action, either in this very life, or in the next rebirth, or on some subsequent occasion.
translations.an3.34:6: When an action done through hatred … When an action done through delusion, born of delusion, sourced in delusion, originated from delusion—wherever their personal existence arises, there that action ripens. Where that action ripens, there they experience the result of that action, either in this very life, or in the next rebirth, or on some subsequent occasion. These, mendicants, are the three sources for the arising of actions.
translations.an3.34:9: When, mendicants, an action done without hatred, born of non-hatred, sourced in non-hatred, originated from non-hatred—when hatred has faded away, that action is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.
translations.an3.35:3: 'Well then, prince, I will ask you about this in return. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, prince? Suppose a householder or householder's son had a gabled house, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and windows shuttered. In it there was a couch spread with rugs, blankets, and covers, with a fine deer-hide as a top cover, with a canopy above, and red pillows at both ends. And an oil lamp was burning there. And four wives were attending to him with whatever is pleasing. What do you think, prince, would he sleep well or not? How does it seem to you?' 'He would sleep well, sir. And of those in the world who sleep well, he would be one of them.'
translations.an3.35:4: "What do you think, prince? Would there arise in that householder or householder's son burning pains born of lust, bodily or mental, burning with which he would sleep in suffering?
translations.an3.35:8: The brahmin who has attained final extinguishment always sleeps happily; who is not smeared by sensual pleasures, cooled, without attachments.
translations.an3.39:10: Living thus, having known the state without attachments; whatever intoxication there is with health, with youth, and with life.
translations.an3.39:2: I had three palaces, mendicants—one for winter, one for summer, and one for the rainy season. I spent the four months of the rainy season in the rainy-season palace, entertained by musicians, none of whom were men, and I didn't go down from the palace. While in other people's homes the food of broken rice with sour gruel is given to slaves, workers, and servants, in my father's home they were given rice and meat.
translations.an3.39:3: Endowed with such fortune and such delicacy, mendicants, this occurred to me: 'An unlearned ordinary person, though themselves subject to old age, not exempt from old age, feels repelled, humiliated, and disgusted when seeing another who is old, overlooking themselves. I too am subject to old age, not exempt from old age. If I were to feel repelled, humiliated, and disgusted when seeing another who is old, that would not be proper for me.' As I reflected thus, mendicants, all intoxication with youth was completely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:4: An unlearned ordinary person, though themselves subject to illness, not exempt from illness, feels repelled, humiliated, and disgusted when seeing another who is ill, overlooking themselves: 'I too am subject to illness, not exempt from illness. If I were to feel repelled, humiliated, and disgusted when seeing another who is ill, that would not be proper for me.' As I reflected thus, mendicants, all intoxication with health was completely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:5: An unlearned ordinary person, though themselves subject to death, not exempt from death, feels repelled, humiliated, and disgusted when seeing another who is dead, overlooking themselves: 'I too am subject to death, not exempt from death. If I were to feel repelled, humiliated, and disgusted when seeing another who is dead, that would not be proper for me.' As I reflected thus, mendicants, all intoxication with life was completely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:7: A mendicant intoxicated with youth, mendicants, rejects the training and returns to the lower life. A mendicant intoxicated with health, mendicants... A mendicant intoxicated with life, mendicants, rejects the training and returns to the lower life.
translations.an3.39:8: Subject to illness, subject to old age, and also subject to death; ordinary people feel disgust for others who are just as their nature dictates.
translations.an3.39:9: If I were to feel disgust for beings whose nature is thus, that would not be proper for one living as I do.
translations.an3.40:1: There are these three authorities, mendicants. What three? The authority of oneself, the authority of the world, and the authority of the Dhamma. And what, mendicants, is the authority of oneself? Here, mendicants, a mendicant gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'It was not for the sake of robes that I went forth from the household life into homelessness. Not for the sake of almsfood, not for the sake of lodgings, not for the sake of this or that state of existence did I go forth from the household life into homelessness. But I am beset by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; beset by suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering can be discerned. If I were to seek the same kind of sensual pleasures that I abandoned when I went forth from the household life into homelessness, or even worse ones, that would not be proper for me.' He reflects thus: 'My energy will be aroused and unsluggish, my mindfulness established and unconfused, my body tranquil and undisturbed, my mind concentrated and unified.' Making oneself the authority, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless, and maintains himself in purity. This, mendicants, is called the authority of oneself.
translations.an3.40:3: And what, mendicants, is the authority of the Dhamma? Here, mendicants, a mendicant gone to the forest, to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: 'It was not for the sake of robes that I went forth from the household life into homelessness. Not for the sake of almsfood, not for the sake of lodgings, not for the sake of this or that state of existence did I go forth from the household life into homelessness. But I am beset by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; beset by suffering, overcome by suffering. Perhaps an end to this entire mass of suffering can be discerned. The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be personally experienced by the wise. There are fellow practitioners of mine who dwell knowing and seeing. If I, having gone forth in such a well-expounded Dhamma and discipline, were to live lazily and negligently, that would not be proper for me.' He reflects thus: 'My energy will be aroused and unsluggish, my mindfulness established and unconfused, my body tranquil and undisturbed, my mind concentrated and unified.' Making the Dhamma the authority, he abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless, and maintains himself in purity. This, mendicants, is called the authority of the Dhamma. These, mendicants, are the three authorities.
translations.an3.40:4: There is no secret in the world for one who does evil deeds; your own self, O person, knows whether it is true or false.
translations.an3.40:5: Indeed, good sir, you disregard yourself as witness, a good one; you who conceal from yourself the evil that exists within yourself.
translations.an3.40:6: The devas and the Tathāgatas see the fool behaving unrighteously in the world; therefore, one who makes oneself the authority, one who makes the world the authority, the wise one who meditates, one who makes the Dhamma the authority and practices in accordance with the Dhamma—the sage of true effort does not decline.
translations.an3.48:2: In the same way, supported by a faithful head of a family, the people in the household grow in three ways. What three? They grow in faith, they grow in ethical conduct, they grow in wisdom. Supported by a faithful head of a family, the people in the household grow in these three ways.
translations.an3.51:3: Life is swept along, short is the lifespan; for one swept on by old age there are no shelters. Seeing this danger in death, one should do deeds of merit that bring happiness.
translations.an3.52:4: Thus the world is on fire with old age and death; one should bring out by giving, for what is given is well brought out.
translations.an3.60:10: Here, brahmin, someone does not read minds by means of signs, but having heard the voice of humans, non-humans, or deities, they declare: 'Your mind is like this, your mind is like that, your thought is thus.' Even if they declare many things, it is exactly so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:11: Here, brahmin, someone does not read minds by means of signs, nor by hearing the voice of humans, non-humans, or deities, but having heard the sound of the spreading of thoughts of one who is thinking and pondering, they declare: 'Your mind is like this, your mind is like that, your thought is thus.' Even if they declare many things, it is exactly so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:12: Here, brahmin, someone does not read minds by means of signs, nor by hearing the voice of humans, non-humans, or deities, nor by hearing the sound of the spreading of thoughts of one who is thinking and pondering, but having attained a concentration without thought and examination, they understand with their mind, having encompassed the mind of another: 'According to how this venerable one's mental formations are directed, immediately after this thought they will think such and such a thought.' Even if they declare many things, it is exactly so, not otherwise. This, brahmin, is called the miracle of mind-reading.
translations.an3.60:13: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Here, brahmin, someone instructs thus: 'Think in this way, don't think in that way; attend in this way, don't attend in that way; abandon this, enter upon and dwell in this.' This, brahmin, is called the miracle of instruction. These, brahmin, are the three miracles. Of these three miracles, brahmin, which miracle do you prefer as the most excellent and sublime?
translations.an3.60:1: Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Buddha: "Master Gotama, we are brahmins. We perform sacrifices and have others perform sacrifices. In this regard, Master Gotama, both the one who performs the sacrifice and the one who has it performed are following a path of merit involving many people, that is, on account of the sacrifice. But, Master Gotama, when someone from whatever family has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, they tame only themselves, calm only themselves, and bring only themselves to final nibbāna. Thus they are following a path of merit involving only one person, that is, on account of the going forth."
translations.an3.51:2: "Indeed, brahmins, you are old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, one hundred and twenty years from birth. And you have not done what is good, not done what is wholesome, not made a shelter from fear. This world, brahmins, is being led on by old age, sickness, and death. When the world is being led on by old age, sickness, and death, restraint of body here, restraint of speech, restraint of mind—that is the shelter, refuge, island, protection, and final resort for one who has passed away."
translations.an3.60:14: "In this regard, Master Gotama, as for the miracle where someone experiences various kinds of psychic powers... and wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahmā world—this miracle, Master Gotama, is experienced only by the one who performs it; it belongs only to the one who performs it. This miracle, Master Gotama, appears to me to be like an illusion."
translations.an3.48:3: Just as a rocky mountain in the forest, in a great wood, trees depending on it, those forest lords grow.
translations.an3.5:1: "A fool can be known by three qualities. What three? They ask questions improperly, they answer questions improperly, and when another has answered a question properly, with well-rounded phrases and expressions that are polished and fitting, they do not approve. A fool can be known by these three qualities."
translations.an3.60:16: As to this demonstration, Master Gotama, where someone instructs others: 'Think like this, don't think like that; attend to this, don't attend to that; give up this, enter and dwell in this'—this demonstration is the most excellent and sublime of these three demonstrations, and it is acceptable to me.
translations.an3.60:17: It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is amazing, Master Gotama! How well this has been stated by Master Gotama! And we consider Master Gotama to be endowed with these three demonstrations. For Master Gotama experiences many kinds of psychic power … he wields bodily mastery as far as the Brahmā realm. For Master Gotama, having encompassed with his mind the mind of one who has attained a state of immersion without thought or examination, understands: 'Given how this person's mental processes are directed, immediately after this state of mind they will think such and such a thought.' For Master Gotama instructs others: 'Think like this, don't think like that; attend to this, don't attend to that; give up this, enter and dwell in this.'
translations.an3.60:3: What do you think, brahmin? This being so, is this practice of merit for one person or for many, that is, on account of going forth?
translations.an3.60:4: When he said this, Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: 'Brahmin, of these two practices, which do you prefer as having fewer requirements, less trouble, greater fruit, and greater benefit?' When he said this, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Just as Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are. These are worthy of my honor, these are worthy of my praise.'
translations.an3.60:8: 'Brahmin, there are these three kinds of miracles. What three? The miracle of psychic power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction. And what, brahmin, is the miracle of psychic power? Here, brahmin, someone wields the many kinds of psychic power: having been one, they become many; having been many, they become one; they appear and vanish; they go unhindered through walls, ramparts, and mountains as if through space; they dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; they walk on water without sinking as if it were earth; they fly cross-legged through the sky like a bird; with their hand they touch and stroke the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful; they control the body as far as the Brahmā realm. This is called the miracle of psychic power.
translations.an3.60:9: And what is the miracle of revealing? It's when someone reveals by means of signs: 'Such is your mind, such is your thinking, such is your thought.' And even if they reveal many things, it is so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.61:13: 'These four noble truths'—this teaching of mine is irrefutable, uncorrupted, blameless, and not criticized by sensible ascetics and brahmins. That's what I said, but why did I say it? Mendicants, conception in a womb takes place dependent on the six elements. When there is conception, there is name and form. Name and form is a condition for the six sense bases. The six sense bases are a condition for contact. Contact is a condition for feeling. For one who feels, I declare: 'This is suffering.' I declare: 'This is the origin of suffering.' I declare: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' I declare: 'This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering.'
translations.an3.61:14: And what is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, old age is suffering, … death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress are suffering, association with what is disliked is suffering, separation from what is liked is suffering, not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates affected by grasping are suffering. This is called the noble truth of suffering.
translations.an3.61:15: And what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? Ignorance is a condition for choices. Choices are a condition for consciousness. Consciousness is a condition for name and form. Name and form is a condition for the six sense bases. The six sense bases are a condition for contact. Contact is a condition for feeling. Feeling is a condition for craving. Craving is a condition for grasping. Grasping is a condition for continued existence. Continued existence is a condition for rebirth. Rebirth is a condition for old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to come to be. That is how this entire mass of suffering originates. This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
translations.an3.61:16: And what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? When ignorance fades away and ceases with nothing left over, choices cease. When choices cease, consciousness ceases. When consciousness ceases, name and form cease. When name and form cease, the six sense bases cease. When the six sense bases cease, contact ceases. When contact ceases, feeling ceases. When feeling ceases, craving ceases. When craving ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases. When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases. When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:3: But for those who accept past deeds as essential, there is no desire or effort, no 'this should be done' or 'this should not be done'. Since what should and should not be done are not truly and actually found, those who live unmindful and unguarded have no legitimate claim to the ascetic life. This is my first legitimate refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who have such doctrines and views.
translations.an3.61:8: These are the three sectarian tenets which, when questioned, pressed, and cross-examined by the wise, end up in inaction even when taken to their conclusion.
translations.an3.61:9: But this teaching of mine is irrefutable, uncorrupted, blameless, and not criticized by sensible ascetics and brahmins. And what is this teaching of mine that is irrefutable, uncorrupted, blameless, and not criticized by sensible ascetics and brahmins? 'These six elements'—this teaching of mine is irrefutable, uncorrupted, blameless, and not criticized by sensible ascetics and brahmins. 'These six bases of contact'—this teaching of mine is irrefutable, uncorrupted, blameless, and not criticized by sensible ascetics and brahmins. 'These eighteen mental preoccupations'—this teaching of mine is irrefutable, uncorrupted, blameless, and not criticized by sensible ascetics and brahmins. 'These four noble truths'—this teaching of mine is irrefutable, uncorrupted, blameless, and not criticized by sensible ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an3.62:1: 'There are these three dangers that separate mother and child,' says the uneducated ordinary person. What three? There comes a time when a great fire breaks out. When a great fire breaks out, villages, towns, and cities are burned. When villages, towns, and cities are burning, a mother cannot find her child, and a child cannot find their mother. This is the first danger that separates mother and child, says the uneducated ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:2: Furthermore, there comes a time when a great storm breaks out. When a great storm breaks out, a great flood arises. When a great flood arises, villages, towns, and cities are swept away. When villages, towns, and cities are being swept away, a mother cannot find her child, and a child cannot find their mother. This is the second danger that separates mother and child, says the uneducated ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:3: Furthermore, there comes a time when there is danger, an invasion from the wilderness, and the people of the country flee on their vehicles. When there is danger, an invasion from the wilderness, and the people of the country are fleeing on their vehicles, a mother cannot find her child, and a child cannot find their mother. This is the third danger that separates mother and child, says the uneducated ordinary person. These are the three dangers that separate mother and child, says the uneducated ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:4: An uneducated ordinary person speaks of these three dangers that separate mother and child as dangers that don't separate mother and child. What three? There comes a time when a great fire breaks out. When a great fire breaks out, it burns villages, towns, and cities. While villages, towns, and cities are burning, there comes a time when sometimes a mother finds her child, and a child finds their mother. This is the first danger that separates mother and child that an uneducated ordinary person speaks of as a danger that doesn't separate mother and child.
translations.an3.62:5: Furthermore, there comes a time when a great storm breaks out. When a great storm breaks out, a great flood arises. When a great flood arises, it sweeps away villages, towns, and cities. While villages, towns, and cities are being swept away, there comes a time when sometimes a mother finds her child, and a child finds their mother. This is the second danger that separates mother and child that an uneducated ordinary person speaks of as a danger that doesn't separate mother and child.
translations.an3.62:6: Furthermore, there comes a time when there is fear and turmoil in the wilderness, and the people of the country mount their vehicles and flee. When there is fear and turmoil in the wilderness, and the people of the country mount their vehicles and flee, there comes a time when sometimes a mother finds her child, and a child finds their mother. This is the third danger that separates mother and child that an uneducated ordinary person speaks of as a danger that doesn't separate mother and child. These are the three dangers that separate mother and child that an uneducated ordinary person speaks of as dangers that don't separate mother and child.
translations.an3.62:7: There are these three dangers that don't separate mother and child. What three? The danger of old age, the danger of illness, and the danger of death. A mother cannot obtain this regarding her aging child: 'Let me age, may my child not age.' Nor can a child obtain this regarding their aging mother: 'Let me age, may my mother not age.'
translations.an3.62:8: A mother cannot obtain this regarding her ill child: 'Let me be ill, may my child not be ill.' Nor can a child obtain this regarding their ill mother: 'Let me be ill, may my mother not be ill.'
translations.an3.62:9: A mother cannot obtain this regarding her dying child: 'Let me die, may my child not die.' Nor can a child obtain this regarding their dying mother: 'Let me die, may my mother not die.' These are the three dangers that don't separate mother and child.
translations.an4.24:2: Whatever is seen, heard, thought, cognized, reached, sought, and explored by the mind in this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, with its people including ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—that I know.
translations.an4.10:9: Bound by the yoke of sensuality, and both by the yoke of existence; bound by the yoke of views, led on by ignorance.
translations.an4.10:10: Beings go on in the cycle of rebirth, heading for birth and death. But those who fully understand sensual pleasures, and the yoke of existence entirely.
translations.an3.63:5: Brahmin, there are these three high and luxurious beds that I now obtain at will, without trouble or difficulty. What three? The divine high and luxurious bed, the brahmā high and luxurious bed, and the noble high and luxurious bed. These are the three high and luxurious beds that I now obtain at will, without trouble or difficulty.
translations.an3.63:11: "It's incredible, Master Gotama, it's amazing! Who else but Master Gotama would get such a noble high and luxurious bed whenever they want, without trouble or difficulty?
translations.an4.1:4: "Ethics, immersion, and wisdom, and the supreme freedom: these things have been understood by the renowned Gotama.
translations.an4.24:5: If I were to say, 'I both know and don't know' … that would be just the same.
translations.an4.24:7: So, mendicants, the Realized One, having seen what is to be seen, does not conceive the seen, does not conceive the unseen, does not conceive what is to be seen, does not conceive a seer; having heard what is to be heard, does not conceive the heard, does not conceive the unheard, does not conceive what is to be heard, does not conceive a hearer; having sensed what is to be sensed, does not conceive the sensed, does not conceive the unsensed, does not conceive what is to be sensed, does not conceive a senser; having cognized what is to be cognized, does not conceive the cognized, does not conceive the uncognized, does not conceive what is to be cognized, does not conceive a cognizer. So, mendicants, the Realized One is 'such' regarding things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—he is simply such. And I say there is no other 'such' superior or more sublime than that.
translations.an4.24:8: Whatever is seen, heard, or sensed, and held as true by others— among those self-restrained, one who is 'such' would not affirm as true or false what others hold.
translations.an4.28:1: Mendicants, there are these four noble traditions that are original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, which are not being adulterated and will not be adulterated, and which are not criticized by wise ascetics and brahmins. What four? Here, a mendicant is content with any kind of robe, praises contentment with any kind of robe, and does not engage in improper and unsuitable search for the sake of a robe. Not getting a robe, they are not anxious. Getting a robe, they use it without greed, infatuation, or attachment, seeing the danger and understanding the escape. And because of this contentment with any kind of robe, they do not exalt themselves or disparage others. One who is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful in this regard is called a mendicant who stands in the ancient, original noble tradition.
translations.an4.28:4: Furthermore, a mendicant delights in meditation and loves meditation, delights in abandoning and loves abandoning. And because of this delight and love for meditation and abandoning, they do not exalt themselves or disparage others. One who is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful in this regard is called a mendicant who stands in the ancient, original noble tradition. These are the four noble traditions that are original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, which are not being adulterated and will not be adulterated, and which are not criticized by wise ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an4.28:5: A mendicant endowed with these four noble traditions, whether dwelling in the eastern direction, overcomes discontent—discontent does not overcome them; whether dwelling in the western direction, overcomes discontent—discontent does not overcome them; whether dwelling in the northern direction, overcomes discontent—discontent does not overcome them; whether dwelling in the southern direction, overcomes discontent—discontent does not overcome them. Why is that? Because the wise one overcomes both discontent and delight.
translations.an4.28:6: Discontent does not overcome the wise, discontent does not overcome the wise; the wise one overcomes discontent, for the wise one conquers discontent.
translations.an4.31:1: Mendicants, there are these four wheels. When gods and humans possess these four wheels, the four wheels roll for them, and possessing them, gods and humans before long attain greatness and abundance in wealth. What four? Living in a suitable place, relying on good people, directing oneself rightly, and having made merit in the past. These are the four wheels.
