When gods and humans possess these four wheels, the four wheels roll for them, and possessing them, gods and humans before long attain greatness and abundance in wealth.
translations.an4.32:1: Mendicants, there are these four ways of being inclusive. What four? Giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. These are the four ways of being inclusive.
translations.an4.32:2: Giving and kind speech, and beneficial conduct here, and impartiality in various situations as appropriate— these ways of being inclusive in the world are like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
translations.an4.32:3: If these ways of being inclusive did not exist, neither mother nor father would receive respect or honor on account of their child.
translations.an4.33:1: Mendicants, in the evening the lion, king of beasts, emerges from its lair. Having emerged from its lair, it stretches. Having stretched, it surveys the four quarters all around. Having surveyed the four quarters all around, it roars its lion's roar three times. Having roared its lion's roar three times, it sets out for hunting. Now, mendicants, those animals who hear the sound of the lion, king of beasts, roaring, for the most part become fearful, anxious, and terrified. Those who live in holes enter their holes, those who live in water enter the water, those who live in the forest enter the forest, and birds take to the sky. Even the royal elephants in villages, towns, and capital cities, bound by strong leather straps and chains, break and burst those bonds, and terrified, releasing urine and feces, flee this way and that. So powerful, mendicants, is the lion, king of beasts, over animals, so mighty, so influential.
translations.an4.33:2: In the same way, mendicants, when a Realized One arises in the world, an Arahant, a Fully Awakened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Fortunate One, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One, he teaches the Dhamma: 'Such is identity, such is the origin of identity, such is the cessation of identity, such is the practice leading to the cessation of identity.' Those gods who are long-lived, beautiful, abounding in happiness, dwelling long in lofty palaces, having heard the Realized One's teaching of the Dhamma, for the most part become fearful, anxious, and terrified: 'It seems, sirs, that we who are impermanent thought we were permanent; it seems, sirs, that we who are unstable thought we were stable; it seems, sirs, that we who are not eternal thought we were eternal. It seems, sirs, that we are impermanent, unstable, not eternal, included within identity.' So powerful, mendicants, is the Realized One over the world with its gods, so mighty, so influential.
translations.an4.33:3: When the Buddha, through direct knowledge, set rolling the Wheel of Dhamma, the teacher without equal in the world with its gods,
translations.an4.33:4: He taught identity and its cessation, and the origin of identity, and the noble eightfold path leading to the stilling of suffering.
translations.an4.37:2: And how is a mendicant accomplished in ethics? It's when a mendicant is ethical, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and seeking alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they've undertaken. That's how a mendicant is accomplished in ethics.
translations.an4.34:6: For those confident in the best teaching, the happiness of fading away and peace; for those confident in the best Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.an4.35:2: 'Master Gotama, we describe a person of great wisdom as a great man when they have four qualities. What four? Firstly, they're very learned in diverse fields of learning. And they understand the meaning of diverse statements: 'This is what that statement means; this is what that statement means.' They're mindful, able to remember and recollect what was done and said long ago. And they're skillful and diligent in household duties, understanding how to go about things so as to get things done and organize them. We describe a person of great wisdom as a great man when they have these four qualities. If Master Gotama should approve, let him approve; if he should reject, let him reject.'
translations.an4.34:3: Of all things conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the best—that is, the crushing of vanity, the removal of thirst, the uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the round, the ending of craving, dispassion, cessation, extinguishment. Those who are confident in the teaching of dispassion are confident in the best. And for those confident in the best, the result is the best.
translations.an4.35:6: He understood the release from the snare of death for all beings. He explained the true teaching for the benefit of gods and humans. When people see and hear this, many gain confidence.
translations.an4.36:2: 'Will you be a god?' 'No, brahmin, I will not be a god.' 'Will you be a gandhabba?' 'No, brahmin, I will not be a gandhabba.' 'Will you be a spirit?' 'No, brahmin, I will not be a spirit.' 'Will you be a human?' 'No, brahmin, I will not be a human.'
translations.an4.34:2: Of all conditioned things, the noble eightfold path is declared the best. Those who are confident in the noble eightfold path are confident in the best. And for those confident in the best, the result is the best.
translations.an4.34:4: Of all communities or groups, the Saṅgha of the Realized One's disciples is declared the best—that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha's disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with joined palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world. Those who are confident in the Saṅgha are confident in the best. And for those confident in the best, the result is the best. These are the four kinds of confidence in the best.
translations.an4.34:5: For those confident in the best, understanding the best teaching; for those confident in the best Buddha, unsurpassed, worthy of offerings.
translations.an4.34:7: For those who give gifts to the best, the best merit grows; the best life, beauty, fame, reputation, happiness, and strength.
translations.an4.36:4: The defilements that, if not abandoned, would make me a god—those defilements have been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are unable to arise in the future. The defilements that, if not abandoned, would make me a gandhabba … a spirit … a human—those defilements have been abandoned by me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that they are unable to arise in the future. Just as a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus, though born in the water and growing in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water, so too, brahmin, though born in the world and growing up in the world, I have overcome the world and dwell unsoiled by the world. Remember me, brahmin, as a Buddha.
translations.an4.37:3: And how does a mendicant guard the sense doors? When a mendicant sees a form with the eye, they don't grasp at signs and features. If the faculty of the eye were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would overwhelm them. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of the eye, and achieving its restraint. When they hear a sound with the ear … When they smell an odor with the nose … When they taste a flavor with the tongue … When they feel a touch with the body … When they know a mental object with the mind, they don't grasp at signs and features. If the faculty of the mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of covetousness and displeasure would overwhelm them. For this reason, they practice restraint, protecting the faculty of the mind, and achieving its restraint. That's how a mendicant guards the sense doors.
translations.an4.37:4: And how does a mendicant eat in moderation? It's when a mendicant reflects properly on the food they eat: 'Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support the holy life. In this way, I shall put an end to old feelings and not give rise to new feelings, and I will live healthy, blameless, and at ease.' That's how a mendicant eats in moderation.
translations.an4.37:5: And how is a mendicant committed to wakefulness? It's when a mendicant purifies their mind from hindrances by walking and sitting meditation during the day. In the first watch of the night, they purify their mind from hindrances by walking and sitting meditation. In the middle watch of the night, they lie down in the lion's posture on their right side, placing one foot on top of the other, mindful and aware, having focused on the perception of getting up. In the last watch of the night, they get up and purify their mind from hindrances by walking and sitting meditation. That's how a mendicant is committed to wakefulness. A mendicant who has these four qualities is incapable of decline, and has drawn near to extinguishment.
translations.an4.37:6: A mendicant grounded in ethics, restrained in the sense faculties, eating in moderation, and committed to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:7: Living like this, ardent, tireless day and night, developing skillful qualities, for the attainment of sanctuary from the yoke.
translations.an4.38:1: 'A mendicant who has rejected individual truths, whose search is over, whose bodily activities have been tranquilized, is said to be withdrawn.' And how has a mendicant rejected individual truths? It's when a mendicant has rejected, dismissed, given up, vomited, released, abandoned, and relinquished all the various individual truths of the many ascetics and brahmins, such as: 'The world is eternal' or 'The world is not eternal' or 'The world is finite' or 'The world is infinite' or 'The soul and the body are the same' or 'The soul and the body are different' or 'A Realized One exists after death' or 'A Realized One doesn't exist after death' or 'A Realized One both exists and doesn't exist after death' or 'A Realized One neither exists nor doesn't exist after death.' That's how a mendicant has rejected individual truths.
translations.an4.38:4: And how is a mendicant withdrawn? It's when a mendicant has given up the conceit 'I am', cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it's unable to arise in the future. That's how a mendicant is withdrawn. 'A mendicant who has rejected individual truths, whose search is over, whose bodily activities have been tranquilized, is said to be withdrawn.'
translations.an4.38:5: The search for sensual pleasures, the search for continued existence, together with the search for the spiritual life; clinging to truth, and the grounds for views—these are accumulated.
translations.an4.38:6: For one dispassionate toward all lust, freed by the ending of craving, searches are relinquished, and the grounds for views are uprooted.
translations.an4.52:1: Mendicants, there are these four kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. They nurture happiness and are conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. They lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. What four? It's when a noble disciple has experiential confidence in the Buddha: 'That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to train, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.' This is the first kind of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. It nurtures happiness and is conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. It leads to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an4.52:2: Furthermore, a noble disciple has experiential confidence in the teaching: 'The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—visible in this very life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.' This is the second kind of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. It nurtures happiness and is conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. It leads to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an4.52:3: Furthermore, a noble disciple has experiential confidence in the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Buddha's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs, the eight individuals. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha's disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with joined palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.' This is the third kind of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. It nurtures happiness and is conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. It leads to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an4.52:4: Furthermore, a noble disciple has the ethical conduct loved by the noble ones—unbroken, impeccable, spotless, unblemished, freeing, praised by sensible people, not mistaken, and leading to immersion. This is the fourth kind of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. It nurtures happiness and is conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. It leads to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. These are the four kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness. They nurture happiness and are conducive to heaven, ripening in happiness and leading to heaven. They lead to what is likable, desirable, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an4.52:5: One whose faith in the Realized One is settled and well grounded, whose ethical conduct is good, loved by the noble ones, praised.
translations.an4.52:6: One who has confidence in the Saṅgha, and whose view is upright; they call them 'not poor', their life is not in vain.
translations.an4.53:10: Both faithful and generous, restrained and living righteously; they are husband and wife, speaking lovingly to each other.
translations.an4.53:11: Many benefits arise, comfort is born; enemies are unhappy, when both are equal in virtue.
translations.an4.53:2: "Householders, there are these four kinds of living together. What four? A wretch lives with a wretch, a wretch lives with a goddess, a god lives with a wretch, a god lives with a goddess.
translations.an4.53:3: And how, householders, does a wretch live with a wretch? Here, householders, a husband kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in intoxicating drinks that cause heedlessness; he is immoral, of bad character, and dwells at home with a heart overcome by the stain of miserliness, abusing and reviling ascetics and brahmins. And his wife also kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in intoxicating drinks that cause heedlessness; she is immoral, of bad character, and dwells at home with a heart overcome by the stain of miserliness, abusing and reviling ascetics and brahmins. Thus, householders, a wretch lives with a wretch.
translations.an4.53:8: The husband is immoral, stingy, and abusive; the wife is virtuous, generous, and free from miserliness; that goddess lives together with a wretched husband.
translations.an4.53:9: The husband is virtuous, generous, and free from miserliness; the wife is immoral, stingy, and abusive; that wretch lives together with a godly husband.
translations.an4.5:1: "Mendicants, these four people are found in the world. What four? One who goes with the stream, one who goes against the stream, one who stands firm, and one who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry ground—a brahmin. And what, mendicants, is the person who goes with the stream? Here, mendicants, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and does bad deeds. This is called the person who goes with the stream.
translations.an4.5:2: And what, mendicants, is the person who goes against the stream? Here, mendicants, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures and does not do bad deeds. Even though it may be with pain and sorrow, weeping with a tearful face, they live the complete and pure spiritual life. This is called the person who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:3: And what, mendicants, is the person who stands firm? Here, mendicants, a certain person, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, is one of spontaneous rebirth, who will attain final Nibbāna there, not liable to return from that world. This is called the person who stands firm.
translations.an4.5:4: And what, mendicants, is the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry ground—a brahmin? Here, mendicants, a certain person, with the destruction of the taints, realizes for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it. This is called the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, and stands on dry ground—a brahmin. These, mendicants, are the four people found in the world.
translations.an4.5:5: Those people who are unrestrained in sensual pleasures, not free from lust, enjoying sensual pleasures here; again and again they go to birth and old age, overcome by craving, going with the stream.
translations.an4.5:6: Therefore the wise one here, with mindfulness established, not indulging in sensual pleasures and evil deeds; even with pain, they should abandon sensual pleasures—they call that person one who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:7: One who has abandoned the five defilements, a trainee complete, not liable to decline; having attained mastery of mind, with faculties composed, that person is truly called one who stands firm.
translations.an4.62:2: "Householder, there are these four kinds of happiness that may be achieved by a layperson enjoying sensual pleasures, from time to time, when the occasion arises. What four? The happiness of ownership, the happiness of enjoyment, the happiness of freedom from debt, and the happiness of blamelessness.
translations.an4.62:3: And what, householder, is the happiness of ownership? Here, householder, a person of good family has wealth acquired by energetic striving, gathered by the strength of their arms, earned by the sweat of their brow, righteous wealth righteously gained. Thinking, 'I have wealth acquired by energetic striving, gathered by the strength of my arms, earned by the sweat of my brow, righteous wealth righteously gained,' they experience happiness and joy. This is called the happiness of ownership.
translations.an4.62:5: And what, householder, is the happiness of freedom from debt? Here, householder, a person of good family owes no debt to anyone, whether small or great. Thinking, 'I owe no debt to anyone, whether small or great,' they experience happiness and joy. This is called the happiness of freedom from debt.
translations.an4.62:6: And what, householder, is the happiness of blamelessness? Here, householder, a noble disciple is endowed with blameless bodily action, blameless verbal action, and blameless mental action. Thinking, 'I am endowed with blameless bodily action, blameless verbal action, and blameless mental action,' they experience happiness and joy. This is called the happiness of blamelessness. These, householder, are the four kinds of happiness that may be achieved by a layperson enjoying sensual pleasures, from time to time, when the occasion arises.
translations.an4.62:7: Having known the happiness of freedom from debt, and then the further happiness of ownership; enjoying the happiness of wealth, a mortal then sees clearly with wisdom.
translations.an5.23:1: "Mendicants, there are these five corruptions of gold. Corrupted by these, gold is not pliable, workable, or radiant; it's powdery and not properly fit for working. What five? Iron, copper, tin, lead, and silver. These are the five corruptions of gold. Corrupted by these, gold is not pliable, workable, or radiant; it's powdery and not properly fit for working. But when gold is freed from these five corruptions, it's pliable, workable, and radiant; it's not powdery and is properly fit for working. Whatever kind of ornament you want to make—whether a ring, earrings, a necklace, or a golden garland—it can serve that purpose.
translations.an5.23:2: In the same way, mendicants, there are these five corruptions of the mind. Corrupted by these, the mind is not pliable, workable, or radiant; it's brittle and not properly immersed in samādhi for the ending of the defilements. What five? Sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. These are the five corruptions of the mind. Corrupted by these, the mind is not pliable, workable, or radiant; it's brittle and not properly immersed in samādhi for the ending of the defilements. But when the mind is freed from these five corruptions, it's pliable, workable, and radiant; it's not brittle and is properly immersed in samādhi for the ending of the defilements. You can turn your mind toward realizing any state that can be realized by insight, and you'll be capable of witnessing it for yourself, in every case, there being a suitable basis.
translations.an5.23:3: If they wish: 'May I wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying myself and becoming one again; appearing and disappearing; going unimpeded through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with my hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; controlling my body as far as the Brahmā realm.' They are capable of witnessing it for themselves, in every case, there being a suitable basis.
translations.an5.23:4: If they wish: 'With clairaudience that is purified and superhuman, may I hear both kinds of sounds, human and divine, whether near or far.' They are capable of witnessing it for themselves, in every case, there being a suitable basis.
translations.an5.23:5: If they wish: 'May I understand the minds of other beings and individuals, having comprehended them with my own mind. May I understand a mind with greed as a mind with greed, and a mind without greed as a mind without greed. May I understand a mind with hate as a mind with hate, and a mind without hate as a mind without hate. May I understand a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion. May I understand a contracted mind as a contracted mind, and a scattered mind as a scattered mind. May I understand an expansive mind as an expansive mind, and an unexpansive mind as an unexpansive mind. May I understand a mind that is not supreme as a mind that is not supreme, and a mind that is supreme as a mind that is supreme. May I understand a mind immersed in samādhi as a mind immersed in samādhi, and a mind not immersed in samādhi as a mind not immersed in samādhi. May I understand a freed mind as a freed mind, and an unfreed mind as an unfreed mind.' They are capable of witnessing it for themselves, in every case, there being a suitable basis.
translations.an5.25:1: "Mendicants, when right view is supported by five factors it has freedom of heart as its fruit and benefit, and freedom by wisdom as its fruit and benefit.
translations.an5.26:1: "Mendicants, there are these five opportunities for freedom. If a mendicant meditates with diligence, keenness, and commitment, their mind is freed if not freed, their defilements come to an end if they haven't ended, and they attain the supreme sanctuary from the yoke if they haven't attained it.
translations.an5.26:3: Furthermore, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a respected fellow spiritual practitioner teaches Dhamma. But the mendicant teaches others the Dhamma in detail as they learned and memorized it. As they teach others the Dhamma in detail as they learned and memorized it, they experience the meaning and the teaching in that Dhamma. Experiencing this, joy springs up. Being joyful, rapture springs up. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one feels bliss. And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi. This is the second opportunity for freedom. If a mendicant meditates with diligence, keenness, and commitment, their mind is freed if not freed, their defilements come to an end if they haven't ended, and they attain the supreme sanctuary from the yoke if they haven't attained it.
translations.an5.26:4: Furthermore, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a respected fellow spiritual practitioner teaches Dhamma, nor does the mendicant teach others. But the mendicant recites the Dhamma in detail as they learned and memorized it. As they recite the Dhamma in detail as they learned and memorized it, they experience the meaning and the teaching in that Dhamma. Experiencing this, joy springs up. Being joyful, rapture springs up. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. When the body is tranquil, one feels bliss. And when blissful, the mind becomes immersed in samādhi. This is the third opportunity for freedom. If a mendicant meditates with diligence … they attain the supreme sanctuary from the yoke if they haven't attained it.
translations.an5.26:6: Furthermore, it may be that neither the Teacher nor a respected fellow spiritual practitioner teaches the Dhamma to a mendicant, nor do they teach the Dhamma in detail to others as they learned and memorized it, nor do they recite the Dhamma in detail as they learned and memorized it, nor do they think about and consider the Dhamma in their mind, examining it with the mind as they learned and memorized it; but they have properly grasped, attended to, borne in mind, and penetrated with wisdom a certain meditation subject. In whatever way a mendicant has properly grasped, attended to, borne in mind, and penetrated with wisdom a certain meditation subject, in that way they experience the meaning and the teaching. Experiencing the meaning and the teaching, joy arises. Being joyful, rapture arises. When the mind is full of rapture, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, one feels bliss. And with bliss, the mind becomes concentrated. This is the fifth basis for liberation, where a mendicant who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, their mind that is not yet freed becomes freed, their defilements that are not yet ended come to an end, and they attain the supreme sanctuary from the yoke that they had not yet attained.
translations.an5.27:1: Mendicants, develop immeasurable concentration, being alert and mindful. When you develop immeasurable concentration, being alert and mindful, five kinds of knowledge arise personally. What five? The knowledge arises personally: 'This concentration is blissful now and results in bliss in the future.' The knowledge arises personally: 'This concentration is noble and free of worldliness.' The knowledge arises personally: 'This concentration is not cultivated by bad people.' The knowledge arises personally: 'This concentration is peaceful and sublime, gained through tranquility, having attained unification, not held in check by forceful suppression.' The knowledge arises personally: 'I mindfully enter into this concentration and mindfully emerge from it.'
translations.an5.28:1: Mendicants, I will teach you the development of the noble five-factored right concentration. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.
translations.an5.28:10: Suppose a fine chariot stood harnessed to thoroughbreds at a crossroads on level ground, with a goad ready. Then a skilled horse trainer, a charioteer, might mount it, take the reins in the left hand and the goad in the right, and drive it forward and back wherever they wish. In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated the noble five-factored right concentration in this way, they become capable of realizing anything that can be realized by direct knowledge, in each and every case, whenever there is an opportunity.
translations.an5.28:15: If they wish: 'With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, may I understand beings … according to their deeds,' they become capable of realizing it, in each and every case, whenever there is an opportunity.
translations.an5.28:7: When a mendicant has developed and cultivated the noble five-factored right concentration in this way, they become capable of realizing anything that can be realized by direct knowledge, in each and every case, whenever there is an opportunity.
translations.an5.28:9: Suppose there was a square lotus pond on level ground, with banks built up, full of water right up to the brim so a crow could drink from it. If a strong man were to open the bank on any side, would water pour out?
translations.an5.2:1: Mendicants, there are these five powers of a trainee. What five? The power of faith, the power of conscience, the power of prudence, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom.
translations.an5.2:2: And what is the power of faith? It's when a noble disciple has faith in the Realized One's awakening: 'That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to train, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.' This is called the power of faith.
translations.an5.2:3: And what is the power of conscience? It's when a noble disciple has a conscience. They're conscientious about bad conduct by body, speech, and mind, and conscientious about acquiring bad, unskillful qualities. This is called the power of conscience.
translations.an5.2:4: And what is the power of prudence? It's when a noble disciple is prudent. They're prudent about bad conduct by body, speech, and mind, and prudent about acquiring bad, unskillful qualities. This is called the power of prudence.
translations.an5.2:5: And what is the power of energy? It's when a noble disciple lives with energy roused up for giving up unskillful qualities and gaining skillful qualities. They're strong, staunchly vigorous, not slacking off when it comes to skillful qualities. This is called the power of energy.
translations.an5.2:6: And what is the power of wisdom? It's when a noble disciple is wise. They have the wisdom of arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete ending of suffering. This is called the power of wisdom. These are the five powers of a trainee.
translations.an5.30:3: 'Sir, may the Blessed One please accept! May the Holy One please accept! Now is the time for the Blessed One to accept. Wherever the Buddha now goes, the brahmins and householders of town and country incline the same way. Just as, sir, when the rain pours down in fat drops, the water flows downhill; so too, sir, wherever the Buddha now goes, the brahmins and householders of town and country incline the same way. Why is that? Because, sir, such is the Blessed One's ethical conduct and wisdom.'
translations.an5.31:10: So too, a faithful person accomplished in ethical conduct outshines all the stingy people in the world through generosity.
translations.an5.31:11: Just as a cloud, thundering, wreathed in lightning, with a hundred peaks, fills both high and low ground, pouring down upon the earth;
translations.an5.31:12: so a wise disciple of the fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in vision, surpasses the stingy in five respects.
translations.an5.31:2: 'Sir, suppose two of the Buddha's disciples were equal in faith, ethical conduct, and wisdom—but one was a giver and one was not. When their body breaks up, after death, they would be reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm. When they have become gods, would there be any distinction or difference between them?'
translations.an5.31:3: 'There would be, Sumanā,' said the Buddha. 'The one who was a giver, when they have become a god, surpasses the non-giver in five respects: divine lifespan, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine glory, and divine authority. The one who was a giver, when they have become a god, surpasses the non-giver in these five respects.'
translations.an5.31:4: 'But sir, if they pass away from there and come back to this state of existence, when they have become human, would there be any distinction or difference between them?' 'There would be, Sumanā,' said the Buddha. 'The one who was a giver, when they have become human, surpasses the non-giver in five respects: human lifespan, human beauty, human happiness, human glory, and human authority. The one who was a giver, when they have become human, surpasses the non-giver in these five respects.'
translations.an5.31:5: 'But sir, if they both go forth from the lay life to homelessness, when they have gone forth, would there be any distinction or difference between them?' 'There would be, Sumanā,' said the Buddha. 'The one who was a giver, when they have gone forth, surpasses the non-giver in five respects: they mostly use robes that were requested, rarely those that were not; they mostly use almsfood that was requested, rarely that which was not; they mostly use lodgings that were requested, rarely those that were not; they mostly use medicines and supplies for the sick that were requested, rarely those that were not. And the spiritual companions they live with mostly treat them agreeably by body, speech, and mind, rarely disagreeably; and mostly give them agreeable gifts, rarely disagreeable ones. The one who was a giver, when they have gone forth, surpasses the non-giver in these five respects.'
translations.an5.31:6: 'But sir, if they both attain perfection, when they have attained perfection, would there be any distinction or difference between them?' 'In that case, I say there is no difference at all, that is, comparing one liberation with another.'
translations.an5.31:9: 'Just as the stainless moon, traveling through the sky, outshines all the stars in the world with its radiance;
translations.an5.34:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then General Sīha went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him: 'Sir, is it possible to point out a fruit of giving that's visible in the present life?'
translations.an5.34:2: 'It is possible, Sīha,' said the Buddha. 'A giver, a donor, is dear and beloved by many people. This is a fruit of giving that's visible in the present life.'
translations.an5.34:8: A giver is loved, and many associate with them. They get a good reputation and their fame grows. An unselfish person enters an assembly bold and confident.
translations.an5.34:9: Therefore, wise people give gifts, having removed the stain of stinginess, seeking happiness. Established for a long time in the triple heaven, they rejoice in the company of the gods.
translations.an5.36:2: The wise, generous, and free from stinginess give at the right time. A timely gift among the noble ones, who are upright and poised,
translations.an5.36:3: given with a clear mind, is an abundant offering. Those who rejoice in it or assist in the giving—their offering is not diminished; they too share in the merit.
translations.an5.41:4: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired through effort and energy, gathered by the strength of their arms, earned by the sweat of their brow, righteous wealth righteously gained, makes five offerings: offerings to relatives, offerings to guests, offerings to the departed, offerings to the king, and offerings to deities. This is the fourth reason for acquiring wealth.
translations.an5.41:5: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired through effort and energy, gathered by the strength of their arms, earned by the sweat of their brow, righteous wealth righteously gained, establishes an uplifting religious donation for those ascetics and brahmins who refrain from intoxication and negligence, who are established in patience and gentleness, who tame themselves, calm themselves, and bring themselves to final extinguishment—a donation leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, conducive to heaven. This is the fifth reason for acquiring wealth. These, householder, are the five reasons for acquiring wealth.
translations.an5.41:6: If, householder, the wealth of a noble disciple who uses wealth for these five reasons comes to an end, they think: 'I have used my wealth for the proper reasons, and my wealth has come to an end.' Thus they have no regret. If, householder, the wealth of a noble disciple who uses wealth for these five reasons increases, they think: 'I have used my wealth for the proper reasons, and my wealth has increased.' Thus they have no regret in either case.
translations.an5.41:8: Whatever purpose a wise person living at home would wish for wealth, that purpose has been achieved by me. What I have done brings no regret.
translations.an5.43:4: Householder, it is not fitting for a noble disciple who desires long life to pray for long life or to delight in it or to do things for the sake of long life. A noble disciple who desires long life should practice the way that leads to long life. For when they practice the way that leads to long life, it leads to the attainment of long life. They gain long life, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:5: Householder, it is not fitting for a noble disciple who desires beauty to pray for beauty or to delight in it or to do things for the sake of beauty. A noble disciple who desires beauty should practice the way that leads to beauty. For when they practice the way that leads to beauty, it leads to the attainment of beauty. They gain beauty, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:6: Householder, it is not fitting for a noble disciple who desires happiness to pray for happiness or to delight in it or to do things for the sake of happiness. A noble disciple who desires happiness should practice the way that leads to happiness. For when they practice the way that leads to happiness, it leads to the attainment of happiness. They gain happiness, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.38:3: With branches, leaves, and fruit, a great tree with a trunk; with roots and bearing fruit, it is a refuge for birds.
translations.an5.38:4: In that delightful place, the birds resort to it; those needing shade go to the shade, those wanting fruit eat the fruit.
translations.an5.41:7: My wealth has been enjoyed, my dependents supported, I have overcome calamities; I have given lofty offerings, and made the five oblations; I have served the virtuous ones, the restrained ones living the spiritual life.
translations.an5.38:6: Free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion, without defilements; fields of merit in the world, they resort to such a person.
translations.an5.38:5: So too, a person of faith, accomplished in virtue, humble in conduct, not stubborn, gentle, amiable, and soft.
translations.an5.41:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. To the householder Anāthapiṇḍika sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this: "Householder, there are these five reasons for acquiring wealth. What five? Here, householder, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired by energetic striving, gathered by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous wealth righteously gained, makes himself happy and pleased and properly maintains happiness; makes his mother and father happy and pleased and properly maintains their happiness; makes his children, wife, slaves, workers, and servants happy and pleased and properly maintains their happiness. This is the first reason for acquiring wealth.
translations.an5.37:2: The wise one who gives life, gives strength, gives beauty, gives eloquence; the intelligent one who gives happiness, attains happiness.
translations.an5.38:2: Just as, bhikkhus, a great banyan tree on good ground at a crossroads is a refuge for birds all around; so too, bhikkhus, a faithful son of good family is a refuge for many people—for bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, and laywomen.
translations.an5.43:7: A noble disciple who desires fame should not pray or hope for it, or expect it to come to them. A noble disciple who desires fame should practice the way that leads to fame. For when they practice the way that leads to fame, it leads to gaining fame. They gain fame, both divine and human.
translations.an5.43:9: One who desires long life, beauty, fame, reputation, heaven, high birth, and ever greater pleasures,
translations.an5.49:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side.
translations.an5.49:2: Now at that time Queen Mallikā had passed away. Then a man went to King Pasenadi and whispered in his ear: 'Your Majesty, Queen Mallikā has passed away.' When this was said, King Pasenadi sat there miserable, sad, with his shoulders drooping, head down, dejected, unable to speak.
translations.an5.51:3: It is impossible for a mendicant who has not given up these five hindrances—obstructions that overwhelm the mind and weaken wisdom—to know what is for their own good, or the good of another, or the good of both, or to realize any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, with their weak and feeble wisdom. Suppose there was a mountain river, flowing far, swift, carrying all before it. And a man were to open channels on both sides. Then the current in the middle of the river would be dispersed, scattered, and dissipated. It would no longer flow far or swift, nor carry all before it. In the same way, it is impossible for a mendicant who has not given up these five hindrances—obstructions that overwhelm the mind and weaken wisdom—to know what is for their own good, or the good of another, or the good of both, or to realize any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, with their weak and feeble wisdom.
translations.an5.56:1: Then a certain mendicant went to his own preceptor and said: 'Sir, my body feels as if it's drugged. I'm disorientated, the teachings don't spring to mind, and dullness and drowsiness fill my mind. I'm dissatisfied with the spiritual life, and I have doubts about the teachings.'
translations.an5.57:15: I have overcome all Māras, seeing renunciation as safety; I had enthusiasm, seeing nibbāna.
translations.an5.57:7: That noble disciple reflects thus: 'I am not the only one who is subject to old age, who has not gone beyond old age. For as far as there is coming and going, passing away and rebirth of beings, all beings are subject to old age, have not gone beyond old age.' When they frequently review this topic, the path is generated. They cultivate, develop, and make much of that path. As they cultivate, develop, and make much of that path, the fetters are completely abandoned and the underlying tendencies come to an end.
translations.an5.57:11: 'I am not the only one who owns my deeds, heir to my deeds, born of my deeds, related to my deeds, supported by my deeds; whatever deed I do, whether good or bad, I will be its heir. For as far as there is coming and going, passing away and rebirth of beings, all beings own their deeds, are heirs to their deeds, born of their deeds, related to their deeds, supported by their deeds; whatever deed they do, whether good or bad, they will be its heirs.' When they frequently review this topic, the path is generated. They cultivate, develop, and make much of that path. As they cultivate, develop, and make much of that path, the fetters are completely abandoned and the underlying tendencies come to an end.
translations.an5.57:10: 'It is not only for me that there is separation and parting from all who are dear and beloved. For as far as there is coming and going, passing away and rebirth of beings, for all beings there is separation and parting from all who are dear and beloved.' When they frequently review this topic, the path is generated. They cultivate, develop, and make much of that path. As they cultivate, develop, and make much of that path, the fetters are completely abandoned and the underlying tendencies come to an end.
translations.an5.57:8: 'I am not the only one who is subject to illness, who has not gone beyond illness. For as far as there is coming and going, passing away and rebirth of beings, all beings are subject to illness, have not gone beyond illness.' When they frequently review this topic, the path is generated. They cultivate, develop, and make much of that path. As they cultivate, develop, and make much of that path, the fetters are completely abandoned and the underlying tendencies come to an end.
translations.an5.56:4: Then that monk, having been advised by the Buddha with this advice, got up from his seat, bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him keeping him on his right, and departed. Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, that monk soon realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, that supreme goal of the spiritual life for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having entered upon it, he dwelt in it. He understood: 'Rebirth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' And that monk became one of the arahants.
translations.an8.14:3: Furthermore, take a bad horse that, when told 'Go!', being goaded and urged by the charioteer, leaps back, strikes the yoke-pole, and breaks the triple bar. There is such a bad horse. This is the second fault of horses.
translations.an8.14:4: Furthermore, take a bad horse that, when told 'Go!', being goaded and urged by the charioteer, throws its leg over the chariot-pole and tramples on the chariot-pole itself. There is such a bad horse. This is the third fault of horses.
translations.an8.14:5: Furthermore, take a bad horse that, when told 'Go!', being goaded and urged by the charioteer, takes the wrong path and makes the chariot swerve off course. There is such a bad horse. This is the fourth fault of horses.
translations.an8.14:6: Furthermore, take a bad horse that, when told 'Go!', being goaded and urged by the charioteer, rears up, lifting its front body and front legs. There is such a bad horse. This is the fifth fault of horses.
translations.an8.14:7: Furthermore, take a bad horse that, when told 'Go!', being goaded and urged by the charioteer, ignores the charioteer, ignores the goad, crushes the bit with its teeth, and goes wherever it wants. There is such a bad horse. This is the sixth fault of horses.
translations.an8.14:8: Furthermore, take a bad horse that, when told 'Go!', being goaded and urged by the charioteer, neither goes forward nor backward, but stands right there like a post. There is such a bad horse. This is the seventh fault of horses.
translations.an8.14:9: Furthermore, take a bad horse that, when told 'Go!', being goaded and urged by the charioteer, draws its front legs together and its back legs together, and squats down right there on all four legs. There is such a bad horse. This is the eighth fault of horses. These are the eight bad horses and eight faults of horses.
translations.an8.22:10: Sir, if I should die before the Buddha, it would not be surprising if the Buddha were to declare of me: 'There is no fetter bound by which the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma would come back to this world.' This is the eighth amazing and wonderful quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:11: These are the eight amazing and wonderful qualities found in me. But I do not know which eight amazing and wonderful qualities the Buddha declared me to possess.
translations.an8.22:12: Then that monk, having received almsfood at the residence of the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and departed. Then that monk, after his meal, on returning from his almsround, approached the Buddha, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that monk reported to the Buddha the entire conversation he had with the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma.
translations.an8.22:2: Then a certain monk robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma. He sat down on the seat spread out. Then the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma approached that monk, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. The monk said to him: 'Householder, you have been declared by the Buddha as possessing eight amazing and wonderful qualities. What are these eight amazing and wonderful qualities that you possess, as declared by the Buddha?'
translations.an8.22:3: 'Sir, I don't know which eight amazing and wonderful qualities the Buddha declared me to possess. However, sir, I do have eight amazing and wonderful qualities. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, householder,' that monk replied to the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma. The householder Ugga of Hatthigāma said: 'Sir, when I was wandering in the Nāga Grove, I first saw the Buddha from afar. As soon as I saw the Buddha, my mind became confident and my intoxication with liquor was abandoned. This is the first amazing and wonderful quality I possess.
translations.an8.22:4: With a confident mind, I attended upon the Buddha. The Buddha gave me a progressive talk—a talk on giving, a talk on ethics, a talk on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation. When the Buddha knew that my mind was ready, softened, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, he explained the teaching unique to the Buddhas: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Just as a clean cloth free from stains would properly absorb dye, so too, while sitting in that very seat, the stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma arose in me: 'Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.' Having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, understood the Dhamma, plunged into the Dhamma, having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having gained confidence, being independent of others in the Teacher's dispensation, right there I went for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and undertook the five training rules with celibacy as the fifth. This is the second amazing and wonderful quality I possess.
translations.an8.22:5: Sir, I had four young wives. I approached them and said: 'Sisters, I have undertaken the five training rules with celibacy as the fifth. Whoever wishes may enjoy the wealth here and make merit, or may return to her own family. Or if you prefer another man, to whom shall I give you?' When I said this, my eldest wife said to me: 'Dear son, give me to such-and-such a man.' Then I summoned that man, and taking my wife with my left hand and a ceremonial water vessel with my right hand, I gave her to that man. Yet even while giving away my young wife, I am not aware of any change in my mind. This is the third amazing and wonderful quality I possess.
translations.an8.22:6: Sir, there is wealth in my family, and it is shared without reservation with those who are virtuous and of good character. This is the fourth amazing and wonderful quality I possess.
translations.an8.22:7: When I attend upon a monk, I attend respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma, I listen respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, I teach him the Dhamma. This is the fifth amazing and wonderful quality I possess.
translations.an8.22:8: It is no wonder that when the Saṅgha is invited, deities approach me and inform me: 'This monk is liberated both ways, this one is liberated by wisdom, this one is a body-witness, this one has attained right view, this one is liberated by faith, this one is a Dhamma-follower, this one is a faith-follower, this one is virtuous and of good character, this one is immoral and of bad character.' Yet when I serve the Saṅgha, I am not aware of generating such a thought: 'I will give less to this one, more to that one.' Rather, I give with an impartial mind. This is the sixth amazing and wonderful quality I possess.
translations.an8.22:9: It is no wonder that deities approach me and say: 'Householder, the Dhamma is well expounded by the Buddha.' When they say this, I reply to those deities: 'Whether or not you say so, the Dhamma is indeed well expounded by the Buddha.' Yet I am not aware of any elation of mind on that account, thinking: 'Deities approach me, and I converse with deities.' This is the seventh amazing and wonderful quality I possess.
translations.an8.23:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava shrine. There the Buddha addressed the monks: 'Monks, remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as possessing seven amazing and wonderful qualities. What seven? Monks, Hatthaka of Āḷavī has faith; Hatthaka of Āḷavī has virtue; Hatthaka of Āḷavī has a sense of shame; Hatthaka of Āḷavī has fear of wrongdoing; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is learned; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is generous; Hatthaka of Āḷavī is wise. Remember Hatthaka of Āḷavī as possessing these seven amazing and wonderful qualities.' This is what the Buddha said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.an8.23:3: 'You, friend, have been declared by the Blessed One to possess seven wonderful and marvelous qualities. What seven? "The lay follower Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful, mendicants; virtuous … has a sense of shame … has a sense of conscience … is learned … is generous … is wise, mendicants, is the lay follower Hatthaka of Āḷavī." You, friend, have been declared by the Blessed One to possess these seven wonderful and marvelous qualities.' 'But sir, I hope there was no householder dressed in white present?' 'No, friend, there was no householder dressed in white present.' 'Good, sir, that no householder dressed in white was present.'
translations.an8.24:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava shrine. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, accompanied by about five hundred lay followers, went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to Hatthaka of Āḷavī as he sat to one side: 'You have a large assembly, Hatthaka. How do you bring together this large assembly?' 'Sir, I bring together this large assembly by means of the four ways of being inclusive taught by the Blessed One. When I know that someone should be brought together by giving, I bring them together by giving. When I know that someone should be brought together by kind speech, I bring them together by kind speech. When I know that someone should be brought together by beneficial conduct, I bring them together by beneficial conduct. When I know that someone should be brought together by impartiality, I bring them together by impartiality. And there is wealth in my family, sir. They don't think they should listen to someone poor.' 'Good, good, Hatthaka! This is the right way to bring together a large assembly. All those in the past who brought together a large assembly did so by means of these same four ways of being inclusive. All those in the future who will bring together a large assembly will do so by means of these same four ways of being inclusive. All those at present who bring together a large assembly do so by means of these same four ways of being inclusive.'
translations.an8.26:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha in Jīvaka's mango grove. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: 'Sir, to what extent is one a lay follower?' 'When, Jīvaka, one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha—to that extent one is a lay follower.'
translations.an8.26:2: 'But sir, to what extent is a lay follower virtuous?' 'When, Jīvaka, a lay follower abstains from killing living beings … abstains from intoxicating drinks and drugs that cause heedlessness—to that extent a lay follower is virtuous.'
translations.an8.28:5: Furthermore, sir, a mendicant with defilements ended has developed and well developed the four establishments of mindfulness. That a mendicant with defilements ended has developed and well developed the four establishments of mindfulness—this too is a strength of a mendicant with defilements ended, relying on which they claim the ending of defilements: 'My defilements are ended.'
translations.an8.28:6: Furthermore, sir, a mendicant with defilements ended has developed and well developed the four bases of psychic power … the five faculties … the seven factors of awakening … the noble eightfold path. That a mendicant with defilements ended has developed and well developed the noble eightfold path—this too is a strength of a mendicant with defilements ended, relying on which they claim the ending of defilements: 'My defilements are ended.'
translations.an8.2:1: 'Mendicants, there are eight causes and conditions that lead to acquiring the wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life, and to its increase, growth, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired. What eight? Here, a mendicant lives in dependence on the Teacher or on a fellow practitioner in a teacher's role, toward whom they have established a keen sense of conscience and moral shame, as well as love and respect. This is the first cause and condition that leads to acquiring the wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life, and to its increase, growth, development, and fulfillment once it has been acquired.
translations.an8.2:11: "And that venerable, having heard the Dhamma, achieves seclusion in two ways—seclusion of body and seclusion of mind. Surely this venerable knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen." This quality too leads to endearment, respect, development, harmony, and unity.
translations.an8.2:15: "And when that venerable has gone to the Saṅgha, they do not engage in various kinds of pointless talk. Either they speak on Dhamma themselves, or they invite another to do so, or they respect noble silence. Surely this venerable knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen." This quality too leads to endearment, respect, development, harmony, and unity.
translations.an8.2:2: Living in dependence on that teacher, or on a fellow spiritual practitioner in a respected position, towards whom they have established keen conscience and prudence, as well as affection and respect, they approach them from time to time and ask questions: 'Sir, what does this mean? What is the meaning of this?' Those venerables reveal what was hidden, clarify what was unclear, and dispel doubt regarding the many teachings that give rise to doubt. This, mendicants, is the second cause and condition that leads to gaining wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life that has not been gained, or to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been gained.
translations.an8.2:4: They are virtuous, living restrained by the monastic code, accomplished in conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and undertaking the training rules. This, mendicants, is the fourth cause and condition that leads to gaining wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life that has not been gained, or to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been gained.
translations.an8.2:5: They are learned, remembering and accumulating what they have learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual life that is entirely complete and pure—they have learned many such teachings, retained them, recited them verbally, investigated them with the mind, and penetrated them well with right view. This, mendicants, is the fifth cause and condition that leads to gaining wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life that has not been gained, or to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been gained.
translations.an8.2:6: They live with energy aroused for abandoning unskillful qualities and gaining skillful qualities, being strong, firmly striving, not neglecting their duty regarding skillful qualities. This, mendicants, is the sixth cause and condition that leads to gaining wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life that has not been gained, or to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been gained.
translations.an8.2:7: When in the Sangha, they do not engage in various kinds of pointless talk. Either they speak the Dhamma themselves, or they invite others to speak, or they do not disregard noble silence. This, mendicants, is the seventh cause and condition that leads to gaining wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life that has not been gained, or to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been gained.
translations.an8.2:8: They dwell contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates of clinging: 'Such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling, such is the arising of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling; such is perception … such are formations … such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.' This, mendicants, is the eighth cause and condition that leads to gaining wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life that has not been gained, or to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom that has been gained.
translations.an8.2:9: Their fellow spiritual practitioners esteem them thus: 'This venerable one lives in dependence on the teacher, or on a fellow spiritual practitioner in a respected position, towards whom they have established keen conscience and prudence, as well as affection and respect. Surely this venerable one knows what they know and sees what they see.' This quality leads to being loved and respected, to development, to harmony, and to unity.
translations.an8.30:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Bhaggas near Suṁsumāragira, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā's Grove. Now at that time Venerable Anuruddha was staying among the Cetīs in the Eastern Bamboo Park. Then, while Venerable Anuruddha was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: 'This Dhamma is for one of few wishes, not for one of many wishes; this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent; this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company; this Dhamma is for one with aroused energy, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma is for one with established mindfulness, not for one who is unmindful; this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated; this Dhamma is for one with wisdom, not for one who is unwise.'
translations.an8.30:10: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great person, and you gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these four jhānas—the higher mental states that are pleasant abidings in this very life—then, Anuruddha, just as a householder or householder's son might have a gabled house, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and shutters closed; so too will a dwelling at the root of a tree appear to you, as you live content, delighting, untroubled, dwelling at ease, and heading for nibbāna.
translations.an8.30:11: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great person, and you gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these four jhānas—the higher mental states that are pleasant abidings in this very life—then, Anuruddha, just as a householder or householder's son might have a couch spread with long-fleeced covers, white woolen covers, embroidered covers, with an excellent antelope-hide spread, with a canopy above and red cushions at both ends; so too will a bed of grass appear to you, as you live content, delighting, untroubled, dwelling at ease, and heading for nibbāna.
translations.an8.30:12: When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great person, and you gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these four jhānas—the higher mental states that are pleasant abidings in this very life—then, Anuruddha, just as a householder or householder's son might have various medicines, such as ghee, butter, oil, honey, and molasses; so too will fermented urine as medicine appear to you, as you live content, delighting, untroubled, dwelling at ease, and heading for nibbāna. Therefore, Anuruddha, you should spend the coming rains residence right here among the Cetīs in the Eastern Bamboo Park.' 'Yes, Bhante,' Venerable Anuruddha replied to the Buddha.
translations.an8.30:13: Then the Buddha, having advised Venerable Anuruddha with this instruction—just as a strong man might extend a bent arm or bend an extended arm—vanished from the Eastern Bamboo Park among the Cetis and appeared at Bhesakaḷā's Grove in the deer park at Crocodile Hill among the Bhaggans. The Buddha sat down on the prepared seat. Seated, the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants, I will teach you the eight thoughts of a great man. Listen to that… And what, mendicants, are the eight thoughts of a great man? This teaching is for one of few wishes, not for one of many wishes. This teaching is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent. This teaching is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company. This teaching is for one of aroused energy, not for one who is lazy. This teaching is for one with established mindfulness, not for one who is unmindful. This teaching is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated. This teaching is for one with wisdom, not for one of poor wisdom. This teaching is for one who delights in non-proliferation and enjoys non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation and enjoys proliferation.'
translations.an8.30:23: 'Knowing my thought, the Teacher unsurpassed in the world approached me by psychic power with a mind-made body.'
translations.an8.30:24: 'According to my thought, he taught even more than that. The Buddha who delights in non-proliferation taught non-proliferation.'
translations.an8.30:7: 'When, Anuruddha, you think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, whenever you wish, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and sorrow, you will enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity.'
translations.an8.39:1: 'Mendicants, there are these eight kinds of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness, that nurture happiness, are conducive to heaven, ripen in happiness, and lead to heaven; they lead to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. What eight? Here, mendicants, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Buddha. This, mendicants, is the first kind of overflowing merit, overflowing goodness, that nurtures happiness, is conducive to heaven, ripens in happiness, and leads to heaven; it leads to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.'
translations.an8.39:2: 'Furthermore, mendicants, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Dhamma. This, mendicants, is the second kind of overflowing merit… leads to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.'
translations.an8.30:4: When you think these eight thoughts of a great man, Anuruddha, then you will, whenever you want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, and the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
translations.an8.30:5: When you think these eight thoughts of a great man, Anuruddha, then you will, whenever you want, with the stilling of thought and examination, enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
translations.an8.30:6: When you think these eight thoughts of a great man, Anuruddha, then you will, whenever you want, with the fading away of rapture, dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; you will enter and dwell in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'One who is equanimous and mindful dwells happily.'
translations.an8.39:3: Furthermore, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. This is the third overflowing of merit, overflowing of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant. These five gifts are great gifts, known as original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, and will not be adulterated, not scorned by wise ascetics and brahmins. What five? Here, a noble disciple, having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings. By abstaining from killing living beings, the noble disciple gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from affliction. Having given to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from affliction, one becomes a partaker of immeasurable freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from affliction. This is the first gift that is a great gift, known as original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, and will not be adulterated, not scorned by wise ascetics and brahmins. This is the fourth overflowing of merit, overflowing of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an8.39:7: having abandoned intoxicating drinks and drugs that cause negligence, abstains from intoxicating drinks and drugs that cause negligence. By abstaining from intoxicating drinks and drugs that cause negligence, the noble disciple gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from affliction. Having given to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from affliction, one becomes a partaker of immeasurable freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from affliction. This is the fifth gift that is a great gift, known as original, long-standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated, not being adulterated, and will not be adulterated, not scorned by wise ascetics and brahmins. This is the eighth overflowing of merit, overflowing of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, leading to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
translations.an8.40:1: Killing living beings, mendicants, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The very lightest result of killing living beings is that, when one becomes a human being, it leads to a short lifespan.
translations.an8.40:2: Taking what is not given, mendicants, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The very lightest result of taking what is not given is that, when one becomes a human being, it leads to loss of wealth.
translations.an8.40:3: Sexual misconduct, mendicants, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The very lightest result of sexual misconduct is that, when one becomes a human being, it leads to rivalry and hostility.
translations.an8.40:4: False speech, mendicants, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The very lightest result of false speech is that, when one becomes a human being, it leads to being falsely accused.
translations.an8.40:5: Divisive speech, mendicants, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The very lightest result of divisive speech is that, when one becomes a human being, it leads to breaking up with friends.
translations.an8.40:6: Harsh speech, mendicants, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The very lightest result of harsh speech is that, when one becomes a human being, it leads to hearing unpleasant sounds.
translations.an8.40:7: Idle chatter, mendicants, when practiced, developed, and cultivated, leads to hell, the animal realm, or the ghost realm. The very lightest result of idle chatter is that, when one becomes a human being, it leads to one's words not being heeded.
translations.an8.6:2: For an unlearned ordinary person, mendicants, there arise gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. For a learned noble disciple too, there arise gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. What, mendicants, is the difference, the distinction, the distinguishing factor between the learned noble disciple and the unlearned ordinary person?
translations.an8.6:4: Gain takes over their mind, and loss takes over their mind; fame takes over their mind, and disgrace takes over their mind; blame takes over their mind, and praise takes over their mind; pleasure takes over their mind, and pain takes over their mind. They approve of gain that has arisen and resent loss; they approve of fame that has arisen and resent disgrace; they approve of praise that has arisen and resent blame; they approve of pleasure that has arisen and resent pain. Being thus caught up in approval and resentment, they are not freed from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. They are not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.an8.6:7: Gain and loss, fame and disgrace, blame and praise, pleasure and pain— these things among humans are impermanent, transient, subject to change.
translations.an8.6:8: Knowing these, the wise and mindful one observes that they are subject to change. Desirable things do not disturb the mind, nor does one become repelled by the undesirable.
translations.an8.7:2: What eight? Overcome and overwhelmed by gain, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, remaining for an eon, irredeemable. By loss … by fame … by disgrace … by honor … by dishonor … by wicked desires … Overcome and overwhelmed by bad friendship, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, remaining for an eon, irredeemable. Overcome and overwhelmed by these eight bad qualities, Devadatta is going to a place of loss, to hell, remaining for an eon, irredeemable.
translations.an8.7:3: It's good for a mendicant to overcome gain when it arises and to live having overcome it. To overcome loss when it arises … fame … disgrace … honor … dishonor … wicked desires … It's good for a mendicant to overcome bad friendship when it arises and to live having overcome it.
translations.an8.8:6: Suppose, lord of the gods, there was a large heap of grain not far from a village or town. A large crowd of people would carry away grain from it—in baskets, in containers, in their laps, or in their cupped hands. Now, lord of the gods, if someone were to approach that large crowd and ask: 'Where did you bring this grain from?', how would that large crowd rightly answer?
translations.mn108:13: Brahmin, ten inspiring qualities have been declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Fully Awakened One. When we find these qualities in someone, we now honor, respect, esteem, and venerate them; and having honored and respected them, we live in dependence on them. What ten?
translations.mn108:14: Here, brahmin, a mendicant is virtuous, restrained in the monastic code, conducting themselves well and seeking alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, they keep the rules they've undertaken.
translations.mn108:15: They are learned, remembering and accumulating what they've learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased, describing a spiritual practice that's entirely full and pure—such teachings are learned by them, remembered, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and well comprehended theoretically.
translations.mn108:17: They get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in the present life that belong to the higher mind—when they want, without trouble or difficulty.
translations.mn108:18: They wield the many kinds of psychic power: multiplying themselves and becoming one again; appearing and disappearing; going unimpeded through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if it were water; walking on water as if it were earth; flying cross-legged through the sky like a bird; touching and stroking with the hand the sun and moon, so mighty and powerful; controlling the body as far as the Brahmā realm.
translations.mn108:19: With clairaudience that is purified and surpasses the human, they hear both kinds of sounds, human and divine, whether near or far.
translations.mn108:2: Now at that time King Ajātasattu Vedehiputta of Magadha was having Rājagaha fortified, being suspicious of King Pajjota.
translations.mn108:1: So I have heard. At one time Venerable Ānanda was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground, not long after the Buddha had become fully extinguished.
translations.mn108:20: They understand the minds of other beings and other individuals, having comprehended them with their own mind. They understand a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust,' and a mind without lust as 'a mind without lust.' They understand a mind with hate as 'a mind with hate,' and a mind without hate as 'a mind without hate.' They understand a mind with delusion as 'a mind with delusion,' and a mind without delusion as 'a mind without delusion.' They understand a contracted mind as 'a contracted mind,' and a scattered mind as 'a scattered mind.' They understand an expansive mind as 'an expansive mind,' and an unexpansive mind as 'an unexpansive mind.' They understand a surpassable mind as 'a surpassable mind,' and an unsurpassable mind as 'an unsurpassable mind.' They understand a concentrated mind as 'a concentrated mind,' and an unconcentrated mind as 'an unconcentrated mind.' They understand a liberated mind as 'a liberated mind,' and an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind.'
translations.mn108:23: With the ending of defilements, they realize for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the undefiled liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, they dwell in it. These, brahmin, are the ten inspiring qualities declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One.
