Whoever among us possesses these qualities, we now honor, respect, esteem, and venerate them; and having honored and respected them, we live in dependence on them.
translations.mn108:25: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, chief minister of Magadha, said to Venerable Ānanda: "But where is Master Ānanda dwelling now?" "I am dwelling at the Bamboo Grove now, brahmin." "But I hope, Master Ānanda, that the Bamboo Grove is pleasant, quiet, undisturbed, secluded from people, and suitable for retreat?" "Indeed, brahmin, the Bamboo Grove is pleasant, quiet, undisturbed, secluded from people, and suitable for retreat, because of guardians and protectors like yourselves." "Indeed, Master Ānanda, the Bamboo Grove is pleasant, quiet, undisturbed, secluded from people, and suitable for retreat, because of meditators like yourselves who are devoted to meditation. The masters are meditators devoted to meditation. Master Ānanda, one time that Master Gotama was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then I approached the Great Wood, the Hall with the Peaked Roof, and that Master Gotama. And there that Master Gotama spoke in many ways about meditation. That Master Gotama was a meditator devoted to meditation. And that Master Gotama praised all meditation.
translations.mn108:28: "So it seems, Master Ānanda, that Master Gotama criticized blameworthy meditation and praised praiseworthy meditation. Well now, Master Ānanda, we must go; we have many duties and much to do." "Now is the time for that, brahmin, as you see fit." Then Vassakāra the brahmin, chief minister of Magadha, having delighted and rejoiced in Venerable Ānanda's words, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn108:3: Then in the morning, Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms. Then Venerable Ānanda thought: "It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha. Why don't I go to the workshop of Gopaka Moggallāna the brahmin, to where Gopaka Moggallāna the brahmin is?"
translations.mn108:5: "Is there, Master Ānanda, even one monk who possesses in each and every way all those qualities that Master Gotama, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One, possessed?" "There is not, brahmin, even one monk who possesses in each and every way all those qualities that the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One, possessed. For, brahmin, the Blessed One was the originator of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path, the declarer of the undeclared path; he was the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path. But now his disciples dwell following the path, having subsequently attained it.
translations.mn108:7: "But is there, Master Ānanda, even one monk appointed by Master Gotama: 'This one will be your refuge after my passing,' whom you might now resort to?" "There is not, brahmin, even one monk appointed by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One: 'This one will be your refuge after my passing,' whom we might now resort to."
translations.mn108:9: "But being without a refuge, Master Ānanda, what is the cause of your unity?" "We are not without a refuge, brahmin; we have a refuge, brahmin; the Dhamma is our refuge."
translations.mn117:10: Therein, monks, right view comes first. And how does right view come first? One understands wrong intention as 'wrong intention' and right intention as 'right intention'; this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:11: And what, monks, is wrong intention? Intention of sensuality, intention of ill will, intention of harmfulness—this, monks, is wrong intention.
translations.mn117:12: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention? I say that right intention is of two kinds, bhikkhus—there is, bhikkhus, right intention that is accompanied by defilements, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions; and there is, bhikkhus, right intention that is noble, without defilements, transcendent, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:13: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention that is accompanied by defilements, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions? Intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill will, intention of non-harming: this, bhikkhus, is right intention that is accompanied by defilements, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions.
translations.mn117:14: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention that is noble, without defilements, transcendent, a factor of the path? For one with a noble mind, a mind without defilements, possessing the noble path, developing the noble path—the thinking, the thought, the intention, the mental absorption, the mental fixation, the application of mind, the verbal formation: this, bhikkhus, is right intention that is noble, without defilements, transcendent, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:15: One makes effort to abandon wrong intention and to acquire right intention: this is one's right effort. Mindfully one abandons wrong intention, mindfully one acquires and dwells in right intention: this is one's right mindfulness. Thus these three things run and circle around right intention, namely: right view, right effort, right mindfulness.
translations.mn117:16: Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong speech as wrong speech and right speech as right speech: this is one's right view.
translations.mn117:18: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? I say that right speech is of two kinds, bhikkhus—there is, bhikkhus, right speech that is accompanied by defilements, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions; and there is, bhikkhus, right speech that is noble, without defilements, transcendent, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:19: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is accompanied by defilements, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter: this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is accompanied by defilements, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions.
translations.mn117:34: Right view, mendicants, is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? For one of right view, right intention arises. For one of right intention, right speech arises. For one of right speech, right action arises. For one of right action, right livelihood arises. For one of right livelihood, right effort arises. For one of right effort, right mindfulness arises. For one of right mindfulness, right immersion arises. For one of right immersion, right knowledge arises. For one of right knowledge, right freedom arises. Thus, mendicants, the trainee possesses eight factors, while the arahant possesses ten factors. And thereby, through right knowledge, many bad, unskillful qualities that have arisen come to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn117:24: And what is right action? Right action, I say, mendicants, is of two kinds: there is right action that is accompanied by defilements, has the attributes of good deeds, and ripens in attachment; and there is right action that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:35: Right view, mendicants, is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? For one of right view, wrong view is worn away. And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong view are worn away. And because of right view, many skillful qualities come to fulfillment by development. For one of right intention, wrong intention is worn away. … For one of right speech, wrong speech is worn away. … For one of right action, wrong action is worn away. … For one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is worn away. … For one of right effort, wrong effort is worn away. … For one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is worn away. … For one of right immersion, wrong immersion is worn away. … For one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is worn away. … For one of right freedom, wrong freedom is worn away. And the many bad, unskillful qualities that arise because of wrong freedom are worn away. And because of right freedom, many skillful qualities come to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn117:31: And what is right livelihood that is accompanied by defilements, has the attributes of good deeds, and ripens in attachment? Here, mendicants, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, earns a living by right livelihood. This is right livelihood that is accompanied by defilements, has the attributes of good deeds, and ripens in attachment.
translations.mn117:22: Right view, mendicants, is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? One understands wrong action as wrong action, and right action as right action. This is one's right view.
translations.mn117:20: And what is right speech that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path? For one of noble mind, undefiled mind, who possesses the noble path and is developing the noble path, the desisting, abstaining, refraining, and abstinence from the four kinds of verbal misconduct—this is right speech that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:25: And what is right action that is accompanied by defilements, has the attributes of good deeds, and ripens in attachment? Abstaining from killing living creatures, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct—this is right action that is accompanied by defilements, has the attributes of good deeds, and ripens in attachment.
translations.mn117:30: And what is right livelihood? Right livelihood, I say, mendicants, is of two kinds: there is right livelihood that is accompanied by defilements, has the attributes of good deeds, and ripens in attachment; and there is right livelihood that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:29: And what is wrong livelihood? Deceit, flattery, hinting, belittling, and pursuing gain with gain—this is wrong livelihood.
translations.mn117:28: Right view, mendicants, is the forerunner. And how is right view the forerunner? One understands wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood, and right livelihood as right livelihood. This is one's right view.
translations.mn117:36: So, mendicants, there are twenty on the side of the wholesome, and twenty on the side of the unwholesome—the Great Forty exposition of the teaching has been rolled forth and cannot be rolled back by any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or by anyone in the world.
translations.mn117:4: In this context, mendicants, right view comes first. And how does right view come first? One understands wrong view as wrong view and right view as right view. This is their right view.
translations.mn117:5: And what is wrong view? 'There's no meaning in giving, sacrifice, or offerings. There's no fruit or result of good and bad deeds. There's no afterlife. There's no obligation to mother and father. No beings are reborn spontaneously. And there's no ascetic or brahmin who is well attained and well practiced, and who describes the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.' This is wrong view.
translations.mn117:6: And what is right view? Right view, I say, is twofold. There is right view that is accompanied by defilements, has the attributes of good deeds, and ripens in attachment. And there is right view that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:7: And what is right view that is accompanied by defilements, has the attributes of good deeds, and ripens in attachment? 'There is meaning in giving, sacrifice, and offerings. There is fruit and result of good and bad deeds. There is an afterlife. There is obligation to mother and father. There are beings reborn spontaneously. And there are ascetics and brahmins who are well attained and well practiced, and who describe the afterlife after realizing it with their own insight.' This is right view that is accompanied by defilements, has the attributes of good deeds, and ripens in attachment.
translations.mn117:8: And what is right view that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path? It is the wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the awakening factor of investigation of principles, and the path factor of right view in one of noble mind and undefiled mind, who possesses the noble path and develops the noble path. This is called right view that is noble, undefiled, transcendent, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:9: They make an effort to give up wrong view and to acquire right view: this is their right effort. Mindfully they give up wrong view and acquire and remain in right view: this is their right mindfulness. So these three things run and circle around right view, that is: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn118:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the stilt longhouse of Migāra's mother, together with many very well-known senior disciples—Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, Venerable Mahākassapa, Venerable Mahākaccāyana, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, Venerable Mahākappina, Venerable Mahācunda, Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Revata, Venerable Ānanda, and other very well-known senior disciples.
translations.mn118:15: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is very fruitful and beneficial. Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four kinds of mindfulness meditation. The four kinds of mindfulness meditation, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven awakening factors. The seven awakening factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and freedom.
translations.mn118:17: Here, a mendicant—gone to a wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—sits down cross-legged, with their body straight, and establishes mindfulness in front of them. Just mindful, they breathe in. Mindful, they breathe out.
translations.mn118:18: Breathing in long, they know: 'I breathe in long.' Breathing out long, they know: 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, they know: 'I breathe in short.' Breathing out short, they know: 'I breathe out short.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in experiencing the whole body.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out experiencing the whole body.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in stilling the body's motion.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out stilling the body's motion.'
translations.mn118:19: They practice like this: 'I will breathe in experiencing rapture.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out experiencing rapture.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in experiencing bliss.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out experiencing bliss.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in experiencing the mind's motion.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out experiencing the mind's motion.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in stilling the mind's motion.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out stilling the mind's motion.'
translations.mn118:2: Now at that time the senior mendicants were advising and instructing the junior mendicants. Some senior mendicants advised and instructed ten mendicants, some advised twenty, some advised thirty, and some advised forty. And the junior mendicants, being advised and instructed by the senior mendicants, realized a higher distinction than they had before.
translations.mn118:20: They practice like this: 'I will breathe in experiencing the mind.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out experiencing the mind.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in gladdening the mind.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out gladdening the mind.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in immersing the mind in samādhi.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out immersing the mind in samādhi.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in freeing the mind.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out freeing the mind.'
translations.mn118:21: They practice like this: 'I will breathe in observing impermanence.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out observing impermanence.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in observing fading away.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out observing fading away.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in observing cessation.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out observing cessation.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe in observing letting go.' They practice like this: 'I will breathe out observing letting go.'
translations.mn118:23: And how is mindfulness of breathing developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the four kinds of mindfulness meditation?
translations.mn118:24: Whenever a mendicant knows that they breathe in long, or knows that they breathe out long; knows that they breathe in short, or knows that they breathe out short; trains to breathe in experiencing the whole body, trains to breathe out experiencing the whole body; trains to breathe in stilling the bodily process, trains to breathe out stilling the bodily process—at that time a mendicant meditates by observing the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and aversion for the world. For I say that the in-breaths and out-breaths are one of the things included in the body. That is why at that time a mendicant meditates by observing the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and aversion for the world.
translations.mn118:25: Whenever a mendicant trains to breathe in experiencing rapture, trains to breathe out experiencing rapture; trains to breathe in experiencing bliss, trains to breathe out experiencing bliss; trains to breathe in experiencing the mental process, trains to breathe out experiencing the mental process; trains to breathe in stilling the mental process, trains to breathe out stilling the mental process—at that time a mendicant meditates by observing feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and aversion for the world. For I say that close attention to the in-breaths and out-breaths is one of the things included in feelings. That is why at that time a mendicant meditates by observing feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and aversion for the world.
translations.mn118:26: Whenever a mendicant trains to breathe in experiencing the mind, trains to breathe out experiencing the mind; trains to breathe in gladdening the mind, trains to breathe out gladdening the mind; trains to breathe in immersing the mind, trains to breathe out immersing the mind; trains to breathe in freeing the mind, trains to breathe out freeing the mind—at that time a mendicant meditates by observing the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and aversion for the world. For I do not speak of mindfulness of breathing for one who is unmindful and lacks clear comprehension. That is why at that time a mendicant meditates by observing the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and aversion for the world.
translations.mn118:27: Whenever a mendicant trains to breathe in observing impermanence, trains to breathe out observing impermanence; trains to breathe in observing fading away, trains to breathe out observing fading away; trains to breathe in observing cessation, trains to breathe out observing cessation; trains to breathe in observing letting go, trains to breathe out observing letting go—at that time a mendicant meditates by observing principles in principles, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and aversion for the world. Having seen with wisdom the giving up of longing and aversion, they look on closely with equanimity. That is why at that time a mendicant meditates by observing principles in principles, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and aversion for the world.
translations.mn118:28: Mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated in this way, fulfills the four kinds of mindfulness meditation.
translations.mn118:29: And how are the four kinds of mindfulness meditation developed and cultivated so as to fulfill the seven awakening factors?
translations.mn118:30: Whenever a mendicant meditates by observing the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and aversion for the world, at that time their mindfulness is established and unforgotten. Whenever a mendicant's mindfulness is established and unforgotten, at that time the awakening factor of mindfulness is aroused in that mendicant. At that time they develop the awakening factor of mindfulness, and the awakening factor of mindfulness reaches fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:31: Meditating in this way with mindfulness, they investigate and examine that principle with wisdom, and undertake a thorough inquiry into it. Whenever a mendicant meditating in this way with mindfulness investigates and examines that principle with wisdom, and undertakes a thorough inquiry into it, at that time the awakening factor of investigation of principles is aroused in that mendicant. At that time they develop the awakening factor of investigation of principles, and the awakening factor of investigation of principles reaches fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:33: When they investigate and examine that principle with wisdom and undertake a thorough inquiry into it, their energy is aroused without slackening. Whenever a mendicant's energy is aroused without slackening as they investigate and examine that principle with wisdom and undertake a thorough inquiry into it, at that time the awakening factor of energy is aroused in that mendicant. At that time they develop the awakening factor of energy, and the awakening factor of energy reaches fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:34: When their energy is aroused, spiritual rapture arises. Whenever spiritual rapture arises in a mendicant whose energy is aroused, at that time the awakening factor of rapture is aroused in that mendicant. At that time they develop the awakening factor of rapture, and the awakening factor of rapture reaches fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:35: When the mind is full of rapture, the body and mind become tranquil. Whenever the body and mind become tranquil in a mendicant whose mind is full of rapture, at that time the awakening factor of tranquility is aroused in that mendicant. At that time they develop the awakening factor of tranquility, and the awakening factor of tranquility reaches fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:36: They closely watch over the mind that is so immersed. At a time when a mendicant closely watches over the mind that is so immersed, the awakening factor of equanimity is aroused in them. They develop the awakening factor of equanimity, and the awakening factor of equanimity goes to fulfillment by development.
translations.mn118:40: The four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated in this way, fulfill the seven awakening factors.
translations.mn118:41: And how are the seven awakening factors developed and cultivated so as to fulfill true knowledge and liberation?
translations.mn118:6: And those senior mendicants were instructing and advising the junior mendicants even more. Some senior mendicants instructed and advised ten mendicants, some instructed and advised twenty mendicants, some instructed and advised thirty mendicants, some instructed and advised forty mendicants. And those junior mendicants, being instructed and advised by the senior mendicants, came to know successive stages of distinction.
translations.mn118:9: There are mendicants in this Saṅgha who are arahants, with defilements ended, who have lived the spiritual life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge—there are such mendicants in this Saṅgha.
translations.mn11:13: In such a teaching and training, confidence in the Teacher is said to be not rightly directed; confidence in the teaching is said to be not rightly directed; fulfillment of the precepts is said to be not rightly directed; affection and love for one's companions in the teaching is said to be not rightly directed. Why is that? Because that is how it is in a teaching and training that is badly explained, badly proclaimed, not leading out, not conducive to peace, not proclaimed by one fully awakened.
translations.mn11:14: But the Realized One, the Arahant, the Fully Awakened One, claiming to teach the full understanding of all kinds of clinging, rightly teaches the full understanding of all kinds of clinging—he teaches the full understanding of clinging to sensual pleasures, the full understanding of clinging to views, the full understanding of clinging to precepts and observances, the full understanding of clinging to a doctrine of self.
translations.mn11:15: In such a teaching and training, confidence in the Teacher is said to be rightly directed; confidence in the teaching is said to be rightly directed; fulfillment of the precepts is said to be rightly directed; affection and love for one's companions in the teaching is said to be rightly directed. Why is that? Because that is how it is in a teaching and training that is well explained, well proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, proclaimed by one fully awakened.
translations.mn11:6: There are these two views, mendicants—the view of existence and the view of non-existence. Whatever ascetics or brahmins cling to the view of existence, have adopted the view of existence, are attached to the view of existence, they are opposed to the view of non-existence. Whatever ascetics or brahmins cling to the view of non-existence, have adopted the view of non-existence, are attached to the view of non-existence, they are opposed to the view of existence.
translations.mn11:7: Whatever ascetics or brahmins do not truly understand the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these two views, they have lust, they have hatred, they have delusion, they have craving, they have clinging, they are ignorant, they favor and oppose, they delight in proliferation, they enjoy proliferation; they are not freed from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; 'they are not freed from suffering,' I say.
translations.mn11:9: There are these four kinds of clinging, mendicants. What four? Clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to precepts and observances, clinging to a doctrine of self.
translations.mn12:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling near Vesālī, outside the city in a forest grove to the west.
translations.mn12:10: Here, Sāriputta, the Realized One truly understands the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. Since the Realized One truly understands the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible, this is a power of the Realized One, relying on which the Realized One claims the bull's place, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the holy wheel.
translations.mn12:19: Furthermore, Sāriputta, the Realized One, through the destruction of the defilements, has realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the defilement-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it. Since the Realized One, through the destruction of the defilements, has realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the defilement-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it, this is a power of the Realized One, relying on which the Realized One claims the bull's place, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the holy wheel.
translations.mn12:20: These are the ten powers of a Realized One that a Realized One possesses. With these powers, the Realized One claims the bull's place, roars the lion's roar in the assemblies, and turns the holy wheel.
translations.mn12:22: These are the four kinds of self-assurance that a Realized One possesses. With these kinds of self-assurance, the Realized One claims the bull's place, roars the lion's roar in the assemblies, and turns the holy wheel. What four?
translations.mn12:23: 'Though you claim to be a fully awakened Buddha, you have not awakened to these things.' I see no reason why any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could legitimately rebuke me for this. Sāriputta, seeing no such reason, I live having attained safety, fearlessness, and self-assurance.
translations.mn12:24: 'Though you claim to have ended the defilements, these defilements have not ended.' I see no reason why any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could legitimately rebuke me for this. Sāriputta, seeing no such reason, I live having attained safety, fearlessness, and self-assurance.
translations.mn12:25: 'The things you have described as obstructive are not really obstructive for one who engages in them.' I see no reason why any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could legitimately rebuke me for this. Sāriputta, seeing no such reason, I live having attained safety, fearlessness, and self-assurance.
translations.mn12:26: 'The teaching you have taught for a certain purpose does not lead one who practices it to the complete ending of suffering.' I see no reason why any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could legitimately rebuke me for this. Sāriputta, seeing no such reason, I live having attained safety, fearlessness, and self-assurance.
translations.mn12:32: Sāriputta, there are these four kinds of reproduction. What four? Reproduction from eggs, reproduction from a womb, reproduction from moisture, and spontaneous reproduction.
translations.mn12:33: And what, Sāriputta, is reproduction from eggs? Those beings who are born by breaking out of an egg shell—this is called reproduction from eggs. And what, Sāriputta, is reproduction from a womb? Those beings who are born by breaking out of the amniotic sac—this is called reproduction from a womb. And what, Sāriputta, is reproduction from moisture? Those beings who are born in rotten fish, or in a rotten corpse, or in rotten dough, or in a cesspit, or in a sewer—this is called reproduction from moisture. And what, Sāriputta, is spontaneous reproduction? Gods, hell beings, some humans, and some beings in the lower realms—this is called spontaneous reproduction. These, Sāriputta, are the four kinds of reproduction.
translations.mn12:35: Sāriputta, there are these five destinations. What five? Hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, humans, and gods.
translations.mn12:36: I understand hell, Sāriputta, and the path and practice that leads to hell; and how one who has practiced in such a way, when the body breaks up, after death, is reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell—that too I understand. I understand the animal realm, Sāriputta, and the path and practice that leads to the animal realm; and how one who has practiced in such a way, when the body breaks up, after death, is reborn in the animal realm—that too I understand. I understand the ghost realm, Sāriputta, and the path and practice that leads to the ghost realm; and how one who has practiced in such a way, when the body breaks up, after death, is reborn in the ghost realm—that too I understand. I understand humans, Sāriputta, and the path and practice that leads to the human world; and how one who has practiced in such a way, when the body breaks up, after death, is reborn among humans—that too I understand. I understand the gods, Sāriputta, and the path and practice that leads to the world of the gods; and how one who has practiced in such a way, when the body breaks up, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world—that too I understand. I understand extinguishment, Sāriputta, and the path and practice that leads to extinguishment; and how one who has practiced in such a way, through the ending of defilements, realizes the defilement-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in this very life, having directly known and realized it for themselves—that too I understand.
translations.mn12:4: Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta is angry. And he spoke those words out of anger. Thinking to discredit me, Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta actually praises the Realized One. For it is praise of the Realized One to say: 'The teaching he has taught for a certain purpose leads one who practices it to the complete ending of suffering.'
translations.mn12:43: Sāriputta, whoever would say of me, knowing and seeing as I do: 'The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; the ascetic Gotama teaches a teaching worked out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry, produced by his own speculation'—unless they give up that speech and that mind and abandon that view, they will be deposited in hell as surely as if they had been carried there. Just as, Sāriputta, a mendicant accomplished in ethics, immersion, and wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life; so too, I say, unless they give up that speech and that mind and abandon that view, they will be deposited in hell as surely as if they had been carried there.
translations.mn12:44: Sāriputta, I recall having practiced the spiritual life with four factors. I was an ascetic—the ultimate ascetic. I was rough—the ultimate in roughness. I was scrupulous—the ultimate in scrupulousness. I was secluded—the ultimate in seclusion.
translations.mn12:46: And here, Sāriputta, was my roughness. Dirt and dust accumulated on my body over many years, forming a crust. Just as, Sāriputta, the stump of a tinduka tree accumulates dirt over many years, forming a crust, so too dirt and dust accumulated on my body over many years, forming a crust. It never occurred to me: 'Oh, let me rub this dirt off with my hand, or let others rub this dirt off with their hands.' It never occurred to me. This, Sāriputta, was my roughness.
translations.mn12:47: And here, Sāriputta, was my scrupulousness. I went forward mindfully and I went back mindfully, with compassion established even for a drop of water, thinking: 'Let me not harm the tiny creatures in the crevices of the ground.' This, Sāriputta, was my scrupulousness.
translations.mn12:49: So, Sāriputta, I would go to a cow-pen where the cattle had gone out and the cowherd had left, and there, on all fours, I would eat the dung of the young suckling calves. As long as my own urine and feces were not exhausted, I would eat my own urine and feces. This was my practice of eating great filth.
translations.mn12:5: For, Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta will not infer of me: 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.'
translations.mn12:50: Sāriputta, I would enter and dwell in a terrifying forest grove. And the terror of that terrifying forest grove was such that normally anyone who entered it without having abandoned lust would have their hair stand on end. So, Sāriputta, on those cold winter nights during the 'eight-day interval' when snow falls, I would dwell in the open at night and in the forest grove by day; in the last month of summer I would dwell in the open by day and in the forest grove at night. And, Sāriputta, this verse, never heard before, occurred to me: 'Scorched by heat and frozen too, alone in the terrifying forest, naked, sitting without fire, the sage is intent on his quest.'
translations.mn12:51: Sāriputta, I would make my bed in a charnel ground, resting on a skeleton. And cowherd boys would come up to me and spit on me, urinate on me, throw dirt on me, and poke sticks in my ears. Yet I do not recall ever generating an evil mind toward them. Such was my abiding in equanimity.
translations.mn12:52: Now, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view: 'Purification is through food.' They say: 'We live on jujube fruits.' They eat jujubes, they eat jujube powder, they drink jujube water—they consume jujubes prepared in many ways. But I recall eating just a single jujube as my food. Now, Sāriputta, you might think: 'Surely the jujube must have been large at that time.' But it should not be seen that way. The jujube then was at most the same size as now. While eating just a single jujube as my food, my body reached a state of extreme emaciation. My limbs became like the joints of vine stems or bamboo stems because of eating so little. My buttocks became like a camel's hoof because of eating so little. My spine stood out like a string of beads because of eating so little. My ribs jutted out like the jutting rafters of an old roofless barn because of eating so little. The gleam of my eyes sank deep in their sockets like the gleam of water deep in a well because of eating so little. My scalp shriveled and withered like a green bitter gourd shrivels and withers in the wind and sun because of eating so little. When I tried to touch my belly skin, I would grab my spine; when I tried to touch my spine, I would grab my belly skin, because my belly skin had stuck to my spine from eating so little. When I tried to urinate or defecate, I would fall over on my face right there from eating so little. When I tried to ease my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, the hair, rotted at its roots, would fall from my body from eating so little.
translations.mn12:56: But, Sāriputta, by that conduct, by that practice, by that performance of austerities, I did not attain any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Why was that? Because I had not attained this noble wisdom, which when attained is noble and emancipating, and leads the one who practices accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering.
translations.mn12:57: Now, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view: 'Purification is through the round of rebirths.' But, Sāriputta, it is not easy to find a realm in the round of rebirths that I have not already passed through in this long journey, except for the gods of the Pure Abodes. If I had been reborn among the gods of the Pure Abodes, I would not have returned to this world.
translations.mn12:6: For, Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta will not infer of me: 'Thus indeed the Blessed One wields the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through walls, through ramparts, through mountains, as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though it were water; he walks on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged, he travels through space like a bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful; he exercises mastery with the body as far as the Brahmā world.'
translations.mn12:60: Now, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view: 'Purification is through sacrifice.' But, Sāriputta, it is not easy to find a sacrifice that I have not already offered in this long journey, either as a king, a head-anointed noble, or as a wealthy brahmin.
translations.mn12:61: Now, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold this doctrine and view: 'Purification is through fire worship.' But, Sāriputta, it is not easy to find a fire that I have not already tended in this long journey, either as a king, a head-anointed noble, or as a wealthy brahmin.
translations.mn12:62: Now, Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: 'As long as this good person is young, youthful, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, just so long is he endowed with the highest wisdom and eloquence. But when this good person is old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, then he declines from that wisdom and eloquence.' But this should not be seen in that way, Sāriputta. I am now old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life; my age is turning eighty. Suppose, Sāriputta, I had four disciples with a lifespan of a hundred years, living for a hundred years, endowed with the highest memory, retention, perseverance, and the highest wisdom and eloquence. Just as, Sāriputta, a skilled archer, trained, practiced, and experienced, could easily shoot a light arrow across the shadow of a palm tree, so possessed of such supreme memory, such supreme retention, such supreme perseverance, and endowed with the highest wisdom and eloquence. If they were to ask me questions about the four foundations of mindfulness again and again, and I were to answer them when asked, and they were to remember my answers as answered, and they were not to ask me a second follow-up question. Apart from eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, apart from defecating and urinating, apart from dispelling sleepiness and fatigue, the Tathāgata's teaching of the Dhamma would not be exhausted, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata's words and phrases of the Dhamma would not be exhausted, the Tathāgata's inspired answers to questions would not be exhausted. Then those four disciples of mine with a lifespan of a hundred years, living for a hundred years, would die at the end of a hundred years. Even if you were to carry me about on a bed, Sāriputta, there would be no change in the Tathāgata's wisdom and eloquence.
translations.mn12:7: Surely, Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta should have inferred this about me: 'Thus the Blessed One, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, hears both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near.'
translations.mn12:8: Surely, Sāriputta, the foolish man Sunakkhatta should have inferred this about me: 'Thus the Blessed One understands the minds of other beings, other persons, having encompassed them with his own mind— he understands a mind with lust as a mind with lust, he understands a mind without lust as a mind without lust; he understands a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred, he understands a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; he understands a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, he understands a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; he understands a contracted mind as a contracted mind, he understands a distracted mind as a distracted mind; he understands an exalted mind as an exalted mind, he understands an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; he understands a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, he understands an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; he understands a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, he understands an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; he understands a liberated mind as a liberated mind, he understands an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.'
translations.mn12:9: Now, Sāriputta, there are these ten Tathāgata powers of the Tathāgata, possessing which the Tathāgata claims the place of the chief bull, roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the divine wheel. What are the ten?
translations.mn135:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.
translations.mn135:13: Here, student, some woman or man is not a giver to ascetics or brahmins of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, lodging, and lighting. Due to having performed and undertaken such action, on the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. But if on the breakup of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell, if they come to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are poor. This is the way, student, leading to poverty, namely—not being a giver to ascetics or brahmins of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, lodging, and lighting.
translations.mn135:20: Beings are owners of their actions, student, heirs of their actions, born of their actions, bound by their actions, have their actions as their refuge. It is action that distinguishes beings as inferior and superior.
translations.mn135:5: "Student, take some woman or man who kills living creatures, being violent, bloody-handed, a hardened killer, merciless to living beings. Due to undertaking such deeds, on the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. But if on the breakup of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell, if they come back to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are short-lived. This is the path leading to short life, student, namely: killing living creatures, being violent, bloody-handed, a hardened killer, merciless to living beings.
translations.mn135:6: But student, take some woman or man who, having given up killing living creatures, abstains from killing living creatures. They have laid down the rod and the sword, and live conscientiously, full of compassion, seeking the welfare of all living beings. Due to undertaking such deeds, on the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good place, a heavenly world. But if on the breakup of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a good place, a heavenly world, if they come back to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are long-lived. This is the path leading to long life, student, namely: having given up killing living creatures, abstaining from killing living creatures, having laid down the rod and the sword, living conscientiously, full of compassion, seeking the welfare of all living beings.
translations.mn13:10: If, mendicants, that gentleman's wealth is produced through such effort, striving, and exertion, they experience suffering and sorrow on account of guarding it: 'How can I prevent my wealth from being taken by kings or thieves, consumed by fire, swept away by floods, or taken by unloved heirs?' And as they guard and protect it, kings or thieves take it, fire consumes it, floods sweep it away, or unloved heirs take it. They sorrow, grieve, and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion: 'What I had is no longer mine!' This too, mendicants, is a drawback of sensual pleasures visible in this very life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, arising from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the cause.
translations.mn13:11: Furthermore, mendicants, because of sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, arising from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the cause, kings quarrel with kings, nobles with nobles, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders, mother with child, child with mother, father with child, child with father, brother with brother, brother with sister, sister with brother, and friend with friend. Having fallen into quarrels, conflicts, and disputes, they attack each other with fists, stones, sticks, and swords. They meet with death or deadly suffering. This too, mendicants, is a drawback of sensual pleasures visible in this very life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, arising from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the cause.
translations.mn13:12: Furthermore, mendicants, because of sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, arising from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the cause, having taken up sword and shield, having strapped on bow and quiver, they charge into battle massed on both sides, while arrows are flying, spears are flying, and swords are flashing. There they are struck by arrows, struck by spears, and their heads are cut off by swords. They meet with death or deadly suffering. This too, mendicants, is a drawback of sensual pleasures visible in this very life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, arising from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the cause.
translations.mn13:13: Furthermore, mendicants, because of sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, arising from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the cause, having taken up sword and shield, having strapped on bow and quiver, they charge at slippery ramparts, while arrows are flying, spears are flying, and swords are flashing. There they are struck by arrows, struck by spears, splashed with dung, crushed with weights, and their heads are cut off by swords. They meet with death or deadly suffering. This too, mendicants, is a drawback of sensual pleasures visible in this very life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, arising from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the cause.
translations.mn13:15: Furthermore, mendicants, because of sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, arising from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the cause, they conduct themselves badly by body, speech, and mind. Having conducted themselves badly by body, speech, and mind, on the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. This too, mendicants, is a drawback of sensual pleasures pertaining to the next life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, arising from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the cause.
translations.mn13:16: And what, mendicants, is the escape from sensual pleasures? The removal and abandoning of desire and lust for sensual pleasures—this is the escape from sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:17: Any ascetics or brahmins who do not truly understand the gratification of sensual pleasures as gratification, the drawback as drawback, and the escape as escape—it is impossible that they will either fully understand sensual pleasures themselves or instruct another so that they will fully understand sensual pleasures by practicing accordingly. But any ascetics or brahmins who truly understand the gratification of sensual pleasures as gratification, the drawback as drawback, and the escape as escape—it is possible that they will either fully understand sensual pleasures themselves or instruct another so that they will fully understand sensual pleasures by practicing accordingly.
translations.mn13:18: And what, mendicants, is the gratification of forms? Suppose there was a girl of the noble, brahmin, or householder class, fifteen or sixteen years old, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair. Is her beauty and radiance then at its peak? 'Yes, sir.' The pleasure and happiness that arise on account of that beauty and radiance—this is the gratification of forms.
translations.mn13:19: And what, mendicants, is the drawback of forms? Suppose that same sister were seen some time later, eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old, aged, bent double, crooked, leaning on a staff, trembling as she walks, ailing, past her prime, with broken teeth, grey hair, balding, with wrinkled skin and blotchy limbs. What do you think, mendicants? Has her former beauty and radiance vanished, and the drawback become evident?
translations.mn13:30: And what, mendicants, is the escape from forms? The removal and giving up of desire and greed for forms—this is the escape from forms.
translations.mn13:32: And what, mendicants, is the gratification of feelings? It's when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and remains in the first jhāna, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. At such a time they don't intend to hurt themselves, hurt others, or hurt both. At that time they feel a feeling that is free from hurt. I say that freedom from hurt is the highest gratification of feelings.
translations.mn13:36: And what, mendicants, is the drawback of feelings? Feelings are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. This is the drawback of feelings.
translations.mn13:37: And what, mendicants, is the escape from feelings? The removal and giving up of desire and greed for feelings—this is the escape from feelings.
translations.mn13:3: 'Reverend, the ascetic Gotama describes the complete understanding of sensual pleasures, and so do we. The ascetic Gotama describes the complete understanding of forms, and so do we. The ascetic Gotama describes the complete understanding of feelings, and so do we. What, then, is the difference, the distinction, the distinguishing feature between the ascetic Gotama and us—that is, regarding the teaching of the Dhamma or the instruction?'
translations.mn13:29: Furthermore, they might see that same sister's corpse discarded in a charnel ground—bones white like shells, bones heaped up over a year old, bones rotted and crumbled to dust. What do you think, mendicants? Has that former beauty and radiance vanished, and the drawback become evident?' 'Yes, sir.' This too is a drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:23-28: Furthermore, they might see that same sister's corpse discarded in a charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh or blood, held together by sinews; bones disconnected and scattered in every direction—here a hand bone, there a foot bone, here an ankle bone, there a shin bone, here a thigh bone, there a hip bone, here a rib bone, there a spine bone, here a shoulder bone, there a neck bone, here a jaw bone, there a tooth, here a skull. What do you think, mendicants? Has that former beauty and radiance vanished, and the drawback become evident?' 'Yes, sir.' This too is a drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:20: Furthermore, they might see that same sister sick, suffering, gravely ill, lying in her own urine and feces, having to be lifted up by some and put down by others. What do you think, mendicants? Has that former beauty and radiance vanished, and the drawback become evident?' 'Yes, sir.' This too is a drawback of forms.
translations.mn13:6: Mendicants, when wanderers of other sects speak like this, they should be asked: 'But reverend, what is the gratification, the drawback, and the escape in the case of sensual pleasures? What is the gratification, the drawback, and the escape in the case of forms? What is the gratification, the drawback, and the escape in the case of feelings?' Questioned like this, the wanderers of other sects would not be able to answer, and, moreover, would get frustrated. Why is that? Because it's not in their domain. Mendicants, I don't see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions except for the Realized One or his disciple or someone who has heard it from them.
translations.mn13:8: And what is the drawback of sensual pleasures? It's when a respectable person earns a living by means of some profession—whether computing, accounting, calculating, farming, trade, raising cattle, archery, government service, or some other craft—they must face cold and heat, being hurt by the touch of flies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and reptiles, and risking death from hunger and thirst. This is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in this very life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its source, its reason, and its cause.
translations.mn13:9: If that respectable person who works hard, strives, and makes an effort does not obtain wealth, they sorrow, grieve, and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion: 'My hard work is in vain, my effort is fruitless!' This too is a drawback of sensual pleasures apparent in this very life, a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its source, its reason, and its cause.
translations.mn140:12: 'One should not neglect wisdom, should preserve truth, should cultivate generosity, and should train only for peace'—so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:14: And what, bhikkhu, is the earth element? The earth element may be internal or external. And what is the internal earth element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung to, that is: head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach contents, feces, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is solid, solidified, and clung to—this is called the internal earth element. Now both the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply earth element. That should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Having seen it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the earth element.
translations.mn140:15: And what, bhikkhu, is the water element? The water element may be internal or external. And what is the internal water element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung to, that is: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is water, watery, and clung to—this is called the internal water element. Now both the internal water element and the external water element are simply water element. That should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Having seen it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the water element.
translations.mn140:16: And what, bhikkhu, is the fire element? The fire element may be internal or external. And what is the internal fire element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung to, that is: that by which one is warmed, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, consumed, and tasted is properly digested, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is fire, fiery, and clung to—this is called the internal fire element. Now both the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply fire element. That should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Having seen it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the fire element.
translations.mn140:17: And what, bhikkhu, is the air element? The air element may be internal or external. And what is the internal air element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung to, that is: up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, in-breath and out-breath, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is air, airy, and clung to—this is called the internal air element. Now both the internal air element and the external air element are simply air element. That should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Having seen it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the air element.
translations.mn140:18: And what, bhikkhu, is the space element? The space element may be internal or external. And what is the internal space element? Whatever internally, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, and clung to, that is: the ear holes, the nostrils, the mouth door, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, consumed, and tasted is swallowed, where it stays, and by which it passes out below, or whatever else internally, belonging to oneself, is space, spatial, hollow, hollowed out, open, opened up, not touched by flesh and blood, and clung to—this is called the internal space element. Now both the internal space element and the external space element are simply space element. That should be seen as it actually is with proper wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' Having seen it thus as it actually is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the space element and makes the mind dispassionate toward the space element.
translations.mn140:20: Then only equanimity remains, pure and bright, soft and workable and radiant. Suppose, monk, a skilled goldsmith or goldsmith's apprentice were to prepare a furnace, and having prepared the furnace, were to heat the mouth of the furnace, and having heated the mouth of the furnace, were to take gold with tongs and place it in the mouth of the furnace. From time to time they would blow on it, from time to time they would sprinkle it with water, from time to time they would just watch over it. That gold becomes well refined, well purified, cleansed, rid of dross, soft and workable and radiant, and whatever kind of ornament they wish to make from it—whether a bracelet, earrings, a necklace, or a golden garland—it serves that purpose. In the same way, monk, then only equanimity remains, pure and bright, soft and workable and radiant.
translations.mn140:23: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand: 'It is impermanent,' they understand: 'It is not clung to,' they understand: 'It is not delighted in.' If they feel a painful feeling, they understand: 'It is impermanent,' they understand: 'It is not clung to,' they understand: 'It is not delighted in.' If they feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, they understand: 'It is impermanent,' they understand: 'It is not clung to,' they understand: 'It is not delighted in.'
translations.mn140:29: 'One should not neglect wisdom, should preserve truth, should cultivate generosity, should train only for peace'—what was said was said in reference to this.
translations.mn140:3: Now at that time a clansman named Pukkusāti had gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, because of the Blessed One. He had arrived first to stay in that potter's workshop. Then the Blessed One approached Venerable Pukkusāti and said to him: 'If it's not inconvenient for you, monk, I will stay one night in the workshop.' 'The potter's workshop is spacious, friend. Let the venerable one stay as they please.'
translations.mn140:30: 'Where one stands, the currents of conceiving do not flow; and when the currents of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace'—this too was said. With reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:31: 'I am'—this is conceiving. 'I am this'—this is conceiving. 'I shall be'—this is conceiving. 'I shall not be'—this is conceiving. 'I shall be with form'—this is conceiving. 'I shall be formless'—this is conceiving. 'I shall be percipient'—this is conceiving. 'I shall be non-percipient'—this is conceiving. 'I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient'—this is conceiving. Conceiving, monk, is a disease, conceiving is a tumor, conceiving is a dart. By transcending all conceiving, monk, one is called a sage at peace. And the sage at peace, monk, is not born, does not age, does not die, is not shaken, and does not yearn. For there is nothing in them by which they would be born. Not being born, how will they age? Not aging, how will they die? Not dying, how will they be shaken? Not being shaken, for what will they yearn?
translations.mn140:32: 'Where one stands, the currents of conceiving do not flow; and when the currents of conceiving do not flow, one is called a sage at peace'—what was said was said in reference to this. Monk, remember this brief analysis of the six elements that I have given you.
translations.mn140:33: Then Venerable Pukkusāti thought: 'The Teacher has come to me! The Fortunate One has come to me! The Perfectly Enlightened One has come to me!' Rising from his seat, arranging his robe over one shoulder, and falling with his head at the Blessed One's feet, he said: 'A transgression overcame me, venerable sir, foolish, confused, and unskillful as I was, in that I presumed to address the Blessed One as "friend." May the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of restraint in the future.' 'Indeed, monk, a transgression overcame you, foolish, confused, and unskillful as you were, in that you presumed to address me as "friend." But since you see your transgression as a transgression and make amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it. For this is growth in the Noble One's discipline: that one sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint in the future.'
translations.mn140:34: 'May I receive the full ordination from the Blessed One, venerable sir?' 'But, monk, are your bowl and robes complete?' 'No, venerable sir, my bowl and robes are not complete.' 'Monk, Tathāgatas do not give full ordination to one whose bowl and robes are not complete.'
translations.mn140:35: Then Venerable Pukkusāti, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and departed to search for a bowl and robes. Then, while Venerable Pukkusāti was wandering in search of a bowl and robes, a stray cow killed him.
translations.mn140:7: 'A person has six elements, six bases of contact, eighteen mental examinations, and four foundations. Established in these, the streams of conceit do not flow; and when the streams of conceit do not flow, one is called a sage at peace. One should not neglect wisdom, should preserve truth, should cultivate generosity, and should train only for peace'—this is the summary of the analysis of the elements.
translations.mn146:12: 'I have made this simile to convey the meaning. This is the meaning here: 'The inner body of flesh,' sisters, is a term for the six internal sense bases. 'The outer skin,' sisters, is a term for the six external sense bases. 'The inner flesh, sinews, and binding,' sisters, is a term for delight and lust. 'The sharp butcher's knife,' sisters, is a term for noble wisdom—the noble wisdom that cuts through, severs, and carves away the inner defilements, fetters, and bonds.
translations.mn146:13: There are, sisters, these seven factors of awakening, through developing and cultivating which a monk, with the ending of defilements, realizes for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the defilement-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it. What seven? Here, sisters, a monk develops the awakening factor of mindfulness, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, ripening in release. He develops the awakening factor of investigation of states … He develops the awakening factor of energy … He develops the awakening factor of rapture … He develops the awakening factor of tranquility … He develops the awakening factor of concentration … He develops the awakening factor of equanimity, based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, ripening in release. These, sisters, are the seven factors of awakening, through developing and cultivating which a monk, with the ending of defilements, realizes for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the defilement-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it.
translations.mn146:14: Then Venerable Nandaka, having instructed those nuns with this instruction, dismissed them: 'Go, sisters; it is time.' Then those nuns, having delighted and rejoiced in Venerable Nandaka's words, rose from their seats, paid homage to Venerable Nandaka, and keeping him on their right, approached the Buddha. Having approached and paid homage to the Buddha, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Buddha said to those nuns: 'Go, nuns; it is time.' Then those nuns, having paid homage to the Buddha and keeping him on their right, departed.
translations.mn146:3: Now at that time the senior monks were instructing the nuns in turn. Venerable Nandaka did not wish to instruct the nuns when his turn came. Then the Buddha addressed Venerable Ānanda: 'Whose turn is it today, Ānanda, to instruct the nuns?' 'Venerable sir, everyone has taken their turn to instruct the nuns. This Venerable Nandaka does not wish to instruct the nuns when his turn comes.'
translations.mn147:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's park. Then, while the Buddha was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: 'The qualities that ripen in liberation have ripened in Rāhula. Why don't I lead Rāhula further to the ending of the defilements?' Then, in the morning, the Buddha dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on returning from the alms round, he addressed Venerable Rāhula: 'Take your sitting cloth, Rāhula; let us go to the Blind Men's Grove for the day's meditation.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' Venerable Rāhula replied to the Buddha. Taking his sitting cloth, he followed behind the Buddha.
translations.mn148:34: Dependent on the eye and sights, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Contact is a condition for the arising of a feeling that is pleasant, painful, or neutral. When touched by a pleasant feeling, one doesn't approve, welcome, or keep clinging to it. The underlying tendency to greed does not underlie that. When touched by a painful feeling, one doesn't sorrow, tire, lament, beat one's breast, or become confused. The underlying tendency to repulsion does not underlie that. When touched by a neutral feeling, one truly understands that feeling's origin, ending, gratification, drawback, and escape. The underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie that. That one, mendicants, having abandoned the underlying tendency to greed for pleasant feeling, having dispelled the underlying tendency to repulsion for painful feeling, having eradicated the underlying tendency to ignorance for neutral feeling, having abandoned ignorance and given rise to knowledge, will make an end of suffering in this very life—this is possible.
translations.mn148:40: Seeing this, mendicants, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with the eye, grows disillusioned with sights, grows disillusioned with eye-consciousness, grows disillusioned with eye-contact, grows disillusioned with feeling, grows disillusioned with craving.
translations.mn149:11: And what things should be directly known and fully understood? It should be said: 'the five aggregates of clinging,' that is, the aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of volitional formations subject to clinging, the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. These are the things that should be directly known and fully understood. And what things should be directly known and abandoned? Ignorance and craving for existence—these are the things that should be directly known and abandoned. And what things should be directly known and developed? Serenity and insight—these are the things that should be directly known and developed. And what things should be directly known and realized? Knowledge and liberation—these are the things that should be directly known and realized.
translations.mn149:8: As they live attached, tied, and deluded, focusing on gratification, the five grasping aggregates build up for them in the future. And their craving—which leads to future rebirth, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure in various things—grows. Their physical and mental troubles grow; their physical and mental torments grow; their physical and mental fevers grow. And they experience physical and mental suffering.
translations.mn148:16: And what is the practice that leads to the origin of identity? You regard the eye: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self.'
translations.mn149:3: Not knowing and seeing the eye as it really is, not knowing and seeing sights as they really are, not knowing and seeing eye consciousness as it really is, not knowing and seeing eye contact as it really is, not knowing and seeing the feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neutral—that arises conditioned by eye contact as it really is, one becomes infatuated with the eye, sights, eye consciousness, eye contact, and the feeling that arises conditioned by eye contact. As they live attached, tied, and deluded, focusing on gratification, the five grasping aggregates build up for them in the future. And their craving—which leads to future rebirth, mixed up with relishing and greed, taking pleasure in various things—grows. Their physical and mental troubles grow; their physical and mental torments grow; their physical and mental fevers grow. And they experience physical and mental suffering.
translations.mn148:3: The six interior sense fields should be understood. The six exterior sense fields should be understood. The six classes of consciousness should be understood. The six classes of contact should be understood. The six classes of feeling should be understood. The six classes of craving should be understood.
translations.mn148:22: And what is the practice that leads to the cessation of identity? You regard the eye: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'
translations.mn149:9: Truly knowing and seeing the eye, truly knowing and seeing sights, truly knowing and seeing eye-consciousness, truly knowing and seeing eye-contact, truly knowing and seeing the feeling that arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful—they don't become lustful for the eye, for sights, for eye-consciousness, for eye-contact, or for the feeling that arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither pleasant nor painful. For them, living unattached, unbound, unconfused, contemplating the drawbacks, the five grasping aggregates head toward diminishment in the future. And their craving—which leads to future rebirth, mixed up with relishing and greed, delighting in various things—is given up. Their physical and mental troubles are given up; their physical and mental torments are given up; their physical and mental fevers are given up. They experience both physical and mental happiness.
translations.mn19:11: Whatever a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers becomes the inclination of their mind. If a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers the thought of renunciation, they've given up the thought of sensuality, and have developed the thought of renunciation. Their mind inclines to the thought of renunciation. If a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers the thought of good will … If a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers the thought of harmlessness, they've given up the thought of harming, and have developed the thought of harmlessness. Their mind inclines to the thought of harmlessness.
translations.mn19:12: Suppose in the last month of summer, when all the crops have been gathered into the neighborhood of a village, a cowherd would look after the cattle. While at the root of a tree or in the open, they'd just have to be mindful: 'Those are the cattle.' In the same way, I just had to be mindful: 'These are the qualities.'
translations.mn19:13: My energy was roused up and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and lucid, my body was tranquil and undisturbed, and my mind was immersed in samādhi.
translations.mn19:14: Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, I entered and remained in the first jhāna, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected.
translations.mn19:24: This was the third knowledge, which I achieved in the last watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed and knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed and light arose, as happens for a meditator who is diligent, keen, and resolute.
translations.mn19:25: Suppose there was a large, low-lying marsh in a forested wilderness, and a large herd of deer was living nearby. Then along comes a person who wants to harm, injure, and threaten them. They close off the safe, secure path that leads to happiness, and open up a false path. They plant a decoy and set up a dummy. After some time that large herd of deer would fall to ruin and disaster. Then along comes a person who wants to help the large herd of deer, to keep them safe. They open up the safe, secure path that leads to happiness, and close off the false path. They get rid of the decoy and dispose of the dummy. After some time that large herd of deer would grow, increase, and mature.
translations.mn19:26: I've made up this simile to make a point. And this is the point: 'A large, low-lying marsh' is a term for sensual pleasures. 'A large herd of deer' is a term for sentient beings. 'A person who wants to harm, injure, and threaten' is a term for Māra the Wicked. 'A false path' is a term for the wrong eightfold path, that is: wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong immersion. 'A decoy' is a term for relishing and greed. 'A dummy' is a term for ignorance. 'A person who wants to help, to keep them safe' is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. 'A safe, secure path that leads to happiness' is a term for the noble eightfold path, that is: right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right immersion. So I have opened up the safe, secure path that leads to happiness, closed off the false path, got rid of the decoy, and disposed of the dummy.
translations.mn19:3: As I meditated—diligent, keen, and resolute—a sensual thought arose. I understood: 'This sensual thought has arisen in me. It leads to hurting myself, hurting others, and hurting both. It blocks wisdom, it's on the side of anguish, and it doesn't lead to extinguishment.' When I reflected that it leads to hurting myself, it went away. When I reflected that it leads to hurting others, it went away. When I reflected that it leads to hurting both, it went away. When I reflected that it blocks wisdom, it's on the side of anguish, and it doesn't lead to extinguishment, it went away. So I gave up, got rid of, and eliminated any sensual thoughts that arose.
translations.mn19:6: Whatever a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers becomes the inclination of their mind.
