If a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers the thought of sensuality, they've given up the thought of renunciation, and have developed the thought of sensuality. Their mind inclines to the thought of sensuality. If a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers the thought of ill will … If a mendicant frequently thinks about and considers the thought of harming, they've given up the thought of harmlessness, and have developed the thought of harming. Their mind inclines to the thought of harming.
translations.mn19:7: Suppose, mendicants, in the last month of summer, when the crops have been gathered into the neighborhood, a cowherd would look after the cattle. He would tap and poke them with his staff on this side and that to keep them in check. Why is that? For that cowherd sees that there could be death, imprisonment, confiscation, or blame on that account. In the same way, mendicants, I saw the danger, degradation, and defilement in unskillful qualities, and the benefit of renunciation and the cleansing nature of skillful qualities.
translations.mn19:8: As I meditated—diligent, keen, and resolute—a thought of renunciation arose. I understood: 'This thought of renunciation has arisen in me. It doesn't lead to my own affliction, or to the affliction of others, or to the affliction of both. It promotes wisdom, it's on the side of non-distress, and it leads to extinguishment.' If I were to think and consider this all night, I see no danger that would come from that. If I were to think and consider this all day, I see no danger that would come from that. If I were to think and consider this all day and all night, I see no danger that would come from that. But thinking and considering for too long would tire my body. When the body is tired, the mind becomes strained. And when the mind is strained, it's far from immersion. So I steadied, settled, unified, and immersed my mind internally. Why is that? So that my mind would not be strained.
translations.mn1:10: They perceive Brahmā as Brahmā. Having perceived Brahmā as Brahmā, they conceive Brahmā, they conceive in Brahmā, they conceive from Brahmā, they conceive 'Brahmā is mine', they delight in Brahmā. Why is that? Because they haven't fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:11: They perceive the Radiant Gods as Radiant Gods. Having perceived the Radiant Gods as Radiant Gods, they conceive the Radiant Gods, they conceive in the Radiant Gods, they conceive from the Radiant Gods, they conceive 'the Radiant Gods are mine', they delight in the Radiant Gods. Why is that? Because they haven't fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:123: A mendicant who is a perfected one, with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own goal, utterly ended the fetters of existence, and is rightly freed through final knowledge—they too directly know earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, they don't conceive earth, they don't conceive in earth, they don't conceive from earth, they don't conceive 'earth is mine', they don't delight in earth. Why is that? Because of the ending of delusion, because they are free from delusion.
translations.mn1:13: They perceive the Gods of Abundant Fruit as Gods of Abundant Fruit. Having perceived the Gods of Abundant Fruit as Gods of Abundant Fruit, they conceive the Gods of Abundant Fruit, they conceive in the Gods of Abundant Fruit, they conceive from the Gods of Abundant Fruit, they conceive 'the Gods of Abundant Fruit are mine', they delight in the Gods of Abundant Fruit. Why is that? Because they haven't fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:14: They perceive the Overlord as the Overlord. Having perceived the Overlord as the Overlord, they conceive the Overlord, they conceive in the Overlord, they conceive from the Overlord, they conceive 'the Overlord is mine', they delight in the Overlord. Why is that? Because they haven't fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:147: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, also directly knows earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, he doesn't conceive earth, he doesn't conceive in earth, he doesn't conceive from earth, he doesn't conceive 'earth is mine', he doesn't delight in earth. Why is that? Because the Realized One has fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:171: The Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, also directly knows earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, he doesn't conceive earth, he doesn't conceive in earth, he doesn't conceive from earth, he doesn't conceive 'earth is mine', he doesn't delight in earth. Why is that? Because he has understood that 'delight is the root of suffering', and that 'from existence comes birth, and for one who has come to be there is old age and death'. Therefore, mendicants, I say that the Realized One has awakened to the supreme perfect awakening through the complete ending, fading away, cessation, giving up, and letting go of all craving.
translations.mn1:19: They perceive the seen as the seen. Having perceived the seen as the seen, they conceive the seen, they conceive in the seen, they conceive from the seen, they conceive 'the seen is mine', they delight in the seen. Why is that? Because they haven't fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:20: They perceive the heard as the heard. Having perceived the heard as the heard, they conceive the heard, they conceive in the heard, they conceive from the heard, they conceive 'the heard is mine', they delight in the heard. Why is that? Because they haven't fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:22: They perceive the cognized as the cognized. Having perceived the cognized as the cognized, they conceive the cognized, they conceive in the cognized, they conceive from the cognized, they conceive 'the cognized is mine', they delight in the cognized. Why is that? Because they haven't fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:23: They perceive unity as unity. Having perceived unity as unity, they conceive unity, they conceive in unity, they conceive from unity, they conceive 'unity is mine', they delight in unity. Why is that? Because they haven't fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:24: They perceive diversity as diversity. Having perceived diversity as diversity, they conceive diversity, they conceive in diversity, they conceive from diversity, they conceive 'diversity is mine', they delight in diversity. Why is that? Because they haven't fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:25: They perceive all as all. Having perceived all as all, they conceive all, they conceive in all, they conceive from all, they conceive 'all is mine', they delight in all. Why is that? Because they haven't fully understood it, I say.
translations.mn1:27: A mendicant who is a trainee, who hasn't achieved their heart's desire, but lives aspiring for the supreme sanctuary from the yoke—they too directly know earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, let them not conceive earth, let them not conceive in earth, let them not conceive from earth, let them not conceive 'earth is mine', let them not delight in earth. Why is that? Because they should fully understand it, I say.
translations.mn1:4: They perceive water as water. Having perceived water as water, they conceive water, they conceive in water, they conceive from water, they conceive 'water is mine', they relish water. Why is that? I say it is because they haven't fully understood it.
translations.mn1:5: They perceive fire as fire. Having perceived fire as fire, they conceive fire, they conceive in fire, they conceive from fire, they conceive 'fire is mine', they relish fire. Why is that? I say it is because they haven't fully understood it.
translations.mn1:51: A mendicant who is a perfected one, with defilements ended, who has completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own true goal, utterly ended the fetters of existence, and is rightly freed through final knowledge: they directly know earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, they don't conceive earth, they don't conceive in earth, they don't conceive from earth, they don't conceive 'earth is mine', they don't relish earth. Why is that? I say it is because they have fully understood it.
translations.mn1:7: They perceive creatures as creatures. Having perceived creatures as creatures, they conceive creatures, they conceive in creatures, they conceive from creatures, they conceive 'creatures are mine', they relish creatures. Why is that? I say it is because they haven't fully understood it.
translations.mn1:8: They perceive gods as gods. Having perceived gods as gods, they conceive gods, they conceive in gods, they conceive from gods, they conceive 'gods are mine', they relish gods. Why is that? I say it is because they haven't fully understood it.
translations.mn1:9: They perceive Pajāpati as Pajāpati. Having perceived Pajāpati as Pajāpati, they conceive Pajāpati, they conceive in Pajāpati, they conceive from Pajāpati, they conceive 'Pajāpati is mine', they relish Pajāpati. Why is that? I say it is because they haven't fully understood it.
translations.mn22:12: So, mendicants, when you understand the meaning of what I've said, you should remember it accordingly. But when you don't understand the meaning of what I've said, you should ask me about it, or the mendicants who are learned.
translations.mn22:14: I've taught you that the Dhamma is like a raft: for those who understand, even good teachings should be given up, how much more so bad teachings.
translations.mn22:23: Mendicants, you should grasp that attachment to a doctrine of self which, when grasped, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. But do you see any such attachment to a doctrine of self?
translations.mn22:24: Mendicants, you should rely on that support of views which, when relied upon, would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. But do you see any such support of views?
translations.mn22:27: So, mendicants, you should truly see any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all form—with right understanding: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' You should truly see any kind of feeling … any kind of perception … any kind of volitional formations … any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness—with right understanding: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'
translations.mn22:28: Seeing this, mendicants, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness.
translations.mn22:29: Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate. Being dispassionate, they are freed. When freed, there is knowledge that they are freed. They understand: 'Birth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'
translations.mn22:30: This is called a mendicant who has raised the bar, filled in the moat, pulled up the pillar, and withdrawn the bolts; a noble one with banner lowered, burden put down, and detached.
translations.mn22:31: And how has a mendicant raised the bar? It's when a mendicant has given up ignorance, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it's unable to arise in the future. That's how a mendicant has raised the bar.
translations.mn22:32: And how has a mendicant filled in the moat? It's when a mendicant has given up the wandering on in rebirth from one life to the next, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it's unable to arise in the future. That's how a mendicant has filled in the moat.
translations.mn22:33: And how has a mendicant pulled up the pillar? It's when a mendicant has given up craving, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it's unable to arise in the future. That's how a mendicant has pulled up the pillar.
translations.mn22:34: And how has a mendicant withdrawn the bolts? It's when a mendicant has given up the five lower fetters, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, obliterated them, so they're unable to arise in the future. That's how a mendicant has withdrawn the bolts.
translations.mn22:35: And how is a mendicant a noble one with banner lowered, burden put down, and detached? It's when a mendicant has given up the conceit 'I am', cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it, so it's unable to arise in the future. That's how a mendicant is a noble one with banner lowered, burden put down, and detached.
translations.mn22:38: If others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Realized One, the Realized One doesn't feel elated, joyful, or uplifted because of that. If others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate the Realized One, the Realized One thinks: 'They're doing these things for what was previously fully understood.'
translations.mn22:39: So, mendicants, if others abuse, insult, anger, or harass you, you should not harbor resentment, displeasure, or ill will in your heart. And if others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate you, you should not feel elated, joyful, or uplifted because of that. If others honor, respect, esteem, and venerate you, you should think: 'They're doing these things for what was previously fully understood.'
translations.mn22:40: So, mendicants, give up what is not yours; giving it up will be for your lasting welfare and happiness.
translations.mn22:42: So well explained by me, mendicants, is the teaching, made clear, opened up, illuminated, stripped of patchwork. In this teaching so well explained by me, made clear, opened up, illuminated, stripped of patchwork, those mendicants who are perfected—who have ended defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own goal, utterly ended the fetters of existence, and are rightly freed through final knowledge—for them there is no cycle to be described.
translations.mn22:43: So well explained by me, mendicants, is the teaching, made clear, opened up, illuminated, stripped of patchwork. In this teaching so well explained by me, made clear, opened up, illuminated, stripped of patchwork, those mendicants who have given up the five lower fetters are all reborn spontaneously, and will be extinguished there, not liable to return from that world.
translations.mn22:44: So well explained by me, mendicants, is the teaching, made clear, opened up, illuminated, stripped of patchwork. In this teaching so well explained by me, made clear, opened up, illuminated, stripped of patchwork, those mendicants who have given up three fetters, with greed, hatred, and delusion weakened, are all once-returners, who will come back to this world once only, then make an end of suffering.
translations.mn22:45: So well explained by me, mendicants, is the teaching, made clear, opened up, illuminated, stripped of patchwork. In this teaching so well explained by me, made clear, opened up, illuminated, stripped of patchwork, those mendicants who have given up three fetters are all stream-enterers, not liable to be reborn in the lower realms, bound for awakening.
translations.mn22:46: So well explained by me, mendicants, is the teaching, made clear, opened up, illuminated, stripped of patchwork. In this teaching so well explained by me, made clear, opened up, illuminated, stripped of patchwork, those mendicants who are Dhamma-followers or faith-followers are all bound for awakening.
translations.mn26:10: And what, monks, do I call subject to sorrow? Sons and wife, monks, are subject to sorrow; male and female slaves are subject to sorrow; goats and sheep are subject to sorrow; chickens and pigs are subject to sorrow; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to sorrow. These acquisitions, monks, are subject to sorrow. One who is tied to these, infatuated with them, and absorbed in them, being himself subject to sorrow, seeks what is also subject to sorrow.
translations.mn26:11: And what, monks, do I call subject to defilement? Sons and wife, monks, are subject to defilement; male and female slaves are subject to defilement; goats and sheep are subject to defilement; chickens and pigs are subject to defilement; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to defilement; gold and silver are subject to defilement. These acquisitions, monks, are subject to defilement. One who is tied to these, infatuated with them, and absorbed in them, being himself subject to defilement, seeks what is also subject to defilement. This, monks, is the ignoble search.
translations.mn26:13: Before my awakening, monks, while I was still an unawakened bodhisatta, being myself subject to birth, I sought what was also subject to birth; being myself subject to aging, I sought what was also subject to aging; being myself subject to illness, I sought what was also subject to illness; being myself subject to death, I sought what was also subject to death; being myself subject to sorrow, I sought what was also subject to sorrow; being myself subject to defilement, I sought what was also subject to defilement. Then it occurred to me: 'Why, being myself subject to birth, do I seek what is also subject to birth? Being myself subject to aging … illness … death … sorrow … being myself subject to defilement, do I seek what is also subject to defilement? What if I, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, were to seek the unborn, the supreme security from bondage, nibbāna? Being myself subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, were to seek the unaging, the supreme security from bondage, nibbāna? Being myself subject to illness, having understood the danger in what is subject to illness, were to seek the unailing, the supreme security from bondage, nibbāna? Being myself subject to death, having understood the danger in what is subject to death, were to seek the deathless, the supreme security from bondage, nibbāna? Being myself subject to sorrow, having understood the danger in what is subject to sorrow, were to seek the sorrowless, the supreme security from bondage, nibbāna? Being myself subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, were to seek the undefiled, the supreme security from bondage, nibbāna?'
translations.mn26:14: Then, monks, some time later, while still young, a black-haired youth endowed with the blessing of youth, in the prime of life, though my mother and father wished otherwise and wept with tearful faces, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
translations.mn26:17: Then, monks, being a seeker of what is wholesome, searching for the supreme state of sublime peace, I wandered by stages through the Magadhan country until I arrived at Senānigama near Uruvelā. There I saw a delightful piece of ground, a lovely grove of trees, a clear-flowing river with pleasant, delightful banks, and a village for alms-gathering nearby. It occurred to me: 'Delightful is this piece of ground, lovely is the grove of trees, the river flows clear with pleasant, delightful banks, and there is a village for alms-gathering nearby. This is suitable for the striving of a clansman intent on striving.' So I sat down there, thinking: 'This is suitable for striving.'
translations.mn22:9: That someone without sensual pleasures, sensual perceptions, and sensual thoughts could still indulge in sensual pleasures—this is not possible.
translations.mn26:21: Then, mendicants, knowing Brahmā's request, and having compassion for sentient beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha's eye. And I saw sentient beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, and some who lived seeing the danger in the fault of the next world, and some who did not. It's like a pool with blue water lilies, or pink or white lotuses. Some of them sprout and grow in the water without rising above it, thriving underwater. Some of them sprout and grow in the water reaching the water's surface. And some of them sprout and grow in the water but rise up above the water and stand with no water clinging to them. In the same way, I surveyed the world with the Buddha's eye and saw sentient beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to teach and hard to teach, and some who lived seeing the danger in the fault of the next world, and some who did not. Then I replied to Brahmā Sahampati in verse: 'Flung open are the doors to the deathless! Let those with ears release their faith. Perceiving harm, I did not teach the refined and excellent Dhamma among humans, O Brahmā.' Then Brahmā Sahampati, thinking, 'I have created an opportunity for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma,' bowed to me, circumambulated me keeping me on his right, and vanished right there.
translations.mn26:25: Mendicants, Upaka the Ājīvaka saw me traveling along the road between Gayā and the Bodhi tree. Seeing me, he said: 'Your faculties are clear, friend, and your complexion is pure and bright. In whose name have you gone forth, friend? Who is your teacher? Whose teaching do you prefer?' When he said this, I replied to Upaka the Ājīvaka in verses: 'I am the vanquisher of all, the knower of all, unsullied in all things. I have given up all, freed through the ending of craving. Having known by myself, whom should I point to? I have no teacher, and one like me does not exist. In the world with its gods, I have no counterpart. For I am the perfected one in the world, I am the supreme teacher. I alone am fully awakened, cooled, extinguished. I am going to the city of Kāsi to set the Wheel of Dhamma rolling. In a world that has become blind, I shall beat the drum of the deathless.' 'According to your claims, friend, you ought to be the infinite victor.' 'Those who have attained the ending of defilements are victors like me. I have conquered bad qualities, Upaka, that's why I'm a victor.' When I said this, mendicants, Upaka the Ājīvaka said 'May it be so, friend,' shook his head, took a side path, and left.
translations.mn26:26: Then, mendicants, traveling stage by stage, I approached the group of five mendicants in the deer park at Isipatana near Benares. The group of five mendicants saw me coming from afar. Seeing me, they agreed among themselves: 'Here comes the ascetic Gotama, who lives in luxury, who gave up the struggle and reverted to luxury. We shouldn't bow to him, or rise for him, or receive his bowl and robe. But a seat may be set out; he can sit if he wishes.' But as I approached, the group of five mendicants were unable to keep to their agreement. Some came out to greet me and receive my bowl and robe, some prepared a seat, and some set out water for washing my feet. But they addressed me by name and as 'friend.'
translations.mn26:28: When they said this, I said to the group of five mendicants: 'Do you acknowledge, mendicants, that I have never spoken like this before?' 'No, sir.' 'The Realized One is a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha. Listen, mendicants, the deathless has been attained. I will instruct you, I will teach you the Dhamma. By practicing as instructed you will soon realize for yourselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the supreme end of the spiritual life for which people of good family rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness, and you will live having achieved it.'
translations.mn26:29: I was able to convince the group of five mendicants. Sometimes I would advise two mendicants, while three went for alms. Then the six of us lived on what those three brought back. Sometimes I would advise three mendicants, while two went for alms. Then the six of us lived on what those two brought back.
translations.mn26:30: Then the group of five mendicants—instructed and advised by me like this—being themselves subject to rebirth, understanding the drawback in what is subject to rebirth, seeking the unborn supreme sanctuary, extinguishment, found the unborn supreme sanctuary, extinguishment. Being themselves subject to old age, understanding the drawback in what is subject to old age, seeking the unaging supreme sanctuary, extinguishment, they found the unaging supreme sanctuary, extinguishment. Being themselves subject to sickness … Being themselves subject to death … Being themselves subject to sorrow … Being themselves subject to defilement, understanding the drawback in what is subject to defilement, seeking the undefiled supreme sanctuary, extinguishment, they found the undefiled supreme sanctuary, extinguishment. And the knowledge and vision arose in them: 'Our liberation is unshakable; this is our last rebirth; now there is no more renewed existence.'
translations.mn26:31: Mendicants, there are these five kinds of sensual stimulation. What five? Sights known by the eye that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. Sounds known by the ear … Smells known by the nose … Tastes known by the tongue … Touches known by the body that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. These are the five kinds of sensual stimulation.
translations.mn26:34: Suppose a wild deer is wandering in the wilderness. It walks, stands, sits down, and lies down free of worry. Why is that? Because it's out of the hunter's range. In the same way, a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. This mendicant is said to have blinded Māra, put out his eyes without a trace, and gone where the Wicked One cannot see.
translations.mn26:35: Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected. This mendicant is said … where the Wicked One cannot see.
translations.mn26:36: Furthermore, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, personally experiencing the bliss of which the noble ones declare, 'Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.' This mendicant is said … where the Wicked One cannot see.
translations.mn26:37: Furthermore, giving up pleasure and pain, and ending former happiness and sadness, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, without pleasure or pain, with pure equanimity and mindfulness. This mendicant is said … where the Wicked One cannot see.
translations.mn26:38: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite', enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space. This mendicant is said … where the Wicked One cannot see.
translations.mn26:39: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite', enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness. This mendicant is said … where the Wicked One cannot see.
translations.mn26:4: Then the Buddha went to the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka. Now at that time several mendicants were sitting together at Rammaka's hermitage having a Dhamma discussion. The Buddha stood outside the porch waiting for the discussion to end. When he knew the discussion had ended, he coughed and knocked on the door. The mendicants opened the door for him. Then the Buddha entered the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka, sat down on the seat spread out, and addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants, what were you sitting together talking about just now? What conversation was left unfinished?' 'Sir, we were having a Dhamma discussion about the Buddha himself when he arrived.' 'Good, mendicants. It's appropriate for gentlemen like yourselves, who have gone forth from the lay life to homelessness out of faith, to sit together for a Dhamma discussion. When you're sitting together you should do one of two things: discuss the teachings or keep noble silence.
translations.mn26:40: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing at all', enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness. This mendicant is said … where the Wicked One cannot see.
translations.mn26:41: Furthermore, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, enters and remains in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. This mendicant is said … where the Wicked One cannot see.
translations.mn26:5: Mendicants, there are these two kinds of search: the noble search and the ignoble search. And what is the ignoble search? It's when someone who is themselves subject to rebirth seeks what is also subject to rebirth; who is themselves subject to old age seeks what is also subject to old age; who is themselves subject to sickness seeks what is also subject to sickness; who is themselves subject to death seeks what is also subject to death; who is themselves subject to sorrow seeks what is also subject to sorrow; who is themselves subject to defilement seeks what is also subject to defilement.
translations.mn26:6: And what would you say is subject to rebirth? Partners and children are subject to rebirth. Bondservants, male and female, are subject to rebirth. Goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, and elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to rebirth. Gold and money are subject to rebirth. These attachments are subject to rebirth. Someone who is tied, infatuated, and attached to such things, being themselves subject to rebirth, seeks what is also subject to rebirth.
translations.mn27:12: A householder hears that teaching, or a householder's child, or someone reborn in some clan. They gain faith in the Realized One, and reflect: 'Living in a house is cramped and dusty, but the life of one gone forth is wide open. It's not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell. Why don't I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?' After some time they give up a small or large fortune, and a small or large family circle. They shave off their hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness.
translations.mn27:13: When they have gone forth in this way, possessing the training and livelihood of the mendicants, they give up killing living creatures, renouncing the rod and the sword. They are scrupulous and kind, living full of compassion for all living beings. They give up stealing. They take only what is given, expecting only what is given, living without stealing, pure in themselves. They give up unchastity. They are celibate, set apart, avoiding the common practice of sex. They give up lying. They speak the truth, are devoted to truth, trustworthy, and reliable, not deceiving the world. They give up divisive speech. They don't repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. Instead, they reconcile those who are divided, supporting unity, delighting in harmony, loving harmony, speaking words that promote harmony. They give up harsh speech. They speak in a way that is gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, going to the heart, polite, likable and agreeable to the people. They give up idle chatter. Their words are timely, true, meaningful, in line with the teaching and training. They speak words worth treasuring, timely, reasonable, succinct, and beneficial. They refrain from injuring plants and seeds. They eat in one part of the day, abstaining from eating at night and food at the wrong time. They refrain from dancing, singing, music, and seeing shows. They refrain from wearing garlands, perfumes, and makeup, and from beautifying and adorning themselves. They refrain from high and luxurious beds. They refrain from accepting gold and silver. They refrain from accepting raw grain. They refrain from accepting raw meat. They refrain from accepting women and girls. They refrain from accepting male and female bondservants. They refrain from accepting goats and sheep. They refrain from accepting chickens and pigs. They refrain from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares. They refrain from accepting fields and land. They refrain from running errands and messages. They refrain from buying and selling. They refrain from falsifying weights, metals, and measures. They refrain from bribery, fraud, cheating, and deception. They refrain from mutilation, murder, abduction, banditry, plunder, and violence.
translations.mn27:14: They are content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they take only these things. Just as a bird flies with wings as its only burden, so too, a mendicant is content with robes to look after the body and almsfood to look after the belly. Wherever they go, they take only these things. Possessing this entire spectrum of noble ethics, they experience a blameless happiness inside themselves.
translations.mn27:15: When they see a sight with their eyes, they don't get caught up in the features and details. If the faculty of sight were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of desire and aversion would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, guarding the faculty of sight, and achieving its restraint. When they hear a sound with their ears … When they smell an odor with their nose … When they taste a flavor with their tongue … When they feel a touch with their body … When they know a mental phenomenon with their mind, they don't get caught up in the features and details. If the faculty of mind were left unrestrained, bad unskillful qualities of desire and aversion would become overwhelming. For this reason, they practice restraint, guarding the faculty of mind, and achieving its restraint. Possessing this noble sense restraint, they experience an unsullied happiness inside themselves.
translations.mn27:16: They act with situational awareness when going out and coming back; when looking ahead and looking aside; when bending and extending the limbs; when bearing the outer robe, bowl, and robes; when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; when urinating and defecating; when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.
translations.mn27:17: Possessing this entire spectrum of noble ethics, this noble contentment, this noble sense restraint, and this noble mindfulness and situational awareness, they frequent a secluded lodging—a wilderness, the root of a tree, a hill, a ravine, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a forest, the open air, a heap of straw.
translations.mn27:18: After the meal, they return from almsround, sit down cross-legged, set their body straight, and establish mindfulness in front of them. Giving up desire for the world, they meditate with a heart rid of desire, cleansing the mind of desire. Giving up ill will and malevolence, they meditate with a mind rid of ill will, full of compassion for all living beings, cleansing the mind of ill will. Giving up dullness and drowsiness, they meditate with a mind rid of dullness and drowsiness, perceiving light, mindful and aware, cleansing the mind of dullness and drowsiness. Giving up restlessness and remorse, they meditate without restlessness, their mind peaceful inside, cleansing the mind of restlessness and remorse. Giving up doubt, they meditate having gone beyond doubt, not uncertain about skillful qualities, cleansing the mind of doubt.
translations.mn27:19: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom. Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. This too is called a footprint of the Realized One, or a place frequented by the Realized One, or a scratch mark of the Realized One. But a noble disciple does not yet come to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha. The teaching is well explained by the Blessed One. The Blessed One's community of disciples is practicing well.'
translations.mn27:2: Now at that time the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was driving out of Sāvatthī in the middle of the day in an all-white chariot drawn by mares. The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi saw the wanderer Pilotika coming from a distance. Seeing him, he said to the wanderer Pilotika: 'Well now, where is Master Vacchāyana coming from in the middle of the day?' 'Sir, I am coming from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.' 'What does Master Vacchāyana think about the ascetic Gotama's wisdom and intelligence? He is wise, I suppose?' 'Sir, who am I to know the ascetic Gotama's wisdom and intelligence? Surely one would have to be just like him to know the ascetic Gotama's wisdom and intelligence.' 'Master Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with lofty praise indeed.' 'Sir, who am I to praise the ascetic Gotama? That Master Gotama is praised by the praised, the best among gods and humans.' 'But seeing what reason is Master Vacchāyana so confident in the ascetic Gotama?'
translations.mn27:20: Furthermore, brahmin, with the stilling of thought and examination, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of immersion. This too is called, brahmin … the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well.'
translations.mn27:21: Furthermore, brahmin, with the fading away of rapture, a mendicant remains equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body, and enters and remains in the third absorption, of which the noble ones declare: 'Equanimous and mindful, one dwells happily.' This too is called, brahmin … the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well.'
translations.mn27:22: Furthermore, brahmin, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, a mendicant enters and remains in the fourth absorption, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes the purification of mindfulness by equanimity. This too is called, brahmin, a footprint of the Realized One, or scratched by the Realized One, or marked by the Realized One. But a noble disciple still does not come to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is fully awakened, the Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well.'
translations.mn27:4: What four? Here, sir, I see certain aristocratic scholars who are subtle, practiced in the doctrines of others, hair-splitters. They seem to go about demolishing views with their wisdom. They hear: 'The ascetic Gotama will be visiting such and such village or town.' They formulate a question: 'We will approach the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question. If he answers like this when asked, we will refute him in this way. And if he answers like that when asked, we will refute him in that way.' They hear: 'The ascetic Gotama has arrived at such and such village or town.' They approach the ascetic Gotama. The ascetic Gotama instructs, encourages, rouses, and inspires them with a Dhamma talk. Having been instructed, encouraged, roused, and inspired by the ascetic Gotama with a Dhamma talk, they don't even ask the ascetic Gotama the question, so how could they refute him? Instead, they become disciples of the ascetic Gotama. When, sir, I saw this first footprint in the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion: 'The Blessed One is fully awakened, the Dhamma is well taught by the Blessed One, the Sangha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well.'
translations.mn28:10: If, friends, when that mendicant recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established, they are moved by that and feel a sense of urgency: 'It is my loss, it is not my gain; it is my misfortune, it is not my good fortune, that when I recollect the Buddha in this way, recollect the Dhamma in this way, recollect the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established.' Just as, friends, a daughter-in-law, seeing her father-in-law, is moved and feels a sense of urgency; so too, friends, if when that mendicant recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established, they are moved by that and feel a sense of urgency: 'It is my loss, it is not my gain; it is my misfortune, it is not my good fortune, that when I recollect the Buddha in this way, recollect the Dhamma in this way, recollect the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the wholesome does not become established.' If, friends, when that mendicant recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the wholesome becomes established, they are satisfied with that. Even this much, friends, is of great benefit for a mendicant.
translations.mn28:12: There comes a time, friends, when the external water element is disturbed. It sweeps away villages, sweeps away towns, sweeps away cities, sweeps away countries, sweeps away regions of countries. There comes a time, friends, when the waters in the great ocean recede one hundred leagues, two hundred leagues, three hundred leagues, four hundred leagues, five hundred leagues, six hundred leagues, seven hundred leagues. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands at seven palm trees deep, six palm trees deep, five palm trees deep, four palm trees deep, three palm trees deep, two palm trees deep, one palm tree deep. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands at seven persons deep, six persons deep, five persons deep, four persons deep, three persons deep, two persons deep, one person deep. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean stands at half a person deep, waist deep, knee deep, ankle deep. There comes a time, friends, when the water in the great ocean is not even enough to wet a finger joint. Since even the external water element, so vast, is seen to be impermanent, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to change.
translations.mn28:13: What then of this body, so small, taken up by craving, as 'I' or 'mine' or 'I am'? There is simply no basis for that. …
translations.mn28:14: If, friends, when that mendicant recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the wholesome becomes established, they are satisfied with that.
translations.mn28:17: There comes a time, friends, when the external fire element is disturbed. It burns up villages, burns up towns, burns up cities, burns up countries, burns up regions of countries. It comes to the edge of green vegetation, or the edge of a road, or the edge of a rock, or the edge of water, or a pleasant stretch of land, and goes out for lack of fuel. There comes a time, friends, when they seek fire with a chicken feather or strips of sinew. Since even the external fire element, so vast, is seen to be impermanent, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to change. What then of this body, so small, taken up by craving, as 'I' or 'mine' or 'I am'?
translations.mn28:18-20: There is simply no basis for that. … If, friends, when that mendicant recollects the Buddha in this way, recollects the Dhamma in this way, recollects the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity based on the wholesome becomes established, they are satisfied with that. Even this much, friends, is of great benefit for a mendicant.
translations.mn28:2: Friends, just as the footprints of all creatures that walk can be placed within an elephant's footprint, and so the elephant's footprint is declared the chief of them because of its great size; so too, friends, all wholesome qualities are included in the four noble truths. In which four? In the noble truth of suffering, in the noble truth of the origin of suffering, in the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, in the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn28:22: There comes a time, friends, when the external air element is disturbed. It sweeps away villages, sweeps away towns, sweeps away cities, sweeps away countries, sweeps away regions of countries. There comes a time, friends, when in the last month of summer they seek wind with a palm leaf fan or a bellows fan, and even the grass at the drip-line of the eaves does not stir. Since even the external air element, so vast, is seen to be impermanent, subject to destruction, subject to decay, subject to change. What then of this body, so small, taken up by craving, as 'I' or 'mine' or 'I am'? There is simply no basis for that.
translations.mn28:23: If, friends, others abuse, revile, scold, and harass that mendicant, they understand: 'This painful feeling born of ear contact has arisen in me. That is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact.' They see that contact is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent. Their mind, taking the element as its object, enters into it, gains confidence, becomes steady, and resolute.
translations.mn28:26: Just as, reverend, when space is enclosed by sticks, creepers, grass, and mud, it's called a 'house'; so too, when space is enclosed by bones, sinews, flesh, and skin, it's called 'form'.
translations.mn28:27: When the internal eye is intact, reverend, but external forms don't come into range, and there's no corresponding engagement, there's no manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness. When the internal eye is intact and external forms come into range, but there's no corresponding engagement, there's no manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness. But when the internal eye is intact and external forms come into range and there is corresponding engagement, there is the manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness.
translations.mn28:7: There comes a time, reverend, when the external water element rages. At that time the external earth element vanishes. The impermanence of that great external earth element will be known, its nature of being consumed will be known, its nature of perishing will be known, its nature of changing will be known. So what of this short-lived body, clung to by craving, as 'I' or 'mine' or 'I am'? There's no ground for that.
translations.mn29:3: Here, monks, a certain person of good family has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, thinking: 'I am beset by birth, aging, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I am beset by suffering, afflicted by suffering. Perhaps an end to this whole mass of suffering can be found.' Having gone forth thus, they generate material gains, honor, and fame. They are not pleased with those material gains, honor, and fame, and their intention is not fulfilled. They don't exalt themselves and disparage others because of those material gains, honor, and fame. They don't become intoxicated with those material gains, honor, and fame, nor grow negligent, nor fall into heedlessness. Being diligent, they achieve accomplishment in virtue. They are pleased with that accomplishment in virtue, and their intention is fulfilled. They exalt themselves and disparage others because of that accomplishment in virtue: 'I am virtuous, of good character, but these other monks are immoral, of bad character.' They become intoxicated with that accomplishment in virtue, grow negligent, and fall into heedlessness. Being heedless, they dwell in suffering. Suppose, monks, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a great tree standing with heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the softwood, passing over the bark, he would cut off the outer bark and depart taking it, thinking it was heartwood. A man with good eyesight seeing him would say: 'This good man didn't know the heartwood, didn't know the softwood, didn't know the bark, didn't know the outer bark, didn't know the branches and foliage. So this good man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, came to a great tree standing with heartwood. Passing over the heartwood, passing over the softwood, passing over the bark, he cut off the outer bark and departed taking it, thinking it was heartwood. Whatever he needs to do with heartwood, his purpose will not be served.'
translations.mn28:3: And what, reverend, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. And what, reverend, are the five aggregates subject to clinging? They are: the aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of volitional formations subject to clinging, the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.
translations.mn28:37: the mind is unimpaired, but external thoughts don't come into range and there's no corresponding engagement, then there's no manifestation of the corresponding type of consciousness.
translations.mn2:10: And what are the things not fit for attention that they don't attend to? They are things that, when attended to, give rise to the defilement of sensuality, or make it grow if it has already arisen; give rise to the defilement of continued existence, or make it grow if it has already arisen; give rise to the defilement of ignorance, or make it grow if it has already arisen. These are the things not fit for attention that they don't attend to. And what are the things fit for attention that they do attend to? They are things that, when attended to, don't give rise to the defilement of sensuality, or make it decline if it has already arisen; don't give rise to the defilement of continued existence, or make it decline if it has already arisen; don't give rise to the defilement of ignorance, or make it decline if it has already arisen. These are the things fit for attention that they do attend to. By not attending to things unfit for attention and by attending to things fit for attention, defilements that have not arisen don't arise, and defilements that have arisen are given up.
translations.mn2:11: They properly attend: 'This is suffering' … 'This is the origin of suffering' … 'This is the cessation of suffering' … 'This is the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering'. As they attend properly in this way, three fetters are given up: identity view, doubt, and misapprehension of precepts and observances. These are called the defilements that should be given up by seeing.
translations.mn2:12: 2. Defilements Given Up by Restraint And what are the defilements to be given up by restraint? Take a mendicant who, reflecting properly, lives restraining the eye faculty. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in one who lives without restraint over the eye faculty do not arise when there is such restraint. Reflecting properly, they live restraining the ear faculty … the nose faculty … the tongue faculty … the body faculty … the mind faculty. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in one who lives without restraint over the mind faculty do not arise when there is such restraint. For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in one who lives without restraint do not arise when there is such restraint. These are called the defilements to be given up by restraint.
translations.mn2:14: Reflecting properly, they use alms-food: 'Not for fun, indulgence, adornment, or decoration, but only to sustain this body, to avoid harm, and to support the spiritual life. In this way, I shall put an end to old discomfort and not give rise to new discomfort, and I will live blamelessly and at ease.'
translations.mn2:16: Reflecting properly, they use medicines and supplies for the sick: 'Only to ward off arisen afflictive feelings, and for the maximum freedom from illness.'
translations.mn2:17: For the distressing and feverish defilements that might arise in one who lives without using these things do not arise when they are used. These are called the defilements to be given up by using.
translations.mn2:3: I say that the ending of defilements is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know or see. For one who knows and sees what? Proper attention and improper attention. When you attend improperly, defilements arise that have not arisen, and defilements that have arisen grow. When you attend properly, defilements that have not arisen don't arise, and defilements that have arisen are given up.
translations.mn2:6: And what are the things not fit for attention that they attend to? They are things that, when attended to, give rise to the defilement of sensuality, or make it grow if it has already arisen; give rise to the defilement of continued existence, or make it grow if it has already arisen; give rise to the defilement of ignorance, or make it grow if it has already arisen. These are the things not fit for attention that they attend to. And what are the things fit for attention that they don't attend to? They are things that, when attended to, don't give rise to the defilement of sensuality, or make it decline if it has already arisen; don't give rise to the defilement of continued existence, or make it decline if it has already arisen; don't give rise to the defilement of ignorance, or make it decline if it has already arisen. These are the things fit for attention that they don't attend to.
translations.mn2:7: Because they attend to things unfit for attention and don't attend to things fit for attention, defilements arise that have not arisen, and defilements that have arisen grow. This is how they attend improperly: 'Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what did I become in the past? Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I become in the future?' Or they are undecided about the present: 'Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? This sentient being—where did it come from? And where will it go?'
translations.mn2:8: When they attend improperly in this way, one of six views arises in them. The view 'I have a self' arises in them as true and established; or the view 'I have no self' arises in them as true and established; or the view 'I perceive self with self' arises in them as true and established; or the view 'I perceive not-self with self' arises in them as true and established; or the view 'I perceive self with not-self' arises in them as true and established; or else they have this view: 'This self of mine that speaks and feels, and experiences the results of good and bad deeds here and there, this self of mine is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same for all eternity.' This is called a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a writhing of views, a fetter of views. Bound by the fetter of views, the unlearned ordinary person is not freed from birth, old age, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they are not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.mn2:9: But the learned noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones, is skilled and trained in their teaching; who has seen good persons, is skilled and trained in their teaching—understands what things should be attended to and what things should not be attended to. Understanding what things should be attended to and what things should not be attended to, they do not attend to things that should not be attended to, and they attend to things that should be attended to.
translations.mn31:4: Venerable Anuruddha heard the park keeper speaking with the Buddha. When he heard, he said to the park keeper: 'Don't hinder the Buddha, friend park keeper. Our Teacher, the Buddha, has arrived.' Then Venerable Anuruddha approached Venerable Nandiya and Venerable Kimbila. Having approached, he said to Venerable Nandiya and Venerable Kimbila: 'Come, venerables, come, venerables! Our Teacher, the Buddha, has arrived.'
translations.mn31:15: 'Good, good, Anuruddhas. But going beyond this meditation, transcending this meditation, have you attained another superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding?' 'Why not, sir? Here, sir, whenever we wish, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, we enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes purification of mindfulness by equanimity. Going beyond this meditation, transcending this meditation, this is another superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding that we have attained.'
translations.mn31:11-13: 'Good, good, Anuruddhas. But going beyond this meditation, transcending this meditation, have you attained another superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding?' 'Why not, sir? Here, sir, whenever we wish, with the subsiding of thought and examination, we enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. Going beyond this meditation, transcending this meditation, this is another superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding that we have attained.'
translations.mn31:3: Then in the evening, the Buddha emerged from seclusion and approached the Gosiṅga Sal-tree Wood. The park keeper saw the Buddha coming from afar. Seeing him, he said to the Buddha: 'Don't enter this park, ascetic. There are three gentlemen here dwelling for their own pleasure. Don't disturb them.'
translations.mn31:19: Then the Buddha, having instructed, encouraged, inspired, and gladdened Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn31:2: Now at that time Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila were dwelling in the Gosiṅga Sal-tree Wood.
translations.mn31:5: Then the venerables Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila went out to meet the Buddha. One received his bowl and robe, one spread out a seat, and one set out water for washing his feet. The Buddha sat on the seat spread out, and washed his feet. Then those venerables bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to Venerable Anuruddha, who was seated to one side: "I hope you're keeping well, Anuruddhas; I hope you're getting by alright; I hope you're not troubled by alms-gathering." "We're keeping well, Blessed One; we're getting by alright, Blessed One; and we're not troubled by alms-gathering, sir."
translations.mn31:6: "But I hope, Anuruddhas, that you're living in harmony, appreciating each other, without quarreling, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kind eyes?" "Indeed, sir, we live in harmony, appreciating each other, without quarreling, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kind eyes." "But how do you live in harmony, appreciating each other, without quarreling, blending like milk and water, and regarding each other with kind eyes?"
translations.mn31:9: "Indeed, sir, we live diligent, ardent, and resolute." "But how do you live diligent, ardent, and resolute?" "Here, sir, whoever returns first from alms-gathering in the village sets out the seats, and sets out the drinking water and washing water, and sets out the refuse bucket. Whoever returns last eats any food left over, if they wish; otherwise they throw it away where there is no greenery or drop it into water that has no living creatures. They put away the seats, put away the drinking water and washing water, put away the refuse bucket, and sweep the dining hall. Whoever sees that the drinking water pot, washing water pot, or toilet pot is empty sets it up. If it's too heavy for them, they summon another with a hand gesture, and we set it up by joining hands; but we don't break into speech on that account, sir. And every five days we sit together all night for Dhamma discussion. That is how we live diligent, ardent, and resolute, sir."
translations.mn36:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.
translations.mn36:10: "I am so confident in Master Gotama. For Master Gotama has developed body and developed mind." "Surely, Aggivessana, these words of yours are spoken offensively and provocatively, but still I will answer you. Ever since I shaved off my hair and beard, dressed in ocher robes, and went forth from the lay life to homelessness, it has not been possible for arisen pleasant feeling to occupy my mind, or for arisen painful feeling to occupy my mind."
translations.mn36:12: "How could it be otherwise, Aggivessana? Here, Aggivessana, before my awakening, while I was still an unawakened bodhisatta, it occurred to me: 'Household life is cramped and dusty; going forth is wide open. It's not easy for someone living at home to lead the spiritual life utterly full and pure, like a polished shell. Why don't I shave off my hair and beard, dress in ocher robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?'
translations.mn36:2: Now on that occasion, in the morning, the Buddha was properly dressed, and taking his bowl and robe, he wished to enter Vesālī for alms.
translations.mn36:20: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Why don't I, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the palate, restrain, subdue, and crush mind with mind?' So, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the palate, I restrained, subdued, and crushed mind with mind. While I did so, sweat ran from my armpits. It was like a strong man seizing a weaker man by the head or shoulders and restraining, subduing, and crushing him. In the same way, with teeth clenched and tongue pressed against the palate, I restrained, subdued, and crushed mind with mind, and sweat ran from my armpits. My energy was roused and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and unconfused, but my body was afflicted and not tranquil, being overwhelmed by that painful striving. But such painful feeling that arose in me did not occupy my mind.
translations.mn36:26: Some deities, seeing me, said: 'The ascetic Gotama is dead.' Other deities said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not dead, but he is dying.' Other deities said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not dead, nor is he dying; the ascetic Gotama is an arahant, for such is the way an arahant abides.'
translations.mn36:27: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Why don't I practice completely cutting off food?' Then deities approached me and said: 'Good sir, do not practice completely cutting off food. If you do so, we will infuse divine nutriment through your pores, and you will survive on that.' It occurred to me: 'If I claim to be completely fasting, and these deities infuse divine nutriment through my pores, and I survive on that, that would be a lie on my part.' So I dismissed those deities, saying 'There's no need.'
translations.mn36:28: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Why don't I take just a little food at a time, a handful at a time, whether it's mung bean soup, lentil soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup?' So I took just a little food at a time, a handful at a time, whether it was mung bean soup, lentil soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup. When I was taking just a little food at a time, a handful at a time, whether it was mung bean soup, lentil soup, chickpea soup, or pea soup, my body became extremely emaciated. Just like jointed reeds or jointed bamboo, so were my limbs because of eating so little. Just like a camel's hoof, so was my backside because of eating so little. Just like a string of beads, so was my spine, with vertebrae protruding, because of eating so little. Just like the rafters of an old, dilapidated hall, so were my ribs, jutting out and caved in, because of eating so little. Just like the reflection of stars in a deep well appears deep down, so did my eyeballs appear deep in their sockets because of eating so little. Just like a bitter gourd, cut off unripe, shrivels and withers in the wind and sun, so did my scalp shrivel and wither because of eating so little. When I tried to touch my belly skin, Aggivessana, I would grab hold of my spine; when I tried to touch my spine, I would grab hold of my belly skin—so closely had my belly skin clung to my spine because of eating so little. When I tried to urinate or defecate, Aggivessana, I would fall down on my face right there because of eating so little. When I tried to relieve my body by rubbing my limbs with my hands, Aggivessana, the hair, rotted at its roots, fell from my body as I rubbed because of eating so little.
translations.mn36:29: People who saw me, Aggivessana, said: 'The ascetic Gotama is black.' Some people said: 'The ascetic Gotama is not black, he is brown.' Some people said: 'The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor brown, he has golden skin.' So much had my pure, bright complexion been ruined because of eating so little.
translations.mn36:30: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have experienced painful, sharp, severe, piercing feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, sharp, severe, piercing feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this. Whatever ascetics or brahmins at present experience painful, sharp, severe, piercing feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost, there is none beyond this. Yet by this severe, difficult practice I have not attained any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. Could there be another path to awakening?'
translations.mn36:32: It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'Why do I fear that pleasure, which is a pleasure apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states?' It occurred to me, Aggivessana: 'I do not fear that pleasure, which is a pleasure apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states.'
translations.mn36:34: So, Aggivessana, having eaten solid food and regained strength, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, and rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Yet even such pleasant feeling that arose in me, Aggivessana, did not invade my mind and remain.
translations.mn36:38: With my mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of recollection of past lives. I recollected my manifold past lives, that is, one birth… thus with their aspects and particulars I recollected my manifold past lives.
translations.mn36:39: This, Aggivessana, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed, true knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose; as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute. Yet even such pleasant feeling that arose in me, Aggivessana, did not invade my mind and remain.
translations.mn36:40: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfections, malleable, workable, steady, and imperturbable, I directed it to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good places and bad. I understood how beings fare according to their deeds …
translations.mn36:42: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfections, malleable, workable, steady, and imperturbable, I directed it to the knowledge of the destruction of the defilements. I truly understood: 'This is suffering.' I truly understood: 'This is the origin of suffering.' I truly understood: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' I truly understood: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' I truly understood: 'These are the defilements.' I truly understood: 'This is the origin of the defilements.' I truly understood: 'This is the cessation of the defilements.' I truly understood: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of the defilements.'
translations.mn36:43: When I knew and saw thus, my mind was freed from the defilement of sensual desire, from the defilement of existence, and from the defilement of ignorance. When it was freed, there came the knowledge: 'It is freed.' I understood: 'Birth is destroyed, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'
translations.mn36:45: I recall, Aggivessana, teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds. Perhaps each person thinks: 'The ascetic Gotama is teaching the Dhamma just for me.' But it should not be seen like that; the Realized One teaches the Dhamma to others only for the purpose of giving them understanding. At the end of that talk, Aggivessana, I steady, settle, unify, and concentrate my mind internally on that same sign of concentration as before, in which I constantly dwell.
translations.mn36:9: And how, Aggivessana, is one developed in body and developed in mind? Here, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling arises in a learned noble disciple. Being touched by that pleasant feeling, they do not become attached to pleasure and do not fall into attachment to pleasure. That pleasant feeling of theirs ceases. With the cessation of pleasant feeling, painful feeling arises. Being touched by that painful feeling, they do not sorrow, do not tire, do not lament, do not beat their breast and cry, and do not fall into confusion. For them, Aggivessana, that arisen pleasant feeling does not overwhelm the mind and remain because of development of body; that arisen painful feeling does not overwhelm the mind and remain because of development of mind. For anyone, Aggivessana, in whom both these things occur—arisen pleasant feeling does not overwhelm the mind and remain because of development of body, and arisen painful feeling does not overwhelm the mind and remain because of development of mind—that is how one is developed in body and developed in mind.
translations.mn38:17: Thus, mendicants, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:14: "Mendicants, if you clung to, cherished, treasured, and treated as your own this view that is so pure and so bright, would you be understanding that the teaching is similar to a raft, for the purpose of crossing over, not for the purpose of holding on?
translations.mn36:8: "And how, Aggivessana, is one undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind? Here, Aggivessana, a pleasant feeling arises in an uneducated ordinary person. Touched by that pleasant feeling, they become infatuated with pleasure and fall into infatuation with pleasure. That pleasant feeling of theirs ceases. With the cessation of pleasant feeling, painful feeling arises. Touched by that painful feeling, they sorrow, tire, lament, beat their breast, and fall into confusion. That arisen pleasant feeling, Aggivessana, overwhelms their mind and remains because of undevelopment of body, and that arisen painful feeling overwhelms their mind and remains because of undevelopment of mind. For anyone, Aggivessana, in whom both these things happen—that arisen pleasant feeling overwhelms their mind and remains because of undevelopment of body, and that arisen painful feeling overwhelms their mind and remains because of undevelopment of mind—this is how one is undeveloped in body and undeveloped in mind.
translations.mn38:28: As the boy grows up and his faculties mature, he plays with the toys that children play with, such as toy plows, tipcat, somersaults, pinwheels, toy measures, toy carts, and toy bows.
translations.mn38:26: The conception of an embryo in a womb takes place when three things come together. The mother and father come together, but the mother is not in her fertile period, and no being is present—then no embryo is conceived. The mother and father come together, and the mother is in her fertile period, but no being is present—then no embryo is conceived. But when the mother and father come together, the mother is in her fertile period, and a being is present—when these three things come together, an embryo is conceived in a womb.
translations.mn38:27: The mother carries the embryo in her womb for nine or ten months, with much worry, as a heavy burden. When nine or ten months have passed, the mother gives birth, with much worry, to a heavy burden. She nourishes the newborn with her own blood. For mother's milk is regarded as blood in the training of the noble one.
translations.mn38:20: When ignorance fades away and ceases with nothing left over, choices cease. When choices cease, consciousness ceases. When consciousness ceases, name and form cease. When name and form cease, the six sense bases cease. When the six sense bases cease, contact ceases. When contact ceases, feeling ceases. When feeling ceases, craving ceases. When craving ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases. When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases. When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. That is how this whole mass of suffering ceases.
translations.mn38:39: They give up these five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom. Then, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, they enter and remain in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. Furthermore, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, a mendicant enters and remains in the second absorption … third absorption … fourth absorption.
translations.mn38:25: "Good, mendicants, you have been brought up by me with this teaching that is visible in this very life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. 'This teaching is visible in this very life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise'—that's what I said, and this is why I said it.
translations.mn38:9: 'Do you see that this has come to be?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Do you see that it originated with that fuel?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Do you see that with the cessation of that fuel, what has come to be is subject to cessation?' 'Yes, sir.'
translations.mn41:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large Sangha of monks, and he arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Sālā.
translations.mn41:10: And how, householders, is there threefold unrighteous and unequal conduct by mind? Here, householders, someone is covetous; they covet the wealth and possessions of others: 'Oh, may what belongs to another be mine!' They have an ill-disposed mind with corrupt intentions: 'May these beings be killed or slaughtered or annihilated or destroyed or may they not exist!' They have wrong view with distorted vision: 'There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings who are reborn spontaneously; there are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who have practiced rightly and who proclaim this world and the other world having realized it with their own direct knowledge.' Thus, householders, there is threefold unrighteous and unequal conduct by mind. So it is because of such unrighteous and unequal conduct, householders, that some beings here, on the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell.
translations.mn41:12: And how, householders, is there threefold righteous and equal conduct by body? Here, householders, someone, having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings; with rod and weapon laid aside, conscientious and kindly, they dwell compassionate for the welfare of all living beings. Having abandoned taking what is not given, they abstain from taking what is not given; they do not take by way of theft the wealth and possessions of others, whether in the village or in the forest. Having abandoned sexual misconduct, they abstain from sexual misconduct; they do not have intercourse with women who are protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, clan, or by their religion, or with those who have a husband, or those protected by punishment, or even with those garlanded as betrothed. Thus, householders, there is threefold righteous and equal conduct by body.
translations.mn41:13: And how, householders, is there fourfold righteous and equal conduct by speech? Here, householders, someone, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech. When summoned to a council, to an assembly, to their relatives' presence, to their guild, or to the royal court, and questioned as a witness thus: 'Come, good man, tell what you know,' not knowing, they say 'I do not know,' or knowing, they say 'I know'; not seeing, they say 'I do not see,' or seeing, they say 'I see.' Thus they do not knowingly speak falsehood for their own sake, for another's sake, or for some trifling worldly gain.
