Having abandoned divisive speech, they abstain from divisive speech; they do not repeat elsewhere what they have heard here in order to divide those people from these, nor do they repeat here what they have heard elsewhere in order to divide these people from those. Thus they are one who reunites those who are divided, a promoter of friendships, who enjoys concord, rejoices in concord, delights in concord, a speaker of words that promote concord. Having abandoned harsh speech, they abstain from harsh speech; they speak words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, going to the heart, courteous, desired by many, agreeable to many. Having abandoned idle chatter, they abstain from idle chatter; they speak at the right time, speak what is fact, speak what is beneficial, speak on the Dhamma and the Discipline; they speak words worth treasuring, timely, reasonable, well-defined, connected with the goal. Thus, householders, there is fourfold righteous and equal conduct by speech.
translations.mn41:14: And how, householders, is there threefold righteous and equal conduct by mind? Here, householders, someone is not covetous; they do not covet the wealth and possessions of others: 'Oh, may what belongs to another be mine!' They have a mind without ill will, with uncorrupted intentions: 'May these beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from trouble, and may they live happily!' They have right view with undistorted vision: 'There is what is given, what is offered, what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings who are reborn spontaneously; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who have practiced rightly and who proclaim this world and the other world having realized it with their own direct knowledge.' Thus, householders, there is threefold righteous and equal conduct by mind. So it is because of such righteous and equal conduct, householders, that some beings here, on the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
translations.mn41:15: If one who practices righteously and equally should wish: 'Oh, may I, on the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in the company of wealthy nobles!' it is possible that they may, on the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in the company of wealthy nobles. Why is that? Because they practice righteously and equally.
translations.mn41:4: 'What, Master Gotama, is the cause and condition why some beings here, on the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower realms, in hell? And what, Master Gotama, is the cause and condition why some beings here, on the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world?'
translations.mn41:43: If they wish: 'May I realize the undefiled freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom in this very life, and live having realized it with my own insight due to the ending of defilements!' This is possible. Why is that? Because they live by the teaching and they live justly.
translations.mn41:5: It is because of unprincipled and unjust conduct that some beings here, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a place of loss, a bad place, the underworld, hell. It is because of principled and just conduct that some beings here, when their body breaks up, after death, are reborn in a good place, a heavenly realm.
translations.mn41:6: We don't understand the detailed meaning of Master Gotama's brief statement. Master Gotama, please teach us the Dhamma so that we may understand the detailed meaning.
translations.mn41:8: And how is unprincipled and immoral conduct of three kinds by body? It's when a certain person kills living creatures. They're violent, bloody-handed, a hardened killer, merciless to living beings. They steal. They take, by way of theft, parsing belonging to others in the village or wilderness that they haven't been given. They commit sexual misconduct. They have sexual relations with women who are protected by their mother, father, mother and father, brother, sister, relatives, or clan; who have a husband; who are protected by law; or even one who has been garlanded as a betrothed. This is how unprincipled and immoral conduct is of three kinds by body.
translations.mn41:9: And how is unprincipled and immoral conduct of four kinds by speech? It's when a certain person lies. They're summoned to a council, an assembly, a family meeting, a guild, or to the royal court, and asked to bear witness: 'Please, mister, say what you know.' Not knowing, they say 'I know.' Knowing, they say 'I don't know.' Not seeing, they say 'I see.' Seeing, they say 'I don't see.' So they deliberately lie for the sake of themselves or another, or for some trivial worldly reason. They speak divisively. They repeat in one place what they heard in another so as to divide people against each other. And so they divide those who are united, supporting division, delighting in division, loving division, speaking words that promote division. They speak harshly. They use hurtful, harsh, bitter words that attack others, bordering on anger, not leading to immersion. They talk nonsense. They speak at the wrong time, saying what is not true, unhelpful, not in line with the teaching and training. Their words have no value, spoken at the wrong time, with no reason or limit, and not beneficial. This is how unprincipled and immoral conduct is of four kinds by speech.
translations.mn4:20: I thought: 'Why don't I, on those recognized and acknowledged nights—the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight—stay in such awe-inspiring and hair-raising shrines as park-shrines, forest-shrines, and tree-shrines? Then perhaps I will see that fear and terror.' So, some time later, on those recognized and acknowledged nights—the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight—I stayed in such awe-inspiring and hair-raising shrines as park-shrines, forest-shrines, and tree-shrines. While I was staying there a deer would come, or a peacock would knock a twig, or the wind would rustle the leaves. I thought: 'Is this that fear and terror coming?' I thought: 'Why do I just keep waiting for fear? Why don't I, in whatever posture fear and terror come upon me, dispel them in that same posture?' While I was walking, fear and terror came upon me. I didn't stand still or sit down or lie down until I had dispelled that fear and terror while walking. While I was standing, fear and terror came upon me. I didn't walk or sit down or lie down until I had dispelled that fear and terror while standing. While I was sitting, fear and terror came upon me. I didn't lie down or stand up or walk until I had dispelled that fear and terror while sitting. While I was lying down, fear and terror came upon me. I didn't sit up or stand up or walk until I had dispelled that fear and terror while lying down.
translations.mn4:22-26: My energy was roused up and unflagging, brahmin, my mindfulness was established and lucid, my body was tranquil and undisturbed, my mind was concentrated and unified. Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, and the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of thought and examination, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has the rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, I dwelt equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and I experienced happiness with the body; I entered and dwelt in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'Equanimous and mindful, one dwells happily.' With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
translations.mn4:27: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of recollection of past lives. I recollected my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world contraction, many eons of world expansion, many eons of world contraction and expansion: 'There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere. There too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus I recollected my manifold past lives with their aspects and details.
translations.mn4:28: This, brahmin, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed, true knowledge arose, darkness was destroyed, light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:29: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilements, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings fare according to their actions: 'These beings who engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook actions based on wrong view—with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell. But these beings who engaged in good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view—with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.' Thus with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, I saw beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood how beings fare according to their actions.
translations.mn4:3: Before my enlightenment, brahmin, while I was still just an unenlightened bodhisatta, I too thought: 'Remote jungle-thicket lodgings in the wilderness are hard to endure, seclusion is hard to practice, it is hard to enjoy being alone. The forests seem to rob the mind of a monk who has not attained concentration.'
translations.mn4:30: This, brahmin, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night. Ignorance was destroyed, true knowledge arose, darkness was destroyed, light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:34: Now, brahmin, you might think: 'Perhaps the ascetic Gotama is still not free from lust, hate, and delusion, and that is why he frequents remote jungle-thicket lodgings in the wilderness.' But it should not be seen in that way. I see two reasons why I frequent remote jungle-thicket lodgings in the wilderness: seeing my own pleasant dwelling in this very life, and out of compassion for future generations.
translations.mn4:4: Then I thought: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins whose bodily conduct is impure frequent remote jungle-thicket lodgings in the wilderness, because of the defect of their impure bodily conduct those venerable ascetics and brahmins evoke unwholesome fear and dread. But I do not frequent remote jungle-thicket lodgings in the wilderness with impure bodily conduct. My bodily conduct is pure. I am one of those noble ones whose bodily conduct is pure who frequent remote jungle-thicket lodgings in the wilderness.' Seeing this purity of bodily conduct in myself, brahmin, I found greater confidence for dwelling in the wilderness.
translations.mn4:5: Then I thought: 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins whose verbal conduct is impure … whose mental conduct is impure … whose livelihood is impure frequent remote jungle-thicket lodgings in the wilderness, because of the defect of their impure livelihood those venerable ascetics and brahmins evoke unwholesome fear and dread.
translations.mn4:6: But I do not frequent remote jungle-thicket lodgings in the wilderness with impure livelihood. My livelihood is pure.
translations.mn4:7: I am one of those noble ones whose livelihood is pure who frequent remote jungle-thicket lodgings in the wilderness.' Seeing this purity of livelihood in myself, brahmin, I found greater confidence for dwelling in the wilderness.
translations.mn52:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in Beluvagāmaka. Now on that occasion the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business.
translations.mn52:12: Furthermore, householder, a mendicant, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite', enters and remains in the dimension of infinite space. They reflect on this: 'This attainment of the dimension of infinite space is produced by choices and intentions. But whatever is produced by choices and intentions is impermanent and liable to cessation.' Grounded on that … they reach the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
translations.mn52:14: Furthermore, householder, a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing at all', enters and remains in the dimension of nothingness. They reflect on this: 'This attainment of the dimension of nothingness is produced by choices and intentions. But whatever is produced by choices and intentions is impermanent and liable to cessation.' Grounded on that they reach the ending of defilements. If they don't reach the ending of defilements, with the ending of the five lower fetters, they're reborn spontaneously, because of their passion and delight for that teaching. They are extinguished there, and are not liable to return from that world. This too is one thing declared by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha, practicing which a mendicant who is diligent, keen, and resolute frees their mind, ends the defilements, and reaches the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.
translations.mn52:3: Then, having finished his business in Pāṭaliputta, Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara went to Vesālī, to Beluvagāmaka, to Venerable Ānanda. He approached and, having paid homage to Venerable Ānanda, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara said to Venerable Ānanda: "Venerable Ānanda, is there one thing declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, where a mendicant who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, whose mind is not yet liberated becomes liberated, whose defilements are not yet ended reach their end, and who has not yet attained the supreme security from bondage attains it?" "There is, householder, one thing declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, where a mendicant who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, whose mind is not yet liberated becomes liberated, whose defilements are not yet ended reach their end, and who has not yet attained the supreme security from bondage attains it." "But what, Venerable Ānanda, is that one thing declared by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, where a mendicant who is diligent, ardent, and resolute, whose mind is not yet liberated becomes liberated, whose defilements are not yet ended reach their end, and who has not yet attained the supreme security from bondage attains it?"
translations.mn52:8: Furthermore, householder, a mendicant dwells pervading one direction with a mind full of loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, to all as to oneself, they dwell pervading the entire world with a mind full of loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. They reflect thus: 'This liberation of mind through loving-kindness is conditioned and volitionally produced. But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, subject to cessation.' Standing firm in that … they attain the supreme security from bondage.
translations.mn52:2: Then Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara went to the Kukkuṭārāma, to a certain mendicant. He approached and, having paid homage to that mendicant, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Dasama the householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara said to that mendicant: "Venerable sir, where is Venerable Ānanda staying at present? For I wish to see Venerable Ānanda." "Householder, Venerable Ānanda is staying at Beluvagāmaka near Vesālī."
translations.mn54:18: Suppose, householder, there was a pit of glowing coals, deeper than a man's height, full of coals that neither flamed nor smoked. Then a man would come along who wants to live and doesn't want to die, who wants happiness and recoils from suffering. Then two strong men would grab him by both arms and drag him toward the pit of glowing coals. What do you think, householder, would that man twist his body this way and that?
translations.mn54:23: Based on this supreme purity of equanimity and mindfulness, that noble disciple, householder, with the divine eye that is purified and surpasses the human, sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good places and bad places … they understand how beings are reborn according to their actions.
translations.mn54:24: Based on this supreme purity of equanimity and mindfulness, that noble disciple, householder, with the ending of defilements, realizes for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life the defilement-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells in it.
translations.mn60:10: Now, householders, those ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: 'There is what is given … who declare this world and the other world, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge'—it can be expected of them that they will avoid these three unskillful qualities—bad conduct by body, speech, and mind—and will undertake and practice these three skillful qualities—good conduct by body, speech, and mind. Why is that? Because those good ascetics and brahmins see the danger, degradation, and defilement in unskillful qualities, and the benefit of renunciation and the cleansing nature of skillful qualities.
translations.mn60:12: In this case, householders, a wise person reflects: 'If there is another world, then this good person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Even if there is no other world, and the statement of those good ascetics and brahmins is true, still this good person is praised by the wise in this very life as a virtuous person with right view who affirms that there is something.' If there really is another world, then this good person has made a good throw on both counts—in that they are praised by the wise in this very life, and in that with the breakup of the body, after death, they will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus this safe course, when properly undertaken, spreads over both sides and leaves behind the unskillful position.
translations.mn60:13: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: 'For one who acts or makes others act, who mutilates or makes others mutilate, who tortures or makes others torture, who causes grief or makes others cause grief, who trembles or makes others tremble, who kills living beings, who takes what is not given, who breaks into houses, who plunders wealth, who commits burglary, who waits in ambush, who goes to another's wife, who speaks falsely—no evil is done by the doer. If with a razor-edged wheel one were to make the living beings of this earth into one mass of flesh, one heap of flesh, there would be no evil from that, no coming of evil. If one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing and slaughtering, mutilating and making others mutilate, torturing and making others torture, there would be no evil from that, no coming of evil. If one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and making others give, sacrificing and making others sacrifice, there would be no merit from that, no coming of merit. By giving, by self-control, by restraint, by speaking the truth, there is no merit, no coming of merit.'
translations.mn60:14: Directly opposed to those ascetics and brahmins, there are some ascetics and brahmins who say this: 'For one who acts or makes others act, who mutilates or makes others mutilate, who tortures or makes others torture, who causes grief or makes others cause grief, who trembles or makes others tremble, who kills living beings, who takes what is not given, who breaks into houses, who plunders wealth, who commits burglary, who waits in ambush, who goes to another's wife, who speaks falsely—evil is done by the doer. If with a razor-edged wheel one were to make the living beings of this earth into one mass of flesh, one heap of flesh, there would be evil from that, there would be a coming of evil. If one were to go along the south bank of the Ganges killing and slaughtering, mutilating and making others mutilate, torturing and making others torture, there would be evil from that, there would be a coming of evil. If one were to go along the north bank of the Ganges giving and making others give, sacrificing and making others sacrifice, there would be merit from that, there would be a coming of merit. By giving, by self-control, by restraint, by speaking the truth, there is merit, there is a coming of merit.' What do you think, householders, don't these ascetics and brahmins hold doctrines directly opposed to each other?
translations.mn60:16: When there really is action, the view 'there is no action' is wrong view. When there really is action, the intention 'there is no action' is wrong intention. When there really is action, the speech 'there is no action' is wrong speech. When there really is action, saying 'there is no action' is opposition to those arahants who teach that there is action. When there really is action, convincing another 'there is no action' is convincing them of an untrue teaching. And by that convincing of an untrue teaching, one exalts oneself and disparages others. Thus their former good conduct is abandoned and bad conduct is established—this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to the noble ones, convincing others of an untrue teaching, self-exaltation, and disparagement of others. Thus these many bad, unskillful qualities come to be conditioned by wrong view.
translations.mn60:17: In this case, a sensible person reflects: 'If there is no efficacy of action, this individual will keep themselves safe after the breakup of the body. But if there is efficacy of action, this individual will be reborn after the breakup of the body, after death, in a place of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell. Regardless of whether there is efficacy of action or not, and the statement of those ascetics and brahmins is true, still this individual is criticized by the wise in this very life as an immoral individual with wrong view, one who denies efficacy of action. And if there really is efficacy of action, then this individual has made a bad throw on both counts: they are criticized by the wise in this very life, and after the breakup of the body, after death, they will be reborn in a place of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell. This guaranteed teaching has been poorly grasped and adopted by them; it covers only one side and neglects the skillful standpoint.'
translations.mn60:19: Since there is efficacy of action, the view 'there is efficacy of action' is their right view. Since there is efficacy of action, the intention 'there is efficacy of action' is their right intention. Since there is efficacy of action, the speech 'there is efficacy of action' is their right speech. Since there is efficacy of action, in saying 'there is efficacy of action' they do not contradict those perfected ones who teach efficacy of action. Since there is efficacy of action, in convincing another 'there is efficacy of action,' that is convincing them of the true teaching. And by that convincing of the true teaching they do not praise themselves or disparage others. So their former bad conduct is abandoned and good conduct is established—this right view, right intention, right speech, non-contradiction of the noble ones, convincing of the true teaching, not praising oneself, and not disparaging others. Thus these many skillful qualities come into being with right view as condition.
translations.mn60:21: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: 'There is no cause, there is no condition for the corruption of beings; beings are corrupted without cause or condition. There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause or condition. There is no power, no energy, no human strength, no human effort. All beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, without energy, without strength, transformed by destiny, circumstance, and nature, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.'
translations.mn60:22: But there are some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine directly contradicts those ascetics and brahmins. They say: 'There is cause, there is condition for the corruption of beings; beings are corrupted with cause and condition. There is cause, there is condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause and condition. There is power, there is energy, there is human strength, there is human effort. It is not the case that all beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are powerless, without energy, without strength, transformed by destiny, circumstance, and nature, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.' What do you think, householders? Don't these ascetics and brahmins directly contradict each other?
translations.mn60:29: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: 'There are no formless states at all.'
translations.mn60:30: But there are some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine directly contradicts those ascetics and brahmins. They say: 'There are formless states.' What do you think, householders? Don't these ascetics and brahmins directly contradict each other?
translations.mn60:32: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: 'There is no complete cessation of existence.'
translations.mn60:35: Householders, these four kinds of persons are found in the world. What four? Here, householders, a certain person is one who mortifies themselves, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves. Here, householders, a certain person is one who mortifies others, pursuing the practice of mortifying others. Here, householders, a certain person is one who mortifies themselves, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves, and also mortifies others, pursuing the practice of mortifying others. Here, householders, a certain person is one who neither mortifies themselves nor pursues the practice of mortifying themselves, nor mortifies others nor pursues the practice of mortifying others; not mortifying themselves or others, they dwell in this very life free from craving, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, having become holy themselves.
translations.mn60:36: And what, householders, is the person who mortifies themselves, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves? Here, householders, a certain person is a naked ascetic, rejecting conventions, licking their hands … they dwell pursuing the practice of tormenting and mortifying the body in various ways. This, householders, is called the person who mortifies themselves, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves.
translations.mn60:37: And what, householders, is the person who mortifies others, pursuing the practice of mortifying others? Here, householders, a certain person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs … or one who follows some other cruel occupation. This, householders, is called the person who mortifies others, pursuing the practice of mortifying others.
translations.mn60:38: And what, householders, is the person who mortifies themselves, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves, and also mortifies others, pursuing the practice of mortifying others? Here, householders, a certain person is a king, an anointed noble … and those people, threatened with punishment, threatened with danger, with tearful faces, weeping, perform their tasks. This, householders, is called the person who mortifies themselves, pursuing the practice of mortifying themselves, and also mortifies others, pursuing the practice of mortifying others.
translations.mn60:39: And what, householders, is the person who neither mortifies themselves nor pursues the practice of mortifying themselves, nor mortifies others nor pursues the practice of mortifying others; not mortifying themselves or others, they dwell in this very life free from craving, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, having become holy themselves?
translations.mn60:5: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: 'There is nothing given, nothing sacrificed, nothing offered; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings who are reborn spontaneously; there are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who are rightly practicing and rightly progressing, who proclaim this world and the other world having realized it themselves with direct knowledge.'
translations.mn60:6: Householders, there are some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine directly contradicts those ascetics and brahmins. They say this: 'There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings who are reborn spontaneously; there are ascetics and brahmins in the world who are rightly practicing and rightly progressing, who proclaim this world and the other world having realized it themselves with direct knowledge.' What do you think, householders: don't these ascetics and brahmins directly contradict each other?
translations.mn64:9: And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a mendicant—due to seclusion from attachments, due to the abandoning of unskillful qualities, due to the complete tranquilization of bodily discomfort—quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unskillful qualities, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, and has rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Whatever there is of form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, they contemplate those phenomena as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as not-self. They turn their mind away from those phenomena. Having turned their mind away from those phenomena, they direct their mind to the deathless element: 'This is peaceful, this is sublime—that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.' Established in that, they attain the destruction of the taints. But if they do not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that passion for the Dhamma, that delight in the Dhamma, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, they become one who is reborn spontaneously, who attains final Nibbāna there, not liable to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, this is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn6:14: If a mendicant should wish: 'May I wield the various kinds of psychic power—having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through walls, through ramparts, through mountains, as if through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as if it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as if it were earth; may I travel through the sky cross-legged like a bird; may I touch and stroke with my hand the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful; may I exercise mastery with my body as far as the Brahmā world'—they should be one who fulfills the precepts … and who frequents empty huts.
translations.mn64:14: Furthermore, Ānanda, a mendicant, having completely transcended the dimension of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite,' enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite consciousness. Whatever there is of feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness … not liable to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is the path, this is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:7: But, Ānanda, that there is a path, a practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters, and that by relying on that path, that practice, one will know, see, or abandon the five lower fetters—this is possible.
translations.mn63:8: And why, Mālukyaputta, has this not been declared by me? Because, Mālukyaputta, this is not beneficial, it is not fundamental to the spiritual life, it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna. Therefore it has not been declared by me.
translations.mn64:13: Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of impingement, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite', enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. Whatever there is there that belongs to feeling, that belongs to perception, that belongs to formations, that belongs to consciousness … is of a nature not to return to this world. This too, Ānanda, is a path, a practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn70:17: And what person is a body witness? It's when a person contacts with the body and abides in those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending form. And having seen with wisdom, some of their defilements are ended. This person is called a body witness. I say that this mendicant must be diligent. Why is that? Hopefully this venerable—using suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and developing their faculties—will realize for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the supreme end of the spiritual life, for the sake of which people rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness, and will live having achieved it. Seeing this fruit of diligence for this mendicant, I say that they must be diligent.
translations.mn70:15: And what person is freed both ways? It's when a person contacts with the body and abides in those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending form. And having seen with wisdom, their defilements are ended. This person is called freed both ways. I say that this mendicant need not be diligent. Why is that? They have already been diligent. They are incapable of being negligent.
translations.mn70:12: Mendicants, I don't say that all mendicants must be diligent. Nor do I say that all mendicants need not be diligent. Those mendicants who are perfected—who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own goal, utterly ended the fetters of existence, and are rightly freed through final knowledge—I say that such mendicants need not be diligent. Why is that? They have already been diligent. They are incapable of being negligent.
translations.mn6:2: "Mendicants, live with your ethical conduct complete and the monastic code complete. Live restrained in the monastic code, conducting yourselves well and seeking alms in suitable places. Seeing danger in the slightest fault, keep the rules you've undertaken.
translations.mn70:14: These seven persons are found in the world. What seven? One freed both ways, one freed by wisdom, a body witness, one attained to view, one freed by faith, a follower of the teachings, and a follower by faith.
translations.mn70:13: But those mendicants who are trainees, who haven't achieved their heart's desire, but live aspiring for the supreme sanctuary from the yoke—I say that such mendicants must be diligent. Why is that? Hopefully these venerables—using suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and developing their faculties—will realize for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the supreme end of the spiritual life, for the sake of which people rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness, and will live having achieved it. Seeing this fruit of diligence for these mendicants, I say that they must be diligent.
translations.mn6:8: Mendicant, should a mendicant wish: 'May I prevail over fear and dread, and may fear and dread not prevail over me. May I live having overcome fear and dread whenever they arise,' they should fulfill their ethical conduct … and cultivate empty places.
translations.mn6:6: Mendicant, should a mendicant wish: 'When deceased relatives and family members who have passed away recollect me with a confident mind, may that be very fruitful and beneficial for them,' they should fulfill their ethical conduct, be committed to inner serenity of mind, not neglect absorption, be endowed with discernment, and cultivate empty places.
translations.mn70:20: And what person, mendicants, is a follower of the teaching? Here, mendicants, a certain person does not dwell having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms, yet having seen with wisdom, some of their defilements are destroyed, and the teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are accepted by them after being pondered to a sufficient degree with wisdom, and they also have these qualities, namely: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom. This person, mendicants, is called a follower of the teaching. For this mendicant too, mendicants, I say 'diligence is to be practiced.' Why is that? Perhaps this venerable one, using suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, balancing the faculties—for the sake of which gentlemen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, that unsurpassed—culmination of the spiritual life, might in this very life realize for themselves with direct knowledge, and having entered upon it, dwell in it. Seeing this fruit of diligence for this mendicant, mendicants, I say 'diligence is to be practiced.'
translations.mn70:22: Mendicants, I do not speak of the attainment of final knowledge right from the start; rather, mendicants, there is gradual training, gradual practice, gradual progress, and then the attainment of final knowledge.
translations.mn70:23: And how, mendicants, is there gradual training, gradual practice, gradual progress, and then the attainment of final knowledge? Here, mendicants, one who has faith approaches; approaching, they attend; attending, they lend an ear; lending an ear, they hear the teaching; having heard, they remember the teaching; they examine the meaning of teachings they have remembered; examining the meaning, the teachings are accepted after reflection; when the teachings are accepted after reflection, desire arises; with desire arisen, they make effort; having made effort, they weigh it up; having weighed it up, they strive; being resolute, they realize the supreme truth with the body, and penetrating it with wisdom, they see.
translations.mn70:24: That faith, mendicants, was not there; that approaching, mendicants, was not there; that attending, mendicants, was not there; that lending an ear, mendicants, was not there; that hearing the teaching, mendicants, was not there; that remembering the teaching, mendicants, was not there; that examining the meaning, mendicants, was not there; that acceptance of teachings after reflection, mendicants, was not there; that desire, mendicants, was not there; that effort, mendicants, was not there; that weighing up, mendicants, was not there; that striving, mendicants, was not there. You have practiced wrongly, mendicants, you have practiced incorrectly, mendicants. How far these foolish men have strayed from this teaching and discipline!
translations.mn70:25: There is, mendicants, a four-part explanation, which when stated, a wise person would understand the meaning before long. I will state it to you, mendicants; will you understand it from me?
translations.mn70:3: Then the Buddha, wandering on tour through the Kāsī country, arrived at a town of the Kāsīs called Kīṭāgiri. There the Buddha stayed at Kīṭāgiri, a town of the Kāsīs.
translations.mn70:26: "Mendicants, even a teacher who values material things, an heir to material things, living mixed up with material things—even for them such haggling doesn't apply: 'If we get this, we'll do it; if we don't get this, we won't do it.' How much more so when the Realized One lives completely detached from material things!
translations.mn75:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near the Kuru town named Kammāsadamma, on a grass mat in the fire chamber of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan.
translations.mn70:7: "Mendicants, don't you understand that I've taught the Dhamma like this: Here, when someone feels a certain kind of pleasant feeling, unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline. But when someone else feels the same kind of pleasant feeling, unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow. Here, when someone feels a certain kind of painful feeling, unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline. But when someone else feels the same kind of painful feeling, unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow. Here, when someone feels a certain kind of neutral feeling, unskillful qualities grow while skillful qualities decline. But when someone else feels the same kind of neutral feeling, unskillful qualities decline while skillful qualities grow?
translations.mn75:10: "Well, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly when I was a householder I amused myself, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual pleasures: with sights known by the eye that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, connected with sensuality, and arousing; with sounds known by the ear … with smells known by the nose … with tastes known by the tongue … with touches known by the body that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, connected with sensuality, and arousing. I had three palaces—one for the rainy season, one for winter, and one for summer. I stayed in the rainy season palace for the four months of the rainy season, entertained by musicians—none of them men—and I didn't come down from that palace. But some time later, having truly understood the origin, the ending, the gratification, the danger, and the escape when it comes to sensual pleasures, I gave up craving for sensual pleasures, I dispelled the fever of sensual pleasures, and I live without thirst, my mind inwardly at peace. I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I don't envy them, and I don't delight in that. Why is that? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unskillful qualities, which surpasses even divine bliss. Since I take pleasure in that, I don't envy what is inferior, and I don't delight in it.
translations.mn75:12: "In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly when I was a householder I amused myself, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual pleasures: with sights known by the eye that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, connected with sensuality, and arousing; with sounds known by the ear … with smells known by the nose … with tastes known by the tongue … with touches known by the body that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, connected with sensuality, and arousing. But some time later, having truly understood the origin, the ending, the gratification, the danger, and the escape when it comes to sensual pleasures, I gave up craving for sensual pleasures, I dispelled the fever of sensual pleasures, and I live without thirst, my mind inwardly at peace. I see other beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I don't envy them, and I don't delight in that. Why is that? Because, Māgaṇḍiya, there is a delight apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unskillful qualities, which surpasses even divine bliss. Since I take pleasure in that, I don't envy what is inferior, and I don't delight in it.
translations.mn75:13: Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a leper with sores and blisters on his body, being eaten by worms, scratching the scabs off his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a pit of glowing coals. His friends and companions, relatives and kin would bring a doctor to treat him. The doctor would make medicine for him. Relying on that medicine he would be cured of leprosy, and he'd be healthy and happy, free and independent, able to go wherever he wants. Then he'd see another leper with sores and blisters on his body, being eaten by worms, scratching the scabs off his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a pit of glowing coals. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would that man envy that leper for the pit of glowing coals or the use of medicine?
translations.mn75:16: "In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past sensual pleasures were painful to touch, with great misery and great fever. In the future too sensual pleasures will be painful to touch, with great misery and great fever. And at present too sensual pleasures are painful to touch, with great misery and great fever. But these beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, have impaired faculties. So they get a distorted perception of sensual pleasures that are actually painful to touch as pleasant.
translations.mn75:17: Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there was a leper with sores and blisters on his body, being eaten by worms, scratching the scabs off his wounds with his nails, cauterizing his body over a pit of glowing coals. The more that leper cauterizes his body over the pit of glowing coals, the more those wounds become filthy, foul-smelling, and rotten. Yet he still feels a certain pleasure and satisfaction from scratching his wounds. In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, beings who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being consumed by craving for sensual pleasures, burning with the fever of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures. The more those beings indulge in sensual pleasures, the more their craving for sensual pleasures grows, and the more they burn with the fever of sensual pleasures. Yet they still feel a certain pleasure and satisfaction dependent on the five kinds of sensual pleasures.
translations.mn75:2: Then in the morning, the Buddha dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kammāsadhamma for alms. After walking for alms in Kammāsadhamma, after the meal, on returning from the alms round, he went to a certain grove for the day's meditation. Having entered that grove, he sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day's meditation.
translations.mn75:24: In the same way, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: 'This is health, this is Nibbāna,' you would know health, you would see Nibbāna. With the arising of your vision, the desire and lust for the five aggregates of clinging would be abandoned in you. And it would occur to you: 'For a long time indeed I have been cheated, deceived, and deluded by this mind. For when clinging, I was clinging just to form, when clinging, I was clinging just to feeling, when clinging, I was clinging just to perception, when clinging, I was clinging just to formations, when clinging, I was clinging just to consciousness. With clinging as condition, there is existence for me; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.mn75:27: "Māgaṇḍiya, when someone who formerly followed another sect wishes to go forth and receive ordination in this teaching and training, they must spend four months on probation. At the end of four months, if the mendicants are satisfied, they give them the going forth and ordination into monkhood. However, I have recognized individual differences in this matter.
translations.mn75:3: Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering about for exercise, approached the fire chamber of the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta. He saw a grass mat spread out in the fire chamber of the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta. Seeing this, he said to the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta: 'For whom is this grass mat spread out in Master Bhāradvāja's fire chamber? It seems like a bed fit for an ascetic.'
translations.mn75:6: The Buddha heard this conversation between the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya with his divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human. Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha emerged from seclusion and approached the fire chamber of the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta. He sat down on the grass mat that had been spread out. Then the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The Buddha said to the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta sitting to one side: 'Bhāradvāja, did you have some conversation with the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya concerning this grass mat?' When this was said, the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta was shocked and his hair stood on end. He said to the Buddha: 'We were just about to tell Master Gotama about this, but Master Gotama has already told us what was unspoken.'
translations.mn77:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground.
translations.mn77:10: There are, Udāyī, five other qualities because of which my disciples honor, respect, esteem, and venerate me, and having honored and respected me, they live in dependence on me. What five? Here, Udāyī, my disciples esteem me for higher virtue: 'The ascetic Gotama is virtuous, endowed with the supreme aggregate of virtue.'
translations.mn77:15: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught my disciples the practice by which, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the four establishments of mindfulness. Here, Udāyī, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … he dwells contemplating mind in mind … he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure toward the world. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:16: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught my disciples the practice by which, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the four right strivings. Here, Udāyī, a monk generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states, he makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives; he generates desire for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states, he makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives; he generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, he makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives; he generates desire for the continuation, non-confusion, increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states, he makes effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:17: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught my disciples the practice by which, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the four bases of psychic power. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving; he develops the basis of psychic power endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:18: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught my disciples the practice by which, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the five faculties. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops the faculty of faith leading to peace, leading to enlightenment; he develops the faculty of energy … he develops the faculty of mindfulness … he develops the faculty of concentration … he develops the faculty of wisdom leading to peace, leading to enlightenment. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:2: At that time many well-known wanderers were staying at the Peacocks' Feeding Ground, the wanderers' park, such as Annabhāra, Varadhara, the wanderer Sakuludāyī, and other well-known wanderers.
translations.mn77:20: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have taught my disciples the practice by which, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the seven factors of enlightenment. Here, Udāyī, a monk develops the mindfulness factor of enlightenment based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in release; he develops the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment … he develops the energy factor of enlightenment … he develops the rapture factor of enlightenment … he develops the tranquility factor of enlightenment … he develops the concentration factor of enlightenment … he develops the equanimity factor of enlightenment based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in release. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:21: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udāyī, a mendicant develops right view, develops right intention, develops right speech, develops right action, develops right livelihood, develops right effort, develops right mindfulness, develops right immersion. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:22: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the eight liberations. Having form, one sees forms. This is the first liberation. Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally. This is the second liberation. One is focused only on the beautiful. This is the third liberation. Going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite', one enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite space. This is the fourth liberation. Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite', one enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite consciousness. This is the fifth liberation. Going totally beyond the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing', one enters and dwells in the dimension of nothingness. This is the sixth liberation. Going totally beyond the dimension of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. This is the seventh liberation. Going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This is the eighth liberation. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:24: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the ten kasiṇa bases. One perceives the earth kasiṇa above, below, across, non-dual, and limitless. One perceives the water kasiṇa … One perceives the fire kasiṇa … One perceives the air kasiṇa … One perceives the blue kasiṇa … One perceives the yellow kasiṇa … One perceives the red kasiṇa … One perceives the white kasiṇa … One perceives the space kasiṇa … One perceives the consciousness kasiṇa above, below, across, non-dual, and limitless. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:25: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples develop the four jhānas. Here, Udāyī, a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, and the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. They drench, steep, fill, and pervade this body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. There is no part of their whole body that is not pervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Suppose, Udāyī, a skilled bathman or bathman's apprentice were to heap bathing powder in a bronze dish, and knead it while gradually sprinkling water. That ball of bathing powder would be soaked, saturated, and suffused with moisture inside and out, yet would not drip. In the same way, Udāyī, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. There is no part of their whole body that is not pervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.mn77:26: Furthermore, Udāyī, a mendicant, with the stilling of thought and examination, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence … They drench, steep, fill, and pervade this body with the rapture and pleasure born of immersion. There is no part of their whole body that is not pervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of immersion. Suppose, Udāyī, there were a deep lake with water welling up. It had no inlet for water from the east, west, north, or south, and no rainfall to refill it from time to time. But the cool water welling up from the bottom would drench, steep, fill, and pervade that lake. There would be no part of that whole lake that was not pervaded by cool water. In the same way, Udāyī, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this body with the rapture and pleasure born of immersion. There is no part of their whole body that is not pervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of immersion.
translations.mn77:27: Furthermore, Udāyī, a mendicant, with the fading away of rapture … enters and dwells in the third jhāna. They drench, steep, fill, and pervade this body with the pleasure free from rapture. There is no part of their whole body that is not pervaded by the pleasure free from rapture. Suppose, Udāyī, in a pond of blue water lilies, or red or white lotuses, some of the blue water lilies, or red or white lotuses, are born in the water, grow in the water, and thrive submerged in the water, being nourished from the bottom. They are drenched, steeped, filled, and pervaded from root to tip with cool water. There is no part of those blue water lilies, or red or white lotuses, that is not pervaded by cool water. In the same way, Udāyī, a mendicant drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this body with the pleasure free from rapture. There is no part of their whole body that is not pervaded by the pleasure free from rapture.
translations.mn77:28: Furthermore, Udāyī, a mendicant, giving up pleasure and pain, and with the previous ending of happiness and sadness, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which has neither pleasure nor pain, and purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. They sit pervading this body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of their whole body that is not pervaded by a pure, bright mind. Suppose, Udāyī, a man were to sit wrapped from head to foot with a white cloth. There would be no part of his whole body that was not covered by the white cloth. In the same way, Udāyī, a mendicant sits pervading this body with a pure, bright mind. There is no part of their whole body that is not pervaded by a pure, bright mind. And many of my disciples dwell having reached the perfection and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:3: Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the Buddha: 'It's too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha. Why don't I go to the Peacocks' Feeding Ground, the wanderers' park, to see the wanderer Sakuludāyī.'
translations.mn77:32: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples, with clairaudience that is purified and surpasses the human, hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near. Suppose, Udāyī, a powerful conch blower could make themselves heard in the four directions without difficulty. In the same way, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples, with clairaudience that is purified and surpasses the human, hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, whether far or near. And many of my disciples dwell having attained the perfection and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:34: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples recollect their many kinds of past lives, that is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of cosmic contraction, many eons of cosmic expansion, many eons of cosmic contraction and expansion: 'There I was named so-and-so, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere. There too I was named so-and-so, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my lifespan. Passing away from there, I was reborn here.' Thus they recollect their many kinds of past lives with their features and details. Suppose, Udāyī, a person were to go from their own village to another village, and from that village to yet another village, and then return from that village to their own village. They would think: 'I went from my own village to that village, where I stood like this, sat like this, spoke like this, and kept silent like this. From that village I went to that other village, where I stood like this, sat like this, spoke like this, and kept silent like this. And from that village I returned to my own village.' In the same way, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples recollect their many kinds of past lives, that is: one birth … thus they recollect their many kinds of past lives with their features and details. And many of my disciples dwell having attained the perfection and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:35: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples, with the divine eye that is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good places and bad—and they understand how beings fare according to their deeds: 'These beings who engaged in misconduct of body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook actions based on wrong view—with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a place of loss, a bad destination, the underworld, hell. But these beings who engaged in good conduct of body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, held right view, and undertook actions based on right view—with the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.' Thus with the divine eye that is purified and surpasses the human, they see beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good places and bad—and they understand how beings fare according to their deeds. Suppose, Udāyī, there were two houses with doors. A person with good eyesight standing in the middle could see people entering and leaving the houses, walking and wandering about. In the same way, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples, with the divine eye that is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and being reborn … and they understand how beings fare according to their deeds. And many of my disciples dwell having attained the perfection and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:36: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples, with the ending of defilements, realize for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life the defilementless freedom of mind and freedom by wisdom, and having entered upon it, they dwell in it. Suppose, Udāyī, there were a lake in a mountain glen, clear, transparent, and unclouded. A person with good eyesight standing on the bank would see shells, gravel, and pebbles, and schools of fish swimming about and resting. They would think: 'This lake is clear, transparent, and unclouded, and here are these shells, gravel, and pebbles, and schools of fish swimming about and resting.' In the same way, Udāyī, I have explained a practice to my disciples, practicing in accordance with which my disciples, with the ending of defilements, realize for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life the defilementless freedom of mind and freedom by wisdom, and having entered upon it, they dwell in it. And many of my disciples dwell having attained the perfection and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:5: Then the Buddha went to the wanderer Sakuludāyī. Then the wanderer Sakuludāyī said to the Buddha: 'Come, venerable sir, Blessed One. Welcome, venerable sir, Blessed One. It has been a long time, venerable sir, since the Blessed One made an occasion to come here. Please sit, venerable sir, Blessed One; this seat is prepared.' The Buddha sat on the prepared seat. The wanderer Sakuludāyī also took a low seat and sat to one side. The Buddha said to the wanderer Sakuludāyī sitting to one side: 'What were you sitting here discussing just now, Udāyī? And what conversation was left unfinished?'
translations.mn77:7: 'But how many qualities do you see in me, Udāyī, because of which my disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate me, and live in dependence on me, honoring and respecting me?'
translations.mn77:9: 'The ascetic Gotama eats little and praises eating little.' If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this, and were to live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me, Udāyī, I have disciples who eat only a cupful or half a cupful, a wood-apple's worth or half a wood-apple's worth. But sometimes, Udāyī, I eat from this bowl filled to the brim or even more. 'The ascetic Gotama eats little and praises eating little.' If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this, and were to live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me, those disciples of mine who eat only a cupful or half a cupful, a wood-apple's worth or half a wood-apple's worth, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this reason, nor would they live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me. 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe and praises contentment with any kind of robe.' If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this, and were to live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me, Udāyī, I have disciples who are rag-robe wearers, wearing coarse robes, who collect rags from cemeteries, rubbish heaps, or shops, make them into a patchwork robe, and wear it. But sometimes, Udāyī, I wear robes given by householders, finely woven, as soft as gourd-down. 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of robe and praises contentment with any kind of robe.' If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this, and were to live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me, those disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers, wearing coarse robes, who collect rags from cemeteries, rubbish heaps, or shops, make them into a patchwork robe, and wear it, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this reason, nor would they live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me. 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood and praises contentment with any kind of almsfood.' If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this, and were to live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me, Udāyī, I have disciples who are almsfood eaters, who go on continuous almsround, who delight in the practice of gleaning, who, having entered among houses, do not accept even when invited to sit. But sometimes, Udāyī, I eat on invitation—rice with the dark grains picked out, with many sauces and curries. 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of almsfood and praises contentment with any kind of almsfood.' If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this, and were to live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me, those disciples of mine who are almsfood eaters, who go on continuous almsround, who delight in the practice of gleaning, who, having entered among houses, do not accept even when invited to sit, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this reason, nor would they live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me. 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging and praises contentment with any kind of lodging.' If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this, and were to live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me, Udāyī, I have disciples who are tree-root dwellers, open-air dwellers, who for eight months do not go under a roof. But sometimes, Udāyī, I live in gabled houses, plastered inside and out, draft-free, with bolts fastened and shutters closed. 'The ascetic Gotama is content with any kind of lodging and praises contentment with any kind of lodging.' If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this, and were to live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me, those disciples of mine who are tree-root dwellers, open-air dwellers, who for eight months do not go under a roof, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this reason, nor would they live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me. 'The ascetic Gotama is secluded and praises seclusion.' If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this, and were to live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me, Udāyī, I have disciples who are forest dwellers, who frequent remote lodgings, having plunged into remote forest and wilderness lodgings they dwell there, and they come to the midst of the Sangha every fortnight for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. But sometimes, Udāyī, I live surrounded by monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen, kings and royal ministers, sectarians and their disciples. 'The ascetic Gotama is secluded and praises seclusion.' If my disciples were to honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this, and were to live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me, those disciples of mine who are forest dwellers, who frequent remote lodgings, having plunged into remote forest and wilderness lodgings they dwell there, and come to the midst of the Sangha every fortnight for the recitation of the Pātimokkha, would not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for this reason, nor would they live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me. Thus, Udāyī, my disciples do not honor, respect, revere, and venerate me for these five reasons, nor do they live in dependence on me after honoring and respecting me.
translations.mn7:11: 'This has been given up by me, discarded, released, abandoned, relinquished'—gaining inspiration in the meaning, gaining inspiration in the Dhamma, gaining gladness connected with the Dhamma; when one is gladdened, rapture arises; when the mind is uplifted by rapture, the body becomes tranquil; one tranquil in body feels pleasure; the mind of one feeling pleasure becomes concentrated.
translations.mn7:13: They meditate spreading a heart full of love to one direction, and to the second, and to the third, and to the fourth. In the same way above, below, across, everywhere, all around, they spread a heart full of love to the whole world—abundant, expansive, limitless, free of enmity and ill will.
translations.mn7:17: They understand: 'There is this, there is what is inferior, there is what is superior, there is a higher escape from this perception.'
translations.mn7:18: Knowing and seeing like this, their mind is freed from the defilements of sensuality, desire for rebirth, and ignorance. When they're freed, they know they're freed. They understand: 'Rebirth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no return to any state of existence.' This is called, mendicants: 'A mendicant who has bathed with the inner bathing.'
translations.mn7:19: Now at that time the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja was sitting not far from the Buddha. He said to the Buddha: 'But does Master Gotama go to the Bāhukā river to bathe?' 'Brahmin, what is the Bāhukā river for? What can the Bāhukā river do?' 'Master Gotama, the Bāhukā river is agreed by many people to be a means of liberation. The Bāhukā river is agreed by many people to be a means of merit. Many people wash away their bad deeds in the Bāhukā river.'
translations.mn7:2: Suppose, mendicants, there was a cloth that was dirty and stained. Whatever dye the dyer applied—whether blue, yellow, red, or magenta—it would look poorly dyed and impure in color. Why is that? Because of the impurity of the cloth. In the same way, when the mind is defiled, a bad destination is to be expected. Suppose there was a cloth that was pure and clean. Whatever dye the dyer applied—whether blue, yellow, red, or magenta—it would look well dyed and pure in color. Why is that? Because of the purity of the cloth. In the same way, when the mind is undefiled, a good destination is to be expected.
translations.mn7:20: Then the Buddha addressed the brahmin Sundarika Bhāradvāja in verses: 'The Bāhukā, Adhikakkā, Gayā, Sundarikā, Sarassatī, Payāga, and the Bāhumatī river—a fool can plunge into them forever, but it won't purify their dark deeds. What can the Sundarikā do? What the Payāga or Bāhukā river? They cannot purify an evil-doer, a man who has done violent and cruel deeds. For one who is pure, it's always the spring festival; for one who is pure, it's always the sabbath. For one who is pure, with clean actions, their vows are always fulfilled. Bathe just here, brahmin, make yourself safe for all living beings. If you don't speak lies, if you don't harm living creatures, if you don't take what isn't given, if you're faithful and not stingy—what will you do by going to Gayā? Any well is your Gayā!'
translations.mn7:3: And what, mendicants, are the corruptions of the mind? Covetousness and immoral greed is a corruption of the mind. Ill will is a corruption of the mind. Anger is a corruption of the mind. Hostility is a corruption of the mind. Denigration is a corruption of the mind. Contempt is a corruption of the mind. Jealousy is a corruption of the mind. Stinginess is a corruption of the mind. Deceit is a corruption of the mind. Deviousness is a corruption of the mind. Obstinacy is a corruption of the mind. Aggression is a corruption of the mind. Conceit is a corruption of the mind. Arrogance is a corruption of the mind. Vanity is a corruption of the mind. Negligence is a corruption of the mind.
translations.mn7:6: They have experiential confidence in the teaching: 'The teaching is well explained by the Buddha—visible in this very life, immediately effective, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.'
translations.mn7:7: They have experiential confidence in the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Buddha's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This is the Saṅgha of the Buddha's disciples that is worthy of offerings dedicated to the gods, worthy of hospitality, worthy of a religious donation, worthy of greeting with joined palms, and is the supreme field of merit for the world.'
translations.mn82:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kurus together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a town of the Kurus named Thullakotthika.
translations.mn82:12: Then the gentleman Raṭṭhapāla got up, and when he had regained his strength he went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the gentleman Raṭṭhapāla said to the Buddha: 'Sir, I have my parents' permission to go forth from the lay life to homelessness. May the Buddha give me the going forth.'
translations.mn82:13: And the gentleman Raṭṭhapāla received the going forth and ordination in the Buddha's presence. Then, a fortnight after Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's ordination, the Buddha set out for Sāvatthī, having stayed in Thullakoṭṭhika as long as he wished. Traveling stage by stage, he arrived at Sāvatthī, where he stayed in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery.
