translations.mn82:14: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the supreme goal of the spiritual life for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness, and having entered upon it, he dwelt in it. He understood: 'Birth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' And Venerable Raṭṭhapāla became one of the arahants.
translations.mn82:16: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla rose from his seat, bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him, put his lodging in order, took his bowl and robe, and set out for Thullakoṭṭhika. Traveling stage by stage, he arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. There Venerable Raṭṭhapāla stayed in King Koravya's deer park at Thullakoṭṭhika. Then in the morning, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Thullakoṭṭhika for alms. Walking for alms from house to house in Thullakoṭṭhika, he approached his own father's residence.
translations.mn82:17: Now at that time Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father was having his hair combed in the middle porch. He saw Venerable Raṭṭhapāla coming from afar. Seeing him, he said: 'Our only son, dear and beloved, was made to go forth by these bald-headed ascetics.' Then at his own father's residence, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla received neither a gift nor a polite refusal; he only received abuse.
translations.mn82:18: Now at that time a female slave of Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's relatives wanted to throw away some day-old porridge. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to that female slave: 'Sister, if that is to be thrown away, pour it here into my bowl.' Then as the female slave was pouring that day-old porridge into Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's bowl, she recognized the features of his hands, feet, and voice. Then the female slave went to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother and said: 'Please know, madam, that the young master Raṭṭhapāla has arrived.' 'If what you say is true, I make you a free woman.' Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's mother went to his father and said: 'Please know, householder, that the gentleman Raṭṭhapāla has apparently arrived.'
translations.mn82:19: Now at that time Venerable Raṭṭhapāla was eating that day-old porridge leaning against a wall. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father approached him and said: 'Dear Raṭṭhapāla, is it really the case that you would eat day-old porridge? Shouldn't you go to your own home, dear Raṭṭhapāla?' 'Where would we have a home, householder, having gone forth from the lay life to homelessness? We are homeless, householder. We did go to your home, householder, but there we received neither a gift nor a polite refusal; we only received abuse.' 'Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, let us go to the house.' 'Enough, householder, my meal is finished for today.' 'Then, dear Raṭṭhapāla, please accept a meal for tomorrow.' Venerable Raṭṭhapāla consented by remaining silent.
translations.mn82:20: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father, understanding his consent, went to his own residence. Having had a large heap of gold and silver piled up and covered with mats, he addressed Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's former wives: 'Come, daughters-in-law, adorn yourselves with the ornaments that the gentleman Raṭṭhapāla used to find you dear and pleasing in.'
translations.mn82:21: Then when the night had passed, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father had delicious foods prepared in his own residence and announced the time to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'It is time, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.'
translations.mn82:22: Then in the morning, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to his own father's residence. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's father had the heap of gold and silver uncovered and said to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'This, dear Raṭṭhapāla, is your maternal inheritance; other wealth is paternal, and other is from your grandfather. It is possible, dear Raṭṭhapāla, to enjoy wealth and make merit. Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and make merit.' 'If you would do as I say, householder, you would have this heap of gold and silver loaded onto carts, taken out, and dumped in the middle of the Ganges river's current. Why is that? Because, householder, whatever sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise from it will arise for you.'
translations.mn82:23: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla's former wives each clasped his feet and said to him: 'What are they like, young master, those nymphs for whose sake you live the spiritual life?' 'We do not live the spiritual life for the sake of nymphs, sisters.' When Venerable Raṭṭhapāla addressed them as 'sisters,' they fainted and fell down right there.
translations.mn82:26: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having spoken these verses while still standing, went to King Koravya's Migācīra deer park. Having arrived, he sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day's meditation.
translations.mn82:27: Then King Koravya addressed the gamekeeper: 'Clean up the Migācīra pleasure garden, my good gamekeeper. We shall go to see the beautiful grounds.' 'Yes, Your Majesty,' the gamekeeper replied to King Koravya. While cleaning up the Migācīra, he saw Venerable Raṭṭhapāla sitting at the root of a certain tree for the day's meditation. Having seen him, he approached King Koravya and said: 'Your Majesty, the Migācīra is clean. And there is a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the leading family in this very Thullakotthita, whom you have often praised. He is sitting at the root of a certain tree for the day's meditation.' 'Then, my good gamekeeper, enough with the pleasure garden for today. We shall now pay respects to that Master Raṭṭhapāla.'
translations.mn82:29: 'Master Raṭṭhapāla, there are these four kinds of loss, due to which some people here shave off their hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness. What four? Loss through old age, loss through illness, loss of wealth, and loss of relatives.
translations.mn82:3: Then the brahmins and householders of Thullakotthita approached the Buddha. Having approached, some paid homage to the Buddha and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Buddha, and when the greetings and polite conversation were over, sat down to one side; some raised their joined palms toward the Buddha and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan before the Buddha and sat down to one side; some remained silent and sat down to one side. When the brahmins and householders of Thullakotthita were seated to one side, the Buddha instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened them with a Dhamma talk.
translations.mn82:34: These are the four kinds of loss, Master Raṭṭhapāla, due to which some people here shave off their hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness. Master Raṭṭhapāla has none of these. What did Master Raṭṭhapāla know or see or hear that he went forth from the lay life to homelessness?'
translations.mn82:35: 'Great king, there are four summaries of the Dhamma that have been taught by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having known and seen and heard which I went forth from the lay life to homelessness. What four?
translations.mn82:4: Now at that time a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, the son of the leading family in that very Thullakotthita, was sitting in that assembly. Then the clansman Raṭṭhapāla thought: 'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Buddha, it is not easy living at home to practice the spiritual life that is utterly perfect and pure, like a polished shell. Why don't I shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness?'
translations.mn95:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a village of the Kosalan brahmins named Opāsāda. There the Buddha stayed to the north of Opāsāda, in a forest of sal trees called the Gods' Grove.
translations.mn95:10: Then the brahmin Caṅkī, together with a large group of brahmins, approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side.
translations.mn9:11: But what is fuel, what is the origin of fuel, what is the cessation of fuel, and what is the practice that leads to the cessation of fuel? There are these four fuels for the maintenance of beings that already exist and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What four? Physical food, whether coarse or fine, is the first. Contact is the second. Mental intention is the third. Consciousness is the fourth. Fuel originates from craving. When craving ceases, fuel ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of fuel is simply this noble eightfold path, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
translations.mn95:20: When, upon investigating, they see that he is purified of qualities that defile, they place faith in him. Having faith, they approach. Approaching, they pay respect. Paying respect, they lend an ear. Lending an ear, they hear the teaching. Having heard, they memorize the teaching. They examine the meaning of the teachings they have memorized. Examining the meaning, they accept the teachings after reflection. When one has accepted the teachings after reflection, enthusiasm arises. When enthusiasm has arisen, one makes an effort. Having made an effort, one weighs it up. Having weighed it up, one strives. Striving, one personally realizes the ultimate truth and sees it, having penetrated it with wisdom. To this extent, Bhāradvāja, there is the awakening to truth; to this extent one awakens to truth; and to this extent we describe the awakening to truth. But this is not yet the attainment of truth.
translations.mn95:33: "But Master Gotama, what quality is most helpful for approaching? We ask Master Gotama about the quality most helpful for approaching.
translations.mn9:12: When a noble disciple understands fuel in this way, understands the origin of fuel in this way, understands the cessation of fuel in this way, and understands the practice that leads to the cessation of fuel in this way—having entirely abandoned the underlying tendency to greed, having dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion, having uprooted the underlying tendency to the view and conceit 'I am,' having abandoned ignorance and given rise to knowledge—they make an end of suffering in this very life. To this extent also, friends, a noble disciple has right view, their view is straight, they have unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and they have arrived at this true Dhamma.
translations.mn95:2: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī was residing at Opāsāda, a place teeming with living creatures, with grass, wood, and water, with grain, a royal endowment given by King Pasenadi of Kosala, a royal gift, a brahmin grant.
translations.mn9:15: And what, friends, is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering, association with what is disliked is suffering, separation from what is liked is suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering, in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering—this, friends, is called suffering.
translations.mn9:16: And what, friends, is the origin of suffering? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence—this, friends, is called the origin of suffering.
translations.mn9:17: And what, friends, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it—this, friends, is called the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:18: And what, friends, is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is just this noble eightfold path; that is, right view … right concentration—this, friends, is called the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn9:4: And what, friends, is the unwholesome, what is the root of the unwholesome, what is the wholesome, what is the root of the wholesome? Killing living beings, friends, is unwholesome, taking what is not given is unwholesome, sexual misconduct is unwholesome, false speech is unwholesome, divisive speech is unwholesome, harsh speech is unwholesome, idle chatter is unwholesome, covetousness is unwholesome, ill will is unwholesome, wrong view is unwholesome—this, friends, is called the unwholesome.
translations.mn9:5: And what, friends, is the root of the unwholesome? Greed is a root of the unwholesome, hatred is a root of the unwholesome, delusion is a root of the unwholesome—this, friends, is called the root of the unwholesome.
translations.mn9:7: And what, friends, is the root of the wholesome? Non-greed is a root of the wholesome, non-hatred is a root of the wholesome, non-delusion is a root of the wholesome—this, friends, is called the root of the wholesome.
translations.mn9:70: And what, friends, are the taints, what is the origin of the taints, what is the cessation of the taints, what is the way leading to the cessation of the taints? There are these three taints, friends: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of ignorance. With the arising of ignorance there is the arising of the taints, with the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of the taints. This noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of the taints; that is, right view … right concentration.
translations.mn9:8: When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands the unwholesome, thus understands the root of the unwholesome, thus understands the wholesome, thus understands the root of the wholesome, having entirely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust, having removed the underlying tendency to aversion, having uprooted the underlying tendency to the view and conceit 'I am,' having abandoned ignorance and aroused true knowledge, he here and now makes an end of suffering—in that way too, friends, a noble disciple is one of right view, whose view is straight, who has perfect confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma.
translations.sn1.17:3: Like a tortoise drawing its limbs into its own shell, a monk, drawing in the mind's thoughts, independent, not harming others, fully quenched, would not blame anyone.
translations.sn1.20:21: But having fully understood what can be expressed, one does not conceive 'the one who expresses'. For that does not exist for them, that by which one might describe them—that does not exist for them. If you understand, spirit, say so.
translations.sn1.36:6: Don't devote yourself to negligence, nor to intimacy with sensual delight. For one who meditates diligently attains the highest happiness.
translations.sn1.25:5: They would say 'they say to me,' having understood the world's conventions as a skilled person; they would use such expressions as mere conventions.
translations.sn1.38:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi deer park. Now at that time the Buddha's foot had been cut by a stone splinter. The Buddha's pain was severe—physical feelings that were painful, sharp, severe, acute, unpleasant, and disagreeable. But the Buddha endured it, mindful and aware, without being distressed. Then the Buddha spread out his outer robe folded in four and lay down in the lion's posture on his right side, placing one foot on top of the other, mindful and aware.
translations.sn1.38:10: Overcome by craving, bound by vows and rituals, practicing harsh austerities for a hundred years; but their minds are not rightly freed—those of inferior nature don't reach the far shore.
translations.sn1.38:11: There's no taming here for one who loves conceit, no sagacity for one who is not composed. Living alone in the wilderness, heedless, one cannot cross over to the far shore of death's domain.
translations.sn1.38:12: Having abandoned conceit, well-composed, with clear mind, everywhere freed; living alone in the wilderness, heedful, one can cross over to the far shore of death's domain.
translations.sn1.38:9: Brahmins learned in the five Vedas may practice austerities for a hundred years; but their minds are not rightly freed—those of inferior nature don't reach the far shore.
translations.sn1.41:4: What is given yields pleasant fruit, but what is not given does not. Thieves take it, or kings, fire burns it, or it's lost.
translations.sn1.41:5: Then in the end one leaves the body together with possessions. Knowing this, the wise person should enjoy and give. Having given and enjoyed according to their means, blameless they go to a heavenly place.
translations.sn1.42:3: The one who gives a dwelling is the giver of all. But the one who teaches the Dhamma is the giver of the deathless.
translations.sn11.24:4: 'May anger come under your control, and may there be no falling out with friends. Do not blame the blameless, and do not speak divisively. For anger crushes evil people like a mountain.'
translations.sn11.3:10: If you cannot recollect me, then recollect the teaching: 'The teaching is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be personally experienced by the wise.' For when you recollect the teaching, mendicants, whatever fear or terror or hair-raising there may be will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:11: If you cannot recollect the teaching, then recollect the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.' For when you recollect the Saṅgha, mendicants, whatever fear or terror or hair-raising there may be will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:12: Why is that? Because, mendicants, the Realized One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One, is free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, fearless, unafraid, unalarmed, not fleeing.
translations.sn11.3:14: If you cannot recollect the Buddha, the eldest in the world, the bull among men, then you should recollect the Dhamma, emancipating, well-taught.
translations.sn11.14:6: Therefore the wise should cultivate faith and virtue, confidence and vision of the Dhamma, remembering the teaching of the Buddhas.'
translations.sn11.3:13: 'In the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty hut, mendicants, recollect the Awakened One, and there will be no fear for you.
translations.sn11.15:1: At Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One: 'What, venerable sir, is a delightful place?'

translations.sn1.7:2: 'Those who have not fully understood the teachings, who are led astray by the doctrines of others—they are asleep and do not awaken; it is time for them to awaken.'

translations.sn11.22:4: 'My mind is not easily crushed, nor am I easily swept away by anger. I do not stay angry for long; anger does not persist in me.
translations.sn11.24:2: 'There are, mendicants, these two fools. Which two? One who does not see a transgression as a transgression, and one who does not properly accept another's confession of a transgression—these, mendicants, are the two fools. There are, mendicants, these two wise people. Which two? One who sees a transgression as a transgression, and one who properly accepts another's confession of a transgression—these, mendicants, are the two wise people.
translations.sn11.3:16: Thus for those recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, mendicants, there will be no fear, no terror, no hair-raising.'
translations.sn11.5:12: One acts for the good of both, one's own and that of the other; knowing the other is provoked, one who is mindful becomes calm.
translations.sn11.5:14: When these verses were spoken by Sakka, lord of the gods, the gods applauded, while the demons were silent. Then the attendants of the gods and the demons said: 'The verses spoken by Vepacitti, lord of demons, involve punishment and violence, and thus quarreling, conflict, and strife. The victory goes to Sakka, lord of the gods, because of his well-spoken words.' And so, mendicants, the victory went to Sakka, lord of the gods, because of his well-spoken words.
translations.sn11.5:4: 'This alone I consider to be the restraint of a fool: knowing the other is provoked, one who is mindful becomes calm.'
translations.sn11.3:4: If you don't look up at my banner-top, then look up at the banner-top of Pajāpati, lord of gods. For when you look up at the banner-top of Pajāpati, lord of gods, whatever fear or terror or hair-raising you may have will be abandoned.
translations.sn12.15:2: "This world, Kaccāna, for the most part depends on a duality—on the notion of existence and the notion of non-existence. But for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with right wisdom, there is no notion of non-existence regarding the world. And for one who sees the cessation of the world as it really is with right wisdom, there is no notion of existence regarding the world. This world, Kaccāna, for the most part is bound by engagement, clinging, and adherence. But one who does not engage with or cling to that engagement and clinging, that mental fixation, adherence, and underlying tendency, who does not take a stand about 'my self'—such a one does not doubt or waver that what arises is only suffering arising, and what ceases is only suffering ceasing. Their knowledge about this is independent of others. To this extent, Kaccāna, there is right view.
translations.sn11.3:8: Why is that? Because Sakka, lord of gods, is not free from lust, not free from hate, not free from delusion—he is fearful, anxious, alarmed, and prone to flee.
translations.sn11.3:3: 'If, dear sirs, when the gods have gone into battle, fear or terror or hair-raising should arise, then at that time look up at my banner-top. For when you look up at my banner-top, whatever fear or terror or hair-raising you may have will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.5:2: 'More fools would break out, if there were no one to restrain them; therefore the wise one should restrain the fool with a strong punishment.'
translations.sn12.12:1: At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings that already exist and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What four? Physical food, whether gross or subtle; contact is the second; mental intention is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings that already exist and for the support of those seeking a new existence.
translations.sn12.17:5: 'The one who acts is the same one who experiences the result'—Kassapa, saying 'suffering is self-made' to one who has been here from the beginning, this amounts to eternalism. 'One acts and another experiences the result'—Kassapa, saying 'suffering is made by another' to one who is struck by feeling, this amounts to annihilationism. Not approaching either of these extremes, Kassapa, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness comes to be … Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations comes cessation of consciousness … Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.sn12.17:6: When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Blessed One: 'Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned … "Those with eyes will see forms"—in the same way the Dhamma has been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May I receive the going forth in the Blessed One's presence, may I receive the full ordination.'
translations.sn12.17:7: 'Kassapa, one who formerly belonged to another sect and desires the going forth and full ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline must spend four months on probation. At the end of four months, if the monks are satisfied, they give him the going forth and full ordination to the state of a monk. But I recognize individual differences in this matter.'
translations.sn12.18:4: 'That feeling and the one who feels it are the same'—Timbaruka, to one who has been here from the beginning, I do not say 'pleasure and pain are self-made.' 'The feeling is one thing and the one who feels it is another'—Timbaruka, to one who is struck by feeling, I do not say 'pleasure and pain are made by another.' Not approaching either of these extremes, Timbaruka, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness comes to be … Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations comes cessation of consciousness … Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.sn12.19:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. 'Monks, for the fool, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has thus originated. So there is this body and external name-and-form—thus there is this duality. Dependent on the duality there is contact through the six sense bases, contacted through which the fool experiences pleasure and pain, or through one or another of them.
translations.sn12.19:2: Monks, for the wise person, hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, this body has thus originated. So there is this body and external name-and-form—thus there is this duality. Dependent on the duality there is contact through the six sense bases, contacted through which the wise person experiences pleasure and pain, or through one or another of them.
translations.sn12.19:3: Therein, monks, what is the distinction, what is the difference, what is the disparity between the wise person and the fool?' 'Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, have the Blessed One as refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.'
translations.sn12.19:5: 'The ignorance by which the fool was hindered and the craving by which he was fettered, through which this body originated—that ignorance has not been abandoned by the fool and that craving has not been exhausted. For what reason? Because the fool has not lived the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, at the breakup of the body, the fool goes on to another body. Going on to another body, he is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. He is not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.23:5: And what, monks, is the proximate cause of craving? 'Feeling' should be the answer … 'Contact' should be the answer … 'The six sense bases' should be the answer … 'Name-and-form' should be the answer … 'Consciousness' should be the answer … 'Volitional formations' should be the answer. Monks, I say that volitional formations have a proximate cause, not that they are without a proximate cause. And what, monks, is the proximate cause of volitional formations? 'Ignorance' should be the answer.
translations.sn12.23:6: Thus, monks, with ignorance as proximate cause, volitional formations; with volitional formations as proximate cause, consciousness; with consciousness as proximate cause, name-and-form; with name-and-form as proximate cause, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as proximate cause, contact; with contact as proximate cause, feeling; with feeling as proximate cause, craving; with craving as proximate cause, clinging; with clinging as proximate cause, existence; with existence as proximate cause, birth; with birth as proximate cause, suffering; with suffering as proximate cause, faith; with faith as proximate cause, gladness; with gladness as proximate cause, rapture; with rapture as proximate cause, tranquility; with tranquility as proximate cause, happiness; with happiness as proximate cause, concentration; with concentration as proximate cause, knowledge and vision of things as they really are; with knowledge and vision of things as they really are as proximate cause, disenchantment; with disenchantment as proximate cause, dispassion; with dispassion as proximate cause, liberation; with liberation as proximate cause, knowledge of destruction.
translations.sn12.23:7: Just as, monks, when the gods pour down heavy rain on the upper mountains, the water flows down along the slopes and fills the mountain clefts, gullies, and creeks. These being full, fill up the pools. The pools being full, fill up the lakes. The lakes being full, fill up the small rivers. The small rivers being full, fill up the great rivers. The great rivers being full, fill up the great ocean.
translations.sn12.25:10: Ānanda, when there is the body, because of bodily intention, pleasure and pain arise internally. Ānanda, when there is speech, because of verbal intention, pleasure and pain arise internally. Ānanda, when there is the mind, because of mental intention, pleasure and pain arise internally—and with ignorance as condition.
translations.sn12.25:11: Either they generate that bodily volition themselves, which is a condition for that internal pleasure and pain to arise. Or others generate that bodily volition for them, which is a condition for that internal pleasure and pain to arise. Either they generate that bodily volition with full awareness, which is a condition for that internal pleasure and pain to arise. Or they generate that bodily volition without full awareness, which is a condition for that internal pleasure and pain to arise.
translations.sn12.25:3: 'Pleasure and pain are dependently originated,' said the Buddha. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. Saying this, one would be saying what the Buddha has said, and would not misrepresent him with what is untrue. One would explain in line with the teaching, and no legitimate criticism could be grounds for censure.
translations.sn12.25:6: Venerable Ānanda heard this discussion between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija. Then Venerable Ānanda went to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and informed the Buddha of the entire discussion between Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Bhūmija.
translations.sn12.2:6: And what, mendicants, is grasping? There are these four kinds of grasping: grasping at sensual pleasures, grasping at views, grasping at precepts and observances, and grasping at theories of a self. This is called grasping.
translations.sn12.2:14: And what, mendicants, is ignorance? Not knowing about suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice that leads to the cessation of suffering. This is called ignorance.
translations.sn12.25:5: Now, reverend, those ascetics and brahmins who teach about karma and assert that pleasure and pain are made by oneself—it is impossible for them to experience that without contact. Those who … Those who … Those ascetics and brahmins who teach about karma and assert that pleasure and pain are made neither by oneself nor by another, but arise by chance—it is impossible for them to experience that without contact.
translations.sn12.2:11: And what, mendicants, is name and form? Feeling, perception, intention, contact, and attention—this is called name. The four great elements and form derived from the four great elements—this is called form. Such is name and such is form. This is called name and form.
translations.sn12.2:13: And what, mendicants, are volitional formations? There are these three kinds of volitional formations: bodily, verbal, and mental. These are called volitional formations.
translations.sn12.31:3: How should the meaning of this brief statement be understood in detail?" When this was said, Venerable Sāriputta remained silent.
translations.sn12.2:12: And what, mendicants, is consciousness? There are these six classes of consciousness: eye consciousness, ear consciousness, nose consciousness, tongue consciousness, body consciousness, and mind consciousness. This is called consciousness.
translations.sn12.25:4: Now, reverend, those ascetics and brahmins who teach about karma and assert that pleasure and pain are made by oneself—that too is conditioned by contact. Those who … Those who … Those ascetics and brahmins who teach about karma and assert that pleasure and pain are made neither by oneself nor by another, but arise by chance—that too is conditioned by contact.
translations.sn12.2:5: And what, mendicants, is continued existence? There are these three kinds of continued existence: existence in the sensual realm, existence in the realm of luminous form, and existence in the formless realm. This is called continued existence.
translations.sn12.31:2: 'Those who have comprehended the teachings, and the many trainees here—being a wise one, when asked, tell me, dear sir, how they should conduct themselves.'
translations.sn12.38:2: If, mendicants, one does not intend and does not plan, but still has underlying tendencies, this becomes a basis for the continuation of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is a support for consciousness. When that consciousness is established and grows, there is future rebirth into a new state of existence. When there is future rebirth into a new state of existence, future birth, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.35:5: Mendicant, with the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, all those various speculations, contortions, and vacillations—such as 'What is old age and death? And whose is this old age and death?' or 'Old age and death is one thing, the one to whom old age and death belongs is another,' or 'The soul and the body are the same,' or 'The soul and the body are different'—all these are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future.
translations.sn12.35:7: Mendicant, with the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance, all those various speculations, contortions, and vacillations—such as 'What is existence?' … 'What is clinging?' … 'What is craving?' … 'What is feeling?' … 'What is contact?' … 'What is the six sense bases?' … 'What is name and form?' … 'What is consciousness?' …
translations.sn12.51:5: Then, investigating further, they investigate: 'But what is the source of this birth, what is its origin, what is its birthplace, what is its provenance? When what exists does birth come to be? When what does not exist does birth not come to be?' Investigating, they understand thus: 'Birth has existence as its source, existence as its origin, existence as its birthplace, existence as its provenance. When there is existence, birth comes to be. When there is no existence, birth does not come to be.'
translations.sn12.44:3: Ear consciousness arises dependent on the ear and sounds … Nose consciousness arises dependent on the nose and odors … Tongue consciousness arises dependent on the tongue and tastes … Body consciousness arises dependent on the body and touches … Mind consciousness arises dependent on the mind and mental phenomena. The meeting of the three is contact. Feeling is conditioned by contact … Rebirth is a condition for old age and death, and for sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress to arise. This, mendicants, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.51:14: "When there are no choices at all, with the cessation of choices, would consciousness still be found?
translations.sn12.44:4: And what, mendicants, is the ending of the world? Eye consciousness arises dependent on the eye and sights. The meeting of the three is contact. Feeling is conditioned by contact. Craving is conditioned by feeling. When that craving fades away and ceases with nothing left over, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases. This, mendicants, is the ending of the world.
translations.sn12.51:10: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand that it's impermanent, that they're not attached to it, and that they don't relish it. If they feel a painful feeling, they understand that it's impermanent, that they're not attached to it, and that they don't relish it. If they feel a neutral feeling, they understand that it's impermanent, that they're not attached to it, and that they don't relish it. If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it detached. If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it detached. If they feel a neutral feeling, they feel it detached.
translations.sn12.51:13: What do you think, mendicants? Would a mendicant who has ended the defilements make a choice by way of merit, or demerit, or the imperturbable?
translations.sn12.51:3: "Here, a mendicant, while investigating, investigates: 'The suffering that arises in the world in many and various ways, such as old age and death—what is the source, origin, birthplace, and cause of this suffering? When what exists does old age and death come to be? When what doesn't exist does old age and death not come to be?' While investigating they understand: 'The suffering that arises in the world in many and various ways, such as old age and death—rebirth is the source, origin, birthplace, and cause of this suffering. When there is rebirth, old age and death come to be. When there is no rebirth, old age and death don't come to be.'
translations.sn12.51:11: When they feel a feeling that ends with the body, they understand: 'I feel a feeling that ends with the body.' When they feel a feeling that ends with life, they understand: 'I feel a feeling that ends with life.' They understand: 'When the body breaks up, with the ending of life, everything that's felt, not being relished, will become cool right here. Only bodily remains will be left.'
translations.sn12.51:4: They understand old age and death, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation. And they practice accordingly, following that path. This is called a mendicant who is practicing for the complete ending of suffering, for the cessation of old age and death.
translations.sn12.51:12: Suppose a potter were to take a hot pot from the kiln and place it on smooth ground. Its heat would dissipate right there, and the potsherds would remain. In the same way, when they feel a feeling that ends with the body, they understand: 'I feel a feeling that ends with the body.' When they feel a feeling that ends with life, they understand: 'I feel a feeling that ends with life.' They understand: 'When the body breaks up, with the ending of life, everything that's felt, not being relished, will become cool right here. Only bodily remains will be left.'
translations.sn12.51:6: They understand rebirth, its origin, its cessation, and the practice that leads to its cessation. And they practice accordingly. This is called a mendicant who is practicing for the complete ending of suffering, for the cessation of rebirth.
translations.sn12.51:7: Then, examining further, they examine: 'But what is the source of this continued existence? … What is the source of this grasping? … What is the source of this craving? … feeling … contact … What is the source of these six sense bases? … What is the source of this name-and-form? … What is the source of this consciousness? … What is the source, origin, birthplace, and cause of these choices? When what exists do choices exist? When what doesn't exist do choices not exist?' Examining, they understand: 'Choices have ignorance as their source, origin, birthplace, and cause. When ignorance exists, choices exist. When ignorance doesn't exist, choices don't exist.'
translations.sn12.51:8: They understand choices, their origin, their cessation, and the practice that leads to their cessation. And they practice accordingly. This is called a mendicant who is practicing for the complete ending of suffering, for the cessation of choices.
translations.sn12.51:9: Mendicants, when an ignorant individual makes a meritorious choice, consciousness proceeds to merit. When they make a demeritorious choice, consciousness proceeds to demerit. When they make an imperturbable choice, consciousness proceeds to the imperturbable. But when a mendicant has abandoned ignorance and given rise to knowledge, then with the fading of ignorance and the arising of knowledge, they don't make a meritorious choice, a demeritorious choice, or an imperturbable choice. Not choosing, not intending, they don't grasp at anything in the world. Not grasping, they're not anxious. Not being anxious, they personally become extinguished. They understand: 'Rebirth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no return to any state of existence.'
translations.sn12.52:2: Suppose a great bonfire was burning, fueled by ten, twenty, thirty, or forty cartloads of wood. And from time to time someone would toss in dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry wood. Fueled and sustained by that, the great bonfire would burn for a long, long time. In the same way, when someone lives observing the gratification in things that are prone to being grasped, craving grows. Craving is a condition for grasping … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn12.52:3: When someone lives observing the drawback in things that are prone to being grasped, craving ceases. When craving ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases. When continued existence ceases, rebirth ceases. When rebirth ceases, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress cease. That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.
translations.sn12.55:1: At Sāvatthī. "Mendicants, when someone lives observing the gratification in things that are prone to being grasped, craving grows. Craving is a condition for grasping. Grasping is a condition for continued existence … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn12.55:2: Suppose there was a great tree. Its roots going downwards and across all draw the sap upwards. Fueled and sustained by that, the great tree would stand for a long, long time. In the same way, when someone lives observing the gratification in things that are prone to being grasped, craving grows. Craving is a condition for grasping … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn12.55:3: When someone lives observing the drawback in things that are prone to being grasped, craving ceases. When craving ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.
translations.sn12.61:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. "Mendicants, an uneducated ordinary person might become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding this body made up of the four primary elements. Why is that? This body made up of the four primary elements is seen to accumulate and disperse, to be taken up and laid down. That's why an uneducated ordinary person might become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding it.
translations.sn12.61:2: But as for that which is called 'mind' or 'sentience' or 'consciousness'—an uneducated ordinary person is unable to become disillusioned, dispassionate, or freed regarding it. Why is that? For a long time they've clung to it, appropriated it, and grasped it: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self.' That's why an uneducated ordinary person is unable to become disillusioned, dispassionate, or freed regarding it.
translations.sn12.61:3: It would be better for an uneducated ordinary person to regard this body made up of the four primary elements as self, rather than the mind. Why is that? This body made up of the four primary elements is seen to last for a year, or two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred years, or even longer.
translations.sn12.61:5: In this case, a learned noble disciple carefully and properly attends to dependent origination itself: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases—that is, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness … So there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, cessation of consciousness … So there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.'
translations.sn12.62:3: In this case, a learned noble disciple carefully and properly attends to dependent origination itself: 'When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.' Dependent on contact to be experienced as pleasant, mendicants, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the pleasant feeling that arose dependent on contact to be experienced as pleasant—ceases and subsides. Dependent on contact to be experienced as painful, mendicants, painful feeling arises. With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as painful, the corresponding feeling—the painful feeling that arose dependent on contact to be experienced as painful—ceases and subsides. Dependent on contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, mendicants, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose dependent on contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant—ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.62:4: Just as, mendicants, from the rubbing and friction of two sticks, heat is generated and fire is produced. But when those same two sticks are separated and set apart, the corresponding heat ceases and subsides. In the same way, dependent on contact to be experienced as pleasant, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the pleasant feeling that arose dependent on contact to be experienced as pleasant—ceases and subsides … dependent on contact to be experienced as painful … dependent on contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the corresponding feeling—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that arose dependent on contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant—ceases and subsides.
translations.sn12.63:3: What do you think, mendicants? Would they eat that food for fun, for enjoyment, for adornment, or for beautification?' 'No, sir.' 'Wouldn't they eat that food only for the purpose of crossing over the wilderness?' 'Yes, sir.' 'I say that edible food should be seen in the same way. When edible food is fully understood, lust for the five kinds of sensual pleasures is fully understood. When lust for the five kinds of sensual pleasures is fully understood, there is no fetter bound by which a noble disciple would come back to this world again.
translations.sn12.63:4: And how should contact as food be seen? Suppose there was a flayed cow. If she stands by a wall, the creatures living in the wall would eat her. If she stands by a tree, the creatures living in the tree would eat her. If she stands by water, the creatures living in the water would eat her. If she stands in the open, the creatures living in the open would eat her. Wherever that flayed cow stands, the creatures living there would eat her. I say that contact as food should be seen in the same way. When contact as food is fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood. When the three feelings are fully understood, I say there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.63:5: And how should mental intention as food be seen? Suppose there was a pit of glowing coals, deeper than a man's height, full of coals that neither flamed nor smoked. Then a man would come along who wants to live, who doesn't want to die, who wants happiness and recoils from suffering. Then two strong men would grab him by both arms and drag him towards that pit of glowing coals. Then, mendicants, that man's intention would be far away, his wish would be far away, his aspiration would be far away. For what reason? Because that man would think: 'If I fall into this pit of glowing coals, I will meet death or deadly suffering on that account.' I say that mental intention as food should be seen in the same way. When mental intention as food is fully understood, the three cravings are fully understood. When the three cravings are fully understood, I say there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do.
translations.sn12.64:2: If, mendicants, there is lust, delight, and craving for edible food, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is descent of name-and-form. Where there is descent of name-and-form, there is growth of volitional formations. Where there is growth of volitional formations, there is production of future renewed existence. Where there is production of future renewed existence, there is future birth, old age, and death. Where there is future birth, old age, and death, I say that is with sorrow, with distress, with despair.
translations.sn12.64:4: Suppose a dyer or painter had some dye, lac, turmeric, indigo, or madder. On a well-polished plank or wall or canvas they'd create the image of a woman or a man, complete in all its parts. In the same way, when there is greed, relishing, and craving for solid food, consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name and form. Where there is the descent of name and form, there is the growth of choices. Where there is the growth of choices, there is the production of future renewed existence. Where there is the production of future renewed existence, there is future rebirth, old age, and death. Where there is future rebirth, old age, and death, I say that is with sorrow, distress, and despair.
translations.sn12.64:6: When there is no greed, relishing, and craving for solid food, consciousness is not established there and does not grow. Where consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no descent of name and form. Where there is no descent of name and form, there is no growth of choices. Where there is no growth of choices, there is no production of future renewed existence. Where there is no production of future renewed existence, there is no future rebirth, old age, and death. Where there is no future rebirth, old age, and death, I say that is without sorrow, distress, and despair.
translations.sn12.65:5: Then I thought: 'When what doesn't exist is there no consciousness? When what ceases does consciousness cease?' Then, through proper attention, I comprehended with wisdom: 'When there is no name and form, there is no consciousness. When name and form cease, consciousness ceases.'
translations.sn12.65:6: Then I thought: 'I have discovered this path to awakening, that is: When name and form cease, consciousness ceases. When consciousness ceases, name and form cease. When name and form cease, the six sense bases cease. When the six sense bases cease, contact ceases. … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.' 'Cessation, cessation.' Such was the vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light that arose in me regarding teachings not learned before from another.
translations.sn12.65:7: Suppose a man wandering in a forest saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of the past. He would follow it, and following it he would see an ancient city, an ancient capital, inhabited by people of the past, with parks, groves, lotus ponds, and walls—a delightful place. Then that man would inform the king or the king's minister: 'Please sir, you should know that while wandering in the forest I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by people of the past. I followed it, and following it I saw an ancient city, an ancient capital, inhabited by people of the past, with parks, groves, lotus ponds, and walls—a delightful place. Sir, you should rebuild that city.' Then the king or the king's minister would rebuild that city. And some time later that city would become successful and prosperous, populous and crowded with people, grown to fullness. In the same way, I saw an ancient path, an ancient road traveled by the fully awakened ones of the past.
translations.sn12.65:3: It occurred to me, mendicants: 'This consciousness turns back from name and form, it doesn't go further. This is the extent to which one may be born, grow old, die, pass away, or be reborn, that is: consciousness is a condition for name and form; name and form is a condition for the six sense bases; the six sense bases are a condition for contact … That is how this whole mass of suffering originates. "Origination, origination"—in me, mendicants, regarding things unheard before, there arose vision, knowledge, wisdom, realization, and light.'
translations.sn12.66:5: Then, investigating further, they thoroughly investigate: 'But where does this craving arise when it arises? Where does it settle when it settles?' Investigating, they understand thus: 'Whatever in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature—it is here that this craving arises when it arises, here that it settles when it settles. And what in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature? The eye in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature—it is here that this craving arises when it arises, here that it settles when it settles. The ear in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature … The nose in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature … The tongue in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature … The body in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature … The mind in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature—it is here that this craving arises when it arises, here that it settles when it settles.
translations.sn12.66:6: Mendicants, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past saw what in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature as permanent, as pleasant, as self, as healthy, as secure—they increased craving. Those who increased craving increased attachment. Those who increased attachment increased suffering. Those who increased suffering were not freed from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They were not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.66:7: Mendicants, whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will see what in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature as permanent, as pleasant, as self, as healthy, as secure—they will increase craving. Those who increase craving will increase attachment. Those who increase attachment will increase suffering. Those who increase suffering will not be freed from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They will not be freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.66:8: Mendicants, whatever ascetics or brahmins at present see what in the world has a pleasant and agreeable nature as permanent, as pleasant, as self, as healthy, as secure—they increase craving. Those who increase craving increase attachment. Those who increase attachment increase suffering. Those who increase suffering are not freed from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from suffering, I say.
translations.sn12.67:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were staying near Benares, in the deer park at Isipatana. Then in the evening, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika came out of seclusion and approached Venerable Sāriputta. He exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said to Venerable Sāriputta: 'Friend Sāriputta, is old age and death self-made, made by another, made by both self and another, or has it arisen by chance, without being made by self or another?' 'Friend Koṭṭhika, old age and death is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both self and another, nor has it arisen by chance, without being made by self or another. Rather, old age and death is conditioned by birth.'
translations.sn12.67:2: 'Friend Sāriputta, is birth self-made, made by another, made by both self and another, or has it arisen by chance, without being made by self or another?' 'Friend Koṭṭhika, birth is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both self and another, nor has it arisen by chance, without being made by self or another. Rather, birth is conditioned by continued existence.'
translations.sn12.67:4: 'Friend Sāriputta, is consciousness self-made, made by another, made by both self and another, or has it arisen by chance, without being made by self or another?' 'Friend Koṭṭhika, consciousness is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both self and another, nor has it arisen by chance, without being made by self or another. Rather, consciousness is conditioned by name-and-form.'
translations.sn12.67:5: 'Just now we understand what Venerable Sāriputta said thus: "Friend Koṭṭhika, name-and-form is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both self and another, nor has it arisen by chance, without being made by self or another. Rather, name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness."'
translations.sn12.68:6: Then is Venerable Musīla a perfected one with defilements ended?
translations.sn12.70:11: Well now, venerables, there is this answer, and yet you have not attained these states; how is this to be understood, reverends?
translations.sn12.70:13: Then Venerable Susīma got up from his seat and went to the Buddha. He bowed and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Susīma informed the Buddha of all that had been discussed with those mendicants.
translations.sn12.70:16: So, Susīma, any kind of form at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all form should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Any kind of feeling at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all feeling should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Any kind of perception … Any kind of choices at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all choices should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.' Any kind of consciousness at all—past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or fine; inferior or superior; far or near: all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'
translations.sn12.70:10: "But venerables, knowing and seeing in this way, do you dwell having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are formless, transcending forms?
translations.sn12.70:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground. Now at that time the Blessed One was honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, and revered, and received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The Sangha of monks was also honored, respected, esteemed, venerated, and revered, and received robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. But the wanderers of other sects were not honored, not respected, not esteemed, not venerated, not revered, and did not receive robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
translations.sn12.70:12: "I do not understand in detail the meaning of what the venerables have stated in brief. It would be good if the venerables would speak to me in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of what the venerables have stated in brief.
translations.sn12.70:17: Seeing this, Susīma, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, grows disillusioned with feeling, grows disillusioned with perception, grows disillusioned with volitional formations, grows disillusioned with consciousness. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate. Through dispassion, they are freed. When freed, there is knowledge: 'Freed.' They understand: 'Birth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming back to any state of existence.'
translations.sn12.70:27: Then Venerable Susīma, having bowed his head at the Blessed One's feet, said to the Blessed One: 'A transgression overcame me, venerable sir, foolish, confused, and unskillful as I was, in that I went forth as a thief of the Dhamma in this well-proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya. Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.'
translations.sn12.70:8: 'But, venerables, knowing and seeing thus, do you recollect your manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and expansion: "There I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span. Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere. There too I was so named, of such a clan, with such an appearance, such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span. Passing away from there, I was reborn here." Thus do you recollect your manifold past lives with their aspects and details?' 'No, friend.'
translations.sn12.70:2: Now at that time the wanderer Susīma was staying at Rājagaha with a large assembly of wanderers. Then Susīma the wanderer's assembly said to Susīma the wanderer: 'Come, friend Susīma, live the spiritual life under the ascetic Gotama. Having learned the Dhamma, you can teach it to us. Having learned that Dhamma, we will recite it to householders. Thus we too will be respected, honored, esteemed, venerated, and revered, and we will gain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.' 'Yes, friends,' Susīma the wanderer replied to his assembly, and he approached Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Susīma the wanderer said to Venerable Ānanda: 'I wish, friend Ānanda, to live the spiritual life in this Dhamma and Vinaya.'
translations.sn16.11:13: Then, friend, the Buddha, having advised me with this advice, got up from his seat and left. For just seven days, friend, I ate the country's almsfood; on the eighth day, final knowledge arose.
translations.sn16.11:10: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train like this: 'I will have keen conscience and prudence established toward the senior, junior, and middle monks.' That's how you should train, Kassapa.
translations.sn16.11:12: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train like this: 'I will not abandon mindfulness of the body, which is accompanied by pleasure.' That's how you should train, Kassapa.'
translations.sn16.11:2: Now at that time about thirty of Venerable Ānanda's pupils had given up the training and returned to the lower life, most of them being young men. Then Venerable Ānanda, having wandered in the Southern Hills as long as he wished, went to Rājagaha, to the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground, and approached Venerable Mahākassapa. Having approached and paid homage to Venerable Mahākassapa, he sat down to one side. As Venerable Ānanda was sitting to one side, Venerable Mahākassapa said to him: 'For how many reasons, friend Ānanda, did the Buddha establish the rule of eating in groups of three in families?'
translations.sn16.11:7: Then the nun Thullanandā, being displeased, uttered words of displeasure: 'How can Master Mahākassapa, who was formerly of another sect, think to disparage Master Ānanda, the sage of Videha, with the rebuke of a youngster?' Venerable Mahākassapa heard the nun Thullanandā speaking these words.
translations.sn16.11:1: At one time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground. Now at that time Venerable Ānanda was wandering in the Southern Hills with a large Saṅgha of monks.
translations.sn16.11:14: Then, friend, the Buddha left the path and approached a certain tree root. Then I, friend, having spread out my outer robe of rag-cloth folded in four, said to the Buddha: 'Let the Buddha sit here, sir, for my long-lasting welfare and happiness.' The Buddha sat down on the prepared seat, friend. Having sat down, the Buddha said to me, friend: 'This outer robe of rag-cloth is soft, Kassapa.' 'Let the Buddha accept my outer robe of rag-cloth out of compassion, sir.' 'But will you wear my worn-out hempen rag-robes, Kassapa?' 'I will wear the Buddha's worn-out hempen rag-robes, sir.' So I, friend, gave the outer robe of rag-cloth to the Buddha. And I received the Buddha's worn-out hempen rag-robes.
translations.sn16.11:17: I, friend, through the destruction of the taints, have realized for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, I dwell in it. One might think to cover an elephant seven or seven and a half cubits tall with a palm leaf, who might think to cover my six direct knowledges.
translations.sn16.11:11: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train like this: 'Whatever teaching I hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will listen to that teaching having made it essential, having attended to it, having gathered it with my whole mind, with ears ready to listen.' That's how you should train, Kassapa.
translations.sn16.2:3: And how is someone not conscientious? It's when a monk is not conscientious, thinking: 'If unarisen bad, unskillful qualities were to arise in me, it would be for my lasting harm.' They're not conscientious, thinking: 'If arisen bad, unskillful qualities were to not be given up, it would be for my lasting harm.' They're not conscientious, thinking: 'If unarisen skillful qualities were to not arise in me, it would be for my lasting harm.' They're not conscientious, thinking: 'If arisen skillful qualities were to cease in me, it would be for my lasting harm.' That's how someone is not conscientious. That's how one who is not keen or conscientious is incapable of awakening, incapable of extinguishment, incapable of reaching the supreme sanctuary.
translations.sn16.13:2: It's like gold, Kassapa: it doesn't disappear so long as counterfeit gold hasn't appeared in the world. But when counterfeit gold appears in the world, real gold disappears. In the same way, the true teaching doesn't disappear so long as a counterfeit of the true teaching hasn't appeared in the world. But when a counterfeit of the true teaching appears in the world, the true teaching disappears.
translations.sn16.2:4: And how is someone keen? It's when a monk makes an effort, thinking: 'If unarisen bad, unskillful qualities were to arise in me, it would be for my lasting harm.' They make an effort, thinking: 'If arisen bad, unskillful qualities were to not be given up, it would be for my lasting harm.' They make an effort regarding unarisen skillful qualities … That's how someone is keen.
translations.sn16.13:4: Kassapa, there are five things that lead to the decline and disappearance of the true teaching. What five? It's when monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen lack respect and reverence for the Teacher, the teaching, the Saṅgha, the training, and immersion. These five things lead to the decline and disappearance of the true teaching.
translations.sn21.3:6: 'In wisdom, virtue, and peace, Sāriputta is the standard; a bhikkhu who has gone beyond could at most be equal to him.'
translations.sn22.100:3: Monks, I don't see any other order of beings so variegated as the animal realm. Even those animals were designed by the mind. But the mind is even more variegated than those animals. Therefore, monks, you should frequently reflect on your own mind: 'For a long time this mind has been defiled by greed, hate, and delusion.' Beings are defiled because of the defilement of the mind; beings are purified because of the purification of the mind.
translations.sn22.101:3: Suppose there was a hen with eight, ten, or twelve eggs. But she had not properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated. Even if that hen should wish: 'If only my chicks could break out of the eggshell with their claws and beak and hatch safely!' Still they can't break out and hatch safely. Why is that? Because that hen with eight, ten, or twelve eggs has not properly sat on them to keep them warm and incubated. In the same way, when a mendicant is not committed to development, even if they should wish: 'If only my mind was freed from the defilements by not grasping!' Still their mind is not freed from the defilements by not grasping. Why is that? It should be said: 'Because of not developing.' Not developing what? Not developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation … the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.101:2: When a mendicant is not committed to development, even if they should wish: 'If only my mind was freed from the defilements by not grasping!' Still their mind is not freed from the defilements by not grasping. Why is that? It should be said: 'Because of not developing.' Not developing what? Not developing the four kinds of mindfulness meditation, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven awakening factors, and the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.1:12: They regard choices as self, self as having choices, choices in self, or self in choices. They're obsessed with the thought: 'I am choices, choices are mine.' But those choices of theirs change and become otherwise. When their choices change and become otherwise, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise.
translations.sn22.1:11: They regard perception as self, self as having perception, perception in self, or self in perception. They're obsessed with the thought: 'I am perception, perception is mine.' But that perception of theirs changes and becomes otherwise. When their perception changes and becomes otherwise, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise.
translations.sn22.1:10: They regard feeling as self, self as having feeling, feeling in self, or self in feeling. They're obsessed with the thought: 'I am feeling, feeling is mine.' But that feeling of theirs changes and becomes otherwise. When their feeling changes and becomes otherwise, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress arise.
translations.sn22.1:13: They regard consciousness as self, or self as having consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness. They are obsessed with the thought: 'I am consciousness, consciousness is mine.' As they are obsessed with this, that consciousness changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the change and alteration of consciousness, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise. That is how, householder, one is sick in body and sick in mind.
translations.sn22.1:14: And how, householder, is one sick in body but not sick in mind? Here, householder, a learned noble disciple, who sees the noble ones, is skilled in the teaching of the noble ones, and well trained in the teaching of the noble ones; who sees good persons, is skilled in the teaching of good persons, and well trained in the teaching of good persons— does not regard form as self, or self as having form, or form as in self, or self as in form. They are not obsessed with the thought: 'I am form, form is mine.' As they are not obsessed with this, that form changes and becomes otherwise. Due to the change and alteration of form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair do not arise.
translations.sn22.22:2: And what, monks, is the carrier of the burden? It should be called 'the person.' This venerable one of such a name and such a clan— this is called, monks, the carrier of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:3: And what, monks, is the taking up of the burden? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This is called, monks, the taking up of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:4: And what, monks, is the laying down of the burden? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, the giving up, the relinquishing, the release, the letting go. This is called, monks, the laying down of the burden.
translations.sn22.2:10: If, friend, for one dwelling having entered upon unwholesome states, there were pleasant dwelling in this very life, without distress, without despair, without fever, and a good destination could be expected after the breakup of the body, after death, the Blessed One would not praise the abandoning of unwholesome states. But because, friend, for one dwelling having entered upon unwholesome states, there is painful dwelling in this very life, with distress, with despair, with fever, and a bad destination can be expected after the breakup of the body, after death, therefore the Blessed One praises the abandoning of unwholesome states.
translations.sn22.2:3: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Buddha in a certain clump of golden shower trees. Then those mendicants, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, got up from their seats, bowed, and respectfully circled the Buddha, keeping him on their right, before going up to Venerable Sāriputta. They exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those mendicants said to Venerable Sāriputta: 'Reverend Sāriputta, we wish to go to the western lands, to take up residence in the western lands. We have taken leave of the Teacher.'
translations.sn22.36:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain mendicant went up to the Buddha … Seated to one side, that mendicant said to the Buddha: 'Bhante, may the Buddha please teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Buddha, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.' 'Mendicant, what one has a tendency towards, by that one is measured; what one is measured by, by that one is reckoned. What one does not have a tendency towards, by that one is not measured; what one is not measured by, by that one one is not reckoned.' 'Understood, Blessed One! Understood, Fortunate One!'
translations.sn22.3:1: Thus have I heard. At one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in the land of the Avantis on Steep Mountain near Kuraraghara. Then the householder Hāliddikāni went up to Venerable Mahākaccāna, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said to Venerable Mahākaccāna: 'Bhante, this was said by the Buddha in the Māgaṇḍiya Questions of the Aṭṭhakavagga:'
translations.sn22.3:10: And how, householder, is one not rid of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone has not abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, not abandoned desire, not abandoned affection, not abandoned thirst, not abandoned fever, not abandoned craving. Thus, householder, one is not rid of sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:11: And how, householder, is one rid of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone has abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, abandoned desire, abandoned affection, abandoned thirst, abandoned fever, abandoned craving. Thus, householder, one is rid of sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:12: And how, householder, does one look forward? Here, householder, someone thinks: 'May I be of such form in the future, may I be of such feeling in the future, may I be of such perception in the future, may I be of such volitional formations in the future, may I be of such consciousness in the future.' Thus, householder, one looks forward.
translations.sn22.3:14: And how, householder, does one engage in arguments with people? Here, householder, someone engages in such talk: 'You don't understand this Dhamma and discipline; I understand this Dhamma and discipline. How could you understand this Dhamma and discipline? You're practicing wrongly; I'm practicing rightly. What should have been said before you said after; what should have been said after you said before. What I say is consistent; what you say is not. What you've long practiced has been overturned. Your doctrine is refuted; go and try to save your doctrine. You're defeated; work yourself free if you can.' Thus, householder, one engages in arguments with people.
translations.sn22.3:17: 'Having left home, wandering without abode, not forming intimacies in the village; rid of sensual pleasures, not looking forward, one would not engage in arguments with people.'
translations.sn22.3:6: And how, householder, does one wander with an abode? One who is bound by the bondage of wandering through the abode of the sign of form is called 'one who wanders with an abode.' The sign of sounds … the sign of smells … the sign of tastes … the sign of touches … One who is bound by the bondage of wandering through the abode of the sign of mental phenomena is called 'one who wanders with an abode.' Thus, householder, one wanders with an abode.
translations.sn22.3:8: And how, householder, does one form intimacies in the village?
