Here, householder, someone lives in association with householders, rejoicing with them and sorrowing with them, happy when they are happy, sad when they are sad, and involving oneself in their affairs and duties. Thus, householder, one forms intimacies in the village.
translations.sn22.3:9: And how, householder, does one not form intimacies in the village? Here, householder, a mendicant lives unassociated with householders, not rejoicing with them and not sorrowing with them, not happy when they are happy, not sad when they are sad, and not involving oneself in their affairs and duties. Thus, householder, one does not form intimacies in the village.
translations.sn22.47:1: At Sāvatthī. 'Mendicants, whatever ascetics or brahmins regard self in various ways, all of them regard the five aggregates subject to clinging, or one of them. What five? Here, mendicants, an unlearned ordinary person, who has not seen the noble ones, is unskilled and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has not seen good persons, is unskilled and undisciplined in the Dhamma of good persons— regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. Feeling … Perception … Volitional formations … They regard consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as in self, or self as in consciousness.
translations.sn22.47:2: Thus this regarding and the notion 'I am' has not departed from them. When the notion 'I am' has not departed, mendicants, there is the descent of the five faculties—the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, and the body faculty. There is mind, mendicants, there are mental phenomena, there is the element of ignorance. Touched by a feeling born of contact with ignorance, the unlearned ordinary person has the notion 'I am'; they have the notion 'I am this'; they have the notion 'I will be'; they have the notion 'I will not be'; they have the notion 'I will be with form'; they have the notion 'I will be formless'; they have the notion 'I will be percipient'; they have the notion 'I will be non-percipient'; they have the notion 'I will be neither percipient nor non-percipient.'
translations.sn22.53:2: Mendicants, if anyone should say: 'Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from choices, I will describe the coming and going of consciousness, its passing away and rebirth, its growth, increase, and maturity'—that is not possible.
translations.sn22.54:2: If consciousness remains while clinging to form, supported by form, founded on form, sprinkled with delight, it would grow, increase, and mature. If consciousness remains while clinging to feeling … If consciousness remains while clinging to perception … If consciousness remains while clinging to choices, supported by choices, founded on choices, sprinkled with delight, it would grow, increase, and mature.
translations.sn22.56:13: And what is consciousness? There are these six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. This is called consciousness. Consciousness originates from name and form. When name and form cease, consciousness ceases. The practice that leads to the cessation of consciousness is simply this noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right immersion.
translations.sn22.55:5: They don't truly understand not-self form as 'form is not-self'. They don't truly understand not-self feeling as 'feeling is not-self'. They don't truly understand not-self perception as 'perception is not-self'. They don't truly understand not-self choices as 'choices are not-self'. They don't truly understand not-self consciousness as 'consciousness is not-self'.
translations.sn22.55:4: They don't truly understand form as suffering, feeling as suffering, perception as suffering, choices as suffering, or consciousness as suffering.
translations.sn22.55:6: They don't truly understand form as conditioned, feeling as conditioned, perception as conditioned, choices as conditioned, or consciousness as conditioned. They don't truly understand that form will cease to be, that feeling will cease to be, that perception will cease to be, that choices will cease to be, or that consciousness will cease to be.
translations.sn22.55:9: With the cessation of form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness—this is how, mendicant, a mendicant who is committed to the idea that 'I might not be, and it might not be mine; I will not be, and it will not be mine' would cut off the lower fetters.
translations.sn22.55:8: They truly understand impermanent form as 'impermanent form'. Impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent choices … They truly understand impermanent consciousness as 'impermanent consciousness'. Suffering form … suffering consciousness … not-self form … not-self consciousness … conditioned form … They truly understand conditioned consciousness as 'conditioned consciousness'. They truly understand that form will be destroyed. Feeling … perception … choices … They truly understand that consciousness will be destroyed.
translations.sn22.56:14: Whatever ascetics and brahmins, mendicants, having directly known consciousness in this way, having directly known the origin of consciousness in this way, having directly known the cessation of consciousness in this way, having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness in this way, are practicing for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, they are practicing well. Those who are practicing well gain a foothold in this teaching and training.
translations.sn22.56:2: And how is it with four aspects? I directly knew form, I directly knew the origin of form, I directly knew the cessation of form, I directly knew the practice leading to the cessation of form; feeling … perception … volitional formations … I directly knew consciousness, I directly knew the origin of consciousness, I directly knew the cessation of consciousness, I directly knew the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness.
translations.sn22.56:5: Whatever ascetics and brahmins, mendicants, having directly known form in this way … having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of form in this way, are freed through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, without grasping, they are well freed. Those who are well freed are consummate ones. For those who are consummate ones, there is no cycle to be described.
translations.sn22.57:1: At Sāvatthī. "Mendicants, a mendicant who is skilled in seven bases and investigates in three ways is called a consummate one in this teaching and training, one who has lived the spiritual life, the supreme person. And how is a mendicant skilled in seven bases? Here, a mendicant understands form, understands the origin of form, understands the cessation of form, understands the practice leading to the cessation of form; understands the gratification in form, understands the danger in form, understands the escape from form; feeling … perception … volitional formations … understands consciousness, understands the origin of consciousness, understands the cessation of consciousness, understands the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness; understands the gratification in consciousness, understands the danger in consciousness, understands the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:11: And what, mendicants, are volitional formations? There are these six classes of intention—intention regarding sights … intention regarding thoughts. These are called volitional formations. From the arising of contact is the arising of volitional formations; from the cessation of contact is the cessation of volitional formations. This noble eightfold path is the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations, that is: right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:15: The pleasure and happiness that arise dependent on consciousness—this is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in consciousness. The removal and abandoning of desire and lust for consciousness—this is the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:17: Whatever ascetics and brahmins, mendicants, having directly known consciousness in this way, having directly known the origin of consciousness in this way, having directly known the cessation of consciousness in this way, having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness in this way; having directly known the gratification in consciousness in this way, having directly known the danger in consciousness in this way, having directly known the escape from consciousness in this way, are freed through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, without grasping, they are well freed. Those who are well freed are consummate ones. For those who are consummate ones, there is no cycle to be described. This is how a mendicant is skilled in seven bases.
translations.sn22.57:2: And what, mendicants, is form? The four great elements and form derived from the four great elements. This is called form. From the arising of nutriment is the arising of form; from the cessation of nutriment is the cessation of form. This noble eightfold path is the practice leading to the cessation of form, that is: right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:5: Whatever ascetics and brahmins, mendicants, having directly known form in this way, having directly known the origin of form in this way, having directly known the cessation of form in this way, having directly known the practice leading to the cessation of form in this way; having directly known the gratification in form in this way, having directly known the danger in form in this way, having directly known the escape from form in this way, are freed through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, without grasping, they are well freed. Those who are well freed are consummate ones. For those who are consummate ones, there is no cycle to be described.
translations.sn22.57:6: And what, mendicants, is feeling? There are these six classes of feeling—feeling born of eye contact … feeling born of mind contact. This is called feeling. From the arising of contact is the arising of feeling; from the cessation of contact is the cessation of feeling. This noble eightfold path is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling, that is: right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:7: The pleasure and happiness that arise dependent on feeling—this is the gratification in feeling. That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in feeling. The removal and abandoning of desire and lust for feeling—this is the escape from feeling.
translations.sn22.58:1: At Sāvatthī. "Mendicants, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One, freed through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, without grasping, is called 'Perfectly Awakened One.' A mendicant freed by wisdom, freed through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding form, without grasping, is called 'freed by wisdom.'
translations.sn22.58:3: The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One, freed through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding perception … volitional formations … consciousness, without grasping, is called 'Perfectly Awakened One.' A mendicant freed by wisdom, freed through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding consciousness, without grasping, is called 'freed by wisdom.'
translations.sn22.59:10: Whatever consciousness—past, future, or present, internal or external, coarse or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'
translations.sn22.76:2: Seeing this, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness. Being disillusioned, desire fades away. When desire fades away they're freed. When they're freed, they know they're freed. They understand: 'Rebirth is ended, the spiritual journey has been completed, what had to be done has been done, there is no return to any state of existence.' As many as there are abodes of sentient beings, even up to the pinnacle of existence, these are the foremost, the best in the world, namely, the perfected ones.
translations.sn22.5:11: They don't relish, welcome, or remain attached to consciousness. When they don't relish, welcome, or remain attached to consciousness, the delight in consciousness ceases. When their delight ceases, grasping ceases. … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.
translations.sn22.5:2: And what is the origin of form, the origin of feeling, the origin of perception, the origin of choices, the origin of consciousness? It's when a mendicant relishes, welcomes, and remains attached.
translations.sn22.76:9: The knowledge of the adept has arisen; this bag of bones is their last. They're independent of others in the core of the spiritual life.
translations.sn22.5:4: They relish feeling … perception … choices … They relish, welcome, and remain attached to consciousness. When they relish, welcome, and remain attached to consciousness, delight arises. Delight in consciousness is grasping. Their grasping is a condition for continued existence. Continued existence is a condition for rebirth. Rebirth is a condition for … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn22.76:8: Endowed with ten factors, the great elephants are serene. They are the best in the world; craving is not found in them.
translations.sn22.60:8: Mahāli, if consciousness were exclusively suffering, steeped in suffering, soaked in suffering, and not also steeped in pleasure, sentient beings wouldn't become enamored with it. But because consciousness is pleasurable, steeped in pleasure, soaked in pleasure, and not only steeped in suffering, sentient beings become enamored with it. Being enamored, they're fettered. Being fettered, they're corrupted. This too is a cause and condition for the corruption of sentient beings. This is how sentient beings are corrupted when there is a cause and condition.
translations.sn22.76:7: Endowed with the seven treasures, trained in the three trainings, these great heroes wander, having abandoned fear and dread.
translations.sn22.76:6: Having fully understood the five aggregates, they range in the domain of the true teaching. Praiseworthy are these good people, true children of the Buddha.
translations.sn22.5:8: And what don't they relish, welcome, or remain attached to? They don't relish, welcome, or remain attached to form. When they don't relish, welcome, or remain attached to form, the delight in form ceases. When their delight ceases, grasping ceases. When grasping ceases, continued existence ceases. … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.
translations.sn22.5:3: And what do they relish, welcome, and remain attached to? They relish, welcome, and remain attached to form. When they relish, welcome, and remain attached to form, delight arises. Delight in form is grasping. With their grasping as condition, existence comes to be; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress come to be. That is how this whole mass of suffering originates.
translations.sn22.60:4: But sir, what is the cause and condition for the corruption of sentient beings? How is it that sentient beings are corrupted with cause and condition?
translations.sn22.60:3: There is, Mahāli, a cause and condition for the corruption of sentient beings. Sentient beings are corrupted with cause and condition. There is, Mahāli, a cause and condition for the purification of sentient beings. Sentient beings are purified with cause and condition.
translations.sn22.60:2: Sir, Pūraṇa Kassapa says this: 'There is no cause and no condition for the corruption of sentient beings. Sentient beings are corrupted without cause and condition. There is no cause and no condition for the purification of sentient beings. Sentient beings are purified without cause and condition.' What does the Buddha say about this?
translations.sn22.79:1: At Sāvatthī. "Mendicants, whatever ascetics or brahmins recollect many kinds of past lives, all of them recollect the five aggregates subject to clinging, or one of them. What five? 'I had such form in the past'—recollecting thus, they recollect only form. 'I had such feeling in the past'—recollecting thus, they recollect only feeling. 'I had such perception in the past' … 'I had such volitional formations in the past' … 'I had such consciousness in the past'—recollecting thus, they recollect only consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:10: 'I am currently being consumed by consciousness. In the past too I was consumed by consciousness in just the same way as I am now being consumed by present consciousness. And if I were to delight in future consciousness, in the future too I would be consumed by consciousness in just the same way as I am now being consumed by present consciousness.' Having reflected thus, they become indifferent to past consciousness; they don't delight in future consciousness; they practice for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:7: In this regard, mendicants, a learned noble disciple reflects thus: 'I am currently being consumed by form. In the past too I was consumed by form in just the same way as I am now being consumed by present form. And if I were to delight in future form, in the future too I would be consumed by form in just the same way as I am now being consumed by present form.' Having reflected thus, they become indifferent to past form; they don't delight in future form; they practice for disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form.
translations.sn22.80:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Tree Monastery. Then the Buddha, having dismissed the Saṅgha of mendicants for some reason, robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kapilavatthu, after the meal, on returning from alms-round, he went to the Great Wood for the day's meditation. Having plunged into the Great Wood, he sat down at the root of a bilva sapling for the day's meditation.
translations.sn22.80:4: The Buddha consented by remaining silent. Then Brahmā Sahampati, knowing the Buddha had consented, bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him keeping him on his right, and vanished right there.
translations.sn22.80:6: "Mendicants, this is the lowest of livelihoods, that is, alms-gathering. It is a curse in the world to say: 'You wander about with bowl in hand, a beggar!' Yet this is what gentlemen of good family undertake for a good reason, because of a good reason; not because they were forced by kings, or by bandits, or because of debt, or out of fear, or because they lost their livelihood; but because: 'I am swamped by rebirth, old age, and death; by sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. I am swamped by suffering, mired in suffering. Hopefully I can find an end to this entire mass of suffering.'
translations.sn22.80:7: This is how a gentleman of good family has gone forth. Yet he is covetous, with intense desire for sensual pleasures, with a mind full of ill will, with corrupt intentions, with muddled mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a scattered mind, with unrestrained faculties. Just as a firebrand from a funeral pyre, burning at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle, serves neither as timber in the village nor as timber in the forest; I say that this person is like that: they have missed out on the pleasures of a householder, and they don't fulfill the goal of the ascetic life.
translations.sn22.80:9: Mendicants, there are these two views: the view of existence and the view of non-existence. In this regard, a learned noble disciple reflects thus: 'Is there anything in the world that I could cling to without being blameworthy?' They understand: 'There is nothing in the world that I could cling to without being blameworthy. For if I were to cling, I would cling only to form, only to feeling, only to perception, only to volitional formations, only to consciousness. With that clinging as condition, there would be existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress would come to be. That is how this entire mass of suffering originates.'
translations.sn22.81:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Kosambī in Ghosita's Monastery. Then the Buddha robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kosambī, after the meal, on returning from alms-round, he put away his own lodgings, took his bowl and robe, and without informing his attendants or taking leave of the Saṅgha of mendicants, he set out wandering alone, without a companion.
translations.sn22.81:10: They don't regard form as self, they don't regard feeling as self, they don't regard perception … they don't regard volitional formations … they don't regard consciousness as self; but they have such a view: 'That self is the same as the world. After death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change.' But mendicants, that eternalist view is a volitional formation. And what is the source of that volitional formation? … Thus too, mendicants, for one who knows and sees thus, there is the immediate ending of the defilements.
translations.sn22.81:3: Then the Buddha wandered by stages until he arrived at Pālileyyaka, where he stayed at the foot of a lovely sal tree. Then several mendicants went to Venerable Ānanda, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Reverend Ānanda, it's been a long time since we heard a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Buddha. We'd like to hear a Dhamma talk in the Buddha's presence.'
translations.sn22.82:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the stilt longhouse of Migāra's mother, together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants. Now, at that time it was the sabbath—the full moon on the fifteenth day—and the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of mendicants.
translations.sn22.82:13: 'It's possible that some foolish person here—unknowing and ignorant, their mind dominated by craving—thinks they can overstep the Teacher's instructions. "So it seems, good sir, that form, feeling, perception, choices, and consciousness are not-self. Then what self will the deeds done by not-self affect?" Now, mendicants, you have been trained by me in questioning with regard to various topics in various contexts.
translations.sn22.83:3: Suppose a woman or man who was young, youthful, and fond of adornments was examining the reflection of their own face in a clean bright mirror or a clear bowl of water. They would see it because of grasping, not without grasping. In the same way, Reverend Ānanda, the conceit 'I am' occurs because of grasping form, not without grasping. Because of grasping feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness the conceit 'I am' occurs, not without grasping.
translations.sn22.84:10: I've made up this simile, Tissa, to make a point. And this is the point: 'The man who doesn't know the road' is a term for an ordinary person. 'The man who knows the road' is a term for the Realized One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. 'The fork in the road' is a term for doubt. 'The left road' is a term for the wrong eightfold path, that is: wrong view … wrong immersion. 'The right road' is a term for the noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right immersion. 'The thick forest grove' is a term for ignorance. 'The large swampy marsh' is a term for sensual pleasures. 'The cliff and precipice' is a term for anger and distress. 'The level, pleasant terrain' is a term for extinguishment. Rejoice, Tissa, rejoice! I am here to advise, help, and instruct you.
translations.sn22.85:16: They don't truly understand impermanent form as 'impermanent form'. They don't truly understand impermanent feeling as 'impermanent feeling'. They don't truly understand impermanent perception as 'impermanent perception'. They don't truly understand impermanent volitional formations as 'impermanent volitional formations'. They don't truly understand impermanent consciousness as 'impermanent consciousness'.
translations.sn22.85:19: They don't truly understand conditioned form as 'conditioned form'. Conditioned feeling … conditioned perception … conditioned volitional formations … They don't truly understand conditioned consciousness as 'conditioned consciousness'.
translations.sn22.85:20: They don't truly understand form as a killer: 'Form is a killer.' They don't truly understand feeling as a killer: 'Feeling is a killer.' … perception as a killer: 'Perception is a killer.' … They don't truly understand formations as killers: 'Formations are killers.' They don't truly understand consciousness as a killer: 'Consciousness is a killer.'
translations.sn22.85:21: They approach form, grasp it, and take a stand on it: 'This is my self.' They approach feeling … perception … formations … consciousness, grasp it, and take a stand on it: 'This is my self.' These five grasping aggregates, being approached and grasped, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time.
translations.sn22.85:23: They truly understand impermanent form as: 'Form is impermanent.' They truly understand impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent formations … impermanent consciousness as: 'Consciousness is impermanent.'
translations.sn22.85:25: They truly understand not-self form as: 'Form is not-self.' They truly understand not-self feeling … not-self perception … not-self formations … not-self consciousness as: 'Consciousness is not-self.'
translations.sn22.86:10: 'What do you think, Anurādha? Do you regard form … feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as the Realized One?' 'No, sir.'
translations.sn22.86:11: 'What do you think, Anurādha? Do you regard the Realized One as one who is without form … without feeling … without perception … without formations … without consciousness?' 'No, sir.'
translations.sn22.89:11: Even though a noble disciple has given up the five lower fetters, still they have a lingering residue of the conceit 'I am', the desire 'I am', and the underlying tendency 'I am' regarding the five grasping aggregates that has not been uprooted. After some time they meditate observing rise and fall in the five grasping aggregates: 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the ending of form. Such is feeling … Such is perception … Such are choices … Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the ending of consciousness.' As they meditate observing rise and fall in these five grasping aggregates, that lingering residue of the conceit 'I am', the desire 'I am', and the underlying tendency 'I am' regarding the five grasping aggregates that had not been uprooted—that comes to be uprooted.
translations.sn22.89:12: Suppose, reverends, there was a cloth that was soiled and stained. Its owners gave it to a laundryman. The laundryman would scrub it with salt, lye, or cow dung, and rinse it in clean water. Even though that cloth was pure and clean, it would still retain a residual smell of salt, lye, or cow dung that had not been removed. The laundryman would give it back to the owners. The owners would put it in a scented casket. Whatever residual smell of salt, lye, or cow dung that had not been removed would be eliminated. In the same way, reverends, even though a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, there still remains regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging a residual conceit 'I am,' a desire 'I am,' an underlying tendency 'I am' that has not been removed. At a later time they dwell contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates subject to clinging: 'Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such are volitional formations … such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.' As they dwell contemplating rise and fall in these five aggregates subject to clinging, whatever residual conceit 'I am,' desire 'I am,' underlying tendency 'I am' regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging that had not been removed—that is eliminated.
translations.sn22.90:8: 'Even with just this much we are pleased with Venerable Channa, in that Venerable Channa has revealed his mind and cut through the deadlock. Lend an ear, friend Channa; you are capable of understanding the Dhamma.' Then right there a great rapture and joy arose in Venerable Channa: 'It seems I am capable of understanding the Dhamma!'
translations.sn22.94:1: At Sāvatthī. 'Mendicants, I do not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me. One who speaks the Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world. What the wise in the world agree does not exist, I too say does not exist. What the wise in the world agree exists, I too say exists.
translations.sn22.94:3: And what do the wise in the world agree exists, which I too say exists? Form that is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—the wise in the world agree this exists; I too say it exists. Feeling is impermanent … Consciousness that is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—the wise in the world agree this exists; I too say it exists. This is what the wise in the world agree exists; I too say it exists.
translations.sn22.94:4: There is a principle in the world that the Tathāgata has awakened to and comprehended. Having awakened to and comprehended it, he explains, teaches, asserts, establishes, discloses, analyzes, and makes it plain.
translations.sn22.94:7: When the Tathāgata is explaining, teaching, asserting, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, and making it plain in this way, if someone does not know and see—what can I do with that foolish ordinary person, blind and sightless, who does not know and does not see?
translations.sn22.95:10: However they meditate on it, examining it carefully, it appears empty and hollow to one who sees it carefully.
translations.sn22.95:11: Regarding this body, the one of vast wisdom has taught: when three things are abandoned, you see form discarded.
translations.sn22.95:12: When vitality, warmth, and consciousness leave this body, then it lies there cast aside, food for others, without awareness.
translations.sn22.95:13: Such is this continuum, this illusion that beguiles fools. It is declared to be a killer; no core is found here.
translations.sn22.95:2: 'Suppose, mendicants, this Ganges river was carrying along a great lump of foam. A person with good eyesight would see it, meditate on it, and examine it carefully. Seeing, meditating, and examining it carefully, it would appear empty, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a lump of foam? In the same way, a mendicant sees, meditates on, and examines carefully any form whatsoever—past, future, or present … far or near. Seeing, meditating, and examining it carefully, it appears empty, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in form?
translations.sn22.95:3: Suppose that in autumn, when it's raining heavily, a water bubble arises and bursts on the water. A person with good eyesight would see it, meditate on it, and examine it carefully. Seeing, meditating, and examining it carefully, it would appear empty, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a water bubble? In the same way, a mendicant sees, meditates on, and examines carefully any feeling whatsoever—past, future, or present … far or near. Seeing, meditating, and examining it carefully, it appears empty, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in feeling?
translations.sn22.95:5: Suppose a person needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, took a sharp axe and entered a forest. There they'd see a large banana tree, straight, young, and grown tall. They'd cut it down at the root, cut off the top, and unroll the leaf sheaths. Unrolling the leaf sheaths, they wouldn't even find sapwood, let alone heartwood. A person with good eyesight would see it, meditate on it, and examine it carefully. Seeing, meditating, and examining it carefully, it would appear empty, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a banana tree? In the same way, a mendicant sees, meditates on, and examines carefully any choices whatsoever—past, future, or present … far or near. Seeing, meditating, and examining it carefully, they appear empty, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in choices?
translations.sn22.95:6: Suppose, mendicants, a magician or their apprentice were to display a magic trick at a crossroads. A person with good eyesight would see it, contemplate it, and carefully investigate it. And it would appear to them to be void, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in a magic trick? In the same way, a mendicant sees, contemplates, and carefully investigates any consciousness—past, future, or present … far or near. And it appears to them to be void, hollow, and insubstantial. For what substance could there be in consciousness?
translations.sn22.95:7: Seeing this, mendicants, a learned noble disciple grows disillusioned with form, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness. Being disillusioned, they become dispassionate. Through dispassion, they are freed. When freed, there is knowledge that they are freed … They understand: 'there is no more coming to any state of being.'
translations.sn22.95:9: Form is like a lump of foam, feeling is like a water bubble; perception is like a mirage, volitional formations are like a plantain tree; consciousness is like a magic trick— so taught the Kinsman of the Sun.
translations.sn22.96:1: At Sāvatthī. Seated to one side, that mendicant said to the Buddha: "Sir, is there any form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever? Is there any feeling that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever? Is there any perception that … Is there any volitional formations that are permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever? Is there any consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever?" "Mendicant, there is no form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever. There is no feeling … no perception … no volitional formations … no consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever."
translations.sn22.96:2: Then the Buddha, picking up a little ball of cow dung in his hand, said to that mendicant: "Mendicant, there is not even this much personal existence that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever. If there were even this much personal existence that was permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering would not be evident. But since there is not even this much personal existence that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, the living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering is evident.
translations.sn22.96:3: Mendicant, I was once a king, a head-anointed noble. As such a king, I had eighty-four thousand cities, chief of which was the royal capital of Kusāvatī. I had eighty-four thousand palaces, chief of which was the Dhamma Palace. I had eighty-four thousand peaked mansions, chief of which was the Great Array peaked mansion. I had eighty-four thousand couches made of ivory, heartwood, gold, and silver, spread with long-haired covers, woolen covers, embroidered covers, and fine deer-hide covers, with canopies above and red pillows at both ends. I had eighty-four thousand elephants, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with gold netting, chief of which was the elephant king Uposatha. I had eighty-four thousand horses, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with gold netting, chief of which was the horse king Valāhaka. I had eighty-four thousand chariots, adorned with gold ornaments and gold banners, covered with gold netting, chief of which was the chariot Vejayanta. I had eighty-four thousand jewels, chief of which was the jewel treasure. I had … eighty-four thousand women, chief of whom was Queen Subhaddā. I had … eighty-four thousand nobles as vassals, chief of whom was the counselor treasure. I had … eighty-four thousand milk cows with fine cloth tethers and bronze milk pails. I had … eighty-four thousand ten million garments of fine linen, fine silk, fine wool, and fine cotton. I had … eighty-four thousand dishes from which meals were served morning and evening.
translations.sn22.97:2: Then the Buddha, having placed a little bit of dirt on his fingernail, said to that mendicant: "Mendicant, there is not even this much form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same forever. If there were even this much form that was permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, this living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering would not be evident. But since there is not even this much form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, the living of the spiritual life for the complete ending of suffering is evident."
translations.sn35.101:4: Suppose people were to carry off the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta's Grove, or burn them, or do with them as they wish. Would you think: 'People are carrying us off, burning us, or doing with us as they wish'?
translations.sn35.118:3: Lord of the gods, there are tastes cognizable by the tongue … Lord of the gods, there are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are wished for, desirable, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and arousing. This, lord of the gods, is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life.
translations.sn35.118:4: Lord of the gods, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desirable, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and arousing. A mendicant without attachment, lord of the gods, attains final Nibbāna …
translations.sn35.116:5: "Reverends, suppose there was a person in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood. But when they come to a great tree standing with heartwood, they'd pass over the roots and trunk, imagining that the heartwood should be sought in the branches and leaves. Such is the case with the venerables. When the Teacher was right here, you passed over the Buddha and thought you should ask me about this matter. For, reverends, the Buddha knows and sees. He is vision, he is knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the holy one. He is the teacher, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the giver of the deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Realized One. translations.sn35.88:1: Then Venerable Puṇṇa approached the Buddha; having approached … Seated to one side, Venerable Puṇṇa said to the Buddha: 'Venerable sir, it would be good if the Buddha would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Buddha, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.'

translations.sn35.88:18: Then Venerable Puṇṇa, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One's words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him on his right, packed up his dwelling, and taking his bowl and robe, set out wandering toward the Sunāparanta country. translations.sn35.95:18: Having tasted a flavor, with mindfulness lost, attending to the pleasant sign; with a mind full of desire one feels it, and remains clinging to it.

translations.sn35.95:22: Having cognized a thought, with mindfulness lost, attending to the pleasant sign; with a mind full of desire one feels it, and remains clinging to it.

translations.sn35.95:25: As one sees a sight, and also experiences feeling; it wears away and does not accumulate, thus one lives mindfully; thus diminishing suffering, nibbāna is said to be near.

translations.sn35.95:30: One does not lust for tastes, having tasted a flavor, one is mindful; with a dispassionate mind one feels it, and does not remain clinging to it.

translations.sn36.19:8: And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure? It's when a mendicant, as the placing of the mind and keeping it connected are stilled, enters and remains in the second absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of immersion, with internal clarity and mind at one, without placing the mind and keeping it connected. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure. If anyone should say: 'This is the highest peaceful pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience'—I would not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:7: And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure? It's when a mendicant, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and remains in the first absorption, which has the rapture and bliss born of seclusion, while placing the mind and keeping it connected. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure. If anyone should say: 'This is the highest peaceful pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience'—I would not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:12: And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure? It's when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite', enters and remains in the dimension of infinite consciousness. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure. If anyone should say: 'This is the highest peaceful pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience'—I would not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:15: And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure? It's when a mendicant, going totally beyond the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception, enters and remains in the cessation of perception and feeling. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure.
translations.sn36.19:9: And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure? It's when a mendicant, with the fading away of rapture, enters and remains in the third absorption, where they meditate with equanimity, mindful and aware, personally experiencing the bliss of which the noble ones declare, 'Equanimous and mindful, one meditates in bliss.' This, Ānanda, is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure. If anyone should say: 'This is the highest peaceful pleasure and happiness that sentient beings experience'—I would not grant them that. Why is that? Because there is another pleasure that is more excellent and refined than that pleasure.
translations.sn36.31:2: And what, monks, is spiritual rapture? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, and rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This, monks, is called spiritual rapture.
translations.sn36.31:3: And what, monks, is spiritual rapture that is even more spiritual? When a monk with defilements destroyed reviews his mind liberated from lust, reviews his mind liberated from hatred, reviews his mind liberated from delusion, the rapture that arises—this, monks, is called spiritual rapture that is even more spiritual.
translations.sn36.31:5: And what, monks, is spiritual pleasure? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, and rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, one who dwells happily.' This, monks, is called spiritual pleasure.
translations.sn36.31:6: And what, monks, is spiritual pleasure that is even more spiritual? When a monk with defilements destroyed reviews his mind liberated from lust, reviews his mind liberated from hatred, reviews his mind liberated from delusion, the pleasure and joy that arises—this, monks, is called spiritual pleasure that is even more spiritual.
translations.sn36.31:8: And what, monks, is spiritual equanimity? Here, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, monks, is called spiritual equanimity.
translations.sn36.31:9: And what, monks, is spiritual equanimity that is even more spiritual? When a monk with defilements destroyed reviews his mind liberated from lust, reviews his mind liberated from hatred, reviews his mind liberated from delusion, the equanimity that arises—this, monks, is called spiritual equanimity that is even more spiritual.

translations.sn36.6:2: But, monks, the instructed noble disciple, when touched by a painful feeling, does not sorrow, does not tire, does not lament, does not beat the breast and weep, does not become confused. He feels one feeling—bodily, not mental.
translations.sn36.6:4: The wise one, learned, does not feel feeling, whether pleasant or painful; this is the great difference between the skilled one and the ordinary person.
translations.sn36.6:5: For the learned one who has comprehended the Dhamma, who sees clearly this world and the next, desirable things do not agitate the mind, and toward the undesirable he does not react with aversion.
translations.sn36.7:3: And how, monks, is a monk mindful? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and grief for the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … he dwells contemplating mind in mind … he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and grief for the world. Thus, monks, a monk is mindful.
translations.sn36.7:4: And how, monks, is a monk clearly comprehending? Here, monks, a monk acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside; acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching; acts with clear comprehension when wearing the outer robe, bowl, and robes; acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating; acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent. Thus, monks, a monk acts with clear comprehension. Monks, a monk should await his time mindful and clearly comprehending. This is our instruction to you.
translations.sn36.7:5: If, while that mendicant is meditating in this way—mindful, aware, diligent, ardent, and resolute—a pleasant feeling arises, they understand: 'A pleasant feeling has arisen in me. That is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very body. But this body is impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated. How could a pleasant feeling that has arisen dependent on an impermanent, conditioned, dependently originated body be permanent?' They meditate observing impermanence in the body and in pleasant feeling, observing vanishing, observing fading away, observing cessation, observing letting go. As they meditate observing impermanence in the body and in pleasant feeling, observing vanishing, observing fading away, observing cessation, observing letting go, the underlying tendency to greed for the body and pleasant feeling is abandoned.
translations.sn36.7:8: If they feel a pleasant feeling, they understand it is impermanent, they understand it is not clung to, they understand it is not delighted in. If they feel a painful feeling … If they feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, they understand it is impermanent, they understand it is not clung to, they understand it is not delighted in. If they feel a pleasant feeling, they feel it detached. If they feel a painful feeling, they feel it detached. If they feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, they feel it detached. Feeling a feeling limited to the body, they understand: 'I feel a feeling limited to the body.' Feeling a feeling limited to life, they understand: 'I feel a feeling limited to life.' translations.sn45.8:6: And what, mendicants, is right action? Abstaining from killing living creatures, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from sexual misconduct—this is called, mendicants, right action.

translations.sn45.8:5: And what, mendicants, is right speech? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter—this is called, mendicants, right speech.
translations.sn45.8:4: And what, mendicants, is right intention? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, the intention of non-harming—this is called, mendicants, right intention.

translations.sn46.38:1: Mendicants, at a time when a noble disciple, treating it as important, paying attention, applying their whole mind, and lending an ear, listens to the Dhamma, the five hindrances are not present at that time. translations.sn46.3:2: At a time when a mendicant, dwelling thus withdrawn, recollects and thinks about that Dhamma, the awakening factor of mindfulness is aroused in that mendicant at that time. translations.sn46.51:20: And what, mendicants, starves the awakening factor of energy so that it doesn't arise, or so that it doesn't grow and reach fulfillment? translations.sn46.51:21: And what, mendicants, starves the awakening factor of rapture so that it doesn't arise, or so that it doesn't grow and reach fulfillment? translations.sn46.51:22: And what, mendicants, starves the awakening factor of tranquility so that it doesn't arise, or so that it doesn't grow and reach fulfillment? translations.sn46.51:23: And what, mendicants, starves the awakening factor of immersion so that it doesn't arise, or so that it doesn't grow and reach fulfillment? I truly understood: 'This is the origin of suffering.' I truly understood: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' I truly understood: 'This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.' Sir, I have comprehended the teaching and gained the path. When I develop and cultivate it, as I dwell in such a way, it will lead me to such a state that I will understand: 'Rebirth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.'
translations.sn46.52:10: And what is the method by which the seven awakening factors become fourteen? Mendicants, mindfulness regarding internal phenomena is the awakening factor of mindfulness, and mindfulness regarding external phenomena is also the awakening factor of mindfulness. 'The awakening factor of mindfulness'—this is how the summary statement goes. But by this method it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:13: Mendicants, rapture accompanied by thought and examination is the awakening factor of rapture, and rapture without thought and examination is also the awakening factor of rapture. 'The awakening factor of rapture'—this is how the summary statement goes. But by this method it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:11: Mendicants, investigating, exploring, and examining internal phenomena with wisdom is the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, and investigating, exploring, and examining external phenomena with wisdom is also the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena. 'The awakening factor of investigation of phenomena'—this is how the summary statement goes. But by this method it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:12: Mendicants, physical energy is the awakening factor of energy, and mental energy is also the awakening factor of energy. 'The awakening factor of energy'—this is how the summary statement goes. But by this method it becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:15: Immersion with placing and keeping the mind on something is the awakening factor of immersion, and immersion without placing and keeping the mind on something is also the awakening factor of immersion. 'The awakening factor of immersion'—this is how the summary goes. But by this method it becomes two.
translations.sn46.53:14: Suppose, mendicants, a person wanted to extinguish a great bonfire. They would throw wet grass on it, wet cow dung, and wet sticks; they would blow moist air on it, and scatter dust over it. Would that person be able to extinguish that great bonfire?
translations.sn46.53:11: Suppose a person wanted to extinguish a large bonfire. They'd add dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry sticks. They'd blow on it, and not scatter dirt over it. Could that person extinguish the large bonfire?
translations.sn46.53:2: Mendicants, when wanderers who follow other paths say this, you should say to them: 'Reverends, when the mind is sluggish, which awakening factors is it the wrong time to develop, and which awakening factors is it the right time to develop? And when the mind is restless, which awakening factors is it the wrong time to develop, and which awakening factors is it the right time to develop?' Questioned like this, the wanderers who follow other paths would be stumped, and, in addition, would get frustrated. Why is that? Because it's outside their domain.
translations.sn46.52:8: Mendicants, when wanderers who follow other paths say this, you should say to them: 'But reverends, is there a way in which the five hindrances become ten, and the seven awakening factors become fourteen?' Questioned like this, the wanderers who follow other paths would be stumped, and, in addition, would get frustrated. Why is that? Because it's outside their domain. I don't see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions except for the Realized One or his disciple or someone who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.53:3: I don't see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions except for the Realized One or his disciple or someone who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.53:10: When the mind is restless, it's the wrong time to develop the awakening factors of investigation of principles, energy, and rapture. Why is that? Because a restless mind is hard to calm with those things.
translations.sn46.53:13: But when the mind is restless, it's the right time to develop the awakening factors of tranquility, immersion, and equanimity. Why is that? Because a restless mind is easy to calm with those things.
translations.sn46.52:9: And what is the way in which the five hindrances become ten? Sensual desire for internal things is a hindrance, and sensual desire for external things is a hindrance. When this is included in the category 'sensual desire as a hindrance', by this method it becomes two. Ill will for internal things is a hindrance, and ill will for external things is a hindrance. When this is included in the category 'ill will as a hindrance', by this method it becomes two. Dullness is a hindrance, and drowsiness is a hindrance. When this is included in the category 'dullness and drowsiness as a hindrance', by this method it becomes two. Restlessness is a hindrance, and remorse is a hindrance. When this is included in the category 'restlessness and remorse as a hindrance', by this method it becomes two. Doubt about internal things is a hindrance, and doubt about external things is a hindrance. When this is included in the category 'doubt as a hindrance', by this method it becomes two. This is the way in which the five hindrances become ten.
translations.sn46.53:4: Mendicants, when the mind is sluggish, that's not the time to develop the awakening factors of tranquility, immersion, or equanimity. Why is that? Because a sluggish mind is hard to arouse with these things.
translations.sn46.53:5: Suppose a person wanted to make a small fire flare up. If they put wet grass, wet cow dung, and wet sticks on it, blew on it with their mouth, and smothered it with dust, would they be able to make it flare up?
translations.sn46.53:7: But when the mind is sluggish, that is the time to develop the awakening factors of investigation of principles, energy, and rapture. Why is that? Because a sluggish mind is easy to arouse with these things.
translations.sn46.53:8: Suppose a person wanted to make a small fire flare up. If they put dry grass, dry cow dung, and dry sticks on it, blew on it with their mouth, and didn't smother it with dust, would they be able to make it flare up?
translations.sn46.54:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Koliyans, where they have a town named Haliddavasana. Then several mendicants robed up in the morning and, taking their bowls and robes, entered Haliddavasana for alms. Then it occurred to those mendicants: 'It's too early to wander for alms in Haliddavasana. Why don't we go to the monastery of the wanderers of other sects?'
translations.sn46.54:11: Mendicants, when wanderers of other sects say this, you should say to them: 'But reverends, how is the heart's release by love developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? How is the heart's release by compassion developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? How is the heart's release by rejoicing developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? How is the heart's release by equanimity developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal?' Questioned like this, the wanderers of other sects would be stumped, and, in addition, would be frustrated. Why is that? Because it's outside their domain. Mendicants, I don't see anyone in this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions except for the Realized One or his disciple or someone who has heard it from them.
translations.sn46.54:12: And how is the heart's release by love developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? It's when a mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness together with love … develops the awakening factor of equanimity together with love, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. If they wish: 'May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,' that's what they do. If they wish: 'May I meditate perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,' that's what they do. If they wish: 'May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive and the repulsive,' that's what they do. If they wish: 'May I meditate perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive and the unrepulsive,' that's what they do. If they wish: 'May I meditate staying equanimous, mindful and aware, rejecting both the unrepulsive and the repulsive,' that's what they do. Or else they enter and remain in the beautiful liberation. I say that the heart's release by love has the beautiful as its culmination for a mendicant who has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:13: And how is the heart's release by compassion developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? It's when a mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness together with compassion … develops the awakening factor of equanimity together with compassion, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. If they wish: 'May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,' that's what they do. … If they wish: 'May I meditate staying equanimous, mindful and aware, rejecting both the unrepulsive and the repulsive,' that's what they do. Or else, going totally beyond perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not focusing on perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite', they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space. I say that the heart's release by compassion has the dimension of infinite space as its culmination for a mendicant who has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:14: And how is the heart's release by rejoicing developed? What is its destination, its culmination, its fruit, its final goal? It's when a mendicant develops the awakening factor of mindfulness together with rejoicing … develops the awakening factor of equanimity together with rejoicing, which relies on seclusion, fading away, and cessation, and ripens as letting go. If they wish: 'May I meditate perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,' that's what they do. … If they wish: 'May I meditate staying equanimous, mindful and aware, rejecting both the unrepulsive and the repulsive,' that's what they do. Or else, going totally beyond the dimension of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite', they enter and remain in the dimension of infinite consciousness. I say that the heart's release by rejoicing has the dimension of infinite consciousness as its culmination for a mendicant who has not penetrated to a higher liberation.
translations.sn47.10:9: And so, Ānanda, I have taught development with direction and development without direction. What a teacher should do for their disciples out of compassion and care, I have done for you. These are the roots of trees, these are empty huts. Meditate, Ānanda! Don't be negligent! Don't be filled with regret later! This is my instruction to you.
translations.sn47.10:7: Furthermore, Ānanda, a monk meditates observing feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed longing and dejection for the world. While meditating observing phenomena in phenomena, there arises in them either burning in the body based on phenomena, or mental sluggishness, or the mind becomes distracted externally. That monk should then direct the mind toward some inspiring sign. When they direct the mind toward some inspiring sign, joy arises. When joyful, rapture arises. When the mind is filled with rapture, the body becomes tranquil. One tranquil in body feels pleasure. The mind of one who feels pleasure becomes concentrated. They reflect thus: 'The purpose for which I directed my mind has been achieved. Let me now withdraw it.' They withdraw and neither think nor examine. They understand: 'I am without thought, without examination, mindful within, I am happy.' This, Ānanda, is how there is development with direction.
translations.sn47.13:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was staying in the Magadhan country at Nālaka village, sick, afflicted, gravely ill. And the novice Cunda was Venerable Sāriputta's attendant.
translations.sn47.13:2: Then Venerable Sāriputta passed away due to that illness. Then the novice Cunda, taking Venerable Sāriputta's bowl and robes, went to Sāvatthī, to Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery, to Venerable Ānanda. Having approached and paid respects to Venerable Ānanda, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the novice Cunda said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Venerable sir, Venerable Sāriputta has passed away. Here are his bowl and robes.'
translations.sn47.38:2: They meditate observing an aspect of feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. As they meditate observing an aspect of feelings, feelings are fully understood. When feelings are fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.20:2: Suppose, mendicants, that a large crowd were to gather, saying: 'The beauty queen! The beauty queen!' Now, that beauty queen was a consummate dancer and singer. And a large crowd would gather even more, saying: 'The beauty queen is dancing and singing!' Then a man would come along who wants to live and doesn't want to die, who wants to be happy and recoils from pain. They'd say to him: 'Mister, you must carry this bowl of oil, full to the brim, between the large crowd and the beauty queen. And a man with a drawn sword will follow behind you. Wherever you spill even a little, he'll chop off your head right there.' What do you think, mendicants? Would that man lose focus on that bowl of oil and carelessly turn his attention outside?
translations.sn47.37:2: They meditate observing feelings in feelings—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. As they meditate observing feelings in feelings, desire for feelings is given up. When desire is given up, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:3: They meditate observing the mind in the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. As they meditate observing the mind in the mind, desire for the mind is given up. When desire is given up, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:3: They meditate observing the mind in the mind—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. As they meditate observing the mind in the mind, the mind is fully understood. Because the mind is fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.40:1: "Mendicants, I will teach you the establishments of mindfulness, the development of the establishments of mindfulness, and the practice that leads to the development of the establishments of mindfulness. Listen to that. And what, mendicants, are the establishments of mindfulness? Here, a mendicant meditates observing the body in the body—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. They meditate observing feelings in feelings … They meditate observing the mind in the mind … They meditate observing phenomena in phenomena—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. These are called, mendicants, the establishments of mindfulness.
translations.sn47.40:2: And what, mendicants, is the development of the establishments of mindfulness? Here, a mendicant meditates observing the body as liable to origination, as liable to vanishing, as liable to origination and vanishing—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. They meditate observing feelings as liable to origination … They meditate observing the mind as liable to origination … They meditate observing phenomena as liable to origination, as liable to vanishing, as liable to origination and vanishing—keen, aware, and mindful, rid of covetousness and displeasure for the world. This is called, mendicants, the development of the establishments of mindfulness.
translations.sn47.4:2: "Mendicants, those mendicants who are junior, recently gone forth, newly come to this teaching and training, should be encouraged, settled, and established in the development of the four establishments of mindfulness. What four? 'Come, friends, meditate observing the body in the body—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—for the true knowledge of the body. Meditate observing feelings in feelings—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—for the true knowledge of feelings. Meditate observing the mind in the mind—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—for the true knowledge of the mind. Meditate observing phenomena in phenomena—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—for the true knowledge of phenomena.'
translations.sn47.4:3: Those mendicants who are trainees—who haven't achieved their heart's desire, but live aspiring for the supreme sanctuary from the yoke—also meditate observing the body in the body—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—for the full understanding of the body. They meditate observing feelings in feelings—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—for the full understanding of feelings. They meditate observing the mind in the mind—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—for the full understanding of the mind. They meditate observing phenomena in phenomena—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—for the full understanding of phenomena.
translations.sn47.4:4: Those mendicants who are perfected—who have ended the defilements, completed the spiritual journey, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, achieved their own goal, utterly ended the fetters of existence, and are rightly freed through final knowledge—also meditate observing the body in the body—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—detached from the body. They meditate observing feelings in feelings—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—detached from feelings. They meditate observing the mind in the mind—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—detached from the mind. They meditate observing phenomena in phenomena—keen, aware, unified, with minds that are clear, immersed in samādhi, and unified—detached from phenomena.
translations.sn47.6:1: "Once upon a time, mendicants, a hawk suddenly swooped down and grabbed a quail. Then the quail, as it was being carried off by the hawk, lamented: 'How unlucky I am, how unfortunate, that I strayed out of my territory into the domain of others! If I had stayed in my own territory today, in my ancestral domain, this hawk wouldn't have been a match for me in a fight.' 'But what is your own territory, quail, your ancestral domain?' 'The freshly plowed field covered with clods.' Then the hawk, not boasting of her own strength, not overconfident in her own strength, released the quail, saying: 'Go, quail! Even when you've gone there you won't escape me!'
translations.sn47.6:2: Then the quail went to a freshly plowed field covered with clods, climbed up on a large clod, and stood there taunting the hawk: 'Come and get me now, hawk! Come and get me now, hawk!' Then the hawk, not boasting of her own strength, not overconfident in her own strength, folded both her wings and suddenly swooped down on the quail. But when the quail knew that the hawk was nearly upon her, she slipped behind that very clod. And the hawk crashed right there, breast first. That's what happens when you stray out of your territory into the domain of others.
translations.sn47.6:3: So, mendicants, don't stray out of your own territory into the domain of others. When you stray outside your own territory into the domain of others, Māra will find a vulnerability, Māra will find a foothold. And what is a mendicant's territory outside their own, the domain of others? It is the five kinds of sensual stimulation. What five? Sights known by the eye that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. Sounds known by the ear … Smells known by the nose … Tastes known by the tongue … Touches known by the body that are likable, desirable, agreeable, pleasant, sensual, and arousing. This is a mendicant's territory outside their own, the domain of others.
translations.sn47.7:1: "Mendicants, there are rugged and uneven regions of the Himalayas, king of mountains, where neither monkeys nor humans travel. There are rugged and uneven regions of the Himalayas where monkeys travel, but not humans. There are level regions of the Himalayas, delightful, where both monkeys and humans travel. There hunters lay traps of sticky pitch on the monkey trails to catch the monkeys.
translations.sn47.8:2: That foolish, incompetent, unskilled cook doesn't pick up on their own employer's preferences: 'Today my employer preferred this sauce,' or 'They reached for this,' or 'They took a lot of this,' or 'They praised this.' 'Today my employer preferred the sour sauce,' or 'They reached for the sour,' or 'They took a lot of the sour,' or 'They praised the sour.' 'Today my employer preferred the bitter …' 'Today my employer preferred the spicy …' 'Today my employer preferred the sweet …' 'Today my employer preferred the alkaline …' 'Today my employer preferred the non-alkaline …' 'Today my employer preferred the salty …' 'Today my employer preferred the mild sauce,' or 'They reached for the mild,' or 'They took a lot of the mild,' or 'They praised the mild.'
translations.sn47.8:4: That foolish, incompetent, unskilled mendicant doesn't gain pleasant meditations in this very life, and doesn't gain mindfulness and clear comprehension. Why is that? Because that foolish, incompetent, unskilled mendicant doesn't pick up on the characteristics of their own mind.
translations.sn47.8:5: Suppose a skilled, competent, clever cook served a king or a royal minister with a variety of sauces—sour, bitter, spicy, sweet, alkaline, non-alkaline, salty, and mild.
translations.sn5.10:6: It's only suffering that arises, suffering that persists and passes away. Nothing but suffering arises, nothing but suffering ceases.
translations.sn5.1:5: Sensual pleasures are like swords and stakes, the aggregates are their chopping block. What you call sensual delight has become no delight for me.
translations.sn5.3:3: Then the nun Kisāgotamī thought: 'Who is this that spoke the verse, a human or a non-human?' Then she thought: 'This is Māra the Wicked, who spoke the verse wanting to make me feel fear, terror, and goosebumps, wanting to make me fall away from immersion.'
translations.sn5.3:6: Delight is destroyed everywhere, the mass of darkness is shattered. Having defeated the army of Death, I dwell without defilements.
translations.sn5.2:5: If anyone should think, 'I am a woman' or 'I am a man' or 'I am anything at all'— Māra's fit to address them.
translations.sn5.10:5: For just as when the parts are assembled, the word 'chariot' is used; So too when the aggregates exist, there is the convention 'a being'.
translations.sn5.10:4: "Why do you believe in a 'being', Māra, is that your view? This is just a heap of conditions, no being is found here.
translations.sn5.4:5: I'm horrified and ashamed by this foul body, so fragile and falling apart. Craving for rebirth has been uprooted.
translations.sn5.4:6: Beings who go to the realm of form, and those who abide in the formless, and the peaceful attainments—darkness is destroyed everywhere.
translations.sn5.5:2: Having approached this sal tree with its flowering crown, you stand alone at its foot, nun. There is no one whose beauty equals yours. Foolish one, aren't you afraid of rogues?
translations.sn5.5:4: Even if a hundred thousand rogues like you were to come here, I wouldn't stir a hair, I wouldn't tremble. I'm not afraid of you, Māra, even alone.
translations.sn5.5:6: I have mastery over my mind, the bases of psychic power are well developed. I am freed from all bonds; I'm not afraid of you, friend.
translations.sn5.6:2: Why don't you approve of birth? One who is born enjoys sensual pleasures. Who has persuaded you of this: 'Nun, don't approve of birth'?
translations.sn5.6:3: For one who is born there is death; one who is born experiences suffering—bondage, slaughter, affliction. Therefore one should not approve of birth.
translations.sn5.6:4: The Buddha taught the Dhamma for transcending birth. For the abandoning of all suffering, he established me in the truth.
translations.sn5.6:5: Beings who go to the realm of form, and those who abide in the formless—not understanding cessation, they return to renewed existence.
translations.sn5.8:2: For whose sake have you shaved your head? You look like a female ascetic, yet you don't approve of any sectarian doctrine. Why do you wander about so confused?
translations.sn5.8:3: Sectarian teachers outside here place their confidence in views. I don't approve of their teaching; they are not skilled in the Dhamma.
translations.sn5.8:5: Freed everywhere, unattached, the one with vision sees all. Having reached the destruction of all kamma, liberated in the ending of acquisitions—that Blessed One is my teacher; I approve of his teaching.
translations.sn5.9:2: By whom was this puppet made? Where is the maker of the puppet? Where has the puppet arisen? Where does the puppet cease?
translations.sn5.9:4: This puppet is not made by oneself, nor is this misery made by another. It has arisen dependent on a cause; with the breaking of the cause it ceases.
translations.sn5.9:6: Just so the aggregates, the elements, and these six sense bases—they have arisen dependent on a cause; with the breaking of the cause they cease.
translations.sn56.11:10: But when, monks, my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths as they really are, in their three phases and twelve aspects, was thoroughly purified, then I declared to the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, with its ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans, that I had awakened to the unsurpassed perfect awakening. Knowledge and vision arose in me: 'My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.'
translations.sn56.11:13: And so at that moment, at that instant, at that second, a cry went up as far as the Brahmā world. And this ten-thousandfold world system shook, quaked, and trembled. And an immeasurable, magnificent radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the divine glory of the gods.
