Having seen a form with the eye, do not grasp at signs or features. Since, if one were to dwell with the eye faculty unrestrained, bad unwholesome states of longing and dejection would flow in, practice restraint for that. Guard the eye faculty; undertake restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear … Having smelled an odor with the nose … Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … Having felt a touch with the body … Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp at signs or features. Since, if one were to dwell with the mind faculty unrestrained, bad unwholesome states of longing and dejection would flow in, practice restraint for that. Guard the mind faculty; undertake restraint of the mind faculty.` This too, great king, is a cause, this is a condition, by which these young mendicants with black hair, blessed with the beauty of youth, in the prime of life, who have not played among sensual pleasures, live the spiritual life completely pure and perfect for their whole life, and sustain it for a long time.'
translations.sn35.136:2: 'Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, touches, and mental phenomena in their entirety—wished for, desired, and agreeable—as far as they are said to exist.
translations.sn35.74:18: 'But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard that thus: `This is mine, I am this, this is my self`?'
translations.sn35.88:17: 'Good, good, Puṇṇa. Possessing this taming and pacification, you will be able to dwell in the Sunāparanta country. Now, Puṇṇa, go when you think it is time.'
translations.sn35.88:4: 'Puṇṇa, having been advised by me with this brief advice, in which country will you dwell?' 'Venerable sir, there is a country called Sunāparanta. I will dwell there.'
translations.sn35.88:5: 'Puṇṇa, the Sunāparanta people are fierce; Puṇṇa, the Sunāparanta people are harsh. If, Puṇṇa, the Sunāparanta people abuse and insult you, what will you think then?'
translations.sn35.95:10: 'And here, Mālukyaputta, regarding things to be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: in the seen there will be merely the seen, in the heard there will be merely the heard, in the sensed there will be merely the sensed, in the cognized there will be merely the cognized. When, Mālukyaputta, regarding things to be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, in the seen there will be merely the seen, in the heard there will be merely the heard, in the sensed there will be merely the sensed, in the cognized there will be merely the cognized; then, Mālukyaputta, you will not be by that. When, Mālukyaputta, you are not by that; then, Mālukyaputta, you will not be therein. When, Mālukyaputta, you are not therein; then, Mālukyaputta, you will be neither here nor beyond nor between the two. This itself is the end of suffering.'
translations.sn35.95:2: 'Now, Mālukyaputta, what shall we say to the younger mendicants, when you, a mendicant who is old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, reached the final stage of life, ask for advice in brief?'
translations.sn35.95:3: 'Although, sir, I am old, elderly, senior, advanced in years, come to the last stage of life. Let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief, let the Fortunate One teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that I might understand the meaning of the Blessed One's words. So that I might become an heir of the Blessed One's words.'
translations.sn35.95:4: 'What do you think, Mālukyaputta? Those forms cognizable by the eye that are unseen, that have never been seen before, that you do not see, and that you have no expectation of seeing—do you have any desire or lust or affection for them?' 'No, sir.'
translations.sn35.95:9: 'Those phenomena cognizable by the mind that are unknown, that have never been known before, that you do not know, and that you have no expectation of knowing—do you have any desire or lust or affection for them?' 'No, sir.'
translations.sn36.21:2: 'Sīvaka, some feelings arise here originating from bile. You yourself should know how some feelings arise here originating from bile. And it is agreed upon as true in the world that some feelings arise here originating from bile. Now, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and view as this: `Whatever this person experiences, whether pleasure or pain or neither-pain-nor-pleasure, all that is caused by what was done in the past`—they overshoot what is personally known, and they overshoot what is agreed upon as true in the world. Therefore I say that those ascetics and brahmins are wrong.
translations.sn36.21:4: When this was said, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: 'Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! … Let Master Gotama consider me a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for life.'
translations.sn4.13:2: 'Are you lying in a daze, or drunk on poetry? Do you have no goals to accomplish? Alone in a secluded dwelling, with drowsy face, why do you sleep?'
translations.sn4.19:5: 'What they speak of is not mine; those who speak are not me. Know this, Evil One: you will not even see my path.'
translations.sn4.24:2: 'Are you meditating in the forest overcome by grief? Have you lost wealth, or are you longing for it? Have you committed some offense in the village? Why do you not make friends with people? You have no friendship with anyone.'
translations.sn4.24:3: 'Having dug up all the root of grief, I meditate without guilt, without sorrow. Having cut off all craving and desire for existence, I meditate free of taints, O kinsman of the negligent.'
translations.sn4.24:6: 'If you have discovered the path, secure, leading to the deathless, go away, go on alone! Why do you instruct others?'
translations.sn4.24:7: 'Those people who wish to go beyond ask about the realm free from death. When asked, I explain to them what is true, that which is without attachment.'
translations.sn4.24:9: 'A crow circled around a stone the color of fat, thinking: `Perhaps we will find something soft here, perhaps there will be something tasty.`
translations.sn4.25:14: 'Having attained the goal, peace of heart, having conquered the army of the pleasant and agreeable, alone, meditating, I awakened to happiness. Therefore I do not make friends with people; friendship is not possible with anyone for me.'
translations.sn4.25:16: 'How does a monk who dwells much here cross over the five floods and cross the sixth as well? How does one who meditates much keep sensual perceptions at bay, not obtaining them?'
translations.sn4.25:17: 'With body tranquil, mind well-liberated, without volitional formations, mindful, homeless, knowing the Dhamma, meditating without thought, one is not agitated, does not drift, is not rigid.
translations.sn4.25:2: 'Why are you so unhappy, dear? What man do you grieve for? We will bind him with the snare of lust, like a forest elephant, and bring him back. He will be under your control.'
translations.sn4.25:20: 'Having cut off craving, wandering among groups and communities, many faithful ones will surely follow. This homeless one will indeed lead many people beyond, to the far shore of the King of Death.'
translations.sn4.25:23: 'Fools, you are grinding a mountain with lotus stalks, digging a rock with your nails, chewing iron with your teeth.
translations.sn4.8:2: 'One with sons delights in sons; one with cattle likewise delights in cattle. Acquisitions are a person's delight; one without acquisitions does not delight.'
translations.sn4.8:3: 'One with sons grieves over sons; one with cattle likewise grieves over cattle. Acquisitions are a person's grief; one without acquisitions does not grieve.'
translations.sn44.1:3: 'Your Majesty, there is no such ascetic or brahmin in the city district whom Your Majesty might attend upon. But there is, Your Majesty, a bhikkhunī named Khemā, a disciple of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. This good report about that venerable lady has spread: `She is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, a brilliant speaker, with good eloquence.` Let Your Majesty attend upon her.'
translations.sn44.1:6: 'Well then, great king, I'll ask you about this in return. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, great king, do you have any accountant or calculator or reckoner who can count the grains of sand in the Ganges—so many grains, or so many hundreds of grains, or so many thousands of grains, or so many hundreds of thousands of grains?' 'No, venerable lady.' 'But do you have any accountant or calculator or reckoner who can count the water in the great ocean—so many gallons, or so many hundreds of gallons, or so many thousands of gallons, or so many hundreds of thousands of gallons?' 'No, venerable lady.' 'Why is that?' 'The great ocean, venerable lady, is deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom.' 'In the same way, great king, any form by which one might describe the Realized One has been given up by the Realized One, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated, and unable to arise in the future. The Realized One is freed from reckoning in terms of form, great king. He is deep, immeasurable, and hard to fathom—like the great ocean. The description `the Realized One exists after death` doesn't apply, nor does `the Realized One doesn't exist after death`, nor `the Realized One both exists and doesn't exist after death`, nor `the Realized One neither exists nor doesn't exist after death`.
translations.sn45.1:2: 'Ignorance, mendicants, is the forerunner in the attainment of unskillful qualities, with lack of conscience and prudence following along. For an ignorant person, lacking wisdom, wrong view arises. For one of wrong view, wrong intention arises. For one of wrong intention, wrong speech arises. For one of wrong speech, wrong action arises. For one of wrong action, wrong livelihood arises. For one of wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises. For one of wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises. For one of wrong mindfulness, wrong immersion arises.
translations.sn45.4:8: 'For one whose faith and wisdom are qualities always yoked at the fore, conscience is the shaft, mind the harness, and mindfulness the watchful charioteer.
translations.sn46.30:2: 'It's incredible, sir, it's amazing! How very helpful to me has been my love, respect, conscience, and prudence for the Buddha. For formerly, when I was a layperson, I had little regard for the teaching and the Saṅgha. But seeing my love, respect, conscience, and prudence for the Buddha, I went forth from the lay life to homelessness. The Buddha taught me the Dhamma: `Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the ending of form. Such is feeling … Such is perception … Such are choices … Such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the ending of consciousness.`
translations.sn46.3:1: 'Mendicants, those mendicants who are accomplished in ethics, immersion, wisdom, freedom, and the knowledge and vision of freedom—I say that even seeing such mendicants is very helpful. I say that even hearing them is very helpful. I say that even approaching them is very helpful. I say that even attending on them is very helpful. I say that even recollecting them is very helpful. I say that even going forth after them is very helpful. Why is that? Because after hearing the teaching of such mendicants, one lives withdrawn in both ways—withdrawn in body and withdrawn in mind. Living withdrawn like this, one recollects and thinks about that teaching.
translations.sn46.52:3: 'Friend, the ascetic Gotama teaches his disciples like this: `Come, mendicants, give up the five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, and truly develop the seven awakening factors.` We too teach our disciples like this: `Come, friends, give up the five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, and truly develop the seven awakening factors.` So what, friend, is the difference, the distinction, the variation between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is, regarding the teaching of the teaching, or the instruction of the instruction?'
translations.sn46.8:2: 'Friend Upavāna, would a mendicant know: `Through my own proper attention, the seven awakening factors are well developed in me, leading to living at ease`?' 'Friend Sāriputta, a mendicant would know: `Through my own proper attention, the seven awakening factors are well developed in me, leading to living at ease.`'
translations.sn47.10:2: 'Here, Venerable Ānanda, several nuns who live with their minds well established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation recognize a higher distinction from before.' 'That's how it is, sisters, that's how it is! Any monk or nun who lives with their mind well established in the four kinds of mindfulness meditation can expect this: they will recognize a higher distinction from before.'
translations.sn47.13:3: 'Friend Cunda, this is a topic of discussion to bring to the Buddha. Come, friend Cunda, let's go to the Buddha and inform him of this matter.' 'Yes, sir,' replied Cunda the novice to Venerable Ānanda.
translations.sn47.19:2: 'That's the right method,' said the Buddha, 'as the pupil Medakathālikā said to the teacher. `I will protect myself`—the establishments of mindfulness should be practiced thus. `I will protect others`—the establishments of mindfulness should be practiced thus. Mendicants, protecting oneself, one protects others; protecting others, one protects oneself.
translations.sn47.25:2: 'Brahmin, when the four kinds of mindfulness meditation have not been developed and cultivated, the true teaching doesn't last long after the Realized One has become fully extinguished. But when the four kinds of mindfulness meditation have been developed and cultivated, the true teaching does last long after the Realized One has become fully extinguished.
translations.sn47.29:3: 'Therefore, householder, you should train like this: 'I will meditate observing the body in the body—keen, aware, and mindful, having set aside desire and aversion for the world. I will meditate observing feelings … mind … I will meditate observing phenomena in phenomena—keen, aware, and mindful, having set aside desire and aversion for the world.' That is how you should train, householder.'
translations.sn47.33:1: 'Whoever has neglected the four kinds of mindfulness meditation has neglected the noble path that leads to the complete ending of suffering. Whoever has undertaken the four kinds of mindfulness meditation has undertaken the noble path that leads to the complete ending of suffering.
translations.sn47.37:1: 'Mendicants, there are these four kinds of mindfulness meditation. What four? It's when a mendicant meditates observing the body in the body—keen, aware, and mindful, having set aside desire and aversion for the world. As they meditate observing the body in the body, desire for the body is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:1: 'Mendicants, there are these four kinds of mindfulness meditation. What four? It's when a mendicant meditates observing the body in the body—keen, aware, and mindful, having set aside desire and aversion for the world. As they meditate observing the body in the body, the body is completely understood. With the complete understanding of the body, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn5.10:2: 'By whom has this being been made? Where is the maker of a being? Where does a being arise? Where does a being cease?'
translations.sn5.1:2: 'There is no escape in the world, so what will you do with seclusion? Enjoy sensual pleasures! Do not be one who regrets it later.'
translations.sn5.1:4: 'There is an escape in the world, which I have touched well with wisdom. O Evil One, kinsman of the negligent, you do not know that state.
translations.sn5.2:2: 'That state attainable by sages, so hard to reach—a woman with her two-fingered wisdom cannot attain it.'
translations.sn5.2:4: 'What does womanhood matter when the mind is well-concentrated, when knowledge is progressing, rightly seeing into the Dhamma?
translations.sn5.3:2: 'Why do you sit alone with tearful face, like one whose children have died? Having gone into the midst of the woods alone, are you looking for a man?'
translations.sn5.3:5: 'I have completely finished with dead children; men are done with for me. I do not grieve, I do not weep, and I do not fear you, friend.
translations.sn5.4:2: 'You are young and beautiful, and I too am a young lad. Come, let us delight together with the music of a five-piece band.'
translations.sn5.4:4: 'Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and pleasant touches—I hand them over to you, Māra. I have no need of them.
translations.sn5.7:2: 'The Thirty-Three and the Yāma gods, the Tusita deities too, the gods who delight in creation, and the gods who control what others create—direct your mind there, and you will experience delight.'
translations.sn5.7:3: 'The Thirty-Three and the Yāma gods, the Tusita deities too, the gods who delight in creation, and the gods who control what others create—they are bound by the bonds of sensuality, they come again under Māra's control.
translations.sn5.7:4: The whole world is ablaze, the whole world is burning, the whole world is on fire, the whole world is quaking.
translations.sn56.35:1: 'Suppose, mendicants, there was a person with a hundred-year lifespan, who would live for a hundred years. Someone would say to them: `Come, good person, in the morning they will strike you with a hundred spears, at midday they will strike you with a hundred spears, and in the evening they will strike you with a hundred spears. And you, good person, being struck day after day with three hundred spears, with a hundred-year lifespan, living for a hundred years, will realize the four noble truths that you had not realized before, at the end of a hundred years.`
translations.sn56.36:1: 'Suppose, mendicants, a person were to cut up whatever grass, sticks, branches, and leaves there are in this Jambudīpa and gather them together in one place. Having gathered them together, they would make stakes. Having made stakes, they would impale the large creatures in the ocean on large stakes, the medium creatures on medium stakes, and the small creatures on small stakes. Yet, mendicants, the large creatures in the ocean would not be exhausted.
translations.sn56.42:2: 'But sir, what other precipice is there greater and more terrifying than this one?' 'Mendicants, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not truly understand: `This is suffering,` do not truly understand: `This is the origin of suffering,` do not truly understand: `This is the cessation of suffering,` do not truly understand: `This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering`—they delight in choices that lead to rebirth, they delight in choices that lead to old age, they delight in choices that lead to death, they delight in choices that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. Delighting in choices that lead to rebirth, old age, death, and sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, they make choices that lead to rebirth, they make choices that lead to old age, they make choices that lead to death, they make choices that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. Having made choices that lead to rebirth, old age, death, and sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress, they fall down the precipice of rebirth, they fall down the precipice of old age, they fall down the precipice of death, they fall down the precipice of sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from rebirth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, sadness, and distress. They are not freed from suffering, I say.'
translations.sn56.46:1: 'Mendicants, there are boundless, abysmal, dark, and gloomy gaps between the worlds, where the light of the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful, does not reach.'
translations.sn56.48:1: 'Suppose, mendicants, this great earth were entirely covered with water. And a man threw in a yoke with a single hole. The east wind would blow it west, the west wind would blow it east, the north wind would blow it south, and the south wind would blow it north. And there was a blind turtle who would surface once every hundred years. What do you think, mendicants? Would that blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, poke its neck through that yoke with a single hole?' 'Only by chance, sir, would that blind turtle, surfacing once every hundred years, poke its neck through that yoke with a single hole.'
translations.sn56.48:2: 'Just so by chance, mendicants, is it to gain a human birth. Just so by chance, mendicants, is it that a Realized One arises in the world, a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha. Just so by chance, mendicants, is it that the teaching and training proclaimed by a Realized One shines in the world. You have gained this human birth, mendicants. A Realized One has arisen in the world, a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha. And the teaching and training proclaimed by a Realized One shines in the world.
translations.an10.24:1: At one time Venerable Mahācunda was staying in the land of the Cetis at Sahajāti. There Venerable Mahācunda addressed the mendicants: 'Reverend mendicants!' 'Reverend,' those mendicants replied to Venerable Mahācunda. Venerable Mahācunda said this:
translations.an10.51:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants!' 'Venerable sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.an10.58:2: 'Well then, mendicants, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.an10.60:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Now at that time Venerable Girimānanda was sick, suffering, gravely ill. Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Buddha, bowed to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Buddha:
translations.an10.7:1: Then Venerable Ānanda approached Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.an3.15:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Benares in the deer park at Isipatana. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants!' 'Venerable sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.an3.32:4: 'Here, Ānanda, a mendicant thinks: `This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all activities, the relinquishment of all attachments, the ending of craving, dispassion, cessation, extinguishment.` In this way, Ānanda, a mendicant might gain such a state of immersion that there would be no underlying tendencies to the conceit `I am,` the conceit `I am this,` and the conceit `mine` regarding this conscious body, and no underlying tendencies to the conceit `I am,` the conceit `I am this,` and the conceit `mine` regarding all external signs; and they would enter and remain in that freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where these underlying tendencies to the conceit `I am,` the conceit `I am this,` and the conceit `mine` do not occur.
translations.an3.33:2: 'Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train like this: `There will be no underlying tendencies to the conceit `I am,` the conceit `I am this,` and the conceit `mine` regarding this conscious body; there will be no underlying tendencies to the conceit `I am,` the conceit `I am this,` and the conceit `mine` regarding all external signs; and we will enter and remain in that freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where these underlying tendencies to the conceit `I am,` the conceit `I am this,` and the conceit `mine` do not occur.` That is how you should train, Sāriputta.
translations.an3.33:3: When, Sāriputta, a mendicant has no underlying tendencies to the conceit 'I am,' the conceit 'I am this,' and the conceit 'mine' regarding this conscious body; has no underlying tendencies to the conceit 'I am,' the conceit 'I am this,' and the conceit 'mine' regarding all external signs; and enters and remains in that freedom of heart and freedom by wisdom where these underlying tendencies to the conceit 'I am,' the conceit 'I am this,' and the conceit 'mine' do not occur; this is called, Sāriputta: 'A mendicant who has cut off craving, untied the fetters, and by completely understanding conceit has made an end of suffering.' And it was with reference to this that I said in the Way to the Beyond, in the Questions of Udaya:
translations.an3.51:1: Then two brahmins who were old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, having reached the final stage, a hundred and twenty years old from birth, approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to the Buddha: 'Master Gotama, we are brahmins who are old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, having reached the final stage, a hundred and twenty years old from birth. And we have not done what is good, not done what is skillful, not made a shelter from fear. Let Master Gotama advise us, let Master Gotama instruct us for our long-term welfare and happiness.'
translations.an3.60:2: 'Well then, brahmin, I will ask you about this in return. Answer as you see fit. What do you think, brahmin? Here a Realized One arises in the world, a perfected one, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to train, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed. He says: `Come, this is the path, this is the practice. Practicing in this way, I have realized for myself with direct knowledge the supreme culmination of the spiritual life and declare it. Come, you too practice in this way, and practicing in this way, you too will realize for yourself with direct knowledge the supreme culmination of the spiritual life and will enter and remain in it.` Thus this teacher teaches the Dhamma, and others practice accordingly. And there are many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands of them.
translations.an3.60:5: For a second time Venerable Ānanda said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: 'Brahmin, I am not asking you: `Who are worthy of your respect, who are worthy of your praise?` I am asking you this, brahmin: `Of these two practices, brahmin, which practice do you prefer as being less complicated, less troublesome, more fruitful, and more beneficial?`' For a second time the brahmin Saṅgārava said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Just like Master Gotama and Master Ānanda. These are worthy of my respect, these are worthy of my praise.'
translations.an3.60:7: Then the Buddha thought: 'Even when asked a legitimate question three times by Ānanda, the brahmin Saṅgārava flounders and does not answer. Why don't I release him?' Then the Buddha said to the brahmin Saṅgārava: 'Brahmin, what topic of conversation arose today among the king's men sitting together in the royal court?' 'Today, Master Gotama, this topic of conversation arose among the king's men sitting together in the royal court: `Formerly there were fewer mendicants, but more displayed superhuman psychic powers. But these days there are more mendicants, but fewer display superhuman psychic powers.` This was the topic of conversation that arose today, Master Gotama, among the king's men sitting together in the royal court.'
translations.an3.63:1: At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a village of Kosalan brahmins named Venāgapura. The brahmins and householders of Venāgapura heard: 'It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Venāgapura. He has this good reputation: `That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to train, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.` He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others. He teaches Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that is entirely complete and pure. It is good to see such perfected ones.'
translations.an3.63:2: Then the brahmins and householders of Venāgapura went to the Buddha. Some bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Buddha, and when the greetings and polite conversation were over, sat down to one side. Some raised their joined palms toward the Buddha and sat down to one side. Some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side. Some kept silent and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Vacchagotta of Venāgapura said to the Buddha:
translations.an4.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Vajjis at Bhaṇḍagāma. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants!' 'Venerable sir,' they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an4.24:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāketa in the Dark Forest. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants!' 'Venerable sir,' they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an4.35:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground. Then Vassakāra, a brahmin who was a chief minister of Magadha, went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Vassakāra, the brahmin who was a chief minister of Magadha, said to the Buddha:
translations.an4.36:1: At one time the Buddha was traveling along the road between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setabya. And the brahmin Doṇa was also traveling along the road between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setabya. The brahmin Doṇa saw on the Buddha's footprints the thousand-spoked wheels with rims and hubs, complete in every detail. Seeing this, he thought: 'How amazing, how wonderful! Surely these cannot be the footprints of a human being.' Then the Buddha left the road and sat down at the root of a tree, cross-legged, with his body straight, and established mindfulness in front of him. Then the brahmin Doṇa, following the Buddha's footprints, saw him sitting at the root of a tree—inspiring and confidence-inspiring, with peaceful faculties and peaceful mind, having attained the highest taming and tranquility, tamed, guarded, with restrained faculties, a great being. Seeing him, he went up to the Buddha and said:
translations.an4.53:1: At one time the Buddha was traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. And a number of householders and their wives were also traveling along the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Then the Buddha left the road and sat down at the root of a certain tree. The householders and their wives saw the Buddha sitting at the root of a tree. Seeing him, they went up to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to the householders and their wives seated to one side:
translations.an5.31:1: At one time … in Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then Princess Sumanā, escorted by five hundred chariots and five hundred princesses, went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Princess Sumanā said to the Buddha:
translations.an5.43:1: Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika seated to one side:
translations.an5.56:3: 'That is how it is, mendicant, for one who does not guard the sense doors, who does not know moderation in eating, who is not devoted to wakefulness, who does not have insight into skillful qualities, and who does not pursue the development of the qualities that lead to awakening in the evening and at dawn—that the body becomes sluggish, the directions are unclear, teachings do not occur to them, dullness and drowsiness overcome the mind, they live discontent in the spiritual life, and they have doubt regarding the teachings. Therefore, mendicant, you should train like this: `I will guard the sense doors, I will know moderation in eating, I will be devoted to wakefulness, I will have insight into skillful qualities, and I will pursue the development of the qualities that lead to awakening in the evening and at dawn.` That is how you should train, mendicant.'
translations.an8.14:1: 'Mendicants, I will teach you eight kinds of wild horses and eight faults in horses, and eight kinds of wild people and eight faults in people. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, venerable sir,' they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.an8.19:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Verañjā at the root of a neem tree used by Naḷeru. Then Pahārāda, lord of demons, went to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. The Buddha said to Pahārāda, lord of demons, standing to one side:
translations.an8.22:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Vajjis at Hatthigāma. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants, you should remember the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma as someone who has eight amazing and incredible qualities.' That is what the Buddha said. When he had spoken, the Holy One got up from his seat and entered his dwelling.
translations.an8.23:2: Then a certain mendicant robed up in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, went to the home of Hatthaka of Āḷavī. When he arrived, he sat down on the seat spread out for him. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī went up to that mendicant, bowed, and sat down to one side. The mendicant said to Hatthaka of Āḷavī:
translations.an8.23:4: Then that mendicant, after receiving almsfood at Hatthaka of Āḷavī's home, got up from his seat and left. Then after the meal, on his return from almsround, that mendicant went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that mendicant said to the Buddha:
translations.an8.30:2: Then the Buddha, knowing with his mind the thoughts in Venerable Anuruddha's mind, just as a strong man might extend a contracted arm or contract an extended arm, vanished from the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the deer park at Suṁsumāragira in the land of the Bhaggas, and reappeared in front of Venerable Anuruddha in the Eastern Bamboo Park in the land of the Cetis. The Buddha sat down on the seat spread out for him. Venerable Anuruddha also bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to Venerable Anuruddha, who was seated to one side:
translations.an8.30:22: Then Venerable Anuruddha stayed for another rains residence right there in the Eastern Bamboo Park in the land of the Cetis. Then, living alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute, Venerable Anuruddha soon realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the supreme culmination of the spiritual life—for the sake of which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness—and having entered upon it, he dwelled in it. He understood: 'Rebirth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being.' And Venerable Anuruddha became one of the perfected ones. Then, on attaining perfection, Venerable Anuruddha at that time spoke these verses:
translations.an8.30:3: 'Good, good, Anuruddha! It is good that you think this thought of a great man: `This teaching is for one of few wishes, not for one of many wishes. This teaching is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent. This teaching is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company. This teaching is for one of aroused energy, not for one who is lazy. This teaching is for one with established mindfulness, not for one who is unmindful. This teaching is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated. This teaching is for one with wisdom, not for one of poor wisdom.` Well then, Anuruddha, you should also think this eighth thought of a great man: `This teaching is for one who delights in non-proliferation, who enjoys non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation, who enjoys proliferation.`
translations.an8.7:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants regarding Devadatta: 'It is good, mendicants, for a mendicant to review their own failings from time to time. It is good, mendicants, for a mendicant to review the failings of others from time to time. It is good, mendicants, for a mendicant to review their own successes from time to time. It is good, mendicants, for a mendicant to review the successes of others from time to time. Mendicants, overcome by eight bad qualities, with his mind overwhelmed, Devadatta is bound for a place of loss, bound for hell, remaining there for an eon, irredeemable.
translations.an8.8:4: Then Sakka, lord of the gods, just as a strong man might extend a contracted arm or contract an extended arm, vanished from among the gods of the Thirty-Three and reappeared in front of Venerable Uttara at Vaṭajālikā on Mount Saṅkheyya in the Mahisa country. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, went up to Venerable Uttara, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the gods, said to Venerable Uttara:
translations.an8.8:7: 'It is amazing, sir! It is incredible, sir! How well said this was by Venerable Uttara: `Whatever is well spoken is all the word of that Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha. Taking it from there, we and others speak.` Sir Uttara, at one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants regarding Devadatta:
translations.mn108:4: Then Venerable Ānanda went to the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna's workplace, to where the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna was. The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna saw Venerable Ānanda coming from a distance. Seeing him, he said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Come, Master Ānanda! Welcome to Master Ānanda! It has been a long time since Master Ānanda made an occasion to come here. Please sit down, Master Ānanda, this seat is prepared.' Venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat. The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna also took a low seat and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn117:2: 'Mendicants, I will teach you noble right immersion with its supports and its requisites. Listen to that and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn118:3: Now at that time, on the observance day of the fifteenth, the full moon night of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, the Buddha was sitting in the open surrounded by the Saṅgha of mendicants. Then the Buddha, looking around the silent Saṅgha of mendicants, addressed the mendicants:
translations.mn12:2: Now at that time Sunakkhatta the Licchavi had recently left this teaching and training. He was saying this to the assembly at Vesālī: 'The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The ascetic Gotama teaches a Dhamma worked out by reasoning, following his own line of inquiry, according to his own inspiration. And the Dhamma for the sake of which he teaches it leads one who practices it to the complete ending of suffering.'
translations.mn135:2: Then Subha, the student, son of Todeyya, approached the Buddha. He exchanged greetings with the Buddha. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Subha, the student, son of Todeyya, said to the Buddha:
translations.mn135:4: 'Student, beings are owners of their actions, heirs of their actions, born of their actions, bound by their actions, and have their actions as their refuge. It is action that distinguishes beings as inferior and superior.' 'I do not understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement of Master Gotama's, which he did not explain in detail. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach me the Dhamma so that I might understand the detailed meaning of this brief statement.' 'Then, student, listen and pay close attention. I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' Subha, the student, son of Todeyya, replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn13:2: Then, in the morning, a number of mendicants robed up, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those mendicants: 'It is too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. Why don't we go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?' Then those mendicants went to the park of the wanderers of other sects. They exchanged greetings with those wanderers. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side. Then those wanderers of other sects said to those mendicants seated to one side:
translations.mn13:4: Then those mendicants neither approved nor rejected what those wanderers of other sects said. Without approving or rejecting, they got up from their seats and left, thinking: 'We will learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Buddha.'
translations.mn140:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Buddha was wandering in the Magadhan lands and arrived at Rājagaha. He approached Bhaggava the potter and said to him:
translations.mn140:4: Then the Buddha entered the potter's workshop, prepared a spread of grass on one side, and sat down, crossing his legs, straightening his body, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Then the Buddha spent most of the night seated. Venerable Pukkusāti also spent most of the night seated. Then it occurred to the Buddha: 'This clansman conducts himself in an inspiring way. Why don't I question him?' Then the Buddha said to Venerable Pukkusāti:
translations.mn140:6: Then it occurred to the Buddha: 'This clansman has gone forth out of faith in me. Why don't I teach him the Dhamma?' Then the Buddha addressed Venerable Pukkusāti: 'I will teach you the Dhamma, mendicant. Listen and pay close attention. I will speak.' 'Yes, friend,' Venerable Pukkusāti replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn146:4: Then the Buddha addressed Venerable Nandaka: 'Advise the nuns, Nandaka. Instruct the nuns, Nandaka. Give the nuns a Dhamma talk, brahmin.' 'Yes, Bhante,' Venerable Nandaka replied to the Buddha. Then, in the morning, he robed up, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. After wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on returning from the alms round, he went with a companion to the Rājakārāma. Those nuns saw Venerable Nandaka coming from afar. Seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for washing the feet. Venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, he washed his feet. Those nuns paid homage to Venerable Nandaka and sat down to one side. To those nuns seated to one side, Venerable Nandaka said this:
translations.mn147:2: Now at that time many thousands of deities were following the Buddha, thinking: 'Today the Buddha will lead Venerable Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints.' Then the Buddha, having plunged into the Blind Men's Grove, sat down on a prepared seat at the foot of a certain tree. Venerable Rāhula also paid homage to the Buddha and sat down to one side. To Venerable Rāhula seated to one side, the Buddha said this: 'What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?' 'Impermanent, Bhante.' 'Is what is impermanent suffering or happiness?' 'Suffering, Bhante.' 'Is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: `This is mine, this I am, this is my self`?' 'No, Bhante.'
translations.mn148:2: 'Mendicants, I will teach you a Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing. I will reveal a spiritual life that is entirely complete and pure, that is, the six sets of six. Listen and pay close attention. I will speak.' 'Yes, Bhante,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn149:2: 'Mendicants, I will teach you the great discourse on the six sense bases. Listen and pay close attention. I will speak.' 'Yes, Bhante,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn1:1: Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Buddha was staying near Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Grove at the foot of a royal sāla tree. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants!' 'Bhante,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn1:2: 'Mendicants, I will teach you a discourse on the root of all things. Listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn22:18: When this was said, a certain mendicant said to the Buddha: 'Sir, can there be anxiety about external things that don't exist?' 'There can be, mendicant,' said the Buddha. 'It's when someone thinks: `I had it, but now I don't. I might get it, but I'm not getting it.` They sorrow and pine and lament, beating their breast and falling into confusion. This is how there is anxiety about external things that don't exist.'
translations.mn22:7: Then the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'What do you think, mendicants? Has this mendicant Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trapper, ever even warmed up in this teaching and training?' 'How could he, sir? No, sir.' When this was said, the mendicant Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture trapper, sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping, head down, dejected, with nothing to say. Then the Buddha, knowing that Ariṭṭha was silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping, head down, dejected, with nothing to say, said to him: 'You will be known by your own bad view, you foolish man. I will question the mendicants about this.'
translations.mn27:3: 'Suppose, sir, a skilled elephant tracker were to enter an elephant wood. There he would see a large elephant's footprint, long and broad. He would conclude: `This must be a big bull elephant.` In the same way, when I saw four footprints of the ascetic Gotama, I came to the conclusion: `The Blessed One is a fully awakened Buddha, the teaching is well explained by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing well.`'
translations.mn27:9: Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. He then informed the Buddha of the entire conversation he had had with the wanderer Pilotika. When he had finished, the Buddha said to him: 'Brahmin, the simile of the elephant's footprint is not yet complete in detail. As to how the simile of the elephant's footprint is complete in detail, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn28:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There Venerable Sāriputta addressed the mendicants: 'Friends, mendicants!' 'Friend,' those mendicants replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn28:24: If others treat that mendicant with disagreeable, unpleasant, and displeasing conduct—by contact with fists, stones, sticks, or knives. They understand: 'Such is this body that contacts with fists, stones, sticks, and knives affect it. But the Buddha has said in his advice on the simile of the saw: `Mendicants, if bandits were to sever you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, anyone who had a malicious thought on that account would not be following my instructions.` My energy shall be roused up and unflagging, my mindfulness established and unconfused, my body tranquil and undisturbed, my mind concentrated and unified. Now let contacts with fists, stones, sticks, and knives affect this body. For this is how the instructions of the Buddhas are practiced.'
translations.mn28:28: The form of such a person is included in the aggregate of form affected by clinging. The feeling of such a person is included in the aggregate of feeling affected by clinging. The perception of such a person is included in the aggregate of perception affected by clinging. The volitional formations of such a person are included in the aggregate of volitional formations affected by clinging. The consciousness of such a person is included in the aggregate of consciousness affected by clinging. They understand: 'So this is how there is inclusion, gathering, and coming together of these five aggregates affected by clinging. And the Buddha has said: `One who sees dependent origination sees the teaching. One who sees the teaching sees dependent origination.` And these five aggregates affected by clinging are dependently originated. Desire, attachment, attraction, and holding to these five aggregates affected by clinging is the origin of suffering. Removal and abandoning of desire and greed for these five aggregates affected by clinging is the cessation of suffering.' To this extent too, friend, a mendicant has done much.
translations.mn29:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha on Vulture's Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants regarding Devadatta:
translations.mn36:3: Then Saccaka, the son of Jain parents, while walking and wandering about for exercise, approached the Great Wood and the hall with the peaked roof. Venerable Ānanda saw Saccaka coming from a distance. Seeing him, he said to the Buddha: 'Sir, here comes Saccaka, the son of Jain parents, a debater and clever speaker, well-regarded by many people. He wants to discredit the Buddha, the teaching, and the Saṅgha. Sir, please sit for a moment out of compassion.' The Buddha sat on the seat prepared. Then Saccaka went up to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Saccaka said to the Buddha:
translations.mn36:46: 'I recall, Aggivessana, that in the last month of summer, after my meal, returning from almsround, I spread out my outer robe folded in four and lay down on my right side, mindful and clearly aware, to sleep.' 'Some ascetics and brahmins call that an abiding in delusion, Master Gotama.' 'That is not how one is deluded or undeluded, Aggivessana. But as to how one is deluded or undeluded, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha son replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn38:2: Now at that time a mendicant named Sāti, a fisherman's son, had the following harmful misconception: 'As I understand the teaching explained by the Buddha, it is this very same consciousness that roams and transmigrates, not another.'
translations.mn38:6: Then the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'What do you think, mendicants? Has this mendicant Sāti, the fisherman's son, kindled even a spark in this teaching and training?' 'How could he, sir? No, sir.' When this was said, the mendicant Sāti, the fisherman's son, sat silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping, head down, dejected, with nothing to say. Then the Buddha, knowing that Sāti was silent, dismayed, with shoulders drooping, head down, dejected, with nothing to say, said to him: 'You will be known by this harmful misconception of your own, foolish man. I will question the mendicants about this.'
translations.mn38:7: Then the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Do you too understand the teaching I have taught in such a way that this mendicant Sāti, the fisherman's son, by his own wrong grasp, misrepresents us, and digs up himself, and generates much demerit?' 'No, sir. For in many ways the Buddha has told us that consciousness is dependently originated, and that apart from conditions there is no arising of consciousness.' 'Good, good, mendicants. It is good that you understand the teaching I have taught in this way. For in many ways I have told you that consciousness is dependently originated, and that apart from conditions there is no arising of consciousness. Yet this mendicant Sāti, the fisherman's son, by his own wrong grasp, misrepresents us, and digs up himself, and generates much demerit. This will be for that foolish man's lasting harm and suffering.
translations.mn41:3: Then the brahmin householders of Sālā went to the Buddha. Having approached, some bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Buddha, and when the cordial and courteous talk was over, sat down to one side; some raised their joined palms toward the Buddha and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan before the Buddha and sat down to one side; some remained silent and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin householders of Sālā said to the Buddha:
translations.mn52:15: When this was said, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Just as, Venerable Ānanda, a man seeking one entrance to a hidden treasure would find eleven entrances all at once; so too, venerable sir, while seeking one door to the deathless, I have found eleven doors to the deathless for development. Just as, venerable sir, if a man had a house with eleven doors, and when that house caught fire, he could escape safely through any one of those doors; so too, venerable sir, through any one of these eleven doors to the deathless I can escape safely. These other sectarians, venerable sir, would seek a teacher's fee for their teacher; why shouldn't I make an offering to Venerable Ānanda?'
translations.mn64:4: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: 'This is the time, Blessed One, this is the time, Fortunate One, for the Buddha to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard from the Buddha, the mendicants will remember it.' 'Then, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' Venerable Ānanda replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.mn6:15: If a mendicant should wish: 'May I hear both kinds of sounds with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human—divine and human, whether far or near,' they should fulfill the precepts … and be devoted to empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:16: If a mendicant should wish: 'May I understand the minds of other beings, other individuals, having encompassed them with my own mind—may I understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust, a mind without lust as a mind without lust; a mind with hate as a mind with hate, a mind without hate as a mind without hate; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; a contracted mind as a contracted mind, a distracted mind as a distracted mind; an expansive mind as an expansive mind, an unexpansive mind as an unexpansive mind; a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; a liberated mind as a liberated mind, an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,' they should fulfill the precepts … and be devoted to empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:3: If a mendicant should wish: 'May I be dear and agreeable to my fellow monastics, respected and esteemed,' they should fulfill the precepts, be devoted to internal serenity of mind, not neglect absorption, be endowed with insight, and be devoted to empty dwellings.
translations.mn6:7: A mendicant might wish: 'May I prevail over desire and discontent, and may discontent not prevail over me. May I live having overcome any desire and discontent that have arisen.' So let them fulfill their precepts … and cultivate empty huts.
translations.mn6:9: A mendicant might wish: 'May I get the four absorptions—blissful meditations in the present life that belong to the higher mind—when I want, without trouble or difficulty.' So let them fulfill their precepts … and cultivate empty huts.
translations.mn70:1: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering in the Kāsī country together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants:
translations.mn70:4: Now at that time the mendicants called Assaji and Punabbasuka were residing at Kīṭāgiri. Then several mendicants approached the mendicants Assaji and Punabbasuka. Having approached, they said to the mendicants Assaji and Punabbasuka: 'Friends, the Buddha eats only outside of the night-time, and so does the Saṅgha of mendicants. Friends, those who eat only outside of the night-time experience few illnesses, few afflictions, lightness, strength, and comfortable living. Come, friends, you too should eat only outside of the night-time. Friends, you too, eating only outside of the night-time, will experience few illnesses, few afflictions, lightness, strength, and comfortable living.' When this was said, the mendicants Assaji and Punabbasuka said to those mendicants: 'Friends, we eat in the evening, in the morning, and during the day at the wrong time. Eating in the evening, in the morning, and during the day at the wrong time, we experience few illnesses, few afflictions, lightness, strength, and comfortable living. Why should we give up what is visible and chase after what is time-dependent? We will eat in the evening, in the morning, and during the day at the wrong time.'
translations.mn75:7: Now this conversation between the Buddha and the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta was left unfinished. Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and wandering about for exercise, approached the fire chamber of the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta, where the Buddha was. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Buddha. When the cordial and amiable talk was finished, he sat down to one side. To the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya seated to one side, the Buddha said this:
translations.mn82:11: Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached his mother and father. Having approached, they said this to the mother and father of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla: 'Mother and father, the clansman Raṭṭhapāla is lying right there on the bare ground, saying: `Either I will die here or I will go forth.` If you do not give the clansman Raṭṭhapāla permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness, he will die right there. But if you do give the clansman Raṭṭhapāla permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness, you will see him even after he has gone forth. If the clansman Raṭṭhapāla does not find satisfaction in going forth from the household life into homelessness, what other option will he have? He will return right here. Give the clansman Raṭṭhapāla permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness.' 'Dear ones, we give the clansman Raṭṭhapāla permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness. But after going forth, he must visit his mother and father.' Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla approached the clansman Raṭṭhapāla. Having approached, they said this to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla: 'Get up, friend Raṭṭhapāla, you have been given permission by your mother and father to go forth from the household life into homelessness. But after going forth, you must visit your mother and father.'
translations.mn82:24: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said this to his father: 'Householder, if food is to be given, give it; do not harass us.' 'Eat, dear Raṭṭhapāla, the meal is ready.' Then the father of Venerable Raṭṭhapāla served and satisfied Venerable Raṭṭhapāla with his own hands with fine foods to eat and drink. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having eaten and removed his hand from the bowl, while standing, spoke these verses:
translations.mn82:28: Then King Korabya, having said 'Dispose of all the food to eat and drink that was prepared there,' had fine vehicles harnessed, mounted a fine vehicle, and departed from Thullakotthika with fine vehicles, with great royal pomp, to see Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. Having gone as far as the ground was passable for vehicles, he dismounted from the vehicle and approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla on foot, accompanied by a distinguished retinue. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. When the cordial and amiable talk was finished, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, King Korabya said this to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: 'Let Master Raṭṭhapāla sit here on the elephant rug.' 'It is enough, great king, you sit; I am seated on my own seat.' King Korabya sat on the prepared seat. Having sat down, King Korabya said this to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
translations.mn82:6: Then, not long after the brahmins and householders of Thullakotthita had left, Raṭṭhapāla went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Raṭṭhapāla said to the Buddha: 'As I understand the teaching explained by the Buddha, it is not easy for one living at home to lead the spiritual life that is fully complete and pure, polished like a conch shell. I wish, sir, to shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the lay life to homelessness. May I receive the going forth in the Buddha's presence, may I receive ordination. Let the Buddha give me the going forth.' 'But Raṭṭhapāla, have you been given permission by your mother and father to go forth from the lay life to homelessness?' 'No, sir, I have not been given permission by my mother and father to go forth from the lay life to homelessness.' 'Raṭṭhapāla, Tathāgatas do not give the going forth to a son who has not been given permission by his mother and father.' 'Sir, I will act in such a way that my mother and father will give me permission to go forth from the lay life to homelessness.'
translations.mn95:11: Now at that time the Buddha was sitting, having exchanged some polite conversation with the very senior brahmins. At that time a young man named Kāpaṭika was seated in that assembly. He was young, with shaven head, sixteen years old, a master of the three Vedas with their vocabularies, liturgy, phonology, and etymology, and the histories as a fifth; skilled in philology and grammar, he was fully versed in cosmology and the marks of a great man. While the very senior brahmins were conversing with the Buddha, he kept interrupting their conversation. Then the Buddha rebuked the young man Kāpaṭika: 'Venerable Bhāradvāja should not interrupt while the very senior brahmins are conversing. Venerable Bhāradvāja should wait until the conversation is finished.' When this was said, the brahmin Caṅkī said to the Buddha: 'Let Master Gotama not rebuke the young man Kāpaṭika. The young man Kāpaṭika is of good family, the young man Kāpaṭika is learned, the young man Kāpaṭika is wise, the young man Kāpaṭika is a good speaker, and the young man Kāpaṭika is capable of engaging in discussion with Master Gotama on this matter.'
translations.mn95:5: Now at that time the brahmin Caṅkī had gone to the upper terrace of his house for a midday rest. He saw the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda leaving Opāsāda in groups and crowds, heading north toward the Deva Grove, the sal forest. Seeing this, he addressed his steward: 'My good steward, why are the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda leaving Opāsāda in groups and crowds, heading north toward the Deva Grove, the sal forest?'
translations.sn1.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta's Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said to the Buddha: 'Dear sir, how did you cross the flood?' 'I crossed the flood without halting and without straining, friend.' 'But how, dear sir, did you cross the flood without halting and without straining?' 'When I halted, friend, I sank; when I strained, I was swept away. That is how, friend, I crossed the flood without halting and without straining.'
translations.sn1.20:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Hot Springs Monastery. Then Venerable Samiddhi rose at the last watch of the night and went to the hot springs to bathe. After bathing in the hot springs and coming out, he stood in a single robe drying his limbs. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire hot springs, went up to Venerable Samiddhi. Standing in the air, she addressed Venerable Samiddhi with a verse:
translations.sn1.20:4: Then that deity, standing on the ground, said to Venerable Samiddhi: 'You are young, monk, gone forth while still a youth, black-haired, blessed with the beauty of youth, in the prime of life, without having played among sensual pleasures. Enjoy human sensual pleasures, monk! Do not abandon what is visible here and now to chase after what takes time.'
translations.sn1.20:8: 'Monk, it is not easy for us to approach that Buddha, as he is surrounded by other powerful deities. But if you, monk, would approach that Buddha and ask about this matter, we too would come to hear the teaching.' 'Yes, friend,' Venerable Samiddhi replied to that deity. Then he went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Samiddhi said to the Buddha:
translations.sn1.2:1: At Sāvatthī. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta's Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said to the Buddha:
translations.sn1.36:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then, late at night, several deities of the Satullapa group, glorious, lighting up the entire Jeta's Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity recited this verse in the Buddha's presence:
translations.sn1.38:2: Then, late at night, seven hundred deities of the Satullapa host, of stunning beauty, lighting up the entire Maddakucchi, approached the Buddha, bowed to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity expressed this heartfelt sentiment in the Buddha's presence: 'The ascetic Gotama is truly a serpent! And with serpent-like composure he endures painful, sharp, severe, bitter, unpleasant, disagreeable bodily feelings, mindful and aware, without being distressed.'
translations.sn1.38:3: Then another deity expressed this heartfelt sentiment in the Buddha's presence: 'The ascetic Gotama is truly a lion! And with lion-like composure he endures painful, sharp, severe, bitter, unpleasant, disagreeable bodily feelings, mindful and aware, without being distressed.'
translations.sn1.38:8: Then another deity expressed this heartfelt sentiment in the Buddha's presence: 'See this well-developed immersion and well-liberated mind, neither bent forward nor bent back, nor held in check by forceful suppression. Whoever would think they could look down on such a serpent of a man, such a lion of a man, such a thoroughbred of a man, such a bull of a man, such a beast of burden of a man, such a tamed man—what could that be other than blindness?'
translations.sn1.41:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then, late at night, a deity of stunning beauty, lighting up the entire Jeta's Grove, approached the Buddha, bowed to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity recited these verses in the Buddha's presence:
translations.sn11.14:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants!' 'Venerable sir,' they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.sn11.14:3: Then, mendicants, Sakka, lord of the gods, addressed the gods of the Thirty-Three: 'Good sirs, do not be offended by this young god. This young god, good sirs, when he was formerly a human being, undertook faith in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One, undertook ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Having undertaken faith, ethics, learning, generosity, and wisdom in the teaching and training proclaimed by the Realized One, with the breakup of the body, after death, he was reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world, in the company of the gods of the Thirty-Three. He outshines the other gods in beauty and glory.' Then, mendicants, Sakka, lord of the gods, winning over the gods of the Thirty-Three, on that occasion recited these verses:
translations.sn11.22:1: At Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove. There … he said this: 'Once upon a time, mendicants, a certain ugly, deformed spirit was sitting on the seat of Sakka, lord of the gods. The gods of the Thirty-Three complained, criticized, and grumbled about this: 'It's incredible, it's amazing! This ugly, deformed spirit is sitting on the seat of Sakka, lord of the gods!' But the more the gods of the Thirty-Three complained, criticized, and grumbled, the more handsome, good-looking, and lovely that spirit became.
translations.sn11.22:3: Then, mendicants, Sakka, lord of the gods, approached that anger-eating spirit. He arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, raised his joined palms toward that anger-eating spirit, and announced his name three times: 'Good sir, I am Sakka, lord of the gods! Good sir, I am Sakka, lord of the gods!' The more Sakka announced his name, the uglier and more deformed that spirit became. Having become uglier and more deformed, he vanished right there. Then, mendicants, Sakka, lord of the gods, having sat down on his own seat, winning over the gods of the Thirty-Three, on that occasion recited these verses:
translations.sn11.24:3: Once upon a time, mendicants, Sakka, lord of the gods, in the Sudhamma assembly hall, winning over the gods of the Thirty-Three, on that occasion recited this verse:
translations.sn11.3:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants!' 'Venerable sir,' they replied. The Buddha said this:
translations.sn11.3:2: 'Once upon a time, mendicants, a battle was fought between the gods and the demons. Then, mendicants, Sakka, lord of the gods, addressed the gods of the Thirty-Three:
translations.sn11.3:9: But I say this, mendicants: 'If, mendicants, when you have gone to the wilderness, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, fear or terror or goosebumps should arise, on that occasion you should recollect me: `Indeed, the Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.` For when you recollect me, mendicants, any fear or terror or goosebumps that you have will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.5:3: When this verse was spoken by Vepacitti, lord of the demons, the demons applauded, but the gods remained silent. Then, mendicants, Vepacitti, lord of the demons, said to Sakka, lord of the gods: 'Speak a verse, lord of the gods.' When this was said, mendicants, Sakka, lord of the gods, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:5: When this verse was spoken by Sakka, lord of the gods, the gods applauded, but the demons remained silent. Then, mendicants, Sakka, lord of the gods, said to Vepacitti, lord of the demons: 'Speak a verse, Vepacitti.' When this was said, mendicants, Vepacitti, lord of the demons, spoke this verse:
translations.sn12.15:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Kaccānagotta approached the Buddha, bowed to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Kaccānagotta said to the Buddha: 'Venerable sir, it is said `right view, right view.` To what extent, venerable sir, is there right view?'
translations.sn12.17:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground. Then the Buddha, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Buddha coming from a distance. Seeing him, he approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the naked ascetic Kassapa said to the Buddha: 'We would like to ask Master Gotama about a certain point, if Master Gotama would give us the opportunity to answer a question.' 'Now is not the time for questions, Kassapa; we have entered among the houses.'
translations.sn12.18:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wanderer Timbaruka said to the Buddha:
translations.sn12.25:1: At Sāvatthī. Then in the evening, Venerable Bhūmija came out of seclusion and approached Venerable Sāriputta. He exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Bhūmija said to Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.sn12.31:8: And how, sir, is one a person who has comprehended the teaching? One sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'This has come to be.' Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'This has come to be,' one is freed through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what has come to be, without grasping. One sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'Its origination is from nutriment.' Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'Its origination is from nutriment,' one is freed through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what originates from nutriment, without grasping. One sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation.' Having seen with right wisdom as it really is: 'With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation,' one is freed through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding what is subject to cessation, without grasping. That is how, sir, one is a person who has comprehended the teaching. Thus, sir, regarding what was said in the Pārāyana, in the Questions of Ajita:
translations.sn12.44:1: At Sāvatthī. 'Mendicants, I will teach you the origination and the ending of the world. Listen to this and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.sn12.46:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain brahmin approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that brahmin said to the Buddha:
translations.sn12.51:2: 'How, mendicants, does a mendicant investigate so as to bring about the complete ending of suffering?' 'Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Buddha, guided by the Buddha, with the Buddha as refuge. It would be good if the Buddha himself would clarify the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Buddha, the mendicants will remember it.' 'Then listen, mendicants, and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.sn12.66:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Kurus, near a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadamma. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants!' 'Venerable sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this: 'Do you, mendicants, practice inner exploration?' When this was said, a certain mendicant said to the Buddha: 'I, sir, practice inner exploration.' 'But how do you, mendicant, practice inner exploration?' Then that mendicant explained. As that mendicant explained, he did not satisfy the Buddha's mind.
translations.sn12.66:2: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: 'This is the time for that, Blessed One; this is the time for that, Fortunate One— for the Buddha to speak on inner exploration. Having heard it from the Buddha, the mendicants will remember it.' 'Then, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' those mendicants replied to the Buddha. The Buddha said this:
translations.sn12.67:8: 'It is wonderful, friend Sāriputta! It is amazing, friend Sāriputta! How well this has been spoken by Venerable Sāriputta. And we rejoice in Venerable Sāriputta's statement on these thirty-six grounds:
translations.sn12.70:3: Then Venerable Ānanda, taking the wanderer Susīma, approached the Buddha. Having approached and paid homage to the Buddha, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Ānanda said to the Buddha: 'Sir, this wanderer Susīma says this: `Friend Ānanda, I wish to live the spiritual life in this teaching and training.`' 'Then, Ānanda, give Susīma the going forth.' The wanderer Susīma received the going forth in the Buddha's presence, he received the full ordination.
translations.sn16.11:6: The nun Thullanandā heard: 'It seems that the Venerable Ānanda, the Videhan sage, has been rebuked by Venerable Mahākassapa as if he were a boy.'
translations.sn16.11:8: Then Venerable Mahākassapa said to Venerable Ānanda: 'Indeed, friend Ānanda, the nun Thullanandā has spoken rashly, without reflection. Since I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness, I do not recall having designated any other teacher except that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Formerly, friend, when I was still a householder, this occurred to me: `Household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is wide open. It is not easy living in a house to lead the spiritual life that is utterly perfect and pure, like a polished shell. Why don't I shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?` So, friend, some time later, having made a patchwork robe from rags, having designated the arahants in the world, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the household life into homelessness.
translations.sn16.2:1: So I have heard. At one time Venerable Mahākassapa and Venerable Sāriputta were staying near Benares, in the deer park at Isipatana. Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Sāriputta came out of seclusion and went to Venerable Mahākassapa. He exchanged greetings with Venerable Mahākassapa, and when the greetings and polite conversation were over, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Mahākassapa: 'It is said, friend Kassapa, that one who is not ardent and conscientious is incapable of awakening, incapable of extinguishment, incapable of attaining the supreme sanctuary from the yoke; but one who is ardent and conscientious is capable of awakening, capable of extinguishment, capable of attaining the supreme sanctuary from the yoke.'
translations.sn16.5:1: So I have heard. … at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove. Then Venerable Mahākassapa went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to Venerable Mahākassapa, who was seated to one side: 'Kassapa, you are now old, and these rag robes of yours are heavy and worn out. So Kassapa, you should wear robes given by householders, accept invitations for meals, and stay in my presence.'
translations.sn21.10:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground. Now at that time a certain monk named Thera was a lone dweller and spoke in praise of dwelling alone.
