He entered the village for alms alone, returned alone, sat in private alone, and undertook walking meditation alone. Then several monks went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said to the Buddha: 'Sir, there is a certain monk named Thera who is a lone dweller and speaks in praise of dwelling alone.'
translations.sn21.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks!' 'Friend,' those monks replied to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
translations.sn21.1:2: Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: 'Friends, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind: `Noble silence, noble silence,` it is said. What is noble silence?' Then it occurred to me: 'Here, a monk, with the stilling of thought and examination, enters and dwells in the second absorption, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of immersion. This is called noble silence.' So I, friends, with the stilling of thought and examination, entered and dwelt in the second absorption, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of immersion. While I was dwelling in this state, perceptions and attention accompanied by thought kept occurring to me.
translations.sn21.2:1: At Sāvatthī. There Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks!' 'Friend,' those monks replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn21.3:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna were staying near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground, in a single dwelling. Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Sāriputta came out of seclusion and went to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. He exchanged greetings with Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and when the greetings and polite conversation were over, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
translations.sn21.8:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Nanda, the Buddha's cousin, having dressed in nicely pressed and ironed robes, applied eye makeup, and taking a polished bowl, went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to Venerable Nanda, who was seated to one side: 'Nanda, it is not proper for you, a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, to dress in nicely pressed and ironed robes, apply eye makeup, and carry a polished bowl. This is proper for you, Nanda, a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness: that you be a forest dweller, an alms-food eater, a rag-robe wearer, and dwell without concern for sensual pleasures.' This is what the Buddha said. … The Teacher:
translations.sn21.9:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Tissa, the Buddha's paternal cousin, went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side—miserable, sad, shedding tears. Then the Buddha said to Venerable Tissa: 'Tissa, why are you sitting there miserable, sad, shedding tears?' 'Because, sir, the monks have been attacking me from all sides with piercing words.' 'That is because you admonish others but cannot accept admonishment yourself. Tissa, it is not proper for you, a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, to admonish others but not accept admonishment yourself. This is proper for you, Tissa, a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness: that you both admonish others and accept admonishment yourself.'
translations.sn22.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Bhaggas on Crocodile Hill, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā's Grove. Then the householder Nakulapitā went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Nakulapitā said to the Buddha:
translations.sn22.1:4: And then the householder Nakula's Father, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, got up from his seat, bowed to the Buddha, and keeping him on his right, went to Venerable Sāriputta. He bowed to Venerable Sāriputta and sat down to one side. Venerable Sāriputta said to him: 'Householder, your faculties are serene; your complexion is pure and bright. Did you get to hear a Dhamma talk in the presence of the Buddha today?'
translations.sn22.1:8: 'Well then, householder, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' replied the householder Nakula's Father. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.2:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans, near a Sakyan town called Devadaha. Then several mendicants who were heading for the western lands went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those mendicants said to the Buddha: 'Sir, we wish to go to the western lands, to take up residence in the western lands.'
translations.sn22.2:5: 'Friend, we would come even from far away to learn the meaning of this statement from Venerable Sāriputta. It would be good if Venerable Sāriputta himself would explain the meaning of this statement.' 'Well then, friends, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, friend,' those mendicants replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.55:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Buddha spoke this inspired utterance: 'Resolving thus: `I might not be, and it might not be mine; I will not be, and it will not be mine`—a mendicant would cut off the lower fetters.' When this was said, a certain mendicant said to the Buddha: 'But sir, how does a mendicant who resolves thus: `I might not be, and it might not be mine; I will not be, and it will not be mine`—cut off the lower fetters?'
translations.sn22.60:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī, at the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then Mahāli the Licchavi went to the Buddha … Seated to one side, Mahāli the Licchavi said to the Buddha:
translations.sn22.80:5: Then in the late afternoon, the Buddha came out of seclusion and went to the Nigrodha monastery, where he sat on the seat spread out for him. Having sat down, the Buddha exercised such a psychic power that those mendicants would come to him in ones and twos, looking bashful. And those mendicants came to the Buddha in ones and twos, looking bashful. They bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side. The Buddha said to them:
translations.sn22.82:10: 'But sir, what is the gratification, the drawback, and the escape in the case of form? What is the gratification, the drawback, and the escape in the case of feeling … perception … choices … consciousness?' 'The pleasure and happiness that arise dependent on form: this is the gratification of form. That form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the drawback of form. The removal and giving up of desire and greed for form: this is the escape from form. The pleasure and happiness that arise dependent on feeling … dependent on perception … dependent on choices … dependent on consciousness: this is the gratification of consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the drawback of consciousness. The removal and giving up of desire and greed for consciousness: this is the escape from consciousness.' 'Good, sir!' That mendicant approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, and asked another question:
translations.sn22.82:12: Now at that time a certain mendicant had this thought: 'So it seems, good sirs, that form is not-self, feeling … perception … choices … consciousness is not-self. Then what self will deeds done by not-self affect?' Then the Buddha, knowing that mendicant's train of thought with his own mind, addressed the mendicants:
translations.sn22.82:4: 'But sir, what is the root of these five aggregates of clinging?' 'These five aggregates of clinging are rooted in desire.' … 'But sir, is that clinging the same thing as the five aggregates of clinging, or is clinging one thing and the five aggregates of clinging another?' 'That clinging is not the same thing as the five aggregates of clinging, nor is clinging one thing and the five aggregates of clinging another. Rather, the desire and greed for them is the clinging there.' 'Good, sir!' That mendicant … asked another question:
translations.sn22.82:5: 'But sir, can there be diversity of desire and greed for the five aggregates of clinging?' 'There can, mendicant,' said the Buddha. 'It's when someone thinks: `May I have such form in the future! May I have such feeling in the future! May I have such perception in the future! May I have such choices in the future! May I have such consciousness in the future!` That's how there can be diversity of desire and greed for the five aggregates of clinging.' 'Good, sir!' That mendicant … asked another question:
translations.sn22.82:7: 'But sir, what is the cause and condition for the description of the form aggregate? What is the cause and condition for the description of the feeling aggregate? What is the cause and condition for the description of the perception aggregate? What is the cause and condition for the description of the choices aggregate? What is the cause and condition for the description of the consciousness aggregate?' 'The four great elements are the cause and condition for the description of the form aggregate. Contact is the cause and condition for the description of the feeling aggregate. Contact is the cause and condition for the description of the perception aggregate. Contact is the cause and condition for the description of the choices aggregate. Name and form are the cause and condition for the description of the consciousness aggregate.' 'Good, sir!' That mendicant … asked:
translations.sn22.82:8: 'But sir, how does identity view come about?' 'Bhikkhu, an uneducated ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones, and is unskilled and undisciplined in their teaching; who has not seen good persons, and is unskilled and undisciplined in their teaching—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self, or self in form. They regard feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness. That is how identity view comes about.' 'Good, sir.' That bhikkhu … asked:
translations.sn22.82:9: 'But sir, how does identity view not come about?' 'Bhikkhu, an educated noble disciple who has seen the noble ones, and is skilled and well-trained in their teaching; who has seen good persons, and is skilled and well-trained in their teaching—does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form, or form in self, or self in form. They do not regard feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness. That is how identity view does not come about.' 'Good, sir.' That bhikkhu … asked:
translations.sn22.83:1: At Sāvatthī. There Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: 'Friends, bhikkhus!' 'Friend,' those bhikkhus replied to Venerable Ānanda. Venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn22.85:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Now at that time a bhikkhu named Yamaka had arisen with this evil wrong view: 'As I understand the teaching taught by the Buddha, a bhikkhu with defilements destroyed is annihilated and perishes when the body breaks up, and does not exist after death.'
translations.sn22.85:5: When those bhikkhus were unable to detach Venerable Yamaka from that evil wrong view, they rose from their seats and approached Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, they said to Venerable Sāriputta: 'Friend Sāriputta, a bhikkhu named Yamaka has arisen with this evil wrong view: `As I understand the teaching taught by the Buddha, a bhikkhu with defilements destroyed is annihilated and perishes when the body breaks up, and does not exist after death.` Please, Venerable Sāriputta, approach the bhikkhu Yamaka out of compassion.' Venerable Sāriputta consented by silence. Then in the evening, Venerable Sāriputta emerged from seclusion and approached Venerable Yamaka. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Yamaka … Seated to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said this to Venerable Yamaka:
translations.sn22.86:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Now at that time Venerable Anurādha was staying in a forest hut not far from the Buddha. Then several wanderers of other sects approached Venerable Anurādha. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Anurādha. When they had finished their greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those wanderers of other sects said to Venerable Anurādha: 'Friend Anurādha, the Realized One, the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has attained the highest attainment—when describing him, the Realized One describes him in these four ways: `The Realized One exists after death,` or `The Realized One does not exist after death,` or `The Realized One both exists and does not exist after death,` or `The Realized One neither exists nor does not exist after death.`'
translations.sn22.86:12: 'But Anurādha, when the Realized One is not found as a truth and a reality in this very life, is it fitting for you to declare: `Friends, the Realized One, the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has attained the highest attainment—when describing him, the Realized One describes him apart from these four ways: The Realized One exists after death, or … does not exist … both exists and does not exist … neither exists nor does not exist after death`?' 'No, sir.'
translations.sn22.86:2: When this was said, Venerable Anurādha said to those wanderers of other sects: 'Friends, the Realized One, the supreme person, the highest person, the one who has attained the highest attainment—when describing him, the Realized One describes him apart from these four ways: `The Realized One exists after death,` or `The Realized One does not exist after death,` or `The Realized One both exists and does not exist after death,` or `The Realized One neither exists nor does not exist after death.`' When this was said, those wanderers of other sects said to Venerable Anurādha: 'This bhikkhu must be newly ordained, recently gone forth, or else he is an elder who is foolish and incompetent.' Then those wanderers of other sects, having disparaged Venerable Anurādha with the terms `newly ordained` and `foolish,` rose from their seats and left.
translations.sn22.86:3: Then, not long after those wanderers of other sects had left, this occurred to Venerable Anurādha: 'If those wanderers of other sects were to question me further, how should I answer so that I would state what the Buddha has said, and not misrepresent him with what is untrue, and would explain in accordance with the teaching, and no reasonable follower of the teaching would have grounds for criticism?'
translations.sn22.90:1: At one time several senior bhikkhus were staying near Bārāṇasī in the deer park at Isipatana. Then in the evening, Venerable Channa emerged from seclusion, took a key, and going from dwelling to dwelling, approached the senior bhikkhus and said: 'Let the venerable elders advise me, let the venerable elders instruct me, let the venerable elders give me a Dhamma talk, so that I may see the Dhamma.'
translations.sn22.90:2: When he had spoken, the senior mendicants said to Venerable Channa: 'Form, friend Channa, is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Form is not-self; feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self. All conditioned things are impermanent; all things are not-self.'
translations.sn22.90:3: Then Venerable Channa thought: 'I too think this way: `Form is impermanent, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is impermanent; form is not-self, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self. All conditioned things are impermanent, all things are not-self.` Yet my mind does not leap forward, grow confident, settle, and become resolved regarding the stilling of all activities, the relinquishing of all attachments, the ending of craving, fading away, cessation, extinguishment. Anxiety and grasping arise; the mind turns back, thinking: `Then who is my self?` But this does not happen for one who sees the Dhamma. Who could teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma?'
translations.sn22.90:4: Then Venerable Channa thought: 'This Venerable Ānanda is staying near Kosambi in Ghosita's Monastery. He has been praised by the Teacher and is esteemed by his wise fellow monastics. Venerable Ānanda is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma. And I have such trust in Venerable Ānanda. Why don't I go to Venerable Ānanda?' Then Venerable Channa set his lodging in order, took his bowl and robe, and went to Kosambi, to Ghosita's Monastery, to Venerable Ānanda. He approached and exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda … Seated to one side, Venerable Channa said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn22.95:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Ayujjhā on the bank of the Ganges river. There the Blessed One addressed the mendicants:
translations.sn35.116:3: Then those mendicants approached Venerable Ānanda. They approached and exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. When they had finished their greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those mendicants said to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn35.116:7: 'Well then, friends, listen and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, friend,' those mendicants replied to Venerable Ānanda. Venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn35.116:9: 'Yes, friend,' those mendicants replied to Venerable Ānanda. They got up from their seats and approached the Blessed One. They approached, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those mendicants said to the Blessed One:
translations.sn35.118:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain. Then Sakka, lord of the gods, approached the Blessed One. He approached, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One: 'What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do not attain final extinguishment in this very life? And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here do attain final extinguishment in this very life?'
translations.sn35.127:1: At one time Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was staying near Kosambi in Ghosita's Monastery. Then King Udena approached Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. He approached and exchanged greetings with Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. When they had finished their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Udena said to Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja: 'What, Master Bhāradvāja, is the cause, what is the reason why these young mendicants—with black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life, who have not played among sensual pleasures—live the complete and pure spiritual life for as long as they live, and maintain it for the long term?' 'This has been said, great king, by the Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Awakened One: `Come, mendicants, towards those who are like your mothers, establish the thought of a mother; towards those who are like your sisters, establish the thought of a sister; towards those who are like your daughters, establish the thought of a daughter.` This, great king, is the cause, this is the reason why these young mendicants—with black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life, who have not played among sensual pleasures—live the complete and pure spiritual life for as long as they live, and maintain it for the long term.'
translations.sn35.63:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Migajāla approached the Blessed One … Seated to one side, Venerable Migajāla said to the Blessed One: '`One who dwells alone, one who dwells alone,` venerable sir, it is said. To what extent, venerable sir, does one dwell alone, and to what extent does one dwell with a companion?'
translations.sn35.69:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Upasena were staying near Rājagaha in the Cool Grove, at Snakehead Cave. Now at that time a viper had fallen on Venerable Upasena's body. Then Venerable Upasena addressed the mendicants: 'Come, friends, lift this body of mine onto a stretcher and carry it outside. Before this body scatters right here; like a handful of chaff.'
translations.sn35.74:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain mendicant approached the Blessed One … Seated to one side, that mendicant said to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, in such-and-such a dwelling there is a certain mendicant who is junior and unknown, who is sick, afflicted, gravely ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would approach that mendicant out of compassion.'
translations.sn35.88:12: 'If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with a stick, then I will think: `These people of Sunāparanta are good, these people of Sunāparanta are truly good, in that they don't give me a blow with a knife.` Thus it will be, Blessed One; thus it will be, Fortunate One.'
translations.sn35.88:16: 'If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta take my life with a sharp knife, then I will think: `There are disciples of the Blessed One who, being troubled, ashamed, and disgusted with the body and with life, seek someone to wield the knife. And I have obtained this knife-wielder without even seeking.` Thus it will be, Blessed One; thus it will be, Fortunate One.'
translations.sn35.88:19: Then several mendicants went to the Buddha … Seated to one side, those mendicants said to the Buddha: 'Sir, the clansman named Puṇṇa, who was advised by the Buddha with a brief instruction, has passed away. What is his destination? What is his future state?'
translations.sn35.88:6: 'If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and insult me, I will think: `These people of Sunāparanta are good, so very good, in that they don't strike me with their fists.` That is how it will be, Blessed One. That is how it will be, Fortunate One.'
translations.sn35.88:8: 'If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta strike me with their fists, I will think: `These people of Sunāparanta are good, so very good, in that they don't strike me with stones.` That is how it will be, Blessed One. That is how it will be, Fortunate One.'
translations.sn36.21:1: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground. Then the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka went to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and said to the Buddha: 'Master Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have this doctrine and view: `Everything this individual experiences—pleasant, painful, or neutral—is all caused by past deeds.` What does Master Gotama say about this?'
translations.sn36.23:1: Then a certain mendicant went to the Buddha, bowed, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that mendicant said to the Buddha: 'Sir, what is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the practice that leads to the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the practice that leads to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification of feeling? What is the drawback? What is the escape?'
translations.sn4.13:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the deer park at Maddakucchi. Now at that time the Buddha's foot had been cut by a stone splinter. The Buddha's painful feelings were intense—physical, sharp, severe, unpleasant, and disagreeable. But he endured them, mindful and aware, without being distressed. Then the Buddha spread out his outer robe folded in four and lay down in the lion's posture on his right side, placing one foot on the other, mindful and aware. Then Māra the Wicked went to the Buddha and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn4.18:2: Then the Buddha entered Pañcasālā, a brahmin village, for alms with his bowl just as clean as when he had washed it, and he left with his bowl just as clean. Then Māra the Wicked went to the Buddha and said: 'Ascetic, did you get any alms?' 'Wicked One, did you act in such a way that I wouldn't get alms?' 'Well then, sir, let the Buddha enter Pañcasālā for alms a second time. I will act in such a way that the Buddha will get alms.'
translations.sn4.1:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Uruvelā at the root of the goatherd's banyan tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, just after he had first awakened. Then as the Buddha was in private retreat, this thought came to his mind: 'I am freed from that grueling work! Thank goodness I'm freed from that pointless grueling work! Thank goodness that, steadfast, I have attained awakening!'
translations.sn4.20:1: At one time the Buddha was staying in the Kosalan lands in a wilderness hut in the Himalayan region. Then as the Buddha was in private retreat, this thought came to his mind: 'Is it possible to rule righteously, without killing or having others kill, without conquering or having others conquer, without sorrowing or causing sorrow?'
translations.sn4.21:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the land of the Sakyans at Silāvatī. Now at that time several mendicants were staying near the Buddha, diligent, keen, and resolute. Then Māra the Wicked manifested in the form of a brahmin with a large matted topknot, wearing an antelope hide, old, bent over like a roof-beam, wheezing, and carrying a staff of udumbara wood. He went to those mendicants and said: 'Sirs, you have gone forth while young, lads with black hair, blessed with youth, in the prime of life, without having enjoyed sensual pleasures. Enjoy human sensual pleasures! Don't give up what is visible here and now to chase after what takes time.' 'Brahmin, we are not giving up what is visible here and now to chase after what takes time. Rather, we are giving up what takes time to chase after what is visible here and now. For the Buddha has said that sensual pleasures take time, with much suffering and much distress, and they are all the more full of drawbacks. But this teaching is visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, relevant, so that sensible people can know it for themselves.' When this was said, Māra the Wicked shook his head, waggled his tongue, raised his eyebrows until his forehead had three wrinkles, and left leaning on his staff.
translations.sn4.24:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Uruvelā at the goatherd's banyan tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River. Now at that time Māra the Wicked had been following the Buddha for seven years, seeking an opportunity but not finding one. Then Māra the Wicked went to the Buddha and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn35.95:1: Then Venerable Mālukyaputta went to the Buddha … Seated to one side, Venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Buddha: 'Sir, may the Buddha please teach me the Dhamma in brief. Having heard it, I will live alone, withdrawn, diligent, keen, and resolute.'
translations.sn4.24:8: 'Suppose, sir, there was a crab near a village or town, in a pond. Then several boys or girls would leave that village or town and go to that pond. Having gone, they would pull that crab out of the water and place it on dry ground. Whenever that crab extended a claw, those boys or girls would cut it off, break it, and smash it with a stick or stone. Thus, sir, with all its claws cut off, broken, and smashed, that crab would be unable to return to that pond. Just so, sir, all my distortions, deceptions, and tricks have been cut off, broken, and smashed by the Blessed One. I am now unable to approach the Blessed One again seeking an opportunity.' Then Māra the Evil One spoke these verses of dejection in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn4.25:12: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra's daughters, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, Craving, Māra's daughter, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.25:4: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra's daughters, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they said to the Blessed One: 'We serve at your feet, ascetic.' But the Blessed One paid no attention, being liberated in the supreme ending of attachments.
translations.sn4.25:5: Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra's daughters, withdrew to one side and deliberated: 'Men have varied tastes. Let us each create a hundred forms of young women.' Then Craving, Discontent, and Lust, Māra's daughters, each having created a hundred forms of young women, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they said to the Blessed One: 'We serve at your feet, ascetic.' But the Blessed One paid no attention to that either, being liberated in the supreme ending of attachments.
translations.sn4.8:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn44.1:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. Now at that time the bhikkhunī Khemā, while wandering in the Kosalan lands, had taken up residence at Toraṇavatthu between Sāvatthī and Sāketa. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, traveling from Sāketa to Sāvatthī, stopped for one night at Toraṇavatthu between Sāketa and Sāvatthī. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man: 'Come now, good man, find out if there is any ascetic or brahmin in Toraṇavatthu whom I might visit today.'
translations.sn44.1:2: 'Yes, Your Majesty,' that man replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala. Having wandered through the whole of Toraṇavatthu, he did not see any ascetic or brahmin whom King Pasenadi of Kosala might visit. But that man saw the bhikkhunī Khemā who had taken up residence at Toraṇavatthu. Having seen her, he approached King Pasenadi of Kosala. Having approached, he said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
translations.sn45.2:1: So I have heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans where there was a town of the Sakyans named Nagaraka. Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: 'Sir, this is half of the spiritual life, that is—good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship.'
translations.sn45.4:2: Then Venerable Ānanda, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on returning from the alms round, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn45.4:4: 'It is possible, Ānanda,' said the Blessed One. 'This, Ānanda, is a designation for this Noble Eightfold Path: `the divine vehicle,` `the vehicle of Dhamma,` and `the unsurpassed victory in battle.`'
translations.sn45.8:1: At Sāvatthī. 'Bhikkhus, I will teach and analyze for you the Noble Eightfold Path. Listen to that and pay close attention, I will speak.' 'Yes, sir,' those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn46.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground. Now at that time Venerable Mahākassapa was staying in the Pipphali Cave, sick, suffering, gravely ill. Then in the evening, the Blessed One, having emerged from seclusion, approached Venerable Mahākassapa. Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to Venerable Mahākassapa:
translations.sn46.30:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sumbhas where there was a town of the Sumbhas named Setaka. Then Venerable Udāyī approached the Blessed One ... Seated to one side, Venerable Udāyī said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.52:1: Then several bhikkhus, having dressed in the morning and taking their bowls and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: 'It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. Let us go to the park of the wanderers of other sects.'
translations.sn46.52:2: Then those bhikkhus went to the park of the wanderers of other sects. Having gone, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects. Having exchanged greetings and cordial talk, they sat down to one side. As those bhikkhus were seated to one side, those wanderers of other sects said this to them:
translations.sn46.52:4: And then those mendicants neither approved nor dismissed that statement of those wanderers of other sects; without approving or dismissing, they got up from their seats and left, thinking: 'We will learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.' Then those mendicants, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on returning from alms round, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those mendicants said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.54:3: 'Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples thus: `Come, mendicants, having abandoned the five hindrances, corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom, dwell pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, to all as to oneself, dwell pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. Dwell pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by compassion, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, to all as to oneself, dwell pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by compassion, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. Dwell pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by appreciative joy, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, to all as to oneself, dwell pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by appreciative joy, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. Dwell pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, to all as to oneself, dwell pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will.`
translations.sn46.8:1: At one time Venerable Upavāna and Venerable Sāriputta were staying near Kosambī in Ghosita's Monastery. translations.sn47.10:1: Then in the morning, Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and approached a certain nuns' residence; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. translations.sn47.13:4: Then Venerable Ānanda and Cunda the novice approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: 'Bhante, this Cunda the novice says thus: `Bhante, Venerable Sāriputta has attained final nibbāna; this is his bowl and robe.` And bhante, my body has become as if drugged, the directions are not clear to me, and the teachings do not occur to me, having heard that Venerable Sāriputta has attained final nibbāna.'
translations.sn47.19:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sumbhas, where there was a town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the mendicants: 'Once in the past, mendicants, a bamboo acrobat set up his bamboo pole and addressed his apprentice Medakathālikā: `Come, dear Medakathālikā, climb the bamboo pole and stand on my shoulders.` `Yes, teacher,` the apprentice Medakathālikā replied to the bamboo acrobat, climbed the bamboo pole, and stood on the teacher's shoulders. Then, mendicants, the bamboo acrobat said this to the apprentice Medakathālikā: `You, dear Medakathālikā, protect me, and I will protect you. Thus guarding each other, protecting each other, we will display our skills, gain profit, and descend safely from the bamboo pole.` When this was said, mendicants, the apprentice Medakathālikā said this to the bamboo acrobat: `But that is not how it will be, teacher. You, teacher, protect yourself, and I will protect myself. Thus self-guarded, self-protected, we will display our skills, gain profit, and descend safely from the bamboo pole.'
translations.sn47.20:1: Thus have I heard— at one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sumbhas, where there was a town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants.' 'Bhante,' those mendicants replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn47.25:1: Thus have I heard— at one time the Blessed One was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had finished their friendly and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One: 'What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason why, when the Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna, the true Dhamma does not last long? And what, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason why, when the Tathāgata has attained final nibbāna, the true Dhamma lasts long?'
translations.sn47.29:2: Then in the morning, Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and approached the residence of the householder Sirivaḍḍha; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Seated, Venerable Ānanda said this to the householder Sirivaḍḍha: 'I hope you are bearing up, householder, I hope you are getting by. I hope painful feelings are subsiding, not increasing; that their subsiding is apparent, not their increase?' 'I am not bearing up, bhante, I am not getting by. Strong painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increase is apparent, not their subsiding.'
translations.sn47.4:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying among the Kosalans at the brahmin village of Sālā. There the Blessed One addressed the mendicants … and said this:
translations.sn5.10:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Vajirā robed up in the morning and, taking her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. She wandered for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, on her return from almsround, she went to the Dark Forest for the day's meditation. Having plunged into the Dark Forest, she sat at the root of a certain tree for the day's meditation. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in the nun Vajirā, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her. Having approached, he addressed the nun Vajirā with a verse:
translations.sn5.10:3: Then the nun Vajirā thought: 'Now who is this, human or non-human, speaking a verse?' Then the nun Vajirā thought: 'This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in me, wanting to make me fall away from concentration, speaking a verse.' Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in the nun Āḷavikā, wanting to make her fall away from seclusion, approached her. Having approached, he addressed the nun Āḷavikā with a verse:
translations.sn5.1:3: Then the nun Āḷavikā thought: 'Now who is this, human or non-human, speaking a verse?' Then the nun Āḷavikā thought: 'This is Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in me, wanting to make me fall away from seclusion, speaking a verse.' Then the nun Āḷavikā, having understood 'This is Māra the Wicked,' replied to Māra the Wicked with verses:
translations.sn5.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Vijayā robed up in the morning … she sat at the root of a certain tree for the day's meditation. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in the nun Vijayā, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her. Having approached, he addressed the nun Vijayā with a verse:
translations.sn5.5:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Uppalavaṇṇā robed up in the morning … she stood at the root of a certain sal tree in full bloom. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, terror, and goosebumps in the nun Uppalavaṇṇā, wanting to make her fall away from concentration, approached her. Having approached, he addressed the nun Uppalavaṇṇā with a verse:
translations.sn5.7:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Upacālā robed up in the morning … she sat at the root of a certain tree for the day's meditation. Then Māra the Wicked approached the nun Upacālā. Having approached, he said to the nun Upacālā: 'Where do you wish to be reborn, nun?' 'I do not wish to be reborn anywhere, friend.'
translations.sn5.8:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Sīsupacālā robed up in the morning … she sat at the root of a certain tree for the day's meditation. Then Māra the Wicked approached the nun Sīsupacālā. Having approached, he said to the nun Sīsupacālā: 'Whose doctrine do you approve of, nun?' 'I do not approve of anyone's doctrine, friend.'
translations.sn56.11:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
translations.sn56.11:11: And while this explanation was being spoken, there arose in Venerable Koṇḍañña the dust-free, stainless vision of the Dhamma: 'Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.'
translations.sn56.31:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī in the Siṁsapā Grove. Then the Blessed One, taking up a few siṁsapā leaves in his hand, addressed the monks: 'What do you think, monks, which is more—the few siṁsapā leaves I have taken up in my hand, or those above in the siṁsapā grove?' 'The leaves the Blessed One has taken up in his hand are few, Bhante; those above in the siṁsapā grove are far more.' 'So too, monks, what I have directly known but not declared to you is far more. And why have I not declared it, monks? Because it is not beneficial, not connected with the fundamentals of the spiritual life, not leading to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna; therefore I have not declared it.
translations.sn56.45:3: 'What do you think, Ānanda, which is more difficult and harder to accomplish—that one should shoot an arrow through a keyhole from a distance, shaft after shaft without missing, or that one should pierce the tip of a hair split into seven with the tip of another?' 'This is more difficult and harder to accomplish, Bhante—that one should pierce the tip of a hair split into seven with the tip of another.' 'But, Ānanda, they penetrate something even harder to penetrate, those who penetrate as it really is: `This is suffering` … who penetrate as it really is: `This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.`
translations.sn56.46:2: When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: 'That is indeed a great darkness, Bhante, a very great darkness indeed. But is there, Bhante, another darkness greater and more frightening than this darkness?' 'There is, monk, another darkness greater and more frightening than this darkness.'
translations.an5.28:8: Suppose a water jar was placed on a stand, full to the brim so a crow could drink from it. If a strong man were to tip it any which way, would water pour out?'  'Yes, sir.'  'In the same way, when a mendicant has developed and cultivated the noble right immersion with five factors, they become capable of realizing anything that can be realized by insight to which they extend the mind, in each and every case, there being a suitable basis.
translations.an5.30:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering in the land of the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of mendicants when he arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Icchānaṅgala. There the Buddha stayed in a forest near Icchānaṅgala. The brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala heard: 'It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Icchānaṅgala. He is staying in a forest near Icchānaṅgala. He has this good reputation: `That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those who wish to train, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.` He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras and Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others. He teaches Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that is entirely full and pure. It is good to see such perfected ones.' Then, when the night had passed, the brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala, taking abundant food, went to the forest near Icchānaṅgala. They stood outside the gate, making a great racket.
translations.an8.26:3: 'But sir, how is a lay follower practicing for their own welfare, but not the welfare of others?'  'Jīvaka, it's when a lay follower is accomplished in faith themselves, but doesn't encourage others to be accomplished in faith. … They practice in line with the teaching themselves, understanding the meaning and the teaching, but they don't encourage others to practice in line with the teaching. To this extent a lay follower is practicing for their own welfare, but not the welfare of others.'
translations.mn140:2: 'If it's no trouble, Bhaggava, I'd like to stay one night in the workshop.'  'It's no trouble, sir. But there's a renunciate who has already taken up residence here. If he allows it, stay as long as you like.'
translations.mn22:25: When there is a self, would there be the thought, `that is mine`?'  'Yes, sir.'  'When there is what belongs to a self, would there be the thought, `that is my self`?'  'Yes, sir.'  'Since a self and what belongs to a self are not found as true and established, is not this doctrinal standpoint—`The world is the self. After death I will be permanent, everlasting, eternal, imperishable, and will last forever and ever`—a totally foolish teaching?'  'What else could it be, sir? It is a totally foolish teaching.'
translations.mn31:16: 'Good, good, Anuruddhas! But have you, while living in this way, achieved any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, going beyond this abiding, transcending this abiding?'  'Why not, sir? Here, whenever we want, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, with the passing beyond perceptions of form, with the ending of perceptions of impingement, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that `space is infinite,` we enter and remain in the dimension of infinite space. This, sir, is a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a comfortable abiding, that we have achieved going beyond this abiding, transcending this abiding.'
translations.mn38:10: 'Does doubt arise in one who is uncertain: `Has this come to be or not`?'  'Yes, sir.'  'Does doubt arise in one who is uncertain: `Has it originated from that nutriment or not`?'  'Yes, sir.'  'Does doubt arise in one who is uncertain: `With the cessation of that nutriment, is what has come to be subject to cessation or not`?'  'Yes, sir.'
translations.mn38:12: 'Are you free of doubt about this: `This has come to be`?'  'Yes, sir.'  'Are you free of doubt about this: `It has originated from that nutriment`?'  'Yes, sir.'  'Are you free of doubt about this: `With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation`?'  'Yes, sir.'
translations.mn38:23: Knowing and seeing in this way, would you run back to the past, thinking: `Did we exist in the past? Did we not exist in the past? What were we in the past? How were we in the past? Having been what, what did we become in the past?`'  'No, sir.'  'Knowing and seeing in this way, would you run forward to the future, thinking: `Will we exist in the future? Will we not exist in the future? What will we be in the future? How will we be in the future? Having been what, what will we become in the future?`'  'No, sir.'
translations.mn60:4: 'But householders, is there any teacher you approve of, in whom you have acquired grounded faith?'  'No, sir, there is no teacher we approve of, in whom we have acquired grounded faith.'  'Since you have not found an approved teacher, householders, you should undertake and practice this guaranteed teaching. For when the guaranteed teaching is undertaken in full, it will be for your lasting welfare and happiness. And what is the guaranteed teaching?
translations.sn11.5:6: 'I see only this fault in patience, Vāsava: when a fool thinks, `He endures me out of fear,` the idiot overwhelms him, like a bull one who flees.'
translations.sn11.5:8: 'Let him think or not think, `He endures me out of fear.` Among goals with one's own good as highest, nothing better than patience is found.
translations.sn12.31:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.sn12.64:8: Suppose there was a bungalow or a bungalow hall with windows on the northern, southern, or eastern side. When the sun rises, a beam of light would enter through the window. Where would it land?' 'On the western wall, sir.' 'And if there were no western wall, where would it land?' 'On the ground, sir.' 'And if there were no ground, where would it land?' 'In the water, sir.' 'And if there were no water, where would it land?' 'It would not land anywhere, sir.' 'In the same way, mendicants, if there is no desire, relish, and craving for solid food …
translations.sn12.35:4: 'What are choices, and whose choices are they?' 'That's not a valid question,' said the Buddha. 'Mendicant, whether you say, `What are choices, and whose choices are they?` or whether you say, `Choices are one thing, and the one whose choices they are is another`—both of these mean the same thing, they differ only in the phrasing. Mendicant, when there is the view that the soul and the body are the same thing, there is no living of the spiritual life. And when there is the view that the soul and the body are different things, there is no living of the spiritual life. Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One teaches by the middle: `Ignorance is a condition for choices.`'
translations.sn12.67:7: 'But Reverend Sāriputta, how should the meaning of this statement be understood?' 'Well then, reverend, I shall give you a simile. For by means of a simile some wise people understand the meaning of what is said. Suppose two sheaves of reeds were to stand leaning against each other. In the same way, name and form are conditions for consciousness. Consciousness is a condition for name and form. Name and form are conditions for the six sense bases. The six sense bases are a condition for contact. … That is how this entire mass of suffering originates. If one of those sheaves of reeds were pulled away, the other would fall. And if the other were pulled away, the first would fall. In the same way, when name and form cease, consciousness ceases. When consciousness ceases, name and form cease. When name and form cease, the six sense bases cease. When the six sense bases cease, contact ceases. … That is how this entire mass of suffering ceases.'
translations.sn1.1:3: That is what that deity said. The Teacher approved. Then that deity, thinking, 'The Teacher approves of me,' bowed to the Buddha, circumambulated him keeping him on the right, and vanished right there.
translations.sn12.68:13: 'Then is Venerable Nārada a perfected one with defilements ended?' 'Reverend, though I have clearly seen with right wisdom as it really is that `the cessation of continued existence is extinguishment,` I am not a perfected one with defilements ended. Suppose, reverend, there was a well in a desert, but it had no rope or bucket. Then a man would come along, oppressed and afflicted by the heat, weary, thirsty, and parched. He would look down into that well. He would have the knowledge that `there is water,` but he would not be able to touch it with his body. In the same way, though I have clearly seen with right wisdom as it really is that `the cessation of continued existence is extinguishment,` I am not a perfected one with defilements ended.'
translations.sn12.46:2: 'Master Gotama, does the same one act and experience the result?' 'Brahmin, to say that the same one acts and experiences the result is one extreme.'
translations.sn12.69:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There … 'Mendicants, when the ocean surges it makes the great rivers surge. When the great rivers surge they make the streams surge. When the streams surge they make the large lakes surge. When the large lakes surge they make the small lakes surge. In the same way, when ignorance surges it makes choices surge. When choices surge they make consciousness surge. When consciousness surges it makes name and form surge. When name and form surges it makes the six sense bases surge. When the six sense bases surge they make contact surge. When contact surges it makes feeling surge. When feeling surges it makes craving surge. When craving surges it makes grasping surge. When grasping surges it makes continued existence surge. When continued existence surges it makes rebirth surge. When rebirth surges it makes old age and death surge.
translations.sn12.70:18: 'Rebirth is a condition for old age and death'—do you see this, Susīma?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Continued existence is a condition for rebirth'—do you see this, Susīma?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Grasping is a condition for continued existence'—do you see this, Susīma?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Craving is a condition for grasping'—do you see this, Susīma?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Feeling is a condition for craving … Contact is a condition for feeling … The six sense bases are a condition for contact … Name and form is a condition for the six sense bases … Consciousness is a condition for name and form … Choices are a condition for consciousness … Ignorance is a condition for choices'—do you see this, Susīma?' 'Yes, sir.'
translations.sn21.6:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya went up to the Buddha. The Buddha saw him coming off in the distance, and addressed the mendicants: 'Mendicants, do you see that mendicant coming—ugly, unsightly, deformed, and despised by the mendicants?' 'Yes, sir.' 'That mendicant is very mighty and powerful. There is no attainment that he has not already attained. And he has realized the supreme end of the spiritual life in this very life, having achieved it with his own insight, and lives having achieved it—the goal for which gentlemen rightly go forth from the lay life to homelessness.' That is what the Buddha said. … The Teacher:
translations.sn22.100:2: 'Mendicants, have you seen the picture called `Conduct`?' 'Yes, sir.' 'Even that picture called `Conduct` is produced by the mind. But the mind is even more elaborate than that picture. Therefore, mendicants, you should often reflect on your own mind: `For a long time this mind has been corrupted by greed, hate, and delusion.` Mendicants, sentient beings are corrupted because the mind is corrupted. Sentient beings are purified because the mind is purified.
translations.sn22.85:9: 'What do you think, Reverend Yamaka? Do you regard the Realized One as being in form?' 'No, reverend.' 'Do you regard the Realized One as being apart from form?' 'No, reverend.' 'In feeling …' 'Apart from feeling …' 'In perception …' 'Apart from perception …' 'In choices …' 'Apart from choices …' 'Do you regard the Realized One as being in consciousness?' 'No, reverend.' 'Do you regard the Realized One as being apart from consciousness?' 'No, reverend.'
translations.sn22.89:10: Suppose there was a blue water lily, or a pink or white lotus, and someone were to say that its scent belonged to the petals, or the color, or the filaments. Would they be speaking rightly?' 'No, reverend.' 'Then how should they answer rightly?' 'They should say that the scent belongs to the flower.' 'In the same way, reverend, I don't say `I am` regarding form, nor do I say `I am` apart from form. I don't say `I am` regarding feeling … perception … choices … I don't say `I am` regarding consciousness, nor do I say `I am` apart from consciousness. Yet I have found `I am` with respect to the five grasping aggregates, but I don't regard anything as `I am this.`
translations.sn35.116:2: Then those mendicants thought: 'This Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his sensible spiritual companions. He is capable of explaining in detail the meaning of what the Buddha has stated in brief without analyzing the meaning. Why don't we go to Venerable Ānanda and ask him about this matter?'
translations.sn4.1:2: Then Māra the Wicked, knowing what the Buddha was thinking, went up to him and addressed him in verse:
translations.sn4.1:7: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, 'The Buddha knows me! The Holy One knows me!' miserable and sad, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.1:6: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, 'The nun Āḷavikā knows me!' miserable and sad, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.3:7: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, 'The nun Kisāgotamī knows me!' miserable and sad, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.5:7: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, 'The nun Uppalavaṇṇā knows me!' miserable and sad, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.7:6: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, 'The nun Upacālā knows me!' miserable and sad, vanished right there.
translations.mn75:18: What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Have you ever seen or heard of a king or a king's minister who, supplied and provided with the five kinds of sensual pleasures, enjoying them, without having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, without having dispelled the fever of sensual pleasures, free from thirst, with a mind inwardly at peace, ever lived or lives or will live?
translations.mn9:2: 'Right view, right view,' is said, friends. In what way is a noble disciple one of right view, whose view is straight, who has unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and has arrived at this true Dhamma?
translations.sn22.95:4: Suppose, bhikkhus, in the last month of summer, at midday, a mirage shimmers. A person with good sight would see it, examine it, and carefully investigate it. As they see it, examine it, and carefully investigate it, it would appear empty, it would appear hollow … for what substance could there be in a mirage? So too, bhikkhus, whatever perception …
translations.sn12.11:1: So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery … 'Mendicants, there are these four kinds of nutriment for the sustenance of beings that have been born and for the support of those seeking a new birth. What four? Solid food, whether coarse or fine; contact is the second, mental intention the third, and consciousness the fourth. These are the four kinds of nutriment for the sustenance of beings that have been born and for the support of those seeking a new birth.'
